papers.abstract: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.
authors: Hidir Yesiltepe, Julius Berner, Arash Vahdat, Pinar Yanardag
bullets: Addresses reverse-KL distillation’s mode-seeking bias and resulting loss of sample diversity.
Uses exponentially reweighted student samples to match teacher posterior means at shifted noisy inputs.
Under Gaussian corruption, matching these means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior.
The stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without retraining.
On SDXL and FLUX.2 4B, PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods while remaining competitive on alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 4. PMD Training Framework. A noisy state zt is obtained through the student’s on-policy sampling process. The frozen teacher is evaluated at the shifted input zt + ρtλ, yielding the tilted posterior mean Tλ = Dt(zt + ρtλ, t). Conditioned on the same zt, the stochastic student generates multiple clean-image predictions using independent random inputs. These predictions are combined into an exponentially weighted mean, which is compared with the teacher target Tλ. PMD minimizes the resulting posterior-matching discrepancy through the loss LPMD, encouraging the student to recover the teacher’s conditional posterior distribution.

Figure 5. Qualitative Comparison and Any-Step Generation. PMD demonstrates greater conditional diversity than RTDMD [22] on FLUX.2 [klein] 4B (cat) and DMD2 [61] on SDXL (woman). The bottom row shows diverse PMD samples generated with both four and two sampling steps using the same model, without retraining.

Figure 6. Ablation on the Number of Student Draws. Diversity scores during four-step PMD distillation of FLUX.2 [klein] 4B, using 4, 8, or 16 independent student draws per noisy input. We evaluate sample diversity using DINOv2, DreamSim, Vendi, and LPIPS.
Figure 7. User Study for FLUX.2 [klein] 4B four-step models.

Figure 10. User Study Form.

Figure 3. Exponential Tilting of the Teacher Posterior. Starting from the original teacher posterior q(x | zt), exponential reweighting by exp(λ⊤x) changes the relative prominence of its modes. Under Gaussian corruption, each tilted posterior is equivalent to the posterior at a shifted noisy state, qλ(x | zt) = q(x | zt + ρtλ). Varying λ over an open neighborhood Br emphasizes different modes, producing a family of tilted means that uniquely characterizes the original posterior.

Figure 2. Tilt=Shift Identity. (Left) Estimating a tilted posterior mean requires multiple stochastic reverse-diffusion trajectories from the same noisy state, followed by exponential reweighting of the resulting clean samples. (Right) Under Gaussian corruption, the same mean is obtained with a single frozen-teacher evaluation at a shifted noisy input.

papers.selection_reason: Diffusion distillation method supporting any-step generation, relevant to efficient image and video diffusion.
papers.title: Posterior Matching Distillation
papers.tldr: Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD) distills diffusion models by matching full teacher posteriors rather than favoring dominant modes, enabling diverse any-step generation in few evaluations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.
authors: Tuna Han Salih Meral, Kaan Oktay, Alec Helbling, Atakan Kara, Duen Horng Chau, Pinar Yanardag
bullets: RL improves visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy in diffusion transformers.
The study adds fixed steering vectors to frozen model block outputs, independent of prompts, tokens, and sampling seeds.
These vectors use 65× fewer parameters than an RL-tuned LoRA on SD3.5-M.
They recover 90.0–96.3% of reward gains across six image models and 89.8% and 111.9% across two video models.
Online RL with only steering vectors surpasses weight-based RL on OCR and PickScore for SD3.5-M.

papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.
authors: Jinbin Luo, Xiaozhe Yao, Shang Yang, Zhijian Liu, Song Han, Qinghao Hu
bullets: Targets heterogeneous cache demands in hybrid models under long contexts and concurrent requests.
Uses a transparent cache pool to redistribute GPU pages without changing cache layouts or backend interfaces.
Streams global-attention prefixes layer by layer during bounded-state computation while keeping generated KV resident.
A scheduler selects resident versus streamed execution and adjusts capacity based on request size and queue state.
Across seven configurations on GB300 and GH200, it achieves up to 2.04× more agent turns, 20–59% lower P50 per-token latency, and 1.40–3.05× better agent P50 TTFT than SGLang with HiCache.

papers.abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.
authors: Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, Yuchao Gu, Lvmin Zhang, Ivor Tsang, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning action representations and dynamics without action labels, often requiring dynamics to be learned from scratch.
Uses one pretrained video prior for two roles: inverse dynamics via a transition encoder with learnable action queries, and forward dynamics via a causal action-conditioned generator.
Trains both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck to discover actions transferable across visual contexts and embodiments.
Achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing and stronger zero-shot transfer in navigation and robotic manipulation, according to the abstract.
The framework also works with predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, suggesting applicability beyond generative video models.

papers.abstract: High-resolution generation enables video world models to render fine-grained scene structures and textures, but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. We present ScaleWorld, a causal video model that unifies low-resolution world prediction and high-resolution refinement within a single shared backbone. By refining its own predictions, ScaleWorld produces high-resolution world videos without requiring a separate refinement model. For each video chunk, the shared backbone first completes a low-resolution prediction and then performs one-step high-resolution refinement conditioned on that prediction. To support efficient streaming generation, we maintain separate causal states with a long low-resolution history for prediction and a short high-resolution history for refinement. To address task interference during distillation, we separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation and introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD). This procedure transfers prediction and refinement behaviors from specialized teachers into a shared student through local velocity matching under their respective sampling and history policies. {Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScaleWorld achieves high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.
authors: Yansong Qu, Wesker Zheng, Quanjian Song, Zhiyuan Zhang, Xiao Cao, Shengchuan Zhang, Liujuan Cao
bullets: Targets the high computational and memory cost of direct high-resolution video generation.
Uses a shared backbone to first predict a low-resolution video chunk, then refine it at high resolution without a separate refinement model.
Maintains long low-resolution and short high-resolution causal histories for efficient streaming generation.
Introduces task-asymmetric on-policy distillation to consolidate prediction and refinement capabilities while reducing task interference.
Experiments show high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.
authors: Yiyang Du, Yuxuan Kuang, Qitao Zhao, Yixuan Wang, Zhanqiu Guo, Yi Xu, Xin Li, Wenbin He, Liu Ren, Chenyan Xiong
bullets: Analyzes direct low-level robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks, beyond episode-level success rates.
Pairs each policy action with a stated local intent, then uses a critic to assess outcomes and failure modes.
Finds closed-loop recovery, reliable semantic grounding, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation.
Identifies bottlenecks in grasping and alignment, with uneven recovery across failure types.
Releases 12,844 annotated actions and a fine-tuned open-source critic; failure-mode accuracy improves from 32.58% to 74.24% on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark.

papers.abstract: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/
authors: Peiyun Hu, Marko Mihajlovic, Lyndon Duong, Lahav Lipson, Wei Dong, Ama\"el Delaunoy, Stephan R. Richter, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between sharp boundaries in single-frame methods and temporal consistency in multi-frame methods.
Uses one network to process both still images and video and predict dense metric depth at full resolution.
Reports improvements over prior work in metric accuracy, sharpness, and temporal consistency.
Releases multiple models spanning a Pareto frontier across accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime.
Code and model weights are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx
authors: Kai Lu, Chenyang Ma, Ioannis Havoutis
bullets: Targets failures caused by tightly coupled temporal structure, skill execution, and precision in monolithic VLA models.
Uses a training-free predicate state machine to manage progression, recovery, navigation, waiting, and stage evaluation.
Keeps VLA models focused on stage-specific manipulation dynamics.
Applies world-coordinate locking for base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and anchored contact targets.
Experiments on three simulated tasks and one real Unitree G1 task show improved stage progression and task success rates.

papers.abstract: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.

Controlled studies find that coarse proxies favor natural motion, whereas medium-grained proxies improve consistency; physics simulation and aligned prompting raise average quality.
The framework adaptively switches between proxy-guided and direct generation, selects entity-level granularity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompts.
Experiments show leading instruction following on VTR, strong scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility, and higher realism than compared Code2Video baselines.
Long-video results improve event structure and consistency across interactions, but transition stability and adherence to scene settings remain limitations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.
authors: Jiahao Huang, Jun Wang
bullets: Introduces a multimodal Jacobian lens that maps vision and language states into the decoder vocabulary’s shared semantic space.

Proposes two J-space metrics for tracking cross-modal concept alignment, which develop before reliable selective access.
Observes similar accessibility, query-dependent selectivity, and intervention patterns across VLM families and sizes, despite differing internal organisation.

papers.abstract: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($\Delta d' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.
authors: Jochen Laubrock
bullets: Across six open-weight model families, probes often decoded authorship information well even when model answers did not.
For German human-versus-AI judgments, post-training reduced answer sensitivity on average and altered how models used stated base rates.
Stage-wise analyses linked the change mainly to supervised fine-tuning and later-layer states at positions after the input text.
For truth of negated statements, representations remained highly decodable while post-training improved several models’ answers—the opposite pattern.
Adding 2,000 labeled authorship examples changed answer behavior across text types, including reversals, showing that limited training signals can set readout direction.

figures.caption: Figure 2. How the interventions work. In panels A, C, and D, the horizontal axis shows the positions of the prompt in reading order (the instruction, the text to be judged, the question, and the position at which the answer is produced), and the vertical axis shows the layers of the network. (A) Information flow: through attention, later positions read information from earlier ones. The answer is produced at the last position. Information from the text reaches it through the positions after the text: the question (dark tiles) and the last position itself, which also reads the text directly at every layer (the schematic shows only the route via the question). (B) Steering, sketched in a two-dimensional version of the highdimensional representation space: human texts (open circles) and AI texts (triangles) differ along an AI–human direction (arrow between the class means). Steering moves the state of one text along this direction (diamonds) and measures how the model’s answer changes; the dashed line marks where the answer switches. The two need not be orthogonal: the angle between the AI–human direction and the model’s decision boundary determines how strongly a shift along the direction changes the answer. If the model read the direction correctly, a shift toward the AI texts would move the answer toward “KI”. (C) Model stitching combines the lower layers of one checkpoint (here the base model, blue) with the upper layers of another (here the SFT model, orange). (D) Activation patching replaces the internal states of one model (here SFT) at selected positions and one layer with those of the other model (here the base model’s states at the question positions).

Figure 1. Brunswik’s lens model, applied to a language model as judge and extended by an internal lens. A state of the world (Brunswik’s distal criterion; the ground truth, here whether a text was written by an AI, whether a statement is true, or whether a review is genuine) is reflected in observable cues of the text, some of which are valid and some of which are not (dashed). In the first lens (encoding), the model integrates these cues into its internal representation; whether the ground truth can be decoded from this representation is measured with linear probes, and whether two checkpoints represent it in the same way with probe transfer. In the second lens (readout), the representation is read out into an answer to the question by weighting internal features. Only one of these features wasmeasured directly: the class direction, i.e., the direction that separates the two classes in the representation; its relation to the answer was examined with steering at the answer position (Appendix D). The other features are schematic. Achievement, i.e., the agreement of the answer with the state of the world, requires both lenses. Post-training changes mainly the second lens (orange), and in several cases also the first (Sections 3.4 and 3.6); model stitching and activation patching locate the change in depth and in the prompt. Splitting the judge side of the lens model has precedents in personality judgment (detection vs. utilization of cues; Funder, 1995) and in neuroscience (information encoded in a neural population vs. read out for behavior; Panzeri et al., 2017). Note: for the authorship corpora, probes were fitted both on the text positions and on the last prompt position; for the truth and review sets, only on the last prompt position.

Note that the two rows have different scales. Horizontal lines show the unpatched recipient (dotted) and the donor (dashed). Asterisks mark differences between the base and the final model on the identical raw prompt that survive Holm correction within the family of 18 final-vs-base comparisons; all of them are decreases. papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper--object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3\%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.
authors: Hao Vo, Taisei Hanyu, Yuki Ikebe, Pham Tri Quang, Sreevenkata Anjani Tishita Godavarthi, Nghi D. Q. Bui, Daniel Sonntag, Chase Rainwater, Duy Minh Ho Nguyen, Anh Nguyen, Ngan Le
bullets: Evaluates dynamic extrinsic dexterity involving gravity, friction, inertia, mass, and center of mass—not just gripper–object contact.

Providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success; similar failure patterns appear on a humanoid robot and in real-world tests.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the PhyDEX data generation pipeline. (a) Environment construction: given a task template, we retrieve a target object, a destination, and a scene from the asset library to create a new task. (b) Domain randomization: we diversify each task visually (camera views, lighting, scene layout), in its trajectories (grasp pose, object pose, robot state), and in its physical properties (mass, CoM, friction). (c) Trajectory generation: GraspGen-X proposes grasp poses, cuRobo plans a collision-free approach, and an SLSQP-based optimizer computes the throwing trajectory q(t) from the initial joint state (q0, q̇0), the object properties (m,CoM, µ), and the target p∗, refining it in a closed loop until the throw succeeds. (d) Data storage: each successful episode is saved in LeRobot format with multi-view RGB, force/torque signals, and actions.

papers.abstract: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.
authors: Nathaniel Cohen, Nicolas Dufour, Am\'elie Royer, Alasdair Newson, Patrick P\'erez
bullets: Addresses the latency and multi-second audio look-ahead requirements of existing audio-driven video diffusion models.

AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time at 20.7 fps on one GPU; AURA 5B streams 720p at 9.7 fps.
Released resources include both model weights, 30K synthetic videos, and precomputed teacher trajectories.

papers.abstract: In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer observation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw +0.070 to 0.107 log-space $R^2$ in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe's gain persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72% of it. We therefore report a robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions, the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted +0.014 from 24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned -0.0004. For the sequence families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 between the nominal 1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 for capacity on three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. A team building on this class of data should start by lengthening the window.
authors: Tara Sowrirajan, Yanqiao Wang
bullets: Doubling the observation window from 8 to 16 weeks added 0.070–0.107 raw log-space R² at the 1M tier across model families.
The positive association with longer windows held across five public datasets and persisted outside the holiday season, retaining about 72% of the weekly ridge gain.
Longer windows also admitted up to 10% more and colder training customers on internal data, an effect not removed by cohort matching.
Observed effects of data, architecture, and capacity were much smaller—at most 0.006, 0.0052, and 0.006 respectively—but these are not equivalence bounds.
The study’s blind prediction largely failed, and the design cannot separate history length from calendar coverage.

Among the plotted families trained with squared error, only ridge is meaningfully below the others. The cohort changes at that step, so the dotted connectors to M24 do not trace a within-cohort trajectory. Figure 4). Transformer matched points are seed-42 evaluations, so they sit slightly off the 3-seed matched means printed in Table 2. Figure 1: The observation window outweighs the observed effects of population scale and model capacity, our counterparts of the data and parameter axes swept by a compute-calibration scaling study that does not vary the window in training [Brüel Gabrielsson, 2026]. Extending the input window M8→M24 moves R2 by +0.111 (left). On our counterparts of those axes, it moves by 0.0025 across training-population tiers 1M→10M at fixed window M16 (center) and by 0.006 across width and depth at fixed window M16 and fixed data (right), both as 3-seed means. Both are observed intervals rather than resolved equivalence bounds. The scale interval sits within seed dispersion. The capacity interval does not, but it is unresolved against its own 0.016 equivalence margin (§6). The raw M24 endpoint carries the composition caveat of Table 2; the matched-cohort window climb is larger still (+0.131, 3-seed, §2.3), so the raw delta is the conservative estimate. Every ladder shares one setup (Huber objective, log-space R2, full test split). Apart from the factor each ladder varies, the only differences are a 100→500-step warmup at d512 with 8 layers (§2.1) and, on the tier ladder, the realized learning-rate schedule (§6). Window length also shifts calendar coverage (§6) and training eligibility (§4.1). Filled markers: 3-seed means ± population SD; open markers: weaker evidence, here single-seed (seed-42) runs; dashed lines: levels of the shared base configurations. The inset redraws the two M16 ladders on a y span about nine times tighter, column-aligned to the main axis. The M8 capacity replicate sits at its own level and stays on the main axis.

Figure 3: The saturating law’s 24-week prediction hits, and the activity-mixture model’s 32-week prediction misses. Both were registered internally. (a) At k=24 the observed 0.4296 lies 0.005 below the saturating prediction and 0.066 below the log-linear one, so both internally registered levels sit above the outcome. The two forms were fit on the three-window matched ladder before any 24-week evaluation and are scored across a cohort shift (both scorings in §4.5). The curve plots the log-space R2 of the weekly-aggregate ridge probe (closed-form, no training seed) against history length k=1..24 weeks. Every point is scored on the single four-window matched cohort (n=372,778) and comes from the M24 extract alone, so no training-extract mismatch enters the curve. On the test calendar it flattens (+0.00009/week at k=22→24), but a single exponential underfits it, with fit RMSE 0.0103 and an asymptote of 0.423, below the observed 0.4296. A mixture of per-decile saturation rates predicts this underfit inside the window, and panel (b) rejects the mixture’s extrapolation past k=24. Inset: the more active the customers, the sooner the curve bends. The top three deciles, 10, 9 and 8, reach the half-saturation point k1/2 of their saturating fits (circles) at 3.9, 5.2 and 10.0 weeks. In the fits, deciles 6–7 bend beyond the window (k1/2 of 27.1 and 24.7 weeks), and the bottom five are still climbing at the window’s edge. This is a claim about curve shape, not level, and it rests on the fitted parameters in §2.6. Curves show per-decile refit R2(k), k=1..16, from the M16 extract on the same matched cohort, shaded by prior-activity decile. Each (decile, k) pair has one ridge fit, evaluated on that decile’s test rows. All ten deciles are fitted, but only deciles 1, 5, 8, 9 and 10 are drawn, because the lower eight lie within 0.051 of one another at k=16 and their strokes would overlap. (b) The 32-week miss, drawn against the falsification region of the internally registered extension. This panel uses a separate M32 extract, scored on the matched-cohort rows that also fall in the M32 test split (94.2% coverage, n=351,174). Its level differs from panel (a) by −0.033, an offset between extracts in which the M32 training data and the scored rows change together. The internally registered quantity is therefore the gain within this extract, ∆(24→32), anchored at the observed k=24 point. The activity-mixture model predicted ∆=+0.0142 [0.0126, 0.0231], the internally registered band and the only interval that panel (b) draws. Its lower endpoint is the calibrated and its upper endpoint the raw 90% bootstrap bound, so it is not a single 90% interval. The flat-tail null is ≤ +0.001. The observed gain is ∆=−0.0004, with 95% CI [−0.0014,+0.0004] from the paired customer-clustered bootstrap on the same extract and rows. This observed interval reflects row-sampling uncertainty at the three test anchors, not variation across calendar anchors (§2.3). The curve enters the flat-tail null, and the observed interval excludes the entire internally registered range (discriminating threshold 0.007). The mechanism check fails in the same direction. The three lowest deciles show a mean within-decile gain of 0.018, against a predicted 0.045–0.059.

Figure 4: Through 16 weeks, cohort composition makes raw deltas understate the window effect. Full-test-split vs. matched-cohort window deltas in log-space R2 (transformer, Huber, seed 42) at 1M and 10M. At both scales the matched delta exceeds the full-set delta for every window contrast (e.g. ∆(M16−M8) +0.094 matched vs. +0.075 full at 10M). The gap arises because longer windows admit colder, less active customers, which changes both the error and the target variance in R2. Here the net effect is that raw deltas between these windows understate the window gain measured on a fixed population. The matched delta scores both windows on that fixed population, so it is unaffected by shifts in test composition. Bars are point estimates. Within seed 42, customer-clustered paired bootstrap intervals on the matched 10M deltas are tight.

Figure 5: In log space, structured physical-time positional encoding beats RoPE as implemented and stacks almost additively with the MSE objective. M16-1M configurations, log-space R2 on the full test split (not the matched cohort of Table 2); bars are 3-seed means and dots are individual seeds {42, 123, 456}, including the stacked configuration (0.6060±0.0006). Under the Huber objective, MS-RoPE’s semantic frequency bands beat RoPE (+0.021) and sit above the unconstrained learnable control (§2.10) on means (+0.009, inside the control’s seed-to-seed variation). Stacked on the MSE objective, the two gains are nearly orthogonal (0.6060 observed vs. 0.6083 fully-additive, 96% of the additive gain, 3-seed), giving the best log-space M16 result on the primary dataset. The same stack at M24 reaches 0.6419±0.0024 (3-seed). The y-axis starts at 0.50 (break marked); bar labels carry the values.

Each prediction and its falsifier were committed before the deciding evaluation ran. The last column states what was already known at commit time, since the commitments are not equally blind. Two of the predictions, (ii) and (iv), are mechanical curve fits to already-measured points with no free parameter choices. Of the other two, (i) is a threshold and (iii) is a per-decile extrapolation with a calibration window pinned in advance. What each registration adds is the discriminating criterion, fixed in advance (§4.5). †Commitment (ii) is a hit on levels, scored across a cohort shift. Scored on the gain instead, the observation sits between the two predictions, nearer the saturating one; we report both scorings (observed gain +0.015 vs. saturating −0.008 / log-linear +0.053; each predicted gain is that form’s R2(24) less the fit cohort’s k=16 level, 0.4426, so the negative saturating value is the fit sitting below that point, not a predicted decline; §4.5). Their M8–M16 cells sit on the three-window cohort (n=407,338 customer-weeks), not the four-window cohort the matched M24 entries use (n=372,778): no ∆ in this table crosses that cohort change, and re-scoring the seed-42 M8–M16 models on the four-window cohort moves those levels by ≤0.0004 and ∆(M16−M8) by ≤0.0002. Train-side eligibility. The longer-window models also train on a modestly larger and colder eligible population (up to 10% more customers, §4.1). Matching fixes test composition but not this, so every window contrast here is “window as extracted” (§6).

Table 4: Matched-cohort evaluation of the linear model (6-feature ridge, 1M): full-test-set vs. matched R2 with the constant-denominator MSE column (log-target space). The matched climb exceeds the raw climb.

Table 15: The paper’s transformer on three public datasets. On each dataset, read on its own, the transformer gains from 16 weeks of history over 8 too. Gain = out-of-fold R2 with a 16-week history minus with an 8-week one, in log space, over all rows, each scored by the model whose test fold holds it; the mean over 5 seeds. Seed interval: t on the 5 per-seed gains (4 df). Scoring interval: a customer bootstrap with the models held fixed, 999 draws, the same draws for both windows and every seed. The intervals cover seed noise and the noise of scoring these rows, not the choice of folds. Datasets: Online Retail II, a UK online gift retailer with many wholesale buyers, 2009 to 2011; The Complete Journey, a grocer’s 2,500-household panel over about two years, with no calendar dates; CDNOW, one quarter’s new customers of an online music store, with every purchase they made over 18 months. Rows are the ridge probes’: one per customer and anchor with at least one purchase in the 56 days before the anchor, cross-fit by customer over the ridge probes’ five folds. Earlier anchors’ targets overlap later anchors’ inputs in calendar time, so this is not out-of-time validation. Target: spend over the 364 days from the anchor, as log(1 + max(0, ·)). Model: the paper’s d128, 2-layer transformer and loss, with batch and warmup scaled to these sizes and the learning rate left at 5×10−4, untuned (it was set at a batch of 8,192). It sees each line’s quantity, price and spend and its place in the sequence, oldest first, with no date and no item or category; the paper’s recipe reads no calendar or timing feature on the main data either. So the longer window adds older lines, in order, without their dates. On Online Retail II, cancellations enter as lines with negative quantity. On CDNOW every customer joined in the first quarter of 1997, and for 31% of rows the 16-week history reaches back to the first purchase, which to a model with no dates looks like a shorter sequence, as a light buyer’s does. On 3 of the 15 folds the learning-rate schedule was sized for 0.7% to 5.6% more steps per epoch than ran, so it ends at about 1.0% to 1.75% of its peak rather than at 1%, and one fold’s warmup is 76 steps, not 72. Each dataset is used under its own terms (CC BY 4.0 for Online Retail II; The Complete Journey and CDNOW used as released, with no modification or redistribution), and only aggregate results are reported.

Table 14: Per-family parameter counts, read from the trained checkpoints (M16-1M runs) as sums over state-dict entries. A module shared across layers, such as the rotary encoding, contributes once for the model and once per layer that references it. Same test rows for every model (all models are M161M, n=480,673), seed 42, log-space R2. Best offset is the additive constant c=mean(y)−mean(ŷ); best affine is the maximum over all aŷ+b, which in closed form is Pearson r2(ŷ, y); isotonic is the validation-fit monotone map. The two linear corrections are fit on test, so they are flattered and give an upper bound on what a linear map can gain for each model. The isotonic correction is fit on validation.

The ordering is strict MSE < Huber < pinball on both columns for 9 of 9 models, and the three per-objective ranges do not overlap on either column. Mean-bias ranges are MSE [0.0894, 0.1185], Huber [0.2692, 0.2880] and pinball [0.3184, 0.3648]. Median-bias ranges are MSE [−0.2081,−0.1782], Huber [−0.0795,−0.0646] and pinball [−0.0181,+0.0026]. One recipe serves every transformer run except the recipe-transfer runs (§E.1), the 1,500-event-cap pair (§6), the runs on the corrected-schedule build (§2.1), the corrected-input runs (§4.4), and the public-dataset runs, whose changes are stated with them (§B).

Ridge is the exception among the two families in this table, which are also the two whose training set grows with the tier (see text). Window ladders, log-space R2 on the full test split (seed 42). The ridge M16-10M and M24-10M values were recomputed separately (footnote in text).

The margin over the control sits within the control’s own seed spread, so that ordering is not seed-resolvable. papers.selection_reason: Empirically demonstrates that longer observation windows significantly outperform increases in data, capacity, and architecture in customer behavior forecasting, highlighting the importance of long-context modeling.
papers.title: The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting
papers.tldr: For long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, extending the history window appears far more influential than adding data, model capacity, or newer architectures, though calendar coverage prevents isolating the window’s causal effect.

papers.abstract: Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state. We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision--language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation. To train the model, we curate 3.7 million question--answer pairs, drawing execution supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation. These questions span different stages of an execution and connect task-level judgments with observed progress and outcomes. We then fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this collection together with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data. Across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, ACE-Brain-0.7 achieves an average score of 76.5, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 72.7 and Claude Opus 5.5 at 73.5. Our model also leads the evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and reaching 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg. Controlled evaluations further indicate that our task-only model makes more effective use of visual history and more accurately distinguishes execution states. Together, these results show that ACE-Brain-0.7 effectively combines spatial perception with temporal understanding, delivering strong execution-grounded reasoning and comparing favorably with closed-source models.
authors: Yinhe Wang, Shijun Shi, Feng Pan, Tao Tao, Wei Mao, Jiangning Zhang, Zhiyao Ren, Yihang Jiao, Haoming Gu, Yunpeng Qing, Jiyu Guo, Zhi Hou, Dacheng Tao, Xiaogang Wang
bullets: Combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and execution-progress estimation.
Trained on 3.7 million question–answer pairs from egocentric videos, robot episodes, and simulations, plus related task and grounding data.
Averages 76.5 across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, exceeding the cited GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 scores.
Leads evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and achieving 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg.
Controlled evaluations suggest stronger use of visual history and more accurate execution-state discrimination.

papers.abstract: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, plan4d leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in a dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that plan4d achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project
authors: Hangwei Zhang, Rujing Dang, Ruimin Lin, Jiahong Wu, Xiangxiang Chu, Chuanxia Zheng
bullets: Addresses the weak physical grounding and geometric consistency of video-focused world models.
Uses a model-stitching architecture combining Depth Anything 3 and LongCat-Video, with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction.
Predicts RGB videos, depth, camera poses, point clouds, and scene flow from observed context and text-specified actions.
Supports complex, long-horizon, fine-grained actions and reports improved visual fidelity and geometric accuracy on synthetic and real-world datasets.
The approach targets settings where paired action and dense 4D supervision is scarce by leveraging pretrained video and 3D reconstruction priors.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the PLAN4D pipeline. A video generator produces a denoised latent trajectory, while a stitched DA3 decoder reads the same latent state to recover synchronized depth, camera rays, camera parameters, point clouds, and scene flow. During joint training, the stitched decoder is frozen and acts as a differentiable geometry critic for the video generator; at inference time, RGB video and dense 4D structure are decoded from the shared latent trajectory.

Figure 8: Stitching adapter architecture ablation over DA3 encoder blocks 1–11. Lower MSE means that the adapter reconstructs the frozen DA3 feature grid more accurately from the Wan VAE latent. Figure 3: Qualitative results for scene flow and dynamic reconstruction. Columns from left to right compare the ground truth, results from our DA3-based prediction, Any4D, and MotionCrafter. papers.abstract: Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. Project page: https://dreamtechai.github.io/Direct3D-V3.
authors: Shuang Wu, Jiachen Qian, Youtian Lin, Feihu Zhang, Philip Torr, Yao Yao, Xun Cao
bullets: Addresses the reconstruction bottleneck and representational complexity of VAE-based latent 3D diffusion.
Uses a latent-free diffusion transformer that models raw SDF voxel grids during training and sampling.
Applies neighboring-voxel manifold regularization and rendered normal supervision through Marching Cubes.
Predicts conditioning-image camera parameters as an auxiliary task to improve image-to-geometry alignment.
Supports generative reconstruction by combining diffusion with normal-guided refinement for observed and unseen regions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Framework of Direct3D-V3. Rather than compressing geometry into a learned latent representation, Direct3D-V3 trains and samples directly on raw SDF voxel grids. During training, we extract the SDF voxel grid and surface patch SDF values from the ground-truth mesh, and add Gaussian noise to the surface patch SDF values to form the DiT input x𝑡 . During inference, the first-stage model is used only to provide the surface patch indices; sampling then starts from Gaussian noise on these sparse patches, and the latent-free DiT predicts the clean SDF values directly in the native voxel domain. The patch-level DiT uses the noisy SDF signal, DINOv2 image tokens, and timestep embedding to reason efficiently over global shape semantics, while a lightweight voxel-level DiT refines voxel-level SDF values within each selected patch. In parallel, a camera prediction branch combines patch-level features with image tokens to regress normalized intrinsic and extrinsic parameters, encouraging the generated shape to remain spatially aligned with the conditioning image.

Fig. 5. Generative reconstruction pipeline. Given the input images, we use pre-trained predictors to estimate the corresponding foreground mask and normal map as auxiliary observations. The key reconstruction mechanism lies in how these cues are coupled with the latent-free DiT output: the mask calibrates the predicted camera, while the normal map drives direct refinement of the predicted SDF voxel grid. At each guided sampling step, the DiT proposes a clean SDF grid together with an image-view camera. We first align the rendered mask with the estimated one to correct the camera, and then compare rendered surface normals with the estimated normal map to update the SDF values. The refined SDF is re-noised and passed back to the sampler, coupling observation-driven correction with the learned generative prior for the final reconstruction.
Fig. 3. The architecture of the dual-granularity DiT.

Fig. 4. Illustration of the Implicit Manifold Regularization (IMR). Without the decoder-induced geometric prior used in latent-based pipelines, a latentfree DiT can predict locally inconsistent TSDF fields, leading to abrupt zerolevel crossings and non-watertight meshes after Marching Cubes. Since the surface manifold is implicitly defined by the zero level set of the TSDF, we regularize this manifold by penalizing neighboring voxels whose predicted SDF values differ by more than one voxel length 𝜂. This local constraint encourages coherent TSDF transitions around the surface, reducing holes and producing a more watertight extracted mesh while preserving the generated shape.
Fig. 7. Qualitative comparison with recent open-source image-to-3D generation methods.
Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison for single-view generative reconstruction. The figure compares reconstructed meshes from the same challenging input images.
Fig. 15. Additional qualitative comparisons with recent image-to-3D generation methods.
Fig. 6. User study results for image-to-3D generation. Scores range from 1 to 5, and higher is better.
Fig. 14. Additional visual results generated by Direct3D-V3.
Fig. 9. Qualitative comparison for multi-view generative reconstruction on scenes from the Tanks and Temples dataset.

Fig. 11. Qualitative ablation of the camera prediction branch. Adding the branch improves alignment between the generated mesh and the conditioning image, especially for structures visible from the conditioning view.

Fig. 10. Qualitative ablation of the core components. The patch-level DiT alone produces coarse and incomplete geometry. Adding the voxel-level DiT restores finer details but still leaves many holes; IMR greatly reduces these artifacts, and normal-rendering supervision further improves the quality.

Fig. 12. Ablation of first-stage surface patch indices at 5123 resolution. Comparable results across a pre-trained VecSet DiT, a dense 643 index predictor, and Hunyuan3D 2.1 indicate that the latent-free DiT is robust to different sources of surface patch indices.

Fig. 13. Failure case of single-view generative reconstruction. When the first-stage surface indices are poorly aligned with the conditioning image, normal-guided SDF refinement operates on inaccurate sparse support and can distort the mesh.

Table 2. Quantitative comparison with recent image-to-3Dmethods. Higher is better for all metrics, and the best result is shown in bold. Ours∗ denotes Direct3D-V3 trained with the public training data plus approximately 200K additional private meshes.
Table 1. Progressive training schedule for Direct3D-V3.
Table 3. Quantitative comparison on GSO generative reconstruction. The table reports Chamfer Distance (CD), F1-score at 0.95 and 0.99, and Volume IoU. The best result is shown in bold.

Table 4. Core component ablations on the held-out Objaverse-XL subset. Each checkmark indicates that the corresponding module is enabled. Lower is better for Normal-FID, and the best result is shown in bold.
Table 5. Effect of IMR on boundary artifacts. Lower boundary-edge count indicates fewer open mesh boundaries.
Table 8. Computational cost and scaling across resolutions and patch sizes. Memory and per-step inference time are measured on one A800 GPU.
Table 7. First-stage choices evaluated on the Objaverse-XL validation set at 5123 resolution. Lower is better for Normal-FID.
Table 6. Patch-size ablation for the latent-free DiT. Smaller patches improve Normal-FID but increase the number of patch tokens; we use 𝑝 = 8 as the default patch size.

papers.abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.
authors: Guoxin Chen, Shuang Sun, Fanzhe Meng, Xinyu Tang, Ruihua Song, Wayne Xin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the problem that task success alone does not identify which teacher behaviors should be reinforced.
Skill-FT applies natural-language skills during teacher rollouts, followed by fine-tuning on the resulting trajectories.
AutoMaster automates skill design, trajectory analysis, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation.
Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B models, it improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT by 1.42–8.99 percentage points under fixed training conditions.
Keeping skill instructions during SFT improves performance across all six settings, even though they are absent at evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A correct result is only part of what a teacher demonstrates. AutoMaster designs natural-language skills to guide teacher rollouts and selects demonstrations for fine-tuning. (a) In this example, both pipelines process all 100 records with four workers. The skill-guided teacher also checks whether the fix holds with fewer or more workers. (b) With the same teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe, students trained with AutoMaster achieve higher performance than their Vanilla SFT counterparts on all three benchmarks at both model sizes (4B and 9B). Labels above the bars show gains of 1.42–8.99 percentage points over Vanilla SFT. Error bars show ±1 SD over three evaluation runs per checkpoint.

Figure 2. Overview of AutoMaster. An LLM agent designs skills for subsets of a fixed training task pool and tests them in pilot teacher rollouts. It refines the skills as needed, runs promising interventions on larger batches, and selects demonstrations for SFT. In each outer-loop round, the student is trained from the same initial checkpoint, with any skill instructions used by the teacher retained in the training input. The student is evaluated without generated skills.

Figure 4. Contributions of skill guidance and data selection. w/o Skill Guidance retains agentdirected selection from unguided teacher rollouts. w/o Data Selection retains skill guidance on a fixed random subset of tasks but omits agent-directed trajectory selection. Removing either component lowers the mean score in each of the six settings. Task-Matched SFT uses unguided rollouts from the same teacher and matches the final training set of AutoMaster. Even with this match, AutoMaster scores 1.08–10.11 percentage points higher on average within each setting. Points show mean scores over three evaluation runs per checkpoint. Horizontal bars indicate ±1 standard deviation.

Figure 7. Explicit use of skill context in teacher demonstrations. Two examples from the SFT corpus illustrate how skill instructions inform the teacher’s reasoning and actions. (a) The teacher applies a conditional rule to distinguish interpreter invocation from direct execution, avoiding an unnecessary permission change. (b) The teacher references the supplied grammar to derive an expression’s grouping, then implements and tests the corresponding parser. Skill instructions and trajectory excerpts are condensed. Quotation marks indicate verbatim excerpts.

Figure 5. Skill-guided changes in teacher behavior. Each column compares unguided and skill-guided rollouts by the same teacher on the same task. (a) Terminal: Both solvers meet the error threshold. The unguided teacher claims fourth-order accuracy despite evidence of second-order convergence. The skill-guided teacher switches to a nine-point stencil and verifies fourth-order convergence using direct solves on successively finer grids. (b) Search: Both rollouts identify the same episode. The unguided teacher repeatedly guesses the award, while the skill-guided teacher identifies the director from episode credits and verifies the clues. (c) SWE: The unguided teacher reverses the global sort to satisfy a flawed self-test. The skill-guided teacher checks the UTF-16 encoding, corrects the self-test input, and keeps the required ascending order.

Figure 3. Infrastructure of AutoMaster. The agent accesses data and submits rollout and SFT jobs through the MCP interface. After SFT, the execution controller automatically schedules evaluation on a separate GPU cluster, where SGLang workers load the checkpoint directly from storage shared with the training cluster. Linked experiment records let the agent trace each evaluation back to the training set and the skills that guided the teacher.

Figure 6. Retaining skill instructions during SFT improves performance without test-time skills. Both conditions use the same teacher trajectories and SFT recipe. Keep retains the skill instructions in the training input, whereas Remove omits them. All students are evaluated without skills under the official benchmark protocols. Bars show mean scores over three evaluation runs per checkpoint, circles show individual runs, and error bars indicate ±1 SD. Labels give the gain of Keep over Remove in percentage points.

Table 1. Main results with Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. We report task accuracy for TerminalBench 2.1 and BrowseComp, and mean test pass rate for Doc2Repo, all in percent (higher is better). Results are mean ± SD over three evaluation runs per checkpoint. Bold marks the highest mean in each column. ∆ gives the gain over Vanilla SFT in percentage points.

papers.abstract: Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters. Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens. Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.
authors: Sahibzada Allahyar, Julia White, Dhruv Atreja, George Hurn-Maloney, Urchade Zaratiana
bullets: Targets confidence-aware candidate selection while avoiding the latency and token generation costs of explicit reasoning.
Uses bidirectional full-attention interactions among context, questions, and candidate answers in Qwen-based hybrid models.
Combines soft-target distillation from multiple teachers—including a reasoning model—with progressive post-training across diverse decision tasks.
Provides models from 0.4B to 27B parameters that the abstract reports as lying on the Hugging Face decision-model performance–parameter Pareto frontier.

The 27B variant reaches a hidden-set score of 73.37 with 2.1% expected calibration error after checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth; scope is evaluated on five model sizes and the stated benchmark.

figures.caption: Figure 2: GLiDE V1.2 architecture. Each decision is encoded as a single sequence containing the context, question, coded candidate answers, and an answer prefix. Starting from a 64-layer Qwen hybrid decoder, GLiDE removes causal masking from its 16 full-attention layers, enabling bidirectional interactions while retaining causal recurrence in the 48 Gated DeltaNet layers. A dedicated 255-way readout scores the final hidden state, and a softmax over the offered options produces a normalized probability distribution. Decisions are computed in a single forward pass, without generating tokens or intermediate reasoning. Appendix C details the output semantics and deployment policies.

Figure 4: GLiDE V1.2 compared with the other models on the Hugging Face Decision Index, edition 0.4.1. Scored by the board’s maintainers on hidden test sets. a, Calibration error against Full score, for models scoring above 50. b, Full score against median latency on one GPU. c, Stated confidence against measured accuracy for GLiDE V1.2; larger markers hold more answers.

Figure 8: The GLiDE family on the Hugging Face Decision Index (board of 12 November 2026, 300 models). Scored by the board’s maintainers on hidden test sets. a, Full score on the hidden sets against parameters served, for every model with a declared size. Stage 4 trains GLiDE V1.1 on the rebuilt mixture with routed, gold-anchored soft targets and releases the average of two seeds.

Screenshot of the Hugging Face Decision Index website (Passos, 2026b), taken on 15 November 2026 and reproduced unchanged. Highlighted points are on the frontier. Figure 8a redraws the same data. papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires agents to adapt when the task changes while reusing what they know about the environment. Successor features separate dynamics from task-specific reward, but their effectiveness depends on the choice of base features. Taking the identification of entorhinal grid cells with eigenvectors of the successor representation as a design principle, we build this basis from eigenvectors of the transition matrix of a fixed reference policy. With such a basis, the successor features at a state-action pair are a linear combination of the base features at that same pair, which is not true in general, and the coefficients are known in closed form: each successor feature is its base feature multiplied by $\theta_i = 1/(1-\gamma\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ is its eigenvalue. The long-term return is thus predicted from the same features as the immediate reward, no successor-feature network or replay buffer is needed, and adapting to a new task reduces to a linear regression on the reward. The agent acts greedily on the action values of the reference policy, which is one step of policy improvement over it and suffices to reach a single goal. In a two-goal gridworld, with the uniform random walk as reference policy, whose eigenvectors are the low-frequency Laplacian eigenvectors, agents built this way maintain near-maximal return across every change of goal, whereas SimpleSF and DQN lose most of their return at each change.
authors: \'Elodie C\^ot\'e-Gauthier, Doina Precup, Isabeau Pr\'emont-Schwarz

In a two-goal gridworld, performance remains near maximal across goal changes, unlike SimpleSF and DQN.
