papers.abstract: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.
authors: Shibo Zhou, Tianqi Hong, Zheng Yan, He Yang
bullets: Addresses the human-intensive design–build–test–iterate workflow in power-electronics hardware development.
Uses workspace scanning, machine-specific constraints, and an executable digital twin to rehearse robot actions, fabrication, and circuit behavior before fabrication.
Coordinates a robot arm, PCB printer, pick-and-place machine, cameras, sensors, an OPAL-RT simulator, and an oscilloscope from a single text instruction.
In a 60 Hz notch-filter demonstration, it completed a first-run experiment without human intervention in 2 h 39 min and achieved 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz.
The rehearsal identified five pre-fabrication issues, while the agent also diagnosed and resolved faults during execution.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Architecture of JARVIS. The agent reads and writes the records, its long-term memory, and acts through two channels. In the twin, the agent asks questions and rehearses. The twin’s four layers (geometry, behavior, physics, provenance) mirror the bench. Through the accountable execution layer, the agent runs programs on the real machines. This layer logs every attempt, enforces every safety limit in code and holds the machine skills. The bench consists of unmodified machines. Scans and the machines’ live states keep the twin in step with the bench. Two screens show people what the bench does and what the agent thinks. A person states the need in plain language and agrees to the agent’s plan; once the run starts, no person intervenes.

Fig. 10. What people in the lab see during a run, as recorded in the run of Sec. VII-A. (a) The live display, here as the arm carries the carrier to the pick-and-place machine. The bench overview is the live 3D twin. The device at work is shown large: here the arm, with its pose and joint angles, its place on the bench seen from above, and what its gripper holds. Every other device stays live in the row below: the printed board and the bed’s temperature, the board waiting for its parts, the simulator and the oscilloscope waiting for the test, and the 3D scanner after its survey. The run’s steps appear along the bottom once the agent has worked them out, and the current step is highlighted. (b) The thinking screen at the end of the run. A person types one request in plain language at the start. The agent shows its reasoning as it works (what it observes, checks and compares) and states its conclusions and decisions in its own voice; here, the verdict’s explanation, the next design, and the improvements it proposes from the run itself.

Fig. 4. How the bench is connected. Machines are shown by their role. Line styles show the type of each link. The agent and its twin run on the control computer; the agent’s reasoning comes from a language model in the cloud.

Fig. 7. Physics in the twin. (a) Heat transfer. The heated bed warms the aluminium carrier and the board by conduction; the board loses heat to the air, and the carrier to the arm. The twin runs the cure’s own heating program on a simulated bed and, from the heat path between the bed and the board, predicts the temperature at the board’s surface: it holds at the ink’s cure temperature. The twin also predicts when the carrier is cool enough for the arm to grip. (b) Thermal expansion. Aluminium grows more than the board and more than the cold frame around the carrier. Up to 240 ◦C, a gap stays open around the carrier, and the board stays held. (c) Bending of the aluminium flexures. Two beams, clamped at both ends, hold the carrier in place. As the carrier grows, the beams bend further and push harder; their deflection stays inside the slot behind them. Schematics not to scale; curves computed by the twin’s models.

Fig. 6. From scans to the twin, and a rehearsal in it. (a) The 3D scanner on the arm’s wrist views the bench from several directions; each cone is one view. (b) The agent fuses the views into one panorama of the bench, a point cloud in the arm’s frame, coloured by height above the surface below. (c) The agent places the complete CAD model of every machine, fixture and tool where the scan found it. The result is the executable digital twin. (d) Before anything moves, the agent rehearses the experiment in the twin. It checks motion, heat, time, the circuit and its test, and the machine files.

Fig. 2. The JARVIS bench and the agent’s twin of it. (a) The physical bench. (b) The twin of the same bench at the start of a run. Every machine and fixture is placed where the bench scan found it: the robot arm with its gripper, the printer, the pick-and-place machine with its dock and tape feeders, the tool rack, the test nest holding the carrier, the test head on its stand, the push-out pin, the next blank board, the simulator and the oscilloscope. (c) Close-ups of the twin. Left: the tool rack holds the printer’s probe, paste dispenser and ink dispenser. Middle: in the carrier, the board sits in an adapter and the adapter sits in a base. Right: at the end of a run, the tested board is pushed out of the adapter on the push-out pin, and the empty adapter is set onto the next blank board.

Fig. 5. How a board travels through the bench, and how boards are exchanged. (a) The board clips into an adapter, an open frame. The adapter sits in a base. Through the opening, the board rests directly on the base, and its top stays below the adapter’s rim. The adapter and the base each have a grip tab, by which the arm holds them. A board of another size uses another adapter. (b) Board exchange at the end of a run. The base stays in the test nest, and the arm moves only the adapter. (1) The arm lowers the adapter over a push-out pin, which pushes the tested board out near one edge; the board drops onto the table. (2) The arm lowers the empty adapter onto the next blank board, which clips in. (c) The route of one board. The arm carries the whole carrier from machine to machine, and the whole carrier is heated on the printer’s bed. After the test, the exchange loads the next blank board, and the next run starts again in the test nest. Schematic, not to scale.

Fig. 8. The build, step by step. The board is the agent’s own layout, shown as it is after each step. (a) Before the run, the 3D scanner on the arm’s wrist scans every machine and fixture that the run uses, and the agent matches each scan to its place in the twin; a place that does not match stops the run. (b) The printer’s carriage waits at its tool-change position. A printed marker, found by the 3D scanner, locates the tool rack, and the arm moves a tool head from the rack onto the carriage. (c) The probe touches the bare board at many points. The result is a height map (unevenness exaggerated), so the nozzle can follow the surface. The nozzle follows the map, so an uneven board is printed at a constant gap; the agent decides how large a step between neighbouring points each stage may have, small on a bare board and larger once printed pads stand higher. (d) The ink dispenser draws the traces in ink, at a constant gap above the uneven surface (inset: a section along one trace). (e) The whole carrier stays on the heated bed while the ink cures, then cools until the arm can grip it safely. (f) The probe finds two features of the printed circuit (1, 2), and the paste layer is aligned to them; the paste dispenser sets a dot of solder paste on each pad. (g) The down-looking camera finds the board’s three fiducials. The nozzle picks each part from a tape feeder, the up-looking camera checks it, and the part is set on its paste. (h) The bed heats the whole carrier again; the paste melts and forms the joints (inset: one joint before and after). Schematic, not to scale.
Fig. 12. The board built and tested by JARVIS. The traces printed in ink, the 14 parts placed and reflowed, and the gold discs on the test pads, as the board came out of the run.

Fig. 9. The hardware-in-the-loop test. The board, still in its adapter and base, sits in the test nest. The arm places the test head on the board and holds it there through the sweep; the arm’s gripper holds the head by a fin on its top, and the head’s six contact tips touch the board’s six test pads, each wired out. A and B are not used by this board. An analog output of the simulator drives the board’s input (IN) with a sine wave. Two analog inputs record IN and OUT, and the gain OUT/IN is measured at every frequency. An oscilloscope also measures IN and OUT, as a second instrument. Inset: the twin’s prediction of the gain. Schematic, not to scale.

Fig. 14. The next design. (a) The board that the agent proposed from the measured data, as drawn in KiCad (copper and silkscreen): the same layout, every resistance divided by ten and every capacitance multiplied by ten. (b) The measured board, the twin recalibrated on it, and the next board predicted by the recalibrated twin. (c) The passband near 1 Hz enlarged: the next board meets the limit that the built board missed.

Fig. 13. The requirement as code, the twin’s prediction and the measured board. Red: the acceptance limits derived from the requirement. Green: the twin’s predicted response of the notch board, for nominal parts and for 300 virtual boards with random part values within their tolerances. Orange: the board measured by the simulator; open circles: the oscilloscope’s readings.

Fig. 15. A defect found by simulation in the twin, and the agent’s own redesign. The printer draws its ink-start pattern at the center of the rectangle that encloses the circuit. Simulated in the twin, the pattern on the first layout, v1, would cross the traces (red strokes). No person pointed this out: the agent found it in the rehearsal and changed the design itself, adding two marks that move the center. On the revised layout, v1b, whose marks the built board keeps, the pattern lands on bare board.

Fig. 11. One board through the bench, as measured in the run. Each bar is an activity of one machine. The arm carries the board, changes the printer’s tool heads eight times, holds the test head and exchanges the board. Most of the time is the machines’ own process time: curing, reflow and the cooling after each.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward models have been very successful in 3D reconstruction with ad hoc attention designs that relate all view patches densely. However, the cost of this dense global attention grows quadratically with the number of views, preventing the model from applying to larger-scale reconstruction settings. In this paper, we argue that most dense attention computations are unnecessary from a classical structure-from-motion perspective: 3D structures stem from geometrically matching regions in 2D. We bring this principle to learning-based feed-forward reconstruction with our Sparse Geometric Attention Reconstruction (SGAR) method. In SGAR, each patch token attends to only a small set of patch tokens from other views, chosen by a lightweight learned key selection module trained to predict cross-view 3D proximity of tokens. Thus, dense global attention is replaced by much more efficient geometric-similarity-guided sparse attention. SGAR is a general method that can be applied to different feed-forward models by fine-tuning. In our experiments, we show that SGAR is the fastest among both state-of-the-art dense and sparse methods and the most accurate sparse one. It runs up to 12-times faster than dense attention at 1,000 views with stable pose accuracy where existing sparse methods fail, and shows the best performance in reconstructing more complete geometries on the same time budget.
authors: Aoxiang Fan, Maria Pilligua, Corentin Dumery, Oliver Heinimann, Pascal Fua
bullets: Dense global attention scales quadratically with the number of views, limiting large-scale reconstruction.
A lightweight key-selection module predicts cross-view 3D proximity and selects only relevant patch tokens.
The approach can be integrated into different feed-forward reconstruction models through fine-tuning.
Experiments report the fastest runtime among compared dense and sparse methods, with the strongest accuracy among sparse methods.
At 1,000 views, SGAR runs up to 12× faster than dense attention while maintaining stable pose accuracy and producing more complete geometry under equal time budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison. Point clouds predicted by FastVGGT, ZipMap and SGAR (DejaView), with the ground truth, on one scene of each of 7-Scenes (chess/seq-03), ETH3D (courtyard, laser scan), LaMAR (HGE) and Mip-NeRF 360 (bonsai, SfM points). Left: four of the input views. Below each reconstruction: the AUC@30 of its cameras. SGAR (DejaView) keeps the structure of the scene where the other efficient models fragment it, most visibly on the long LaMAR trajectory.

Figure 3. Overview of SGAR. We replace the global dense attention of DejaView [8] with our sparse geometric attention as an example. The images are encoded by DINOv2 and augmented with camera and register tokens. A single shared block, unrolled over its L steps, runs frame attention, key selection and sparse attention. In sparse attention, each patch attends to the special tokens of all views, the patches of the reference view, a summary of each cluster, and all the patches of the nearest clusters, so that its cost grows near-linearly with the number of views. Key Selection projects the patch tokens by Wadj into a geometric embedding and clusters the embeddings by spherical k-means into √ N clusters, re-clustered at every step. Each cluster probes its m = 4 nearest clusters, itself first. With the patches sorted by cluster, the selected keys form a block-sparse mask over tiles of 128 tokens. A contrastive loss pulls together the embeddings of patches that observe the same surface in the ground-truth geometry and pushes the others apart.

papers.abstract: We present a new adaptive stepsize rule that biases gradient descent toward flatter minima in both theory and practice, and establish the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both sharpness and loss reduction for a broad class of locally quadratic objectives. Our critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes multiply the classical Polyak rule by $4$ and a mild damping factor. The factor $4$ is critical in that it produces equioscillations around the manifold of minimizers $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order. Damping provably drives convergence to $\mathcal{M}$. CDP thus operates at the edge of stability by adapting its stepsizes to local curvature. Once the loss is small, its projected iterates follow gradient descent on $\log{\lambda_1(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L})}$ along $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order, paralleling the flatness bias of normalized gradient descent (Arora et al., 2022). Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths shrink with the distance to $\mathcal{M}$, enabling convergence to an interpolating solution that locally minimizes sharpness at finite learning rate. We establish our theory for a broad class of non-negative losses with locally quadratic Morse-Bott structure near $\mathcal{M}$, capturing regular interpolation regimes in smooth overparameterized neural networks. Empirically, CDP stepsizes produce a flattening effect similar to that of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM, Foret et al., 2021), reducing sharpness even in settings beyond our theory, including nonlinear teacher-student networks and fine-tuning of pre-trained LLMs.
authors: Francesco Caporali, Jason M. Altschuler, Boris Hanin
bullets: Introduces CDP, which scales the classical Polyak stepsize by a critical factor of 4 and a damping term.
Proves uniform-in-time guarantees for loss reduction and sharpness on locally quadratic, Morse-Bott objectives.
Shows damping drives iterates toward the minimizer manifold, while near interpolation they follow sharpness-reducing dynamics along it.
Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths vanish near the minimizer manifold, enabling finite-learning-rate convergence.
Experiments observe SAM-like flattening in nonlinear teacher-student networks and pretrained-LLM fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Data assimilation (DA) in partially observed nonlinear systems requires repeated estimation of both hidden states and their uncertainty. Conventional nonlinear filtering can be computationally expensive and often relies on an explicit dynamical model. In this paper, we develop the Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), a data-driven dynamical model that maps unobserved physical states into a learned latent space, where the dynamics of the latent states follow a conditional Gaussian structure. This structure allows closed-form DA updates in the latent space, while nonlinear encoder-decoder mappings retain the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamics in physical space. A key feature of Neural CGM is its treatment of uncertainty in DA. The latent posterior mean and covariance are mapped to the physical variables through a Gaussian decoder that combines local moment propagation with learned nonlinear corrections. The resulting physical-space posterior statistics depend on the sequentially updated latent distribution rather than on a separate post-processing estimate. The same statistics enter a Gaussian negative log-likelihood during training, so both the posterior mean and uncertainty affect the learned model. Because Neural CGM learns the dynamical model itself, it can also be used for state forecasting and simulation without explicit knowledge of the governing equations. Numerical experiments on benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems show accurate state estimation and forecasting while substantially reducing online assimilation cost relative to conventional nonlinear DA methods. Neural CGM is therefore suited to repeated state estimation, uncertainty quantification, and prediction from partial observations.
authors: Chuanqi Chen, Nan Chen
bullets: Addresses costly state and uncertainty estimation in partially observed nonlinear systems without requiring explicit governing equations.
Maps physical states to a latent space with conditional Gaussian dynamics, enabling closed-form sequential DA updates.

Experiments on benchmark nonlinear systems show accurate estimation and forecasting with substantially lower online assimilation cost than conventional nonlinear DA methods.

papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters. We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-grafting primitives that compile deterministic computation directly into pretrained LM weights using zero training examples and zero runtime hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization drift and preserving natural-language (NL) competence. Our construction combines three analytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scaling into translation along a log-spaced gate grid ($>250\times$ dynamic range) with IEEE 754 error bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned width extension ($d \to d+K$) with $\sqrt{d/(d+K)}$ norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE emission, and differential $(+254,-256)$ tied unembeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4-8 digit signed $\{+,-,\times\}$ circuits in constant $\mathsf{TC}^0$ depth alongside 3-literal Boolean (100%, $N=1{,}728$; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits. On 6-digit arithmetic ($N=1{,}200$, BF16), IBM Granite 4.2 3B (1.07M-1.33M active non-zeros, $\le 0.036\%$) and Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B (2.25M-2.39M non-zeros, $\le 0.057\%$) reach 99.17% and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with an FP32 sidecar) and 98%-100% mid-sentence resumption, outperforming 12.8K-sample LoRA (42.2% / 61.7%, 0% inline continuation). A factorized block-sparse sidecar holds A100 memory at 7.89 / 10.65 GiB (4.60 / 8.14 GiB under INT8/INT4 + FP32 sidecar) while passing all 14/14 pre-registered $>2$K-token Tango splits ($N=4{,}392$; 0/11,134 OOD triggers).

papers.selection_reason: Presents a highly novel zero-gradient method to compile exact circuits into pretrained LLM weights, relevant to LLM capabilities and architecture.
papers.title: A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
papers.tldr: A zero-gradient compiler grafts exact arithmetic and logic circuits into pretrained LMs with minimal sparse weight changes and no runtime hooks, achieving near-perfect reported accuracy while largely preserving language behavior.

papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.
authors: Chenyang Jin, Susanne F. Yelin, Andi Gu
bullets: Addresses the speed–accuracy trade-off in decoding rapid syndrome measurements for superconducting quantum processors.
Uses hardware-efficient operations and training in integer arithmetic to run efficiently on FPGAs.
Decodes distance-19 surface-code syndrome rounds in under a microsecond on one FPGA.
Reports a 240× lower logical error rate than existing real-time hardware decoders for the surface code and 16× higher accuracy than Relay for a bivariate-bicycle code.
Can scale across multiple FPGAs or into custom silicon to improve speed, accuracy, or code size.

papers.selection_reason: Hardware co-designed streaming neural decoder with low-latency integer arithmetic, transferable to efficient AI inference.
papers.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
papers.tldr: Rapids is an FPGA-co-designed neural decoder that enables fast, low-latency, and highly accurate real-time quantum error correction.

papers.abstract: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.
authors: Yuzhi Huang, Jie Wu, Fanding Huang, Junchao Lin, Weichen Zhang, Ziyi Xiong, Yang Li, Zhengwei Xie, Zhimin Wang, Zhen Liu, Jiazhen Huang, Yuzheng Zhang, Yuche Liu, Hongyi Yang, Chen Tang, Shixiang Tang, Hakan Aktas, Adam Wu, Duo Wu, Kangye Ji, Shuzhao Xie, Huanan Liu, Weijue Bu, Chenxin Li, Xinyuan Wang, Tianyi Bai, Yinan Mao, Jiawei Wang, Minglei Li, Heng Yu, Ehsan Adeli, Minchen Li, Yong-Lu Li, Cengiz \"Oztireli, Huazhe Xu, Chao Yu, Jing Zhang, Shanghang Zhang, Weitao Zhou, Wenwu Zhu, Cheng Chi, Jingyan Jiang, Zhi Wang

papers.abstract: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiyaoMou/L2D-Expert-Drift.
authors: Ziyao Mou, Andrea Wynn, Eric Nalisnick
bullets: Addresses a limitation of prior L2D methods that assume fixed human performance.
Conditions the deferral policy on recent expert outcomes using a sequence model.
Evaluated on image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection.
Experiments include realistic deferral settings and irregular expert-reliability shifts.
Reports better adaptation and deferral decisions than prior L2D methods across diverse temporal patterns.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) An example use case of our EDA-L2D framework in a setting with expert performance drift: a radiologist whose performance degrades over a workday. Our model monitors past outcomes to infer current expert reliability in real time, deferring to the expert when reliable and assigning cases to the model when the expert’s performance declines. (b) Overview of our Expert-Drift-Adapted L2D framework. A streaming sequence of inputs is encoded by the backbone into features. At each timestep, the feature vector is concatenated with the expert’s most recently observed correctness, which is available only for inputs previously deferred to the expert, and passed to an RNN module. The classifier head outputs class logits and the defer head outputs a deferral score; a deferral gate then assigns the instance to either the expert or the classifier. Because the expert’s competence drifts over time, this design makes the L2D system timeaware and adaptive to temporal shifts.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models enable efficient test-time adaptation by leveraging expert demonstrations as additional context without updating model parameters. However, even when retrieved demonstrations are relevant to the current task, the VLA may fail to effectively utilize the retrieved information, ultimately leading to task failure. To address this challenge, we propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that enables reliable test-time adaptation by satisfying a user-specified task success rate requirement with minimal expert assistance. Specifically, R2-VLA learns an uncertainty predictor that estimates the uncertainty of the VLA's predicted actions given the retrieved demonstrations, guiding when to act autonomously or request expert assistance. We further introduce a task-level risk-control procedure that calibrates the uncertainty threshold to satisfy a user-specified task-failure risk requirement. Moreover, R2-VLA continually incorporates expert corrections into its retrieval memory to improve future adaptation while preserving the prescribed task-level risk guarantee. Experiments across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites demonstrate that R2-VLA improves average task success by 9.2--11.2 percentage points, achieving the desired target with fewer expert requests. These results highlight the effectiveness of connecting the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations with task-level risk control to enable successful robotic manipulation.
authors: Zixuan Liu, Hashem Haghbayan, Zizhan Zheng, Siavash Khajavi
bullets: Addresses failures where VLA models cannot effectively use relevant retrieved expert demonstrations.
Learns an uncertainty predictor over actions conditioned on retrieved demonstrations to guide assistance requests.
Calibrates an uncertainty threshold with task-level risk control to meet a specified success-rate requirement.
Continually adds expert corrections to retrieval memory while preserving the risk guarantee.
Across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO suites, improves average task success by 9.2–11.2 percentage points with fewer expert requests.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Qualitative comparison of RICL and R2-VLA on the LIBERO-GOAL task “Put the bowl on top of the cabinet” using π0-FAST. (a) RICL retrieves behaviorally relevant demonstrations from the same task, yet still produces an incorrect action at step 85: instead of moving the bowl toward the cabinet, the policy moves it away from the target. This error leads to continued execution in the wrong direction and ultimately task failure. (b) R2-VLA detects such uncertain actions using its learned uncertainty predictor and requests expert assistance when the predicted uncertainty exceeds the threshold λ̂, enabling successful task completion.

Figure 3. Effect of different target risk levels on R2-VLA across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO suites. As the target success rate increases, R2-VLA generally requests more expert assistance to achieve higher task success, demonstrating the trade-off between task-level success and the frequency of expert assistance.

papers.abstract: Frontier text-to-image (T2I) foundation models predominantly rely on multi-billion parameter Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) pretrained across massive compute clusters, creating an accessibility barrier for academic laboratories. When training DiTs from scratch on single consumer GPUs (e.g., an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24\,GB VRAM), practitioners encounter three primary bottlenecks: quadratic attention sequence costs, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation graph breaks induced by variable aspect-ratio bucketing, and an autoencoder throughput wall where frozen Variational Autoencoder (VAE) operations dominate step latency. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Asuka-FM}, an end-to-end system and architectural framework demonstrating that competitive dual-stream DiTs ($\sim$206M parameters) can be pretrained from scratch on a single consumer GPU in $\sim$160 GPU hours for under \$55. Asuka-FM integrates four core designs: (i) an AdaLN-free dual-stream DiT backbone reducing parameter count; (ii) structured sequence sparsification via Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (SPRINT) to cut attention FLOPs by over 50\%; (iii) continuous aspect-normalized Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) coupled with shifted square crop training, guaranteeing static tensor shapes while unlocking zero-shot virtual camera control; and (iv) a pixel adaptation phase utilizing a lightweight (10M parameter) Patch Detailer Head operating under velocity regression ($v$-prediction). Evaluated on open-domain benchmarks without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Asuka-FM achieves GenEval 0.588 / DPG 78.96 scores at 256px and GenEval 0.609 / DPG 78.51 scores at 512px, setting a new Pareto-optimal efficiency standard for democratic foundation modeling.
authors: V\'ictor Rodrigo Gonz\'alez, Pablo M. Olmos, Ignacio Peis, Alejandro Lancho
bullets: Targets quadratic attention, variable-resolution compilation breaks, and VAE throughput bottlenecks in single-GPU DiT pretraining.
Uses an AdaLN-free dual-stream backbone, SPRINT sequence sparsification, continuous aspect-normalized RoPE, and shifted square crops.
Adds a lightweight Patch Detailer Head for pixel adaptation with velocity regression.
Pretrains an approximately 206M-parameter model in about 160 GPU hours for under $55 on consumer hardware.
Reports GenEval scores of 0.588 at 256px and 0.609 at 512px, with DPG scores of 78.96 and 78.51, respectively, without benchmark-specific fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Asuka-FM system-architectural co-design pipeline. Top Row (Stage 1): Raw images Iorig undergo shifted square cropping to enforce static tensor dimensions (X × X) and eliminate JIT recompilations, while continuous aspect-normalized RoPE prevents phase collapse. Precomputed FLUX.2 VAE latents zt receive prepended in-context temporal conditioning (ztime) alongside text representations from a 2-layer adapter without per-block AdaLN parameters. Bottom Row (Stage 2): The 13-layer dual-stream DiT executes SPRINT sequence sparsification: shallow blocks (fθ) supply high-frequency dense skips ft, deep middle blocks (gθ) process macro-semantics over a 75%-sparse grid, and dense decoder blocks (hθ) fuse representations to predict flow trajectories. Finally, the lightweight 10.09M Patch Detailer Head (PDH) transfers representations directly to RGB pixels under native v-prediction.

(B) Center-row coordinate trajectories comparing discrete integer indices [0, 15] against continuous coordinates [−rW , rW ]. papers.abstract: First-person manipulation datasets treat the observation-action pair as the atomic unit and compress the generation and execution of an action into a policy network's weights, rendering the intent state behind the action unobservable. Human motor control research shows that intent mediates between observation and action and leaves observable traces along the intent pathway from decision to effect: gaze reaches the target before the hand, muscle load builds before contact, and cortical activity precedes the motor command. To record this pathway at scale, we present HumanCOIN, a first-person manipulation dataset built around human intent: 12,500 hours across 38 scene classes with three tiers of proxies. At the output end, the L1 attention tier (10,000 h) infers gaze from headband camera video, exposing the operator's next object of attention and reach before the hand moves. Midway, the L2 exertion tier (2,000 h) records surface EMG from armbands, making load expectations readable before execution is complete. At the origin, the L3 cognition tier (500 h) records scalp EEG, giving early readouts of task decisions and monitoring. Each tier inherits all proxies from the tiers below. The dataset further provides multi-view RGB images, depth maps and point clouds, 6-DoF head and wrist pose, and step-level action and object annotations. The controlled L3 setting additionally measures gaze, hand pose and finger kinematics directly. Clock and calibration data are released with the dataset so that any read rate can be re-aligned. The three tiers cover three stations, from visual orienting to cortical preparation, making the process behind visual-action pairs available for modeling at dataset scale. papers.selection_reason: Large egocentric manipulation dataset with intent proxies, directly useful for learning from human videos.
papers.title: HumanCOIN: A 12,500-Hour Dataset for Human Intent in Egocentric Manipulation
papers.tldr: HumanCOIN is a 12,500-hour egocentric manipulation dataset designed to expose human intent through gaze, muscle activity, and EEG alongside actions.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects move in dynamic scenes requires recovering their 3D motion from visual observations and predicting their positions at unobserved times. Existing methods either optimize scene-specific velocity fields or impose predefined physical and kinematic assumptions. We instead study learning a continuous-time dynamics operator across scenes, mapping multi-view visual observations to 3D object kinematics. We introduce Adaptive Pixel Flows (\ours{}), which learns this operator from multi-view RGB-D observations without per-scene optimization or predefined motion models. The method fuses observations from all cameras into a shared voxel grid in world coordinates, from which the network predicts a continuous-time velocity field. Because the operator is trained across scenes, it learns motion priors that carry over to unseen scenes. The field can then be integrated from observed states to predict object positions between observations and beyond the observed sequence. On held-out PhysInOne scenes, \ours{} improves F1 over the strongest competing method by 2.5\% for in-between prediction and 15\% for future prediction. Compared with per-scene velocity-field methods, the improvements are 30\% and 85\%, respectively. Applied zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, it improves future-prediction F1 by 12\%.
authors: Hrishikesh Viswanath, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses 3D motion recovery and temporal prediction without per-scene optimization or predefined physical assumptions.

Improves F1 on held-out PhysInOne scenes by 2.5% for in-between and 15% for future prediction over the strongest competitor.
Transfers zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, achieving a 12% future-prediction F1 improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces FFGaussType, a feed-forward method to convert 2D geometry into 3D Gaussian assets. This advances 3D scene generation and geometry-aware representation, relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: AdaPixFlow: Learning Continuous-Time 3D Dynamics Across Scenes from Sparse Multi-view Observations
papers.tldr: AdaPixFlow learns a cross-scene continuous-time 3D motion operator from sparse multi-view RGB-D observations to predict object positions between and beyond observed frames.

papers.abstract: Immersive 3D content allows text and graphical elements, such as subtitles, annotations, and icons, to be placed inside a scene rather than displayed as flat overlays. Placed this way, they respect occlusion and perspective and take on user-assigned materials and lighting while preserving their original shapes. In Gaussian scenes, however, each new glyph or icon requires its own iterative optimization, which limits scalable content creation. We present FFGaussType, which converts extruded glyph and SVG outlines into Gaussian assets in a single forward pass. A point encoder maps anchors sampled on the known surface to a single feature plane, from which a decoder shared by all assets predicts neural Gaussians carrying surface normals. This separates geometric conversion from material and lighting choices, and the feature plane supports image and video coding for compact delivery. We construct a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets with anchors and calibrated normal and silhouette renderings, holding out font families for evaluation. Conversion from prepared anchors takes 9.1 ms per asset, at a fraction of the compute and memory of prior baselines. On unseen font families and test icons, FFGaussType achieves $1.62^\circ$ normal error and $0.985$ silhouette IoU, the best among the compared feed-forward converters, matching the fidelity that per-asset fitting needs thousands of steps to reach. The code and dataset will be released after publication.
authors: Haoan Feng, Tianfu Wang, Peimeng Guan, Dae Yeol Lee, Guan-ming Su
bullets: Addresses the scalability problem of iteratively optimizing every glyph or icon for Gaussian scenes.
Encodes sampled surface anchors into a shared feature plane, then decodes neural Gaussians with surface normals.
Separates geometry conversion from material and lighting, while supporting compact image and video delivery.
Uses a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets, with font-family holdouts for evaluation.
Achieves 1.62° normal error and 0.985 silhouette IoU on unseen assets; conversion takes 9.1 ms per prepared asset.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes AdaPixFlow, a method to learn continuous-time 3D dynamics across scenes from sparse multi-view observations. This is a significant contribution to world models (predicting future states) and 3D vision (reconstructing motion).
papers.title: FFGaussType: Feed-Forward Conversion of Glyph and SVG Geometry into Compact Gaussian Assets
papers.tldr: FFGaussType converts glyph and SVG geometry into compact, renderable Gaussian assets in one fast forward pass instead of per-asset optimization.

papers.abstract: Long-term agents accumulate large external memory stores as interactions unfold, increasing the costs of storage, retrieval, and response generation. Efficiency is constrained by two coupled factors: a growing record count increases retrieval overhead, while longer retrieved contexts increase prefill computation and decoding-time attention costs. Existing methods prune or consolidate records, but pruning can discard useful evidence, whereas consolidation may produce fewer yet longer retrieval units. We introduce MemFolder, a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces record count and context length. The framework comprises two core components that share memory groups, using cross-record structure to guide both evidence consolidation and compact representation. RecordFolder grounds entity mentions, progressively selects representative yet complementary anchors, and combines semantic and entity affinity with temporal chaining to consolidate compatible records into fewer retrieval units. ContextFolder encodes the original records within these groups into compact text and uses verification feedback to revise encodings when key facts cannot be recovered. Experiments on the three text-based memory benchmarks LoCoMo, PersonaMem, and LongMemEval and the two multimodal benchmarks M3-Bench-web and M3-Bench-robot demonstrate the strong performance of our methods. Notably, on Mem0, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of the original average performance across the three text-based benchmarks with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in performance retention. Combined with ContextFolder, existing record compression methods further shorten their output records while retaining most of their performance.
authors: Xuyang Liu, Chenwen Lu, Junxi Wang, Siyu Ren, Xinying Lin, Siteng Huang, Hongli Sun, Linfeng Zhang, Honggang Chen
bullets: Targets rising storage, retrieval, and context-processing costs in long-term agents.

On Mem0, RecordFolder retained 99.0% of average performance with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in retention.

papers.abstract: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users' devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent's judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent's action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call--response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.
authors: Yuhao Zhou, Yang Zhou, Yuanxi Li, Jindi Lv, Dan Si, Qing Ye, Jiancheng Lv
bullets: Targets privacy- and compute-driven deployment of research agents on user devices, where small models struggle with action selection.
Separates action proposal from consequence prediction and value estimation using a shared tool-response simulator and value estimator.
Uses imagined candidate evaluation without executing discarded tool calls, then commits only the selected action and its real response.
Improves reported GAIA accuracy from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B across evaluated settings.
Broader candidate coverage can offset imperfect simulation, but prediction and scoring errors limit gains from wider search.

papers.abstract: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.

papers.abstract: Each fibre-reinforced composite structure has a unique material architecture. The manufacturing methods used and the presence of defects lead to local variations which require material-scale models that can resolve the response in real time at every location in the structure. Concurrent multi-scale schemes provide this capability, but at a prohibitive computational cost for large structures as the number of integration points and time increments scales with size. Surrogates have been studied extensively as replacements for material-scale models to mitigate these computational limitations. A surrogate must represent an arbitrary local architecture including defects, track the irreversible material state over an unknown number of increments, remain stable when driven recursively by its own predictions, and fit within the memory available at every integration point. Here, a Composites World Model based on a Multi-Modal Spiking Transformer architecture is designed to meet these requirements. The proposed architecture combines a material encoder, a Spiking Neural Network memory block that tracks the long-term internal state of the material, and transformer blocks that learn the short-term applied strain state. The system is trained in three stages: material architecture encoding, base training on short time windows, and recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling to suppress cumulative error drift. The trained model is disassembled at inference and coupled to a non-linear FE solver, enabling structural scale simulation of composites containing embedded defects. Benchmarks against experimental results for IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression and transverse shear, for pristine and wrinkled composites, show that the SNN memory block successfully tracks the material internal state and results in prediction errors between 0.4% and 4.8%.

bullets: Motivation: Conventional concurrent multiscale modelling is too costly for large composite structures with many integration points and time increments.

Training uses architecture encoding, short-window base training, and recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling to reduce prediction drift.

For IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression, and transverse shear, including pristine and wrinkled cases, reported errors range from 0.4% to 4.8%.

papers.abstract: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.
authors: Zixuan Huang, Yang Zhou, Guli Zhang, Sunzhu Li, Hongyan Xie, Zehao Chen, Fuzhen Zhuang, Kaixuan Wang, Xiaozhi Chen, Yikun Ban, Deqing Wang

Reports substantially better performance than representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE benchmarks.
Induces only minor changes to the VLM’s weights, though the abstract does not specify detailed limitations or numerical results.

papers.abstract: Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-N (BoN), improve language model outputs by generating multiple candidates per prompt and selecting among them using a reward model. Much of this cost is wasted: a fixed budget is applied to every prompt, although the computation required by prompts varies widely. Adaptive methods halt once sampled answers appear settled, but their thresholds are tuned heuristics with no statistical control over early-stopping errors. We instead seek an anytime-valid stopping rule that takes an error tolerance $\alpha$ as input and halts only once an answer is certified to hold a majority ($\theta_a > 1/2$) under the generator's distribution. We aggregate candidates by final answer with a reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) score and treat stopping as a sequential test over the resulting clusters. Applying Wald's sequential probability ratio test to these clusters yields SPRT-RWSC, which performs well empirically, but its guarantee fails because the leading answer shifts during sampling, and the run is continuously monitored. Our main contribution, e-RWSC, replaces Wald's test with a betting supermartingale (an e-process) for every answer the policy produces, bounding the probability of ever certifying a non-dominant answer by $\alpha$, uniformly over time and across all answers. The RWSC scores drive the bets, so they affect only how quickly a dominant answer $a^\star$ is certified, not validity; certification takes $O(\log(1/\alpha)/d_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta_{a^\star}\|1/2))$ samples. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward models confirm the predicted $1/d_{\mathrm{KL}}$ scaling of cost and show that accuracy improves over baselines at substantially lower token cost.
authors: Vishesh Kumar Singh, Sayak Ray Chowdhury
bullets: Fixed-budget Best-of-N wastes computation because prompts require different numbers of samples.
The method clusters sampled answers using reward-weighted self-consistency and applies anytime-valid betting tests.
Its e-process guarantee controls the probability of ever certifying a non-dominant answer at tolerance α, despite changing leaders and continuous monitoring.
Certification requires O(log(1/α)/d_KL(θₐ*‖1/2)) samples for a dominant answer.
Experiments across models, datasets, and reward models support the predicted cost scaling and show higher accuracy at substantially lower token cost.

papers.abstract: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce \textbf{WeMM-Video}, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.

papers.abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp
authors: Timo Ropinski, Sebastian Kranz
bullets: Evaluates five LLMs editing convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks.

Compares standard training, label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and Edit-Ready Training (ERT).
ERT rehearses the direct closed-form weight edits performed by LLMs and achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across evaluated baselines.
The framework, tasks, editing trajectories, and scores are planned for release.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Edit-Ready Training (ERT) to prepare vision models for LLM-driven weight-space programming. This explores a novel interaction paradigm between LLMs and vision models, relevant to both language and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
papers.tldr: A benchmark shows that training vision models specifically for LLM-driven weight edits—especially with Edit-Ready Training—substantially improves editability and performance.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is a versatile framework for generative modeling that transports a source distribution to a target data distribution. A key advantage is its flexibility in the choice of source distribution, such as heavy-tailed and multimodal sources. Yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources remain limited. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence theory for Euler discretization of flow matching with linear interpolation. Suppose the source distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an everywhere positive, continuously differentiable density, finite total variance $\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}$, and an $L$-Lipschitz score. Using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, this sampler achieves total variation error at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}(Ld\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}/\varepsilon)$ iterations, provided the target distribution satisfies a mild second-moment condition. These assumptions cover, among many examples, source distributions such as multivariate Student's $t$ distributions with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, while accommodating target distributions with neither a smooth density nor bounded support.
authors: Yuchen Zhou, Lili Zheng, Yuxin Chen, Gen Li
bullets: Addresses limited sampling theory for heavy-tailed and multimodal flow-matching sources.
Analyzes Euler discretization with linear interpolation using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid.
Under positive differentiable source densities, finite total variance, Lipschitz scores, and a mild target second-moment condition, achieves error ε in ~O(Ld·TotVar_base/ε) iterations.
Covers multivariate Student’s t sources with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance.
Allows target distributions without smooth densities or bounded support.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical foundation for efficient sampling in flow matching with non-Gaussian sources, establishing non-asymptotic convergence guarantees that improve sampling efficiency.
papers.title: Flow Matching from Non-Gaussian Sources: A Theory of Efficient Sampling
papers.tldr: Provides finite-step total-variation convergence guarantees for Euler flow-matching samplers initialized from broad non-Gaussian source distributions.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.
authors: Weile Li, Yunfan Lou, Muqing Shi, Zihao Zhang, Zhenbiao Huang, Boxian Yao, Xiyu Zhu, Zhibo Pang
bullets: Addresses inconsistent benefits from adding tactile sensing to vision-language-action models.
A tokenizer conditioned on visual observations and executed actions compresses future tactile changes into discrete innovation codes.
TacInno-VLA predicts these codes as an auxiliary training target, adding no deployment-time tactile module.
Achieves 87.5% average success across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks.
Outperforms the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively; ablations support visual/action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary prediction.

papers.abstract: Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon. In language models, a sink is a token with high incoming attention, a small value, and little effect on the output. We test whether that profile holds, not the horizon rule, in one $\pi_{0.5}$ checkpoint on five RoboCasa tasks. The two endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key mass, 1.4 percentage points above their uniform share, and rotary positional encoding produces this excess: directly in shallow layers and through upstream action-token RoPE deeper in the network. The endpoints do not fit the sink profile. Their value norms stay near the action-token mean in all 18 layers. On 250 paired episodes, masking them or zeroing their values changes success by less than 4 points, and replacing their value directions with those of another observation lowers it by 3.2 to 7.2 points across three donors, whereas the same replacement on two non-endpoint tokens in the executed prefix lowers it by 28.4 points. The token that does fit the sink profile on mass and value norm is the prefix BOS; on this checkpoint, zeroing its value raises success in two paired runs, by +13.2 points (95% CI [+7.0, +19.4]) and +6.0 points ([+0.2, +11.8]). Inside the action chunk, a relative-offset routing profile estimated on other tasks keeps 75% of action-token spread and keeps closed-loop success on three held-out tasks (42.7% against a 38.7% baseline), while uniform or shuffled routing drops success to 3-4%. High attention mass alone does not tell what a token does.
authors: Yuxi Zheng, Yueqian Lin, Yudong Liu, Zijia Tang, Junyu Pan, Yiheng Wang, Hai Helen Li, Yiran Chen
bullets: The study tests the sink interpretation of the first and last action tokens in one π₀.₅ checkpoint, without evaluating the horizon-selection rule.
The endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key attention mass, with excess linked to rotary positional encoding across network depth.
Their value norms remain near the action-token average, and masking or value zeroing changes success by less than 4 percentage points.
Replacing endpoint value directions has a modest effect, while analogous replacement for non-endpoint executed-prefix tokens causes much larger losses.
Relative-offset routing preserves performance on three held-out tasks, whereas uniform or shuffled routing reduces success to 3–4%; prefix BOS more closely matches the sink profile.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes attention structure in flow-based VLA policies for robot manipulation.
papers.title: Beyond the Sink Interpretation: Radial Attention in Flow-Based VLA Policies
papers.tldr: Endpoint action tokens in a flow-based VLA policy attract slightly elevated attention but do not behave like attention sinks; their functional role is better explained by positional routing.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional point clouds are a fundamental data modality, and a large family of machine learning architectures has been developed to respect their natural symmetries to rigid motions and permutations. A principled way to compare these architectures, which vary widely in complexity and cost, is through their expressive power. That is, an architecture is complete if it can distinguish any two inputs not related by the symmetries it respects. Simple distance-based message-passing networks are known to be incomplete, and while there exist complete alternatives, they typically rely on computationally intensive mechanisms like high-order representations of the rotation group or higher-order Weisfeiler-Leman-type tests. In this work, we devise a novel, simple, equivariant message-passing architecture for point clouds, and prove that it is complete. We complement our theoretical result with experiments showing that our architecture separates challenging point clouds that distance-based message passing provably cannot distinguish. Our results suggest that high-order equivariant features may not be necessary to enhance the expressivity of point cloud architectures, and can help settle completeness for other equivariant architectures for which such results are currently unknown. We give initial evidence for this by proving completeness of a slightly modified version of SEGNN.
authors: Nadav Dym, Tal Amir, Gia Chi Dang, Christopher Morris
bullets: Targets the limited expressive power of distance-based message-passing networks under rigid-motion and permutation symmetries.
Develops a novel geometric, equivariant message-passing architecture and proves that it can distinguish any non-equivalent point clouds.
Experiments show it separates challenging point-cloud pairs that distance-based methods cannot distinguish.
Results suggest high-order equivariant features may not be necessary for achieving completeness.
Also proves completeness for a slightly modified version of SEGNN, providing evidence for broader applicability.

(b) The 16 distinct Platonic balanced sets. Rows correspond to a tetrahedron T , octahedron O, or icosahedron I. Blue denotes vertices V , orange denotes edge midpoints E, and green denotes face centers F . All these points are projected radially onto the unit sphere; concatenation denotes union, e.g., V E = V ∪E. The 21 descriptions include five duplicates, identified by congruence labels in shaded cells.

Figure 4: Color atoms in the three Platonic balanced sets with equal-sized color atoms. Colors here distinguish color atoms. (a) The octahedron O(V ) splits into three antipodal pairs of sizes 2 + 2 + 2; proper rotations realize every permutation of the pairs. (b) The cube O(F ) splits into two inscribed tetrahedra of sizes 4 + 4. (c) In O(V F ) the two tetrahedra and the octahedral vertices give color-atom sizes 4 + 4 + 6. A quarter-turn about a coordinate axis interchanges the tetrahedra in (b) and (c) and preserves the octahedron in (c), as verified in Appendix C. Any assignment of colors to whole color atoms is color-balanced, including assignments that merge color atoms into one color class.

Figure 3: Admissible color classes for a color-balanced regular polygon with both poles. (a) For a triangle, the three cycle points have one color and the two poles have one color, giving color-atom sizes 3 + 2. (b) For a square, opposite cycle points share a color, giving two alternating cycle classes and a pole-pair class of sizes 2 + 2 + 2. This support is the octahedron. Colors distinguish the finest classes; any classes may receive the same color. Thus the diagrams also describe all admissible colorings obtained by merging classes.

Figure 1: Four steps of complete geometric message passing. (1) Each node aggregates information from its neighbors into an invariant feature hi. (2) Two equivariant vectors yi,1 and yi,2 are formed from weighted combinations of positions. (3) Together with their cross product yi,1 × yi,2, these vectors define a basis onto which every other point xj is projected. (4) Pooling the invariant feature and projection obtained at every node gives a rotation- and permutation-invariant representation of the point cloud.

papers.selection_reason: Proves completeness of a simple equivariant message-passing architecture for point clouds, a core contribution to 3D geometric deep learning.
papers.title: A Complete Geometric Message-Passing Architecture for Point Clouds

papers.abstract: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.
authors: Yuqi Tang, Yang Shi, Yuran Wang, Tengfei Liu, Rundong Wang, Zongyang Qiu, Qixun Wang, Zhuoran Zhang, Xuanyu Zhu, Yifan Xu, Yiyan Ji, Shujie Li, Shixuan Liu, Haotian Wang, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Chengwei Qin
bullets: Targets missed brief actions, incorrect action order, and confusion about the camera wearer’s motion.
Uses a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline to create structured captions with video overviews, timed steps, adaptive narration, and key moments.
Trains caption refinement with GRPO using rewards for factual accuracy, coverage, temporal alignment, and non-redundancy; pose-derived motion facts strengthen supervision when available.
Built from 50,000 examples across eight egocentric video sources and evaluated on five benchmarks.

Reports leading performance among evaluated open-source models, with additional gains over specified proprietary baselines on PhysCapBench and Minerva-Ego; ablations support the reward design and coarse-to-fine annotation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate broad generalization across tasks and domains. However, comparable generalization in robot manipulation remains challenging. Heterogeneity in robot embodiments, task formulations, geometric conventions, and action interfaces fragments interaction experience across benchmarks and hardware. We rethink robot skill learning through alignment: Can heterogeneous interactions across benchmarks and embodiments jointly improve one shared skillset for robot manipulation? We propose UniCraft, a framework for learning robot manipulation skills by aligning heterogeneous settings. Specifically, UniCraft represents observed scene geometry using consistent coordinate conventions and aligns sensing and control interfaces across robots. It organizes tasks from different benchmarks in a canonical format, allowing interaction feedback to jointly refine shared skills and the orchestration policy that guides their selection and composition, without any demonstrations or model weight updates. We interleave tasks from 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments, collecting 2,700 learning rollouts per agent model. During training, UniCraft improves pooled task success on unseen scenarios and tasks by 9-28 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8-13.3 on RoboTwin 2.0, and 3.1-14.4 on RoboCasa365 (Epochs 1-3). After training, with the learned skills frozen, UniCraft demonstrates zero-shot transfer across 4 new robot embodiments and 5 additional agent models on robosuite and RoboDojo.
authors: Ziyue Wang, Yaopeng Yang, Liyi Zhou
bullets: Addresses fragmented robot-learning experience caused by differing embodiments, task formats, geometry conventions, and action interfaces.
Uses consistent scene coordinates, aligned sensing/control interfaces, and a canonical task format to combine interactions across benchmarks.
Jointly refines reusable skills and an orchestration policy without demonstrations or model-weight updates.
Training across 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments improves unseen-task performance across LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365.
Frozen learned skills transfer zero-shot to 4 new embodiments and 5 additional agent models on robosuite and RoboDojo.

papers.title: Alignment Drives Reuse: Learning Generalizable Robot-Use Agents from Heterogeneous Experience
