papers.abstract: Low-dose and thin-slice computed tomography (CT) images suffer from elevated noise that obscures anatomical detail, while clean references for supervised denoising are often unavailable. Although Noise2Noise permits self-supervised training from noisy pairs, direct regression tends to oversmooth fine structure. Averaging multiple independently generated samples mitigates this blur, though repeating multi-step diffusion sampling is costly. We introduce Noise2Noise with Improved Mean Flow (N2N-iMF) to accelerate this process via few-step sampling. N2N-iMF learns to generate one noisy image conditioned on its paired counterpart; at inference, independent outputs are sampled and averaged to suppress noise. We evaluated image quality and sampling efficiency on simulated thin-slice brain and low-dose abdominal CT across four sampling methods and averaging counts from 1 to 20, and validated the approach on real-world photon-counting CT (PCCT) brain scans. With ten samples per conditioning input and three network evaluations per sample, N2N-iMF achieved a mean absolute error of 2.60 HU on brain CT and 14.02 HU on abdominal CT, outperforming 50-evaluation denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) sampling (2.91 and 14.53 HU). On the same GPU, per-output generation time dropped from 7.29 to 0.43 s. Across eight PCCT cases, N2N-iMF reached a mean gray-white matter contrast-to-noise ratio of 1.341, versus 0.916 for Noise2Noise and 1.176 for DDIM. N2N-iMF accelerates self-supervised generative CT denoising without distillation while keeping the number of averaged outputs adjustable at inference.
authors: Xingyi Yao, Zhengtao Ma, Zhennong Chen
bullets: Addresses noisy low-dose and thin-slice CT when clean reference images are unavailable.
Trains on paired noisy images and uses Improved Mean Flow to generate denoised candidates with only a few network evaluations.
Averages independently sampled outputs to suppress noise and preserve fine anatomical structure.
Using 10 samples and 3 evaluations per sample, it improved MAE over 50-evaluation DDIM and reduced generation time from 7.29 to 0.43 seconds per output.
On eight real PCCT brain cases, it achieved higher gray-white matter contrast-to-noise ratio than Noise2Noise and DDIM.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces N2N-iMF, a method to accelerate self-supervised generative CT denoising via few-step sampling. This technique for improving diffusion model efficiency is directly transferable to video generation and world model research.
papers.title: Fast Self-Supervised Generative CT Denoising via Few-Step Sampling
papers.tldr: N2N-iMF enables fast self-supervised generative CT denoising by averaging independently generated outputs from few-step sampling, improving image quality while greatly reducing inference time.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to simulate physical interactions, but training a separate model for each environment limits scalability. Cross-environment prediction requires identifying the current physical rule, which appearance alone may not reveal. We therefore study visual calibration: using object motion and interactions in a short video as direct evidence to infer the current rule and predict motion under that rule from a different initial state. However, differences in data availability across physical conditions can yield a long-tailed training distribution, biasing models toward common rules even when evidence supports rare ones. To study this challenge, we introduce TailWorld, which evaluates the transfer of demonstrated rules across initial states while independently controlling training imbalance and calibration informativeness. The benchmark compares predictions with two reference futures from the same prediction initial state, one following the demonstrated rule and the other a common rule, to measure prediction bias toward common dynamics. We further propose Rule Inference for Transfer (RIFT), which learns how different rules affect object motion, infers the current rule from calibration interactions, and applies it to prediction from a new initial state. RIFT explicitly controls the influence of training frequency on rule inference, allowing sufficiently informative observational evidence to support rare rules. Experiments on TailWorld show that RIFT improves prediction accuracy and physical consistency across varying training imbalances and distribution shifts, with gains in predicting rare dynamics.
authors: Han Xiao, Zhiyong Bao, Xiaotong Liu, Yanhao Chen, Qingqiang Wu
bullets: Studies visual calibration: inferring a scene’s physical rule from object motion and interactions in a short video.
Introduces TailWorld, a benchmark that independently controls training imbalance and the informativeness of calibration evidence.
Proposes RIFT, which separates rule effects on motion from current-rule inference and applies the inferred rule to a new initial state.
Evaluates bias by comparing predictions under the demonstrated rule versus a common alternative rule.
RIFT improves prediction accuracy and physical consistency across training imbalances and distribution shifts, especially for rare dynamics.

papers.selection_reason: Studies world models for predicting physical dynamics from video, introducing a benchmark and method for rule inference, fitting Video World Models.
papers.title: World Models Favor Learned Priors over Visual Evidence
papers.tldr: World models often favor common learned dynamics over visual evidence, while RIFT improves rule inference from brief interactions and transfers rare physical rules to new states.

papers.abstract: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.
authors: Ambroise Borbely, Mathieu Salzmann, Olivier Verscheure
bullets: Targets the full query-key dot product in LLM attention rather than sparsifying across tokens.
Uses a static, parameter-free rule based on token positions and RoPE structure to omit selected query/key components.
Preserves full query and key projections while computing only a partial attention score.
Training from scratch shows no performance loss and reported improvements over complete dot products.
Extends to FlashAttention-3 and reduces decoding time and memory usage; dense attention also learns to suppress the omitted components.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces hidden-dimension sparse attention for RoPE-based LLMs, reducing attention computation and improving inference speed and memory footprint.
papers.title: HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
papers.tldr: HiSA sparsifies RoPE attention across the hidden feature dimension, reducing query-key computations to about one third while improving performance and inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.
authors: K. R. Jayaram, Vatche Isahagian, Aswath Vaithinathan Aravindan, Vinod Muthusamy, Punleuk Oum, Gaodan Fang, Michal Ulewicz, Gegi Thomas, Evelyn Duesterwald
bullets: The pipeline mines 1–3 lessons per trajectory, consolidates them into weighted guidelines, and supplies either all or a selected subset at inference.
On AppWorld, stronger models benefited from adding more guidelines, while weaker models often performed better with a smaller selected subset.
DeepSeek-V3.2 improved with its full 191-guideline memory; gpt-oss-120b performed better with about 29 selected guidelines than with all 199.
Deployment uncovered risks including misleading high-support guidelines, lost provenance, swallowed API errors, and baseline-comparison confounds.
The system is available in altk-evolve and deployed in IBM’s CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies how much memory LLM agents should retain, mining and consolidating lessons into guidelines, fitting the LLM Memory subtopic.
papers.title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Self-distilled memory improves long-horizon LLM agents, but the optimal number of stored guidelines depends on the model’s strength and requires careful deployment practices.

papers.abstract: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Beam, a large-scale sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 1M context window and extensive RL training, representing a significant architectural advance in LLMs.
papers.title: Beam Model Technical Report
papers.tldr: Beam is a 501.3B-parameter sparse MoE model optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads, combining a 1M-token context window with compute-efficient inference and large-scale RL post-training.

papers.abstract: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router-ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges - collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct, a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, while ClonAct's routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.
authors: Xufei Tian, Han Hu, Wenli Du
bullets: Shared linear contexts cause cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line delays; router hierarchies add lossy handoffs and routing overhead.
ClonAct uses a routerless, single-pass Context MMU with Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus, an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk.
The trial merge gate raises true-conflict merge success from 33.3% to 63.3% across three-run means.
ClonAct achieves this merge ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and avoids compact-model router collapse.
Under continuous surges, it reaches 95.0% completion with the lowest median wait and no timed-out status checks.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on extended reasoning traces, yet the training signals used to shape this behavior remain coarse. Supervised fine-tuning on full trajectories forces the model to imitate an entire demonstration, overconstraining its output distribution, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning provides only weak credit assignment, rewarding or penalizing whole completions without identifying where they succeed or fail. We propose edit-based training, a general framework for learning from a model's own trajectories via localized textual corrections. Given a sampled completion, an editor identifies the first point of failure under a specified criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span. The model is then supervised only on these edited spans. By design, this concentrates supervision where the model's reasoning first breaks down and aims to preserve its existing reasoning patterns elsewhere. The method applies both offline and online, with the latter continually adapting supervision to the model's evolving failure modes. We instantiate this approach on reasoning instruction following with Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark. Compared to full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level reinforcement learning baselines, edit-based training substantially improves compliance with the reasoning instruction while largely preserving the model's skills on untargeted tasks. These results suggest that localized correction is an effective complement to these approaches for shaping how LLMs reason.
authors: Alexandra Yakovleva, Luat Gia Khoi Nguyen, Juho Kannala, Harri Valpola, Alexander Ilin
bullets: Full-trajectory imitation can overconstrain outputs, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning offers weak credit assignment.
The method samples a completion, identifies its first failure under a criterion, and replaces only the problematic span.
Localized supervision is designed to preserve the model’s existing reasoning patterns and can operate offline or online.
On Qwen3-32B evaluated on ReasonIF, the approach substantially improves instruction compliance while largely preserving untargeted-task skills.
The abstract reports scope on reasoning instruction following; broader applicability beyond this setting is not established.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Edit-based training within one example. The instruction asks the model to reason in Chinese; the final answer is to remain in English. Each column shows the state of the trajectory after one editing round. The prompt and instruction are fixed across rounds. A red circle marks the first remaining instruction violation at the current round. A green circle is the editor’s minimal replacement span and is used as a supervised training target. Gray circles are model-generated tokens that are uncorrected in the current round. White circles are tokens accepted as part of the final trajectory but not used as edit targets. In the sampled rollout, the model begins reasoning in English, so the first reasoning step is flagged as the first violation. The editor makes a minimal Chinese replacement, and generation resumes from the corrected prefix. The editor applies replacements until the model continues reasoning in Chinese. Once the model adopts the requested mode, it may overshoot and emit the final answer in Chinese as well, which is itself a violation. The last edit then restores an English answer. The trajectory is now compliant.

papers.abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.
authors: Zilang Cen, Chao Tang, Fangcheng Liu, Weishi Mi, Wei Hao, JiaYu Xu, Dehao Huang, Yehui Tang, Xiaohui Cui, Tingguang Li, Xiaoyuan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the latency and token costs of frequent multimodal-model calls during long-horizon manipulation.
Coordinates a low-level policy with a high-level reasoning agent using an online monitor of visual progress and interaction history.
Triggers agent review to repair execution, revise subtasks, or coordinate both, while verified outcomes update memory and transitions.
On RMBench, improves task success by 24.0 percentage points over the strongest agent-based baseline while reducing token use by 65.3%.
Improves task success by 15.1 percentage points over the strongest policy-based baseline and is validated on three real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: A one-pass decision encoder reads a text, a question and several named options, and returns a probability for each option in a single forward pass. We ask how far Laya, a 421M-parameter encoder of this kind, can be compressed before its decisions change. We count decisions that differ from Laya's own full-precision (fp32) answer, and track calibration (how well confidence matches accuracy, measured by expected calibration error, ECE), on 1,221 synthetic items with the training schemas, 273 with an unseen schema, and 800 out-of-family questions from ARC, MMLU and HellaSwag. Layer pruning of a related model family is known; we add flips, calibration, held-out data and retraining. bf16 changes 0.2% of in-family decisions but 2.2% out of family; 6-bit grouped rounding 1.3% and 5.9%; deleting 6 layers 0.9% and 9.1%, while ECE rises from 5.9% to 39.2%. One fitted temperature, needing no labels, restores it to 3.6%. One scale per tensor fails below six bits, and CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, nearly all through one layer. Total variation tracks flips for rounding but not for deletion, and an early exit saves layers over a static cut only if its confidence gate is first recalibrated. Distilling a 16-layer student cuts its in-family flips from 44% to 9% (45% out of family). At equal stored size, rounding flips fewer decisions than deletion. Data are synthetic and LLM-labelled, for one architecture.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Vrishank Tiwari
bullets: Evaluates decision flips and expected calibration error (ECE) after precision reduction, layer deletion, early exit, and distillation.
bf16 changes 0.2% of in-family versus 2.2% of out-of-family decisions; 6-bit grouped rounding changes 1.3% versus 5.9%.
Deleting six layers causes 0.9% in-family and 9.1% out-of-family flips, with ECE rising from 5.9% to 39.2%; label-free temperature fitting reduces ECE to 3.6%.
Per-tensor scaling fails below six bits, while CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, mostly through one layer.
A 16-layer distilled student reduces in-family flips from 44% to 9%, but still has 45% out-of-family flips; results are limited to one architecture and synthetic, LLM-labelled data.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies model compression (quantization, pruning, distillation) and its effect on decision flips and calibration, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Sirius-Tiamat: How Small Can a One-Pass Decision Encoder Get Before Its Decisions Change?

papers.abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.
authors: Francesco Belardinelli, Flavio Corradini, Matteo Leonesi
bullets: Tests identical scenarios under the open-world, closed-world, and locally closed-world assumptions, changing only missing-information rules.
Includes verified base tasks and agent extensions covering action choice, source scope, and updates.
Requires correct answers across all closure variants and introduces core switch accuracy to expose assumption-sensitive errors.
Across 960 instances, overall accuracy ranges from 71.18% to 99.86%, while core switch accuracy ranges from 18.23% to 99.31%.
Large errors occur under LCWA, showing that high overall accuracy can hide failures to follow stated closure rules.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize this rotation as a tree of $2 \times 2$ planar rotations, each stored with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradients or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple greedy fit is globally optimal for our 'mean-flattening' objective. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as improving other metrics.
authors: Ryan Lucas, Petros Prastakos, Rahul Mazumder
bullets: Temporal KV-cache reuse creates memory bottlenecks, while distant-token quantization suffers from large ranges and errors.
TRQ rotates temporally adjacent cache vectors to flatten per-channel means before quantization.
It uses gradient-free, online-fitted trees of 2-bit planar rotations followed by a shared Hadamard transform.
A greedy fitting procedure is proven globally optimal for the mean-flattening objective, with efficient fused Triton inference kernels.
At matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over QVG on LongCat-Video-13B and HY-WorldPlay-8B, while also improving other metrics.

papers.abstract: Single-photon lidar records the arrival time of each returning photon, enabling 3D reconstruction from few views and scarce photons. However, leading neural methods such as Transientangelo require over an hour of non-convex per-scene optimization, and their accuracy degrades as photon flux decreases. We propose FirstCross, a network-free approach that instead solves a short sequence of convex problems on a voxel grid. For a solid object, the Poisson likelihood of a ray with given signal and background rates depends on the scene solely through its first crossing, the point where the ray first enters the object. Decomposing this likelihood yields two tractable terms. The first penalizes surfaces in front of detected photons and admits a tight convex closure, namely volume rendering with a running-maximum transmittance in place of NeRF's product transmittance. The second accounts for photons that no surface explains and admits a convex upper bound once the object is assumed to be thick behind each detected surface point. Compared with Transientangelo under its own real-data protocol, FirstCross achieves lower depth error across every test scene, view count, and flux level. With three views and 100 times fewer photons than at the protocol's lowest flux, our mean object depth error stays under half of Transientangelo's with all photons. Given our detected surface points, the best classical fusion has 1.3 to 1.8 times our three-view error across flux levels. On real room-scale captures with 1% of their photons, TransientNeRF has 2.8 to 7.7 times our error. FirstCross lets few-view single-photon scanners cut exposure to 1% and reconstruct an object in about a minute on one GPU.
authors: Chi-Wei Lee, Cheng-Han Chiang, Yi-Chun Chang, An-Kai Chen, Po-Chih Kuo
bullets: Addresses the high cost and low-flux sensitivity of neural single-photon reconstruction methods.
Uses a network-free sequence of convex voxel-grid problems based on each ray’s first surface crossing.
Models detected-photon and unexplained-photon likelihood terms with convex relaxations.
Outperforms Transientangelo across tested scenes, view counts, and flux levels under its evaluation protocol.
Reconstructs room-scale objects from 1% of the photons in about a minute on one GPU.

papers.abstract: Agentic visual reasoning improves vision-language models by selectively enlarging evidence without adding new scene content, but the benefit depends on whether fine structure remains accessible and whether local observations stay grounded in the full scene. We identify three recurring bottlenecks: high-frequency detail can be attenuated during visual-token formation; spatially distributed evidence can remain encoded yet difficult for the language model to retrieve; and isolated crops can weaken whole-detail correspondence through scale and positional mismatch. ResVision addresses these limitations with two complementary components. Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) estimates image complexity and selects an adaptive global sampling scale, avoiding unnecessary enlargement on simple inputs while allocating more visual tokens to detail-rich images. Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) returns each inspected crop together with the complete working view, preserving local detail and global context across tool turns. We evaluate Direct and Agentic variants on four frontier VLMs and 29 benchmarks spanning six visual-reasoning families. Complete ResVision (Agentic Base plus SMR plus CPI) is best for every model, improving by 3.36 to 4.94 points over Direct Base and 1.87 to 2.94 points over Agentic Base. These results show that adaptive visual sampling and context-preserving inspection address distinct, complementary constraints in multimodal reasoning.
authors: Guojian Zhan, Jiahao Xu, Yahui Liu, Yao Hu, Chuan Mu
bullets: Targets three bottlenecks: lost high-frequency detail, difficult retrieval of distributed evidence, and weakened crop-to-scene correspondence.
Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) selects a global sampling scale based on image complexity, avoiding unnecessary enlargement while allocating more tokens to detailed images.
Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) pairs each inspected crop with the complete working view to retain local detail and global grounding.
Evaluated across four frontier VLMs and 29 benchmarks covering six visual-reasoning families.
The full Agentic system improved over Direct Base and Agentic Base for every model, with gains of 3.36–4.94 and 1.87–2.94 points, respectively.

papers.abstract: One fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) is enforcing temporal safety constraints, such as satisfying formal specifications. Existing methods often transform logic formulas into automata for state augmentation and reward shaping. However, this approach assumes that automaton construction is both feasible and tractable, which limits its applicability to small specifications and linear temporal logic (LTL). This paper proposes Actor-Predictor, a framework that learns a surrogate representation of logic progress without explicitly constructing an automaton. The predictor continuously estimates whether a partial trajectory will satisfy the formal specification in a later step, and its learned features are provided as auxiliary inputs to the actor, which is then optimized using GRPO and RWR. We show theoretically that, under sufficient predictive accuracy, the learned representation is equivalent to the automaton state. Experiments on grid world and robotic tasks in Isaac Lab demonstrate that Actor-Predictor outperforms automaton-based baselines on LTL-constrained tasks. It also performs well on non-regular formal specifications, such as $(a^n b^n)$, for which finite-automaton-based approaches are not applicable.
authors: Josef Brozovich, Qining Zhang, Lei Ying
bullets: Targets temporal safety constraints and the scalability limits of automata-based reward shaping, especially beyond small LTL specifications.
A predictor estimates whether a partial trajectory will eventually satisfy the specification; its features guide an actor trained with GRPO and RWR.
Theoretically, sufficiently accurate predictions yield a representation equivalent to the corresponding automaton state.
Experiments in grid worlds and Isaac Lab robotic tasks show improved performance over automaton-based baselines on LTL-constrained tasks.
The framework also handles non-regular specifications such as $(a^n b^n)$, which finite-automaton methods cannot represent.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the finite-budget exposure-aware informative path planning (IPP) problem for a fleet of mobile sensing agents. The agents map an unknown scalar field while limiting exposure to high field intensity. Existing IPP methods optimize informativeness under motion or resource constraints, but do not address field exposure constraints. We formulate exposure-aware IPP (EA-IPP) as a scalarized bi-objective belief-state Markov decision process that trades the normalized Gaussian-process (GP) information gain against a normalized measurement-derived fleet exposure index. A parameter-shared proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework with decentralized actors and a centralized fleet critic is trained offline and evaluated on unseen fields. Across the radar, plume, and wildfire field families, the EA-IPP agent achieves the lowest GP reconstruction RMSE among the evaluated baselines while retaining D-optimal information within $10\%$ of the non-learning information baseline. The minimum field exposure is approximately $34.6\%$, $20.1\%$, and $27\%$ below the non-exposure-aware baseline for radar, plume, and wildfire, respectively.
authors: Muzaffar Qureshi, Yihui Mao, James W. Cross, Kyle Volle, Rushikesh Kamalapurkar
bullets: Formulates exposure-aware informative path planning as a scalarized bi-objective belief-state MDP.
Uses parameter-shared PPO with decentralized actors and a centralized fleet critic, trained offline and tested on unseen fields.

Across radar, plume, and wildfire fields, achieves the lowest reported GP reconstruction RMSE among evaluated baselines while retaining D-optimal information within 10% of a non-learning baseline.
Reduces minimum field exposure by approximately 34.6% for radar, 20.1% for plume, and 27% for wildfire relative to a non-exposure-aware baseline.

papers.abstract: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill.png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill.png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill.png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png
authors: Maximilian Seeth, Chengzhi Martin Hu, Marie Kempkes, Paul R\"ottger, Leo Schwinn
bullets: Textual skills are easy to transfer but cannot be continuously optimized; model finetuning is optimizable but model-specific.
The method uses gradient descent to optimize skill-like images through a frozen VLM’s vision encoder.
A single image can be jointly optimized for an ensemble of VLMs, enabling transfer across those models.
Across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks, Skill.png outperformed frontier-LLM-optimized textual skills in 9 of 16 settings.
Combining optimized image and text skills further improves agent performance; image skills use 64–256 tokens versus roughly 900–2,000 text tokens.

papers.abstract: We ask how far a driving model can get with one camera and real-time latency. BADAS-3.0 is a 1B-parameter video encoder with four small heads. From two seconds of one forward camera, it predicts the current speed, the metric path just driven, a collision-risk score and six candidate futures over 6.4 seconds, in under 50 ms. Given the car's current speed, BADAS-3.0 has 44% lower minADE$_6$ over five trajectory benchmarks than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, which reads six cameras and runs over 100x slower. The gain comes from camera rigs that neither model was trained on. On the rig they share, the two are on par. Existing benchmarks are mostly nominal driving, so we add two open-loop safety benchmarks, one of real dashcam collisions and near-misses and one of Euro NCAP scenarios. On both, BADAS-3.0 has a higher pass rate than every published planner we tested.
authors: Roni Goldshmidt, Hamish Scott, Lorenzo Niccolini

papers.abstract: LocoMuJoCo is an open-source benchmark for imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) on whole-body control. The library couples MuJoCo (CPU) with MJX and the MjWarp backend (GPU) under a single API, exposes 9 humanoid, 3 (musculo-)skeletal, and 4 quadruped embodiments, and ships a curated native motion-capture dataset for every humanoid, to which it can also retarget AMASS and LAFAN1. A modular plug-in architecture makes observations, rewards, control modes, terrains, and domain randomization fully interchangeable, while compact JAX implementations of many RL and IL algorithms provide JIT-compiled end-to-end training, and the companion loco-mujoco-real repository provides sim-to-real deployment. We describe the design, the SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting pipeline, and a usage example. LocoMuJoCo is released under MIT at https://github.com/robfiras/loco-mujoco.
authors: Firas Al-Hafez, Davide Tateo, Oleg Kaidanov, Aditya Bhatt, Artur Zelik, Zhengyi Luo, Jan Peters
bullets: Supports 9 humanoid, 3 musculoskeletal, and 4 quadruped embodiments in a unified MuJoCo, MJX, and MjWarp API.
Includes curated native motion-capture data for humanoids and supports retargeting from AMASS and LAFAN1.
Provides interchangeable observations, rewards, control modes, terrains, and domain randomization through a plug-in architecture.
Offers compact JAX implementations of RL and IL algorithms with JIT-compiled end-to-end training.
Includes SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting, plus a companion repository for sim-to-real deployment.

papers.abstract: Reasoning capabilities in large language models have evolved from prompting-based methods to internalized model behaviors. In this paper, we investigate whether the internal thinking model of an LLM can be deliberately changed and whether such a change is beneficial. Instead of relying on Chain-of-Thought, we train models to follow Question--Option--Criteria (QOC), a structured decision process that decomposes a task into explicit questions, competing options, and evaluation criteria. We present a three-generation development pipeline that ranges from a basic QOC decision core to richer answer synthesis and statistically enriched QOC reasoning. We then evaluate the resulting models with respect to both internal consistency and output quality. Across the reported experiments, QOC-based fine-tuning improves answer quality relative to non-fine-tuned base models and yields particularly strong gains once models are large enough to execute the underlying QOC computations reliably. The results suggest that the internal thinking model of an LLM is trainable and that structured alternatives to Chain-of-Thought can provide a promising path toward more reliable, interpretable, and task-adapted decision support.
authors: Marc Jansen
bullets: Investigates whether an LLM’s internal reasoning process can be deliberately changed.
Introduces Question–Option–Criteria (QOC), a structured alternative to Chain-of-Thought.
Develops QOC models through three stages: decision reasoning, answer synthesis, and statistically enriched reasoning.
Evaluates internal consistency and output quality, finding improvements over non-fine-tuned base models.
Benefits are strongest for sufficiently large models that can reliably perform QOC computations.

papers.abstract: Compared to single-robot deployments, multi-robot teams can significantly improve search-and-rescue (SAR) mission success by covering large areas in parallel. To collaborate effectively, these robots must be registered in a common reference frame. Standard registration methods typically rely on external infrastructure or significant map overlap, but real deployments require infrastructure-free, stationary initial alignment for immediate operation. While global LiDAR point cloud registration addresses this, existing single-scan methods often fail silently in aliased or degenerate environments. Approaches scaling beyond two agents also remain rarely evaluated in real-world scenarios. We propose a centralized, deployment-ready framework for pre-mission multi-robot registration. Our system performs pairwise coarse-to-fine alignment and actively rejects impossible pose hypotheses via deterministic plausibility checks. We validate the framework on a real-world custom dataset of four synchronized robots in various environments with ground truth. The checks reject more than a third of the incorrect pairwise registrations while falsely rejecting less than 1% of the correct ones, and reduce the number of team registrations with a wrong robot pose by 38%. Dataset and code are publicly available.
authors: Jonathan Lichtenfeld, Oskar von Stryk
bullets: Addresses infrastructure-free, stationary initial registration for multi-robot search-and-rescue teams.
Uses centralized pairwise coarse-to-fine alignment with deterministic mutual-observation plausibility checks.
Evaluated on a real-world dataset with four synchronized robots across varied environments and ground truth.
Rejects over one-third of incorrect pairwise registrations while falsely rejecting fewer than 1% of correct ones.
Reduces team registrations containing a wrong robot pose by 38%; code and dataset are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support parallel generation, yet they often require many denoising steps because only a fraction of token predictions are sufficiently reliable to be committed at each step. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize confidence learning or commitment policies. However, these approaches operate on the outputs of a single denoising forward pass, in which information from the prompt, previously committed tokens, and uncommitted positions may not yet be fully integrated. Consequently, some predictions remain under-refined when the commitment decision is made, and modifying the commitment policy alone cannot improve their underlying representations. We introduce dLoop, which restructures a pretrained diffusion language model into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture and recurrently applies a parameter-shared intermediate block to the same partially masked state. Rather than advancing the denoising process, each additional loop provides further latent computation, allowing information distributed across uncommitted positions to continue interacting and become more fully integrated before commitment. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval show that dLoop achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on every benchmark. With tokens per forward pass (TPF) adjusted for loop computation, it outperforms Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and TPF on all four benchmarks and dParallel on three, and is more accurate than d3LLM on all four, while d3LLM attains higher TPF; no compared method surpasses dLoop in both. Mechanistic analyses show that extra loops mainly help on slow, unstable trajectories and that updates at uncommitted positions drive changes in token decisions and later generation. Pre-commitment latent computation thus makes predictions more reliable, offering a route to DLM acceleration distinct from forcing confidence through the training loss.
authors: Handa Li, Pengxiang Li, Mingyu Cao, Xilu Wang, Li Shen, Da Li, Lu Yin
bullets: Targets under-refined token predictions caused by committing after a single denoising pass.
Reorganizes a pretrained DLM into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture with a parameter-shared block applied recurrently to the same partially masked state.
Uses extra latent computation to integrate information across prompt, committed tokens, and uncommitted positions before commitment.
Achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval; it outperforms Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and TPF on all four.
Extra loops primarily benefit slow, unstable generation trajectories, with updates at uncommitted positions influencing later token decisions.

papers.abstract: Tracking objects through transformations is essential for understanding real-world dynamics. Recent work has extended traditional object tracking to detect state changes. However, existing methods require an initial object prompt and detect only its decompositions, missing assembly events, which begin with multiple objects rather than one. We therefore introduce a prompt-free formulation of this task, where the goal is to recover all object tracks and detect both decomposition and assembly events given only a video. Our key insight is that assembly is decomposition in reverse. Building on this insight, we present Atlas, a zero-shot system that constructs and jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions to recover object tracks and their transformations. We further introduce OmniST, a benchmark with dense annotations of objects and both transformation types. On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on existing benchmarks that only evaluate decomposition.

bullets: Addresses prompt-dependent tracking methods that miss assembly events involving multiple objects.
Introduces a prompt-free task: recover object tracks and both types of transformations from video alone.
Atlas is a zero-shot system that jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions.
Introduces OmniST, a densely annotated benchmark for objects, assemblies, and decompositions.
On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on decomposition-only benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) aims to enable agents to adapt to changing tasks while preserving previously acquired capabilities. Evaluation often relies on final aggregate metrics that can hide temporary performance degradation during adaptation. This work introduces a simple CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while preserving environment dynamics and rewards, supporting proof-of-concept demonstrations, inexpensive experimentation, and easily reproducible sanity checks. Using this benchmark, we demonstrate the stability gap in CRL: a substantial drop in prior-task performance after the introduction of new tasks, followed by partial or complete recovery. This pattern occurs despite the agent having complete access to past tasks.
authors: Sebastian Pusch, Matthia Sabatelli, Gido M. van de Ven
bullets: CRL must balance adaptation to new tasks with preservation of prior capabilities.
Final aggregate metrics can hide temporary performance degradation during adaptation.
The benchmark changes observation representations while keeping dynamics and rewards fixed.
Experiments demonstrate a stability gap: prior-task performance drops, then partially or fully recovers.
The benchmark supports inexpensive, reproducible proof-of-concept and sanity-check experiments.

(c) All three tasks can be learned by multitask training (left), whereas sequential fine-tuning (right) shows catastrophic forgetting. Illustrated here for SAC-D on CartPole.

papers.tldr: A simple benchmark reveals that continual RL agents can temporarily lose substantial prior-task performance when learning new tasks, even with access to those past tasks.

papers.abstract: Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) models generate scene-conditioned plans, but frequent trajectory updates can repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference. Reusing a prediction reduces this demand while leaving its commands exposed to changes in vehicle motion. FastRoverVLA addresses this mismatch by decoupling visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution. Its training-free interface maintains decoded plans between visual predictions. A speed-curvature action buffer is aligned with measured motion at each update, integrated into a local trajectory, and advanced by consuming the current action. The corrected remainder is written back to the buffer, preserving motion corrections across successive updates. A bounded refresh rule normalizes speed and curvature variations within a newly decoded plan and assigns a short or long reuse budget according to the resulting plan-roughness score. The interface requires neither backbone features nor an additional learned driving policy. Over a 3 s horizon, independent real-request evaluation achieves average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) of 0.328/0.596 m on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at request rates of 6.0% and 4.8%, respectively. These runs retain lower errors across four backbones and both datasets and reduce Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8 under serial replay, while mechanism and motion-only controls identify persistent state correction as the main source of the observed accuracy benefit. The source code and evaluation materials are publicly available at https://github.com/ADEPT-ORG/FastRoverVLA.
authors: Changtao Zhao, Yingxue Guan, Li Wang, Shijie Zhao, Yuhang Zhang, Shengkai Zhang, Qing Wang, Ziying Song
bullets: Addresses the cost of frequent multimodal inference and the risk that reused commands become misaligned with vehicle motion.
Uses a training-free action buffer that aligns speed-curvature commands with measured motion, advances execution, and preserves corrections across updates.
Refreshes plans using a bounded rule based on plan roughness, without backbone features or an additional learned driving policy.
Over a 3 s horizon, it reports lower trajectory errors across four backbones on ORAD-3D and RELLIS-3D, with FDE reductions of 18.0% and 36.7% at the evaluated request rates.
Reduces Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by 16.6× and 20.8× under serial replay; controls attribute the accuracy gains mainly to persistent state correction.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.
authors: Zheyuan Liu, Chuhan Wang, Jinduo Guo, Yue Huang, Xiangchi Yuan, Ningshan Ma, Meng Jiang
bullets: Initial-state refusal may fail after takeover during task execution, and simply failing to complete a task can still cause physical incidents such as dropping objects.
State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) constructs stationary arm and consistent gripper targets for prohibited-task demonstrations.
Joint policy adaptation learns these fallback targets while preserving actions for retained tasks.
On evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduced post-takeover target success to 1.3% with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while maintaining high retained-task success.
The method targets settings where holding is an appropriate fallback response and is evaluated with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid agents in everyday environments are expected to react to diverse cues as humans do, with semantically appropriate and physically executable behaviors. Existing cue-driven reaction generation methods support only a narrow range of cue modalities and are limited to purely kinematic generation, leaving the resulting reactions susceptible to physical artifacts. To this end, we present MixReact, the first unified framework for physics-based reactive humanoid control from text, audio, and video cues, integrating a Discrete--Continuous Mixture of Transformers (DisCo-MoT) for state prediction with a History-aware Action Transformer (HAT) for physical execution. DisCo-MoT couples a discrete masked-modeling branch with a continuous autoregressive diffusion branch via one-way mixture attention within a MoT architecture. Guidance from discrete context mitigates collapse into averaged behaviors in one-to-many reaction generation, while direct prediction in continuous state space bypasses the decoding bottleneck of discrete representations. HAT then maps the predicted next state and observed execution history to executable actions, enabling robust closed-loop control in physics-based simulation. Experiments across all three modalities demonstrate consistent improvements over the baselines in fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency, while ablations validate the complementary contributions of the components. Our code will be released to facilitate future research. Project page: https://binlee26.github.io/MixReact_Page/
authors: Bin Li, Xing Zhu, Jingya Wang
bullets: Addresses limited cue modalities and physically implausible artifacts in existing reactive humanoid generation methods.
Uses DisCo-MoT to combine discrete masked modeling with continuous autoregressive diffusion for multimodal next-state prediction.
Employs HAT to convert predicted states and execution history into actions for robust closed-loop physics-based control.
Experiments across text, audio, and video show improved fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency over baselines.
Ablations support the complementary roles of the framework’s components.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MixReact. MCA maps a text, audio, or video cue to the semantic memory C. Within DisCo-MoT, discrete masked modeling samples a complete reaction once, providing cached intermediate keys and values that guide history-conditioned autoregressive diffusion through one-way mixture attention. HAT converts each predicted next state and observed execution history into an executable action, while simulator feedback updates both prediction and control histories.

papers.abstract: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63$\times$ speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.
authors: Jiaming Li, Lingzhen Li, Xiaze Yang, Chenyu Zhu, Kaiqi Liu, Xiaotong Zhao, Songlian Li, Toyota Li, Alan Zhao, Haobin Zhong, Yue Ma, Zhiyuan Ma
bullets: Replaces decoded-frame reward verification with checks based on the target model’s latent velocity field.
Uses two thresholds to choose among Accept, one-step Refine, and three-step Refine or Reject.
Reuses verification signals to correct drafts, targeting perceptual quality, camera following, and trajectory consistency.
On WBench Navigation, reports 1.63× speedup and raises NavScore from 75.99 to 85.63.
LongSpecBench and Hy-Nomas experiments support sustained rollout performance and applicability across backbones and denoising budgets.

papers.tldr: SpecWM turns speculative verification into latent-space refinement, improving streaming world-model quality and control while accelerating inference.

papers.abstract: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning. However, our analysis shows that the improved accuracy of TwI models does not guarantee faithful tool use; they frequently invoke tools without actually relying on the zoomed region, undermining the reliability of tool-assisted reasoning. We trace this unfaithful behaviour to the training data: when questions are answerable without zooming, the model can answer correctly while ignoring the returned evidence, and this problem is exacerbated during training as the model becomes better at answering without tools. To keep zooming useful throughout training, we adapt the training data to the model's evolving capability and train on questions where correct zoomed evidence can still help the model answer correctly. This selection is supported by a data synthesis pipeline that localises small objects and constructs verifiable questions about their fine details, and complemented by an adaptiveness reward that favours tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary. The experimental results show that our method substantially improves reasoning faithfulness and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual search benchmarks (+11.6% on V*, +7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and +9.4% on HR-Bench 8K). On multimodal hallucination benchmarks, our model also outperforms the compared TwI baselines. These results suggest that improving TwI faithfulness does not sacrifice accuracy and that both can be learnt from the right training data without directly supervising the reasoning process.
authors: Yu Zhao, Jiaxin Zhang, Rohit Saxena, Fazl Barez, Pasquale Minervini, Yiwen Guo
bullets: TwI models often invoke zooming but ignore the returned visual evidence, especially when questions are answerable without tools.
The method dynamically selects questions where zoomed evidence remains necessary and useful as the model improves.
A synthesis pipeline creates fine-detail questions about localized small objects, while an adaptiveness reward discourages unnecessary tool use.
The approach improves visual search performance by 11.6% on V*, 7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and 9.4% on HR-Bench 8K, and outperforms compared TwI baselines on multimodal hallucination benchmarks.
Results indicate that faithfulness and accuracy can improve together without directly supervising the reasoning process.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Question synthesis workflow. We first localise and sample objects from high-resolution, information-dense images using SAM3 [4]. Then, we generate questions for randomly sampled objects using the image overview and zoomed evidence. Finally, we verify questions in several steps: target identification with Set-of-Mark prompting [50] checks if the question refers to unambiguous objects; answer correctness checks if the proposed answer is reliable; visual dependency checks if the question can be guessed without seeing the image.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can act as closed-loop robot-use agents (RUAs) by writing and executing control code through tool interfaces. However, turning an open-weight VLM into a high-performing embodied agent requires a complete post-training stack: out-of-the-box open VLMs fail completely at interactive tool contracts, strong frontier teachers are accessible only as black-box endpoints without exposed weights or token probabilities, and supervised imitation alone plateaus under rollout distribution shift. We present EmbodyAgent, an end-to-end post-training framework with three tightly coupled pipelines: (1) a black-box data synthesis pipeline that queries a strong teacher under a forced think-then-code contract and filters trajectories by task success; (2) an SFT pipeline that distills the explanation-and-program targets into an open-weight 9B VLM with both vision and language encoders trainable; and (3) an online RL pipeline that optimizes student-generated episodes via group-relative advantage with a runtime-error-penalized outcome reward. All three pipelines share one primitive-free Python execution tool exposing only raw visual observation and seven-dimensional end-effector control, with no action decoder and no interface shift across stages. Under a strictly separated evaluation protocol on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks (disjoint state splits, greedy test-time decoding, training-only safeguards), held-out success on 100 test states rises from 0/100 (base 9B VLM) to 14/100 (after SFT) and 84/100 (after RL), while training rollout success climbs from 8.4% to 87.7% and median model calls per episode drop from 36 to 11. We further identify a self-reinforcing runtime-error mode induced by outcome-based RL on executable code, and establish a failure-category monitoring and sampling-side curation protocol that stabilizes training.
authors: Wei Dai, Jinkun Liu, Jiayi Chen, Han Liu, Wenbo Ding, Shaolun Huang
bullets: Addresses failures in tool-contract following, limited access to frontier teacher internals, and imitation degradation under rollout distribution shift.
Synthesizes and filters teacher trajectories, distills explanation-and-code targets into a trainable 9B VLM, then optimizes student rollouts with runtime-error-penalized rewards.
Uses the same primitive-free Python tool throughout, exposing only visual observations and seven-dimensional end-effector control.
On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks, held-out success improves from 0/100 for the base model to 14/100 after SFT and 84/100 after RL; median calls per episode fall from 36 to 11.
Finds and mitigates a self-reinforcing runtime-error failure mode through failure monitoring and sampling-side curation.

papers.abstract: Images under non-uniform coupled degradations require diverse restoration capabilities for different degraded regions. Existing methods employ globally uniform operations, potentially overlooking regional differences and causing incomplete restoration or even damage to image content. Moreover, a degraded region may require successive restoration actions, and earlier actions may alter residual degradation characteristics or introduce artifacts, potentially hindering subsequent restoration. To address these challenges, we propose RegionAgent, an adaptive restoration framework that trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) through two-stage preference learning to generate a region-specific restoration action at each iteration. Specifically, we first train the VLM to select an action suited to the current region through step-level Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), using preferences derived from immediate restoration feedback to supervise only the differing component in each action pair. To account for the effects of current actions on subsequent restoration, we then apply trajectory-level DPO, using preferences derived from complete trajectory scores to supervise the sole differing action in each trajectory pair. Furthermore, as conventional image-pair datasets do not directly provide preferences over regional restoration decisions, we construct a regional restoration preference dataset comprising 10K action pairs and 20K trajectory pairs for two-stage VLM training. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate strong restoration performance under both mixed and single degradations. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of two-stage preference learning in improving restoration quality.
authors: Weiyu Zhou, Jiacong Tang, Tao Hu, Axi Niu, Jinqiu Sun, Peng Wu, Wei Dong, Qingsen Yan
bullets: Targets mixed or coupled degradations where globally uniform restoration can miss regional needs or damage content.
Uses step-level DPO to choose actions based on immediate regional restoration feedback.
Uses trajectory-level DPO to account for how earlier actions affect later restoration and artifacts.
Introduces a regional preference dataset with 10K action pairs and 20K trajectory pairs.
Experiments across multiple datasets show strong performance on mixed and single degradations; ablations support both preference-learning stages.

papers.abstract: Real-time streaming video generation has gained rapid momentum in live content creation and interactive media. Deploying such systems in practice requires flexible scaling factors to accommodate diverse source resolutions, target displays, and computational budgets. However, extending fixed-scale generative video super-resolution (VSR) to varying target scales poses two challenges: downsampling from a larger fixed scale incurs redundant cost, while re-optimizing the diffusion transformer (DiT) is costly and alters the shared generative prior. To address both, we propose FlexVSR, a decoupled framework for continuous-scale streaming generative VSR with supervision at only a few scales. Our key insight is that naively resampling fixed-scale latents onto a new target grid induces scale-dependent input mismatch, which can be effectively addressed through parameter-efficient, scale-aware adaptation of the latent interface without updating the DiT. To this end, FlexVSR introduces ReLSA (Refined Latent Scale Adaptation), a lightweight latent adapter that constructs and refines target-grid latents before they enter the DiT, enabling a shared frozen VSR prior to generalize across continuous scales with only 0.274M trainable parameters and an adaptation cost of 7.3 H100 GPU-hours, while introducing no additional temporal dependencies and preserving the native causal streaming protocol. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive or superior reconstruction and temporal quality, lower latency than most native-scale streaming baselines and offline methods, and effective generalization to unseen continuous scales, filling the continuous-scale gap in real-time streaming generative VSR.
authors: Ji Wang, Haonan An, Jiasheng Zhang, Renlong Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and inefficiency of extending fixed-scale streaming VSR to diverse target resolutions.
Introduces ReLSA, a lightweight scale-aware latent adapter that refines target-grid latents before the diffusion transformer.
Uses supervision at only a few scales while generalizing to unseen continuous scales.
Preserves causal streaming and adds no temporal dependencies, with 0.274M trainable parameters and 7.3 H100 GPU-hours of adaptation.
Reports competitive or better reconstruction and temporal quality with lower latency than most compared streaming and offline methods.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires agents to acquire visual evidence and integrate partial observations into coherent three-dimensional representations. We introduce SpatialScout-V2, which extends SpatialScout's active mapping task from simulation to real residential scenes through three advances: real visual observations, preservation of original scene content, and interactive exploration of recorded views. Built from 100 homes in Realsee3D, the benchmark covers 3,171 target objects across 29 categories. Given a fixed target inventory, agents autonomously select recorded viewpoints and viewing directions, integrate calibrated RGB observations, and iteratively estimate and revise object centers within a fixed interaction budget. We evaluate the localization accuracy and completeness of object-center maps using mean IoU, IoU-threshold hit rates, and target coverage. Evaluating seven frontier vision-language models (VLMs), we find that six achieve an all-target mean IoU below 20\%. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches only 22.52\%, with just 18.36\% of targets exceeding an IoU of 0.5. Further analysis shows that broad submission coverage can coexist with limited localization accuracy, while target omissions further reduce overall scores. These results highlight substantial challenges in constructing accurate and complete object-center maps through active exploration of real scenes.
authors: Zhaoxi Zhang, Hao Liang, Linxuan Wu, Yiming Xu, Yifu Yuan, Kun Liang, Chenming Tang, Meiyi Qiang, Wentao Zhang, Weikang Li, Yunfang Wu

Across seven frontier VLMs, six score below 20% all-target mean IoU; the best model reaches 22.52% mean IoU, with 18.36% of targets above IoU 0.5.
High submission coverage can coexist with poor localization, while omitted targets further reduce map quality.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time. This behavior is known as test-time scaling. However, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually trains them with a fixed rollout cap. We find that this cap changes model behavior, not only training cost. After training, models use few additional tokens beyond the training budget. They outperform the base models near that budget, but their accuracy stops improving and falls below the base model at larger budgets. The rollout cap thus becomes a learned constraint, that limits model's test-time scaling. We call this effect budget internalization. We observe it across Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B and two reasoning training tasks: mathematical reasoning and diverse, procedurally generated problems. This effect also transfers from math training to science and coding tasks. Training-objective level ablations on Qwen3.5-4B show that most changes recover little test-time scaling. Stronger KL regularization and lower training-data truncation preserve more scaling, but stronger KL reduces in-budget accuracy. Forcing an answer on truncated training rollouts largely removes budget internalization, but also removes most of the in-budget gain. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces budget internalization, whereas SFT on naturally short traces does not, which shows that the effect is not specific to RL. This result links budget internalization to length-censored post-training rather than to an RL-specific objective term. Thus, a rollout cap does not only control training cost. It can trade low-budget gains for lower performance when additional inference compute is available.
authors: Ilia Zavidnyi, Alexander Kovrigin, Arina Puchkova, Kirill Gelvan, Sergey Titov
bullets: RLVR-trained models learn to stop near their training token cap, treating it as a behavioral constraint.
Models outperform their base versions around the training budget but can underperform them at larger inference budgets.

Stronger KL regularization and less truncation preserve more scaling but may reduce in-budget accuracy.
The effect also occurs with SFT on artificially truncated traces, indicating it stems from length-censored post-training rather than RL alone.

papers.abstract: Tight-space navigation requires a robot to clear obstacles and stop inside its goal despite uncertainty. We present GeoDiff, a motion-program planner coupling original-goal stopped-set inclusion, witness-guided terminal repair, and factored proof compilation. An exact feasible-translation characterization guides repair; request-local reuse reduces repeated geometric work. We establish conditions for compiler equivalence and reach-and-stop soundness. Across 11,440 floorplan-derived jobs, GeoDiff certifies 61/139 tasks at 5-cm tolerance within 15 s, versus 44/139 for the stop-set baseline. The strongest observed external certificate adapter certifies 13/139 tasks from 119/139 native routes, separating route availability from certification. On tasks derived from public BARN maps, GeoDiff certifies 202/270 at 5-cm tolerance for a Jackal-shaped body, versus 3/270 for the portal baseline. Development analyses distinguish emitter savings from solver coverage, and 1,420 route-tracking episodes characterize the execution interface. These results show how terminal reasoning and proof reuse increase finite-budget certification coverage while preserving the original physical task and goal.
authors: Runtian Zheng, Congpeng Zhang, Ying Liu
bullets: Addresses navigation under uncertainty where a robot must both clear obstacles and stop within its goal.
Combines original-goal stopped-set inclusion, witness-guided terminal repair, exact feasible-translation characterization, and request-local proof reuse.
Establishes compiler-equivalence and reach-and-stop soundness conditions.
Certifies 61/139 floorplan-derived jobs versus 44/139 for a stop-set baseline, and 202/270 BARN-derived tasks versus 3/270 for a portal baseline at 5-cm tolerance.
Results focus on finite-budget certification coverage and distinguish route availability from external certification.

papers.abstract: Exocentric-to-egocentric (Exo2Ego) video generation transforms third-person recordings into first-person viewpoints, unlocking immersive AR/VR experiences and scalable demonstration synthesis for embodied robotics. Extending it to a streaming setting is expected to further enable live applications. However, existing methods suffer from degraded manipulation regions, overfitting and confinement to fixed-length clips with prohibitive latency. To address these limitations, we present StreamEgo, a real-time framework for unbounded, generalizable Exo2Ego video generation. To resolve intricate manipulation dynamics while supporting the streaming pipeline, a streaming dual-branch prior provides pixel-aligned guidance for translating appearance and skeletal kinematics. We also introduce a region-aware loss curriculum to improve generalization and stabilize multi-objective diffusion training. Furthermore, we distill the model into a chunk-wise autoregressive model, augmented with a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum, enabling high-quality, generalizable real-time streaming Exo2Ego generation at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.
authors: Tianyi Xu, Boyang Lyu, Yunkai Tang, Kairan Ding, Jiahang Li, Weiyu Guo, Yandong Guo, Shuchen Weng, Boxin Shi
bullets: Targets live AR/VR and embodied-robotics applications by converting third-person video into first-person views.
Uses a streaming dual-branch prior to provide pixel-aligned appearance and skeletal-kinematic guidance.
Introduces a region-aware loss curriculum to stabilize diffusion training and improve generalization.
Distills the system into a chunk-wise autoregressive model with region-aware corruption and first-chunk training.
Generates streaming video at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.
