papers.abstract: Personalized video generation faces a significant scalability challenge: as the number of custom subjects increases, existing methods suffer from severe identity leakage and semantic entanglement, resulting in videos with blended attributes and incoherent narratives. We identify that this stems from a lack of explicit binding between textual entity phrases and their corresponding visual patterns prior to fusion in diffusion models. To address this, we propose MultiBinder, a novel framework built on a ``bind-then-narrate'' paradigm. Our approach introduces a two-stage conditioning process before video diffusion. First, Cross-modal Entity Binding devises an entity-aware Q-Former to extract identity-centric features from each subject's reference image and tightly align them with its unique entity phrase, yielding disentangled ``identity tokens.'' Second, a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) acts as a ``narrative director'' in the Narrative-Aware Subject Arrangement stage, capturing the action of each subject from the text prompt and synthesizes contextualized subject features that encapsulate ``who is doing what'' and preserve role-specific distinctions. These features are then injected into a video diffusion model via dedicated conditioning pathways, ensuring precise attribute allocation. Extensive experiments on both general and newly curated multi-subject benchmarks show that MultiBinder significantly outperforms existing methods in multi-subject identity fidelity.
authors: Wei Li, Yiheng Zhang, Zhaofan Qiu, Ting Yao, Xiaoyan Sun, Tao Mei
bullets: Addresses identity leakage, blended attributes, and incoherent narratives as the number of custom subjects grows.
Uses an entity-aware Q-Former to align each reference image with its corresponding entity phrase, producing disentangled identity tokens.
Employs an MLLM to determine each subject’s role and action, creating context-aware features that preserve subject distinctions.
Injects these features through dedicated conditioning pathways into a video diffusion model.
Experiments on general and newly curated multi-subject benchmarks report significantly better identity fidelity than existing methods.

papers.abstract: Multi-view vision-language-action (VLA) models still face challenges in spatial generalization, particularly under changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. These models typically receive action supervision only in the robot base frame, requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions. We propose One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), which learns to predict actions in each view's camera frame, allowing the same physical motion to provide diverse, observation-aligned supervision across views. OVOA-VLA jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific action experts, whose robot-state inputs and action targets are expressed in their respective camera frames. Two complementary directed attention graphs model both directions of interaction between the base and view-specific experts, jointly leveraging view-specific action supervision to improve base-frame prediction. Cross Graph Consistency further encourages agreement between the two graphs' base-frame predictions for the same sample. With the same multi-view inputs, the model supports both full and base-only inference. Experiments across multiple simulation benchmarks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization perturbations. Full and base-only inference achieve average success rates of 88.1% and 85.7% on LIBERO-Plus, respectively. In real-world evaluations, base-only inference raises the average success rates from $\pi_{0.5}$'s 28.3% to 58.3% across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts.
authors: Jinxi Liu, Ruifeng Zhai, Hao Liu, Guangrun Wang
bullets: Addresses viewpoint and robot-initialization shifts in multi-view vision-language-action models.
Predicts actions in each camera frame, providing observation-aligned supervision for the same physical motion.
Jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific experts with two directed attention graphs.
Uses Cross Graph Consistency to align the graphs’ base-frame predictions.
Achieves 88.1% full-inference and 85.7% base-only success on LIBERO-Plus; real-world base-only success reaches 58.3% under spatial shifts.

CGC encourages consistency between the two base-frame predictions. (c) Full Inference uses R → B; Base-only Inference uses B → R, omitting view-specific experts while retaining all input views. papers.abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.
authors: Doyeob Kim
bullets: Targets the mismatch between short-text quantization calibration and 100K+-token, tool-using agent sessions.
Uses trellis-coded post-training quantization calibrated on tokens generated by the BF16 model during agent sessions.
At 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight, matches BF16 on DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, AIME, and RealWorldQA.
The 2.0-bit checkpoint performs worse than the higher-bit versions.
Releases Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF and a supporting llama.cpp fork for inference.

papers.abstract: World models can imagine how a physical scene evolves over the next few seconds, but growers need to know how a crop will develop over weeks to months: will this rice plant have headed a month from now, and how will it look at harvest? We introduce agricultural world modeling, the task of predicting how the same plant will look at a requested horizon of days to months, from one photo of it, its cultivar, and its camera view. In preliminary analysis, even state-of-the-art image generators get this wrong: they often grow the plant too little or give it the color and form of the wrong growth stage. We argue that they do not work out the plant's developmental state, which the photo reveals only indirectly. We therefore propose AgroWM, which reasons about development before it draws growth. Its reasoning module, PhenoClock, works out the current growth stage, predicts the future one, and writes a Growth Script with numeric targets for height, plant area, and color; its generation module, the Rooted Renderer, then edits the photo to follow this script, adding new organs and colors to the photographed plant. Because pixel scores can prefer an unchanged copy of the photo, we instead check each forecast's traits and developmental timing against the plant's own later photos. On rice, 54.6% of the forecasts of AgroWM are matched to the target stage (Stage R@1), against 34.8% for GPT Image 2.5, 24.0% for Qwen Image 2.1, and 47.4% for the strongest domain-specific baseline, the same backbone fine-tuned without Growth Scripts; 9 to 20 weeks ahead, it still reaches 46.4%, against 35.7% for that baseline. On maize, a crop with a different body plan and stage scale, the same design again scores best on all four measures.
authors: Wenkai Ji, Zeteng Li, Yinkun Guo, Jie Zhou, Liang He, Zhenong Jin
bullets: The task is long-horizon crop forecasting from one photo, cultivar, camera view, and requested future horizon.
AgroWM’s PhenoClock estimates current and future growth stages and produces a Growth Script with targets for height, area, and color.
Its Rooted Renderer edits the original plant photo to add future organs and colors according to the script.
On rice, AgroWM achieves 54.6% Stage R@1, outperforming the reported general and domain-specific baselines; it remains strongest 9–20 weeks ahead.
The design also performs best across four measures on maize, suggesting transfer beyond rice, though the work is presented as preliminary.

figures.caption: Figure 2. How existing models fail to forecast growth, and why standard scores miss it.

papers.abstract: Post-training recursive self-improvement (RSI) iteratively improves a target capability, operationalized by a fixed anchor benchmark, through repeated intervention, training, and evaluation. Yet most loops use the anchor's aggregate score as their sole observation, so early gains give way to stalled progress and repetitive exploration. When this anchor-only feedback ceases to reveal actionable gaps, a plateau may reflect an exhausted observation rather than an exhausted capability. We introduce adaptive observation (AdaObs), an observation-side mechanism of harness evolution that keeps the anchor objective fixed while adapting the active observation. At a plateau, a controller refines diagnostic granularity, escalates difficulty, and adds related tasks; validated increments are fused back into training, while every checkpoint remains evaluated against the anchor. Across eight independently optimized anchors in long-context reading comprehension and instruction following, AdaObs raises the mean score from $66.4$ to $73.7$ under a matched data budget, outperforming FixedObs, the anchor-only baseline. The evolved harness further improves the seven-task average on the independent PostTrainBench across two agent backends. These results identify observation adaptation as a missing mechanism of harness evolution for sustaining post-training RSI.
authors: Yinhao Tang, Youqing Fang, Yanan Sun, Xintian Shen, Hanyu Sun, Wenran Liu, Yue Wu, Weiming Zhang, Bin Liu, Wenwei Zhang
bullets: Anchor-only aggregate scores can hide actionable capability gaps, making progress appear stalled.
AdaObs adapts observations at plateaus by increasing diagnostic granularity, difficulty, and task coverage.
Validated observations are incorporated into training, while checkpoints remain evaluated on the fixed anchor benchmark.
Across eight anchors, mean performance increased from 66.4 to 73.7 with a matched data budget, outperforming fixed observation.
The evolved harness also improved the seven-task average on the independent PostTrainBench across two agent backends.

At a plateau, the controller climbs an ordered observation ladder from finer diagnosis to harder instances and then to related tasks. papers.abstract: Multi-Robot Motion Planning (MRMP) requires trajectories that avoid environmental obstacles and collisions between robots in a shared workspace. Diffusion-based planners often address obstacle avoidance through sampling-time guidance, while some conditioned approaches aggregate map geometry into a global representation. We present Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion (SCTD), a map-conditioned trajectory generator for multi-robot planning. SCTD retains multiple position-aware occupancy tokens accessed through cross-attention throughout a temporal U-Net, with hard endpoint inpainting enforcing start and goal states. One model trained on single-robot demonstrations across procedural environments generates obstacle-aware trajectories without sampling-time obstacle-cost guidance. High-level Conflict-Based Search (CBS) coordinates these trajectories through constrained replanning, retaining inter-agent guidance during sampling and reusing the model across workspace layouts and team sizes. Experiments assess single-robot success and trajectory quality, generalization to unfamiliar layouts with added obstacles, and coordinated multi-robot planning. On 15,000 held-out tasks, SCTD achieves higher success than the evaluated guided diffusion baseline, with the largest gains on hard-detour tasks, while trajectory-quality comparisons show smoother trajectories. Conditioning ablations show higher success with spatial tokens than with a global map embedding, and map-replacement tests demonstrate dependence on the supplied geometry. The resulting multi-robot system achieves higher team success than the compared diffusion baselines, with experiments covering teams of up to 15 robots.
authors: Yefim Nudelman, Dor Atzmon, Tom Tirer
bullets: Targets multi-robot motion planning with obstacle avoidance and collision-free coordination.
Uses position-aware occupancy tokens throughout a temporal U-Net and hard inpainting for start and goal states.
Trains on single-robot demonstrations and reuses one model across layouts and team sizes; CBS handles inter-robot conflicts.
Outperforms the evaluated guided diffusion baseline in held-out success, especially on hard-detour tasks, while producing smoother trajectories.
Ablations support spatial conditioning and map dependence; experiments cover teams of up to 15 robots.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Training and inference of the map-conditioned trajectory diffuser. During training, the temporal U-Net predicts noise added to normalized expert trajectories, conditioned on spatial occupancy-map tokens and the diffusion timestep. Endpoints are fixed by inpainting and excluded from the loss. During single-agent inference, map tokens depend only on the map and are therefore identical at every reverse step; endpoints are restored after every update. The raw trajectory is converted back to world coordinates without static-obstacle-cost guidance or a separate smoother; this describes the single-agent pipeline, not the multi-agent system. Start/goal markers on the maps are illustrative only.

Figure 4: Trajectory examples for MPD and SCTD on selected tasks in MMD’s Conveyor (a) and Highways (b) environments. The map-conditional model (SCTD) handles new obstacles better than a model that relies on guidance (MPD).

Figure 2: The occupancy encoder Eϕ and its two-stage training. A binary occupancy map is converted into 256 position-aware, 64-dimensional tokens. These tokens condition the denoiser through cross-attention and retain spatial structure instead of compressing the map into a single global vector. In Stage 1 (bottom), the convolutional stem is pretrained to predict clipped analytic signed distances at sampled workspace points using an auxiliary head and an L1 loss. The head is then discarded, and the stem is finetuned jointly with the denoiser in Stage 2 (top). Analytic SDF supplies supervision only; occupancy is the planner’s only learned environmental input. Token and SDF illustrations are schematic; ⊕ denotes concatenation. Additional head and sampling details appear in Appendix A.

papers.abstract: Video-language models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on video-text retrieval and are increasingly used for egocentric video understanding. Yet, despite gains in zero-shot retrieval, they have shown limitations in compositional understanding, and it remains unclear whether they understand compositional relationships between verbs and nouns. In this work, we introduce Ego-ExBind, a compositional diagnostic protocol for analyzing pretraining exposure and verb-noun binding in egocentric video-text retrieval. Ego-ExBind consists of an Exposure Ledger built from the EgoClip pretraining corpus used by EgoVLPv2, which defines Seen Composition, Unseen Composition, and Unseen Atom splits for EPIC-KITCHENS-100 multi-instance retrieval (MIR). We further probe noun and verb binding channels through controlled noun-swap and verb-swap negatives. We find that zero-shot retrieval is positively associated with pair exposure within seen compositions, even after controlling for the marginal frequencies of verbs and nouns. However, higher pair exposure is associated with larger noun-swap margins and slightly smaller verb-swap margins. This asymmetry motivates us to test whether exposure reweighting can improve retrieval with little change in the measured swap margins. To isolate the effect of exposure input, we keep the trained checkpoint fixed and replace only the exposure input at inference. We demonstrate that this exposure reweighting can improve video-text retrieval without stronger verb-noun compositional understanding, and that the gain depends on the correct sample-level exposure correspondence. By separating exposure-driven retrieval gains from verb-noun binding, Ego-ExBind provides a diagnostic framework for evaluating whether future improvements in egocentric MIR reflect compositional understanding rather than pretraining familiarity.
authors: Yuqi Guo, Michael Wray
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic protocol for separating pretraining familiarity from compositional binding in video-text retrieval.
Builds exposure-based Seen Composition, Unseen Composition, and Unseen Atom splits from the EgoClip corpus, with controlled noun- and verb-swap negatives.
Pair exposure correlates with zero-shot retrieval performance even after accounting for separate verb and noun frequencies.
Inference-time exposure reweighting improves retrieval while leaving measured binding largely unchanged, and requires correct sample-level exposure correspondence.
The framework helps assess whether future retrieval gains reflect genuine compositional understanding or pretraining exposure.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Swap margins relate differently to pair exposure. Within Seen Compositions, noun-swap (a) and verb-swap (b) margins are plotted against log10(1+ f (v,n)) over 8,592 frozen-model probes. Light-blue points are individual probes, green circles are bin means with 95% confidence intervals, and dashed lines are OLS fits. Correlations are computed on the raw probes; ∗∗ indicates p < 0.01.

Table 3: Exposure reweighting changes V→T retrieval without binding repair. At the same trained checkpoint, Original uses the true exposure vector, Zeroed removes the exposure signal, and Shuffled breaks the sample–exposure correspondence while preserving the exposure distribution. T→V is unchanged by construction and is omitted for compactness. Binding margins remain essentially unchanged across conditions.

Table 2: Retrieval-oriented interventions improve retrieval without consistently restoring verb–noun binding. We report V→T and T→V retrieval performance, noun and verb binding margins, and their correlations with pair exposure.

papers.abstract: The proliferation of AI-generated videos has raised growing concerns about misinformation, fraud, and potential societal risks, creating an urgent need for detection. Reconstruction-error-based methods have shown strong empirical performance for AI-generated image detection by exploiting discrepancies between an input and its reconstructed version. Their extension to video detection, however, faces two challenges: (i) a fixed reconstructor is not optimized for the detection objective and may yield weak discriminative signals; and (ii) an additional raw-video feature stream is often introduced to model temporal dependencies, increasing architectural overhead. To address these challenges, we develop a detector that learns and exploits reconstruction errors as a unified source of spatiotemporal evidence. First, we jointly optimize a reconstructor and the downstream classifier to produce reconstruction errors that are more informative for detecting AI-generated videos. Second, we show that consecutive reconstruction errors alone carry temporal evidence, and thus a 3D convolution over them captures spatiotemporal evidence without a raw-video stream. Extensive experiments on over 30 existing AI-video generators demonstrate competitive performance against baselines.
authors: Jiahua Jiang, Jinglai Li, Jianru Zhang, Jin Zhu
bullets: Addresses weak detection signals from fixed reconstructors and the overhead of parallel raw-video streams.
Jointly optimizes the reconstructor and classifier for more discriminative reconstruction errors.
Uses consecutive reconstruction errors with 3D convolution to model spatiotemporal evidence.
Evaluated across more than 30 AI-video generators, achieving competitive performance against baselines.

papers.abstract: Active urban sensing orchestrates a mobile sensor fleet to proactively inspect a dynamic road network and gather critical information for system management. This problem simultaneously requires understanding the complex spatio-temporal evolution and making decisions with partial observations. In this work, we focus on active sensing in a large-scale urban road network with utilities grounded in dynamic traffic states, while prior work has rarely considered these factors jointly. We propose \emph{SenseAlign}, a Reinforcement Learning-based (RL) framework that learns decision-aligned predictive representations for coordinating an urban sensing drone fleet. SenseAlign first trains a privileged teacher agent that exploits future ground-truth traffic for optimal sensing choices. The student agent has an auxiliary branch that learns to predict future traffic with partial observations, in addition to the RL-trained actor and critic branches. During student learning, our framework matches the action distributions of the teacher under ground-truth and student-predicted future traffic, while keeping the teacher's observations unchanged. Such a design shapes the latent space for decision-making instead of prediction alone. At inference time, the student agent has no overhead as all this learning is done in training. We conduct comprehensive experiments with the real road network of central Barcelona containing 1570 road segments, and demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms the baselines on multiple utility formulations. The codebase will be made publicly available upon paper acceptance.
authors: Weijiang Xiong, Nikolas Geroliminis
bullets: Addresses active sensing in dynamic, large-scale urban road networks where decisions must be made from partial observations.
Uses a privileged RL teacher with future traffic information and a student with prediction, actor, and critic branches.
Aligns the student’s action distribution with the teacher’s decisions to shape representations for control, not prediction alone.
At inference, the student incurs no additional prediction overhead.
Experiments on central Barcelona’s 1,570-road-segment network show consistent gains over baselines across multiple utility formulations.

(c) Deployment uses only the student’s encoder and actor, with no additional inference cost from the auxiliary training components.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single framework. However, prevailing approaches often separate their visual representations or backbone computation to accommodate the different requirements of these two tasks, which limits the degree of unification. In this paper, we present HiUni, which revisits this design choice and explores whether a pretrained vision language model can be directly extended into a unified model with extensive parameter sharing. Specifically, HiUni reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both capabilities, while confining task-specific computation to the output side. Yet such a design introduces two key challenges. Generation in pixel space is difficult to optimize, and semantic abstraction in pretrained ViT discards fine spatial details required for synthesis. To address these challenges, HiUni introduces a \emph{Pixel Diffusion Head} tailored to direct pixel-space optimization and a lightweight \emph{HiGate} pathway that provides fine-grained spatial details near the output stage. Extensive experiments show that HiUni achieves a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while attaining competitive performance on image generation and editing. Controlled comparisons and analyses further demonstrate that a single dense backbone can effectively support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation, highlighting a simpler path toward unified multimodal modeling.
authors: Jiahao Hu, Jingdong Du, Yichen Zhang, Yi Song, Zhenyu Zhang, Jiaxin Niu, Ruihang Li, Xiangzhao Hao, Yiqian Zhang, Yong Huang, Zefeng Zhang, Zheyuan Gu, Shuohuan Wang
bullets: Targets the fragmented architectures commonly used for multimodal understanding and generation.
Reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both tasks, with specialization confined to the output side.
Introduces a Pixel Diffusion Head for direct pixel-space generation and a HiGate pathway to restore fine spatial details lost by semantic visual representations.
Maintains a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while achieving competitive image generation and editing performance.
Experiments indicate that one shared dense backbone can support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation.

papers.abstract: Predicting future scene or object states does not necessarily reveal how robot-object interactions will advance or hinder a task. This challenge is particularly pronounced in dynamic robotic manipulation, where objects continue moving during perception and execution. Effective action generation therefore requires not only modeling object dynamics but also anticipating how future interactions will shape task progress. To this end, we propose \textbf{PhysVAM}, a Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model that represents anticipated interactions through their effects on future task progress. This value-based formulation provides task-directed foresight without reconstructing future visual states. Conditioned on current observations and historical object and robot motion, PhysVAM jointly learns action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction. The value branch learns horizon-specific latent representations through future task-value prediction from successful and failed trajectories. These future-value representations are integrated into the action policy through gated cross-attention, guiding action generation toward interactions that facilitate task success. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate superior task success, with absolute success-rate improvements of 27.0 and 27.5 percentage points over the strongest baselines in simulation and real-world tasks, respectively. Project page: https://metarobo.github.io/physvam.github.io/.
authors: Yuxiang Yang, Jingbo Zhang, Jiaru Zhong, Junliang Chen, Yirui Zhou, Guangming Wang, Haitao Lin, Huaiyuan Xu, Yi Wang, Lap-Pui Chau
bullets: Addresses the challenge of planning interactions with objects that continue moving during perception and execution.
Uses current observations plus historical robot and object motion to jointly learn action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction.
Learns horizon-specific value representations from successful and failed trajectories.
Integrates future-value features into the policy through gated cross-attention to favor task-progressing interactions.
Reports absolute success-rate gains of 27.0 percentage points in simulation and 27.5 points in real-world tasks over the strongest baselines.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.
authors: Zhengtu Liang, Qiwei Liang, Tao Lin, Shihang Weng, Boyang Cai, Xiangyu Chen, Yikeng Chen, Jiaming Liang, Bohan Tan, Yu Yan, Renjing Xu
bullets: Flow-matching policies face different challenges when recovering noisy actions versus refining nearly clean ones.
Endpoint prediction is more stable at high noise, while velocity prediction provides more accurate corrections near clean actions.
UniVEP jointly trains both targets with consistency supervision and switches between them during inference, using one network run per step.
It improves success and efficiency in simulated and real-world manipulation; on RoboTwin, one StarVLA run reaches 61.36% success versus 59.96% for the best single-target baseline using 16 runs.
With LiLa-WAM, two UniVEP runs outperform the best 16-step single-target baseline while reducing inference latency by 77.1%.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video generation has made remarkable progress with diffusion models and transformer-based video architectures, yet generating coherent long videos from evolving textual descriptions remains challenging. Training long-video models from scratch requires substantial computation and large-scale multi-event data, while training-free multi-prompt generation must activate new prompt semantics without breaking temporal continuity. We identify a frequency-agnostic boundary coupling problem in existing transition strategies: weak coupling causes abrupt changes, flicker, and background jumps, whereas overly strong or coarse coupling may over-preserve source semantics and produce ghosting or duplicated subjects around prompt boundaries. To address this problem, we propose FreqSync, a training-free framework that formulates prompt transitions as frequency-selective boundary coupling. FreqSync combines Frequency-Synchronized Source-Conditioned Attention (FS-SCA) with Residual-Clipped Spectral Stitching (RCSS), enabling adjacent segments to share stable low- and mid-frequency structure and motion cues while keeping high-frequency prompt-specific details target-dominant under explicit residual constraints. Extensive experiments show that FreqSync achieves state-of-the-art transition smoothness and prompt alignment while maintaining strong perceptual video quality, demonstrating its effectiveness for coherent multi-prompt long video generation.
authors: Yipan Xu, Shuyong Gao, Jiyuan Fu, Keliang Yin, Jiayu Chen, Qianyu Guo, Yang Liu, Wenqiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses abrupt transitions, flicker, background jumps, ghosting, and duplicated subjects in multi-prompt long-video generation.
Combines Frequency-Synchronized Source-Conditioned Attention with Residual-Clipped Spectral Stitching.
Shares low- and mid-frequency structure and motion across adjacent segments while preserving target-prompt high-frequency details.
Experiments report state-of-the-art transition smoothness and prompt alignment with strong perceptual video quality.
Scope: training-free generation; effectiveness depends on frequency-selective boundary coupling and explicit residual constraints.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of FREQSYNC. Given a prompt sequence, FREQSYNC first encodes frozen text conditions and initializes overlapped latent segments with noise reuse. During iterative denoising, FS-SCA performs frequency-synchronized source-conditioned attention inside selected attention layers, while RCSS applies residual-clipped spectral stitching to denoised overlap predictions before the sampler update. After denoising, overlapped regions are removed and the clean latent segments are concatenated for VAE decoding, producing the final long video.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. On a three-prompt driving sequence, baselines suffer from viewpoint drift, weak prompt transition, ghosting, or duplicated traces. FREQSYNC preserves vehicle identity and motion while producing smoother semantic transitions.

Figure 6: Visual ablation of FREQSYNC. Isolated generation produces a hard cut. RCSS alone smooths the overlap region but lacks attention-level semantic handover. FS-SCA alone preserves the global layout but changes the chapel structure. Full FREQSYNC combines both modules for smooth transitions and stable identity.

Figure 2: Diagnostic observation. Strong frequency-agnostic coupling may over-preserve sourceside evidence and cause duplicated subjects. FREQSYNC transfers mainly low- and mid-frequency continuity cues while keeping target details controlled.
Figure 1: Teaser of FREQSYNC. Given a prompt sequence, FREQSYNC generates coherent long videos with smooth transitions, stable motion, and prompt-specific details.

Figure 9: Additional three-prompt generated examples. We show three representative three-prompt sequences, where each example spans two rows to cover a longer temporal range and two consecutive prompt boundaries. FREQSYNC maintains coherent temporal evolution across multiple semantic changes, such as scene, illumination, and action transitions. The results suggest that the proposed boundary coupling is not limited to a single transition, but can also support longer prompt sequences with successive target-prompt activations.

Figure 11: Additional qualitative comparison on a skateboarder sequence. The base prompt describes a young skateboarder gliding forward through an open public square, while the segment prompts transition from an empty dawn plaza to a festival plaza and then to a rain-washed night plaza. Kling2.6 [1] produces visually stable frames but shows limited scene progression. MEVG [33] and VideoInfinity [42] suffer from identity, viewpoint, or motion inconsistency. DiTCtrl [7] improves crosssegment continuity but introduces ghosting and blurred boundary artifacts. In contrast, FREQSYNC preserves the skateboarder’s motion trajectory while progressively changing the plaza environment and illumination.

Figure 12: Additional qualitative comparison on a hot-air-balloon sequence. The base prompt describes a hot air balloon, and the segment prompts change the lighting condition from early sunrise glow to bright daylight and then to violet dusk light. Kling-2.6 [1] preserves the balloon appearance but shows limited temporal and illumination transition. MEVG [33] and Video-Infinity [42] produce noticeable subject or scene inconsistencies, including multiple balloons, unstable scale, or abrupt viewpoint changes. DiTCtrl [7] maintains partial continuity but shows over-preserved source-side evidence and boundary-local artifacts. FREQSYNC better preserves the balloon identity and desert layout while producing a smoother lighting transition across the prompt sequence.

Figure 5: Temporal self-similarity around prompt boundaries. FREQSYNC preserves local diagonal continuity while reducing excessive cross-boundary similarity, supporting frequency-selective boundary coupling.

Figure 8: Additional two-prompt generated examples. We show eight representative two-prompt sequences. Each row corresponds to one generated video and visualizes key frames across a single prompt boundary. Across diverse transition types, FREQSYNC preserves the main subject, scene layout, and motion trajectory while allowing the target-prompt condition to emerge progressively. These examples further illustrate that the frequency-synchronized boundary coupling used by FS-SCA and RCSS can reduce abrupt visual changes without suppressing prompt-specific details.

Figure 10: Single-prompt long-video generation with FREQSYNC. We apply FREQSYNC to singleprompt long-video generation by assigning the same prompt to all segments. The four examples show a sunlit courtyard fountain, warm paper lanterns, a drifting maple leaf, and a Mars rover driving across a red crater plain. Even without semantic prompt changes, long-video generation still requires stable cross-segment continuation. FREQSYNC produces smooth motion and coherent visual content over extended durations, suggesting that its boundary-coupling mechanism can also benefit single-prompt video extension.

Figure 7: Boundary temporal-frequency analysis. FREQSYNC shows stronger low-frequency continuation and lower high-frequency variation around prompt boundaries. This supports our frequencysynchronized boundary coupling design, where low-frequency components preserve structural continuity and high-frequency instability is suppressed near transitions.

Table 5: Per-seed quantitative results of all compared methods. We report the results of MEVG [33], Video-Infinity [42], DiTCtrl [7], and FREQSYNC under three random seeds: 42, 123, and 999. The shaded average rows correspond to the results reported in the main paper. CSCV and Motion Smoothness are reported as percentages.

Table 4: Main hyperparameters in the supplementary configuration file. The table lists the core parameters included in config.yaml. FS-SCA controls frequency-selective attention-level source conditioning, while RCSS controls residual-constrained prediction-level boundary stitching.

Best scores are in bold; second-best scores are underlined.

CSCV is the primary boundarytransition metric. Segment-level Text-Image Similarity is reported as a prompt-fidelity reference and is not boundary-aware. Best results are in bold and second-best results are underlined.

papers.abstract: Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors accumulated along simulated trajectories. This includes estimating physical parameters and training neural sub-models in hybrid configurations. Gradients are typically computed using adjoint methods, or backpropagation through time (BPTT), whose computational and memory costs grow with the length of the training window. This limits the duration and resolution of hybrid-model training, a major bottleneck for realistic geophysical applications. Approaches like truncated BPTT reduces memory use by discarding sensitivities across truncation boundaries, introducing gradient bias and neglecting long-range dependencies. We propose a class of gradient approximation methods that preserve the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory while approximating only the pullback operators within it. Exact pullbacks are computed by automatic differentiation at sparse anchor states only. Between anchors, sensitivities propagate either through the identity (Zero-order) or through a reused, frozen pullback (Pullback Reuse). This approximation makes the parameter pullback constant within each chunk, allowing the gradient sum to factorize so that a single evaluation per chunk replaces one per time step. We evaluate both on three systems of increasing complexity, an incomplete Lorenz-63 model, a large-eddy closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence, and bias correction in a multilayer quasi-geostrophic ocean model. Peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude and runtime up to fourfold, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to the exact gradient direction. In all three cases, approximate gradients support hybrid-model training at comparable accuracy, showing that effective online learning does not require exact gradients.
authors: Emilio Gonz\'alez-Zamora, Pierre Tandeo, Laurent Debreu, Said Ouala
bullets: Full-trajectory adjoint methods are costly because memory and computation grow with training-window length, limiting realistic geophysical applications.
The proposed approach keeps the adjoint recurrence but approximates pullback operators between sparse anchor states.
Two variants propagate sensitivities through the identity or reuse a frozen pullback within each chunk, enabling one pullback evaluation per chunk instead of per time step.
Across three geophysical systems, peak memory decreases by up to an order of magnitude and runtime by up to fourfold.
Pullback Reuse most closely matches the exact gradient direction, and both methods support comparable hybrid-model training accuracy.

papers.abstract: Role allocation strategies in human-robot collaboration typically assign tasks to both the human and the robot, limiting the user's ability to take initiative. Furthermore, allocation decisions may conflict with the user's intentions, and the rationale behind such allocations may remain unclear, potentially reducing both acceptance and collaboration fluency. The novelty of the proposed framework is that the human is left free to contribute to the task, while the robot is dynamically allocated activities through a cost-driven Behavior Tree architecture according to user-expressed preferences and behavior. Explicit preferences are extracted from natural language instructions using a large language model, whereas human activity is monitored online through a Shannon entropy-based analysis of hand-object interactions. Furthermore, the framework can recognize anomalies in human execution and autonomously trigger corrective robot actions. The approach was validated through a pilot study and a multi-subject experiment involving 14 participants. Results demonstrate the potential of such an allocation strategy for enabling intuitive and engaging collaboration without increasing the perceived workload.

bullets: Addresses rigid human-robot role allocation, conflicts with user intentions, and unclear allocation rationale.
Uses an LLM to extract explicit preferences from natural-language instructions.
Monitors human hand-object interactions online with Shannon entropy and allocates robot activities through a cost-driven Behavior Tree.
Detects anomalous human execution and triggers corrective robot actions autonomously.
Validated in a pilot study and an experiment with 14 participants, demonstrating potential for engaging collaboration without added perceived workload.

papers.abstract: Artificial Spiking Neural Networks have gained remarkable attention in the last few years due to their proven ability in simulating biological neural cultures and producing similar activity and trends. Nevertheless, whether they can be trained for humanoid locomotion while retaining biological plausibility and robust performance at once remains an open question. We study this problem by proposing a biologically inspired spiking network, trained by different learning schemes and tested on the H1-2 Unitree Humanoid. These schemes differ in how recurrent weights are trained. Ordered from most to least biologically faithful, they are: a fixed reservoir mimicking an in-vitro neural culture, where recurrent weights are kept frozen and only a linear readout is trained, the same network but with its synapses trained by reward-modulated spike timing dependent plasticity and eligibility propagation, and finally backpropagation through time as a non biological baseline for comparison. All schemes relied on distillation of a reinforcement learning expert policy with dataset aggregation. We show that e-prop reached 100% survival rate matching backpropagation through time, whereas both the fixed reservoir and the reward-modulated STDP, though the closest to biological cultures, plateaued at a much lower performance (~43.7% and ~11% survival). We explore in further detail which trends a real culture could and could not produce until now. Finally we demonstrate brief bipedal stepping on a full size humanoid H1-2.
authors: Fatima Atwi (LAAS-GEPETTO, Nantes Univ - ECN), Constant Roux (LAAS-GEPETTO), Christian Bergaud (LAAS-MEMS), Olivier Stasse (LAAS-GEPETTO)
bullets: The study asks whether biologically plausible spiking networks can be trained for robust humanoid locomotion.
It compares a fixed recurrent reservoir, reward-modulated STDP, eligibility propagation (e-prop), and backpropagation through time.
All approaches use reinforcement-learning expert-policy distillation with dataset aggregation.
E-prop achieved 100% survival, matching backpropagation through time; the fixed reservoir and reward-modulated STDP reached about 43.7% and 11%.
The experiments include brief bipedal stepping on a full-size Unitree H1-2 and examine which biological-culture trends can be reproduced.

papers.abstract: Recovering metric-scale geometry from observations at a single viewpoint remains fundamentally ill-posed, limiting the reliability of novel view synthesis. Recent methods rely on learned monocular depth priors, which provide strong structural estimates but can suffer from scale ambiguity and dataset-dependent biases. We propose DfD-GS, a feed-forward framework that predicts a metric-scale 3D Gaussian scene representation from a single-view all-in-focus--defocused image pair. The key idea is to exploit defocus blur as a physical metric depth cue. DfD-GS first estimates a defocus-based metric disparity map from the all-in-focus--defocused image pair and the corresponding defocus strength. This estimate is used to align and refine a monocular depth prior to metric scale. Visible and hidden 3D Gaussians are then predicted for occlusion-aware novel view synthesis. Experiments on synthetic-defocus datasets constructed from Booster and Middlebury show that DfD-GS outperforms single-image baselines in metric depth estimation and novel view synthesis. On WildRGB-D, DfD-GS achieves lower AbsRel and LPIPS but higher depth RMSE than the single-image baselines. Additional analyses show that DfD-GS maintains a more stable metric scale under field-of-view changes. Qualitative results on a real dataset show recovery of the main scene structure under optical defocus.
authors: Shiori Ueda, Rinto Yagawa, Hideo Saito, Shohei Mori
bullets: Addresses scale ambiguity and dataset bias in monocular single-view depth estimation.
Estimates metric disparity from defocus blur and uses it to align and refine a monocular depth prior.
Predicts visible and hidden 3D Gaussians for occlusion-aware novel view synthesis.
Outperforms single-image baselines on synthetic-defocus datasets for metric depth and view synthesis.
Shows more stable metric scale under field-of-view changes; on WildRGB-D, it improves AbsRel and LPIPS but has higher depth RMSE.

The refined depth, all-in-focus image, and DA3 features are then used to predict visible and hidden 3D Gaussians for novel view synthesis.

papers.title: DfD-GS: Defocus Image Prior for Metric-Scale Single-View Depth Estimation and View Synthesis

papers.abstract: Autonomous rendezvous and proximity operations require not only an accurate estimate of the pose of the target spacecraft, but also a reliable indication of when this estimate can be trusted. Conformal prediction provides such an indication with a formal guarantee, by producing pose uncertainty sets that contain the true pose with a specified probability. Such a guarantee, however, assumes that calibration and test data follow the same distribution, an assumption that is violated in orbital perception, where labelled calibration images are available only from synthetic renderings while operational images are real. In this work, we show on the SPEED+ dataset that conformal pose estimation calibrated on synthetic images loses its coverage guarantee on real images, and that many of the resulting failures are silent: the predicted pose set appears valid but excludes the true pose. To address this, we calibrate on synthetic images translated to the appearance of real images. Since translation alters appearance while preserving geometry, the synthetic pose labels remain valid and no labelled real images are required. Experiments with two translation models show that this calibration restores coverage above the specified level for miscoverage levels of 0.1 and above, and reduces silent failures from up to 43.5% to at most 3.3% of the test images, bringing conformal pose estimation a step closer to trustworthy deployment in space.
authors: Nidhal Eddine Chenni, Arunkumar Rathinam, Djamila Aouada
bullets: Synthetic-only calibration loses its formal coverage guarantee on real spacecraft images, causing silent failures where uncertainty sets exclude the true pose.
The method translates labeled synthetic images to real-image appearance while preserving geometry and pose labels.
Evaluated on the SPEED+ dataset with two translation models, it restores coverage above the target for miscoverage levels of 0.1 and higher.
Silent failures decrease from as much as 43.5% to at most 3.3% of test images.
The approach targets trustworthy spacecraft rendezvous and proximity-operation deployment without requiring labeled operational imagery.

papers.title: Domain-Aware Conformal Prediction for Trustworthy Spacecraft Pose Estimation under Sim-to-Real Shift

papers.abstract: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.
authors: Alper Kalle, Theo Rudkiewicz, Mohamed-Oumar Ouerfelli, Mohamed Tamaazousti
bullets: Targets post-training low-rank compression that preserves input-output behavior, not just layer weights.
Linearizes the network and uses a Kronecker-factored approximation to reduce compression to a closed-form weighted SVD.
Estimates the otherwise intractable output-side factor unbiasedly with random probes, requiring K backward passes per sequence.
On WikiText-2 calibration, it reports the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity across matched uniform-rank settings and at ratio 0.7 with LEMS allocation.
KL-SVD usually improves calibration perplexity and downstream accuracy but increases cross-corpus perplexity; Complete-SVD improves IFEval accuracy over prior output-aware methods.
papers.selection_reason: Output-aware low-rank SVD compression for LLMs; reduces model memory while preserving logit behavior.
papers.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
papers.tldr: Complete-SVD compresses LLMs by minimizing equal-weighted changes to the model’s output logits, achieving strong perplexity and instruction-following performance in the reported settings.

papers.abstract: A corridor, its mirror reflection, and its image on a display can look identical, yet their physical surfaces lie at different depths. We test whether bounded camera motions distinguish these explanations. Intervene3D takes an image and an initial geometry estimate, predicts the view under each hypothesis and candidate motion, and selects a motion by maximin separability. It reports the mechanism and first physical surface only if the available motions separate the hypotheses still in contention. Otherwise it abstains. An adequacy test also rejects observations that no hypothesis explains. On a matched synthetic benchmark with exact landmarks, disabling abstention gives confident answers on 76.4% of unresolvable scenes. With abstention, none receives a confident answer under exact or noisy landmarks. At 100% accuracy on answered scenes, maximin selection answers 61.0% of scenes and summed selection 43.1%. The adequacy test lowers wrong answers on strongly curved mirror scenes from 56.8% to 12.4%. Real display experiments compare two hypotheses using one frozen depth-network estimate. The second image supplies photometric evidence and is never passed through the depth network. One executed motion reduces the pooled median surface error of twelve networks by 31.5%. These networks have larger error inside the annotated panel than outside on 33.4% of illusion-benchmark images. They place the first physical surface behind the glass on 36.9% of Mirror3D frames.
authors: Reshad Ul Karim, Abrar Samin, Sammam Mahdi, Syeda Maliha Tabassum, Md Rashad Al Hasan Rony
bullets: Visual observations can be identical for real corridors, mirror reflections, and displays despite different physical surface depths.
The system predicts views under competing hypotheses and candidate motions, choosing the motion that maximizes worst-case separability.
It reports a mechanism and first physical surface only when the available motion distinguishes the remaining hypotheses; an adequacy test rejects unexplained observations.
On synthetic scenes, maximin selection answered 61.0% with 100% accuracy, while disabling abstention produced confident answers for 76.4% of unresolvable scenes.
In real display experiments, one motion reduced pooled median surface error by 31.5% across twelve depth networks; substantial errors remained on illusion images.

papers.selection_reason: Active camera-motion reasoning for disambiguating 3D physical geometry; fits spatial intelligence and 3D vision.
papers.title: Less Than Meets the Eye: Action-Set Identifiability and Principled Abstention for 3D Physical Geometry
papers.tldr: Intervene3D uses targeted camera motion and principled abstention to distinguish ambiguous 3D physical explanations, achieving perfect accuracy on answered synthetic scenes while avoiding confident answers when scenes are unresolvable.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion research has advanced rapidly on walking and running, but \emph {object-mediated} locomotion, in which a robot must coordinate its body with a passive external object, remains difficult. One challenging task is skateboarding, which requires simultaneous interaction with the ground and a passive but movable platform to achieve forward motion. Current methods for tackling skateboarding with humanoid robots either require human demonstrations or utilise analytic steering models that require system identification. In this paper, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework that does not rely on prior data such as demonstrations and enables robots such as the K1 humanoid to learn to skateboard using model-free learning. The method combines task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations. We introduce a number of constraints restricting behaviours such as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board, and unstable board motion. Their changing prevalence during training produces an implicit progression from stance control towards sustained robot--board locomotion.
authors: Ganeshvar Soenessardien, Michael Przystupa, Kevin Sebastian Luck
bullets: Addresses object-mediated locomotion requiring coordination with both the ground and a passive skateboard.
Combines task rewards with exploit-blocking termination conditions during training.
Constrains behaviors including losing the planted foot, placing both feet on the board, excessive twisting, board separation, and unstable board motion.
The changing prevalence of terminations implicitly progresses learning from stance control to sustained robot–board locomotion.
Demonstrated on a K1 humanoid, with no specific quantitative results reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: We present PaveSplat, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting method that adds a learned residual to the analytic surface-aligned covariance, keeping surfels paving the visible surface across rendering resolutions. Pixel-aligned feed-forward Gaussian splatting predicts one primitive per pixel from a few images in a single pass, and its rendering quality depends on how well these primitives cover the surface. Recent surfel-based methods compute the surface-aligned covariance analytically from predicted depth. However, this covariance has no way to correct the surfel orientation where the depth-derived frame is ill-posed. The surfels then cover the surface loosely; at the training resolution each surfel's one-pixel minimum footprint covers the gaps, but they show up as holes when the same prediction is re-rendered at a higher resolution. To address this, we keep the analytic covariance as an initialization, with its axes aligned to the surface tangents, and add an identity-initialized unit-quaternion residual that reorients a surfel only where this improves rendering, turning surfels that the analytic frame mis-aims back onto the surface. On RealEstate10K, PaveSplat achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among single-Gaussian-per-pixel methods at every scale (1x-8x). The native-resolution gain is small; the benefit appears when the same prediction is rendered at higher display resolutions without re-running the network. On zero-shot DL3DV, it leads PSNR within this group at every scale and ranks first or second on SSIM/LPIPS. A coverage-hole analysis shows fewer uncovered pixels than both baselines under high-resolution re-rendering.
authors: Janghun Kim, Hyun-Cheol Kim, Eunbin An, Myeonghun Oh, Hyon-Gon Choo
bullets: Targets holes that appear when pixel-aligned Gaussian predictions are re-rendered above their training resolution.
Initializes each surfel with a depth-derived, surface-aligned covariance.
Adds an identity-initialized unit-quaternion residual to reorient surfels when the analytic frame is ill-posed.
Outperforms single-Gaussian-per-pixel baselines across scales on RealEstate10K and leads or ranks highly on zero-shot DL3DV.
Produces fewer uncovered pixels during high-resolution re-rendering; native-resolution gains are small.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of PaveSplat covariance construction. From the predicted depth, (a) the surface-aligned prior sets the analytic frame Ra=[ê1 ê2 n̂], supplying tangent-aligned shape and the initial orientation. (b) Two per-primitive refinements act on this prior: in-plane scale multipliers (orange) set the anisotropic radii si=s̄i mi, and a residual reorientation (blue) — the only added learned covariance parameter — adapts orientation via q=qa⊗∆q. (c) The two recombine as R=RaR∆ into the final covariance Σ, rendered to the novel view.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison on RealEstate10K. Per scene: inputs, ground truth, DepthSplat [18], SurfSplat [7], and PaveSplat; top row = full-frame native render (crop boxed), bottom row = 8× crop. In these high-margin cases, PaveSplat keeps more support along thin structures.

Fig. 1: Three ways to cover a surface with surfels. Per regime: the per-pixel Gaussians for one scene as covariance ellipsoids from a novel view (top) and a schematic of how surfels lie on the surface (bottom). (a) Fully-learned covariances (DepthSplat [18]) leave scale uncontrolled, so oversized ellipsoids over-spread while small ones fail to tile. (b) The analytic prior (SurfSplat [7]) sets the frame from depth with no pathway to correct it, leaving anisotropic surfels mis-oriented to the tangents. (c) PaveSplat makes the analytic frame per-pixel correctable (q=qa ⊗ ∆q), so surfels reorient to pave the surface. This isolates surfel shape and coverage.

The coverage-hole rate (black-hole fraction) = share of pixels rendering near-black (max RGB channel <0.02) where the GT has content (max channel >0.02). (b) perscene distribution at 8× (box = median/IQR, whiskers to the 10th/90th percentile): PaveSplat < SurfSplat < DepthSplat (per-scene Wilcoxon, both p<10−10).

papers.abstract: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.
authors: Zhihao Hu, Jianqi Ma, Jun Zhang, Jiayang Bai, Haifeng Shi, Yanxiang Zhuang, Zhongqian Sun, Weidong Zhang, Wei Yang
bullets: Targets the challenge of jointly achieving high visual fidelity, frame rate, responsiveness, and long-term stability in interactive game video generation.
Redesigns the VAE for efficient 1080p decoding and real-time synthesis.
Uses diffusion forcing with an extended temporal training horizon to capture long-term dependencies and persistent memory.
Applies post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while preserving visual and temporal quality.
Experiments report improved fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation methods.

papers.abstract: Roadside LiDAR detectors are expensive to train on real labels, and digital twins promise to replace these labels, but a detector trained on a twin meets a different sensor, different objects and different annotation conventions on the real site. We describe the pipeline that placed first in the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge (IEEE BigData 2026 Cup, 0.5541 combined score) and fifth on its V2X-Real track (0.8102). Every detector is a CenterPoint model trained only on synthetic data, on a single 8 GB laptop GPU. Most of the gain came from correcting differences between the twin and the real site rather than from the detector. We align the twin's coordinates, point density and box convention with the test sensor, generate the pedestrians and riders that the twins lack, plus street clutter as unlabeled negatives, and rebuild twin objects at real size and real point density. A non-learned resampling to the per-cell point density of unlabeled real frames lifts LUMPI realism from 0.589 to 0.947, against 0.949 between real frames. Label-free post-processing then exploits what a fixed roadside sensor guarantees: static structures recur in every frame, and real objects have characteristic point statistics. Reporting the validation and test gain of each component side by side, we find that corrections of systematic sim-to-real differences transfer to the test set, typically keeping a quarter to three quarters of their validation gain, while choices that fit the few objects of a validation set do not.
authors: KuanLin Chen, Feng-jui Kuo
bullets: Problem: Digital-twin-trained detectors face real-site differences in sensing, object coverage, and labeling, making real annotation costly but sim-to-real transfer difficult.
Method: Train CenterPoint only on synthetic data, while aligning coordinates, point density, box conventions, object sizes, and clutter with the real roadside sensor.
Method: Add missing pedestrians and riders, use unlabeled real frames for non-learned density resampling, and apply label-free post-processing based on static-scene and point-statistic cues.
Results: The pipeline ranked first on LUMPI (0.5541) and fifth on V2X-Real (0.8102); density resampling improved twin realism from 0.589 to 0.947, near the real-frame value of 0.949.
Contribution: Component-wise validation and test analysis shows systematic sim-to-real corrections transfer better than validation-set-specific object-fitting choices.

papers.abstract: Long-form video understanding, as a fundamental yet crucial vision task, is being revolutionized by multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based video agents. However, the retrieval-driven nature inherent to these agents creates a significant bottleneck, forcing them to reactively fetch clips based on local saliency without a global temporal plan. To address this, we present ForeSeek, a foresight-driven video agent that transforms long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into predictive exploration. Rather than blindly probing the timeline, ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over unseen temporal regions, verifies them through targeted observations, and continuously refines its search based on emerging evidence, where failed expectations serve as informative signals for principled backtracking. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training framework that equips MLLMs with foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making. Extensive experiments on five long-video benchmarks demonstrate that ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off of long-video reasoning, achieving competitive or superior accuracy while observing $2.5$--$4.4\times$ fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent. Code is available at https://github.com/harry0021/ForeSeek
authors: Yuchen Sun, Siyuan Cheng, Shi-Zhe Chen, Yixin Qin, Jinwen Luo, Zheng Wei
bullets: Addresses the lack of global temporal planning in retrieval-driven long-video agents.
Builds visually grounded expectations about unseen regions, verifies them with targeted observations, and backtracks when expectations fail.
Uses a two-stage training framework for foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision-making.
Across five long-video benchmarks, achieves competitive or better accuracy while observing 2.5–4.4× fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models combine self-attention with recurrent layers whose in-place state updates restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions. Saving states on a coarse grid wastes reusable prefixes, whereas existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each mid-prompt checkpoint, adding scheduler steps that outweigh the reuse gains under load. We observe that across multi-turn chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search, prefix reuse almost always ends at structural boundaries predictable in advance, such as turn ends and known branch points. We present FrontierReplay, a prefix caching system that materializes exact checkpoints at these boundaries without cutting the prefill. While the forward pass runs uncut, FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs and invokes a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to build the target state 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation without host synchronization. A frontier-aware retention policy prioritizes active anchors and proven branches while lending dead checkpoint slots to the attention KV cache. Across diverse hybrid architectures, model scales, and workloads, FrontierReplay delivers clear gains over existing exact caches, lowering median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raising 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improving goodput by up to 4.26x (3.67x at larger scales). Compared with approximate replay methods, FrontierReplay delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput while preserving exact task accuracy, avoiding the up to 17% accuracy drop suffered by approximation on long contexts.
authors: Zekun Wang, Yizhuo Wang
bullets: Targets hybrid models whose recurrent states can only be reused from exact saved positions.
Predicts checkpoint frontiers such as chat turn ends and search branch points, avoiding mid-prompt prefill cuts.
Logs recurrent-layer inputs and uses a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to construct checkpoints 6–37× cheaper per token than full recomputation.
A frontier-aware policy prioritizes active and proven branches while reallocating unused checkpoint capacity to attention KV caching.
Across architectures and workloads, it reduces median TTFT by 16–89%, increases SLO capacity by up to 1.73×, and improves goodput by up to 4.26× while preserving exact accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 5: FrontierReplay architecture. The host scheduler maintains a prefix index over 16-token pages and manages checkpoint placement, retention, and dead-slot reclaim. 1⃝ The index returns the deepest checkpoint c on the cached prefix. 2⃝ The worker copies it into the request’s state slot. 3⃝ The uncut prefill over [c,n) writes KV pages and stages recurrent-layer inputs for [c, t) in a temporary log. 4⃝ State-only replay starts from the saved state at c and writes the checkpoint at t into a free slot. 5⃝ The scheduler publishes the checkpoint after the GPU event completes. Solid arrows show data and execution flow. Dashed arrows show control flow, including the reassignment of dead checkpoint slots to the KV pool.

(b) Per-token GPU replay latency b versus full prefill slope c across five hybrid models (Table 1); skipping attention and MLPs yields a 5.8–36.9× leverage that widens with model scale.

papers.abstract: Few-step diffusion models are widely deployed for their efficiency. However, reinforcing them with black-box rewards, as is routine for multi-step models, faces two structural challenges. First, a few-step generator is a sampler rather than a score model, so its velocity is not the forward velocity of the generated distribution. Second, it must be anchored to the undistilled teacher, which shares no transitions with it. Existing few-step RL methods handle the latter with a marginal KL to the teacher, but each pays for the former in its reward credit. We propose Shadow Posterior Matching (SPM), which renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and obtains the credit from their shadow posterior. From the KL-regularized reward objective, we derive a regression loss that turns reward values into a reward direction while anchoring the generator's outputs to the teacher and aligning the shadow inputs with the deployed inputs. Applied to 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step RL methods.
authors: Jingqiao Xiu, Yicong Li
bullets: Few-step diffusion generators are samplers, making standard reward-credit assignment unsuitable because their velocity differs from the generated distribution’s forward velocity.
They also require anchoring to an undistilled teacher despite sharing no transitions with it.
SPM renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and uses their shadow posterior to obtain reward credit.
A regression loss derived from a KL-regularized reward objective converts reward values into a reward direction while aligning deployed and shadow inputs and anchoring outputs to the teacher.
On 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step reinforcement-learning methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Shadow Posterior Matching. (a) The deployed few-step sampler generates final samples without gradients, and their black-box rewards yield group-relative advantages. (b) Renoising with fresh noise pairs each shadow input ys with a posterior sample x and the velocity u. (c) Colored arrows show three velocity differences: u − F (ys, s) for shadow credit, and vT − F̂s and F − F̂s at (ŷ, τ) for teacher anchor and endpoint matching. A regression loss pulls the generator’s velocity vθ(ys, s) along their weighted sum Gs.
Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. Samples are generated from GenEval (left), OCR (center), and PickScore (right) test prompts.

Figure 1. Reward curves with a single black-box reward. The reward is GenEval (top) or OCR (bottom). Left: training reward on test prompts. Right: ImageReward on DrawBench prompts. SPM achieves higher task rewards with better image quality.

Figure 4. Ablation results on visual text rendering. Left: OCR reward on test prompts. Right: ImageReward on DrawBench prompts. EM and AW denote endpoint matching and adaptive weighting, respectively. α is the tilting temperature, with a default value of 0.1.

Table 2. Quantitative results. We report training rewards on test prompts, and image-quality metrics and preference scores on DrawBench prompts. Higher is better for all metrics. The best 4-NFE results within each task are shown in bold and second-best results are underlined.

Table 1. Few-step RL paradigms, distinguished by their reward credit. Reward value: the credit is computed from measured reward values, without the reward’s gradient or a learned proxy. Final call: the deterministic final call receives credit from a black-box reward (◦ means only through a learned proxy, and – means not applicable, since the paradigm needs the reward’s gradient). Sharp sample: no reference in the update is built from the generator’s own velocity, so the samples receive no shift toward the posterior mean and stay sharp. Reward direction: the reward provides an update direction independent of the anchor’s force instead of only reweighting the anchor. Teacher KL: the generator is anchored to the teacher by a KL between their marginal distributions.

papers.selection_reason: Reward fine-tuning method for few-step diffusion generators; technically transferable to video diffusion models.
papers.title: Reinforcing Few-Step Diffusion Models via Shadow Posterior Matching
papers.tldr: Shadow Posterior Matching enables more effective and less reward-hacking reinforcement of few-step diffusion generators by deriving reward guidance from renoised shadow samples.

papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires models to acquire new capabilities while retaining performance on previous tasks. A stability-oriented perspective common in conventional continual learning emphasizes knowledge preservation and interference mitigation. Complementing this perspective, we revisit CRL for vision-language models through policy improvement, a fundamental principle of RL, to preserve acquired performance gains. Using the performance difference lemma, we characterize historical performance changes through the current policy's expected advantages on historical task distributions, motivating replay of historical prompts with the current policy. To allocate limited replay memory, we propose Contrastive Likelihood Replay (CoLiR), which contrasts likelihood gains on correct responses from the final task policy with likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy. Our analysis links correct-response likelihood gains to reference-policy advantages under an idealized KL-regularized optimal update and provides an endogenous-reward interpretation for general policy updates. CoLiR estimates scores from finite training rollouts and cached log-likelihoods, selects prompts at task boundaries, and replays them uniformly during subsequent training, with KL regularization restricted to replayed prompts. Memory construction only requires a small amount of additional cross-policy scoring but no additional response generation. Across three Qwen3-VL model sizes on MRCL, CoLiR achieves the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among the compared methods while maintaining competitive new-task performance.
authors: Qin-Wen Luo, Haoxuan Gao, Sheng Ren, Xiang Chen, Sheng-Jun Huang
bullets: Frames continual RL retention through historical-task advantages and the performance difference lemma.
Scores replay candidates by contrasting correct-response likelihood gains with incorrect-response likelihood reductions.
Selects prompts at task boundaries using cached likelihoods and limited extra cross-policy scoring, without additional response generation.
Replays selected prompts uniformly with KL regularization applied only to replayed prompts.
Across three Qwen3-VL sizes on MRCL, reports the best mean final and mean task accuracy among compared methods while preserving competitive new-task performance.
