papers.abstract: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.
authors: John Won, Yonghoon Dong, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Current video-predictive world models may look realistic while misrepresenting the consequences of similar actions.
AFFECT injects temporally correlated action noise during task-agnostic teleoperation and matches the resulting visual-change distributions.
It avoids requiring repeated executions from the same initial state.
Across OGBench, DROID, and ALOHA-2, AFFECT improves correspondence between simulated and real outcomes, lowers FVD, and boosts planning success.
On DROID, success-rate correlation increases from 0.47 to 0.79, with up to 23% lower FVD and 8.3% higher planning success.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of AFFECT. Frozen encoders ϕ, ψ extract video features from both the recorded and generated futures, and perturbation features from the logged action perturbations. Pairing the centered perturbations with each set of video features gives the recorded and predicted action effects (Φ(O),Φ(Ô)), which measure how visual change moves with the perturbation across rollouts. The AFFECT loss optimizes over the distance between the two distributions, so that generated futures respond to perturbations in the same direction and with the same strength as real ones.

Figure 1: Small action perturbations lead to distinct action effects. From the same initial state, actions drawn from a narrow distribution change the gripper’s approach only slightly, yet produce qualitatively different outcomes, where the cube is grasped, missed, or pushed away. A faithful world model must reproduce how these outcomes shift as the action is perturbed, rather than only rendering a plausible video for generic actions.

papers.abstract: Editing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) capture of a person so that they wear a new garment requires every rendered view to agree on the same garment details. Existing 3D virtual try-on (VTON) pipelines, however, edit training views largely independently and fuse them with hand-designed heuristics such as manually chosen reference views and fixed attention-blending weights. The resulting inconsistencies are baked into the 3D representation and surface as texture drift, blurred prints, and implausible geometry in novel views. We present GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage framework that combines implicit and explicit 3D reasoning for consistent 3DGS try-on. (i) A multi-view inpainting transformer jointly edits a set of training views with full cross-view self-attention, so that cross-view correspondence is learned rather than imposed. (ii) A geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet conditions the diffusion editor on the garment image together with depth and surface normals rendered from the current 3DGS state, supplying explicit structure where visual evidence is weakest. (iii) A pose-adaptive persona-aware attention replaces the fixed blending weight between current-view and reference-view features with weights derived from camera-pose proximity. On the 3D-VTONBench benchmark, GS-VTON-MVT improves FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.
authors: Sarthak Batra, Armin Mustafa, Adrian Hilton
bullets: Addresses texture drift, blurred garment prints, and implausible geometry caused by independently editing views and heuristic fusion.
Uses a multi-view inpainting transformer with full cross-view self-attention to learn view correspondence.
Conditions diffusion editing on the garment image plus 3DGS-rendered depth and surface normals.
Adapts attention blending to camera-pose proximity instead of using fixed weights.
Improves image quality, cross-view consistency, and user preference on 3D-VTONBench versus general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of GS-VTON-MVT. (1) A subject-specific 3DGS scene Gsrc is reconstructed from posed multi-view images. (2) The Multi-View Inpainting Transformer (MVT) jointly edits a subset of training views with cross-view attention, producing a consistent edited set Xtrain that is used to personalize a Stable Diffusion inpainting model with LoRA. (3) During 3DGS editing, RGB, depth, and normal maps are rendered from the current scene; the garment region is masked, and the personalized inpainting model, guided by depth, normal, and garment ControlNet branches fused by cross-attention, produces a geometry-aligned target Iedit that supervises the update of the Gaussians, yielding the edited scene Gtgt.

Fig. 2: Qualitative comparison on in-the-wild subjects. Each subject is captured from multiple views and processed with the full pipeline; we show two of the input views, the target garment, and the same two views produced by GS-VTON-MVT and by the baseline. Baseline outputs are resized to the aspect ratio of the input. Faces are blurred for privacy.

papers.abstract: End-to-end approaches to Optical Music Recognition (OMR) have recently shown promising results, but their performance often degrades on unseen data. A common solution is to pretrain and fine-tune models with annotated samples from the target domain, improving adaptation to new distributions. However, this process typically requires extensive manual annotation to yield competitive models, making it costly and time-consuming. In this work, we explore Active Learning to reduce this burden by selecting informative samples for labeling in low-resource scenarios, where the amount of manual annotation that can be performed is limited. We evaluate both uncertainty- and diversity-based sampling strategies on staff-level and full-page corpora. Results show that confidence-based sampling performs comparably to oracle selection (based on true error), and that each scenario benefits from a tailored strategy.
authors: Eric Ayllon, Francisco J. Castellanos, Antonio Rios-Vila
bullets: OMR models often degrade on unseen data and require costly target-domain annotation for adaptation.
The study evaluates uncertainty- and diversity-based sample selection in low-resource labeling scenarios.
Experiments cover both staff-level and full-page corpora.
Confidence-based sampling performs comparably to oracle selection based on true error.
The best sampling strategy depends on the evaluation scenario.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing interactive physical twins from video requires accurately capturing how objects deform while maintaining efficient simulation. We observe that reproducing motion in a video does not guarantee correct responses to new forces when the physical representation restricts how an object can deform. In spring-based twins, coupling between volume and shape responses creates such a limitation. We present MorphTwin, which enriches local deformation modes to capture and independently control these responses while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation. To support interpretable material editing and transfer, we use offline calibration to map shared relative response changes to stiffness updates on each reconstructed graph. Under identical inverse settings on synthetic scenes, MorphTwin reduces the mean absolute error of Poisson's ratio by 75.8% and the mean relative error of Young's modulus by 22.1% compared to PhysTwin. We introduce an egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark covering interactions with objects of varying stiffness. Real-world experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error than PhysTwin at interactive speeds.
authors: Haoqin Hong, Ding Fan, Fubin Dou, Tianyu Huang, Yuzhuo Chen, Zhemeng Zhang, Hanxiao Jiang, Congcong Zhu, Gerhard Petrus Hancke, Jingrun Chen, Rynson WH Lau
bullets: Addresses the limitation that matching observed video motion may not yield correct responses to new forces, especially in spring-based models coupling volume and shape changes.
Enriches local deformation modes while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation.
Uses offline calibration to translate shared relative response edits into stiffness updates for interpretable material editing and transfer.
On synthetic scenes, reduces Poisson’s-ratio error by 75.8% and Young’s-modulus relative error by 22.1% versus PhysTwin.
A new egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark and real-world tests show improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error at interactive speeds.

papers.tldr: MorphTwin reconstructs deformable physical twins from video with independently controllable deformation responses, improving material accuracy and future-motion prediction over PhysTwin.

papers.abstract: Audio LLMs can know when a queried sound occurs but fail to say it. We find a few attention heads that track the queried sound: they shift when the query changes, follow the sound when it moves, and removing or blocking them often hurts the model's timestamps. Yet the answer does not express what they track. Intervals read directly from these heads outperform the model's original answer and recover events that its timestamps miss. To bring this timing into the answer, we introduce head-guided decoding, which needs no training. It keeps the model's decision on whether the sound is present and rescores its candidate timestamps with a prior from these heads. Heads selected on development data transfer unchanged to new recordings and free-text queries, where head-guided decoding improves the timestamps of three audio LLMs, scores above their head readout on every benchmark, and, in most settings, outperforms random-head guidance. On recordings released after the models were trained, head-guided decoding raises mIoU from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56. These results suggest that poor temporal answers in audio LLMs partly reflect a failure to say rather than to hear, and that the model's own attention can close part of this gap.
authors: Jongbhin Woo, Jaewook Jeong, Joon Son Chung
bullets: The identified attention heads shift with the queried sound and follow it as it moves, while disrupting them often harms timestamp accuracy.
Intervals read directly from these heads recover events missed by the model’s original timestamps and outperform its answer.
Head-guided decoding preserves the model’s sound-presence decision and rescores candidate timestamps using attention-derived priors.
Heads selected on development data transfer to new recordings and free-text queries, improving timestamps across three audio LLMs.
On post-training recordings, mIoU increases from 0.07–0.36 to 0.48–0.56.

papers.abstract: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.
authors: Dong An, Tianyu Liu, Haoran Ding, Wen Yang, Anqing Duan, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Problem: Video world models often follow robot actions but predict inconsistent or collapsed object motion because scene dynamics and appearance are inferred together.
Method: Lift the initial frame into 3D points, predict their response to robot motion with a learned dynamics model, then render the simulated points into pixel-aligned videos for a video model.
Results: Object-motion error decreases by 8.6% and 6.2% with two DROID video renderers, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot, without reducing image quality.
The rendered video tracks the simulated dynamics: better point predictions produce better object motion, while editing points can steer the generated video.
Scope: Results are demonstrated in controlled DROID experiments and on a real bimanual robot.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.
authors: Emre U\u{g}ur, Jiawen Qi, Qinyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the prefill bottleneck of long-context attention, where accurately scoring skippable blocks can be costly.
Uses training-free, content-adaptive delta scoring with fewer anchors in redundant regions and more in heterogeneous ones.
Accelerates scoring through parallel, tile-aligned local scans, then computes selected tiles with the original vectors.
Maintains average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, including RULER up to 128K tokens.
Reports 38% lower scoring-pipeline latency than XAttention at 128K tokens and 3.3× prefill speedup over a FlashAttention-2 PyTorch baseline at 512K tokens on four H100 GPUs.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse block attention scoring for long-context LLMs; directly targets efficient attention and long-context processing.

papers.abstract: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. A blob twin blends an altered copy of a real frame with the frame itself, targeting blending artifacts. It needs no generator and no face-shaped mask. Together, these twins provide two complementary forensic cues that generalize to unseen manipulations. TwinDreaches a mean AUROC of 96.3%, 8.9 points above the prior state-of-the-art, with 98.1% on the blending datasets and 95.6% on the EFS datasets. Trained on twins alone, without a deepfake dataset, single models still reach 94.3% on average over three seeds. For reproducibility, the code, trained model, and training data are at: https://github.com/yermandy/TwinD
authors: Andrii Yermakov, Jan Cech, Mario Fritz, Jiri Matas
bullets: Existing detectors perform well on blending fakes but struggle on entire face synthesis (EFS), where blending traces are absent.
TwinD uses reconstruction twins to target neural decoder traces and blob twins to target blending artifacts, without requiring a generator or face-shaped mask.
Across 19 datasets, TwinD achieves 96.3% mean AUROC: 98.1% on blending datasets and 95.6% on EFS datasets.
Training on twins alone still achieves 94.3% mean AUROC across three seeds.
Code, trained models, and training data are publicly released.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of TwinD. (a) A twin is a fake made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is an autoencoder reconstruction with the real pixels put back inside a random grid or noise mask. A blob twin blends an altered copy of the frame with the frame itself through a blob mask. Right halves of the twins show the difference to the real frame. The traces of the autoencoder are amplified 10× for visualization. (b) Each fake is paired with the real frame it was made from. Both get the same augmentation, so they differ only by the manipulation. TwinD is a frozen PEcoreL with LoRA, trained on batches of such pairs. (c) Mean video-level AUROC (%) on the EFS and Blending datasets of Tab. 1. Gray bars show the best prior detector of each kind.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the generalization gap in deepfake detection by training on 'twins' (reconstruction and blob twins) to handle entire face synthesis, a task within video understanding and manipulation detection.
papers.title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis
papers.tldr: TwinD improves deepfake detection on unseen entire-face synthesis by training on two generator-free synthetic “twin” manipulations that capture decoder traces and blending artifacts.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis, but Gaussian rasterization attenuates fine-scale scene structure through the projected covariance of each primitive. We show that contracting these projected covariances at inference time can mitigate the effective bandwidth limitation induced by finite Gaussian footprints, motivating a multi-aperture rendering framework for super-resolution. Based on this insight, we propose AGSR (Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution), a lightweight inference-time framework that progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues. AGSR operates as a plug-in enhancement for pre-trained 3DGS models. Experiments on the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark show that AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with gains increasing as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates. The results provide evidence that covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues attenuated by native Gaussian rasterization. AGSR achieves these improvements while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.
authors: Ayman Alkhateeb, Hadi Amirpour, Christian Timmerer
bullets: Addresses fine-scale detail loss caused by the finite projected footprints of 3DGS Gaussians.
Uses progressive multi-aperture rendering with covariance contraction, uncertainty-guided feature aggregation, and transmittance/depth conditioning.
Acts as a lightweight plug-in for pre-trained 3DGS models without retraining.
Outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines on Mip-NeRF 360, with larger gains for lower-quality Gaussian representations.
Maintains real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of AGSR. Covariance contraction produces multi-aperture RGB, transmittance, and depth renderings with progressively smaller projected footprints and correspondingly higher effective bandwidth. Cross-aperture variations form a structural uncertainty field that guides a three-stage geometry-aware fusion network. Higher-bandwidth observations are fused sequentially and refined through residual PixelShuffle reconstruction to produce the final super-resolved output.

Fig. 1: Projected Gaussian covariances influence the effective bandwidth of individual rasterization kernels. By systematically contracting the covariance, AGSR generates multiaperture observations that reveal structural cues attenuated by native rasterization. The resulting uncertainty field guides geometry-aware super-resolution for enhanced detail reconstruction.

Fig. 3: Visual comparison of 2× and 4× super-resolution on 3DGS representations trained on highly subsampled images (tf = 8). AGSR exploits structural cues revealed by multi-aperture rendering to recover fine-scale detail that is poorly reproduced by degraded Gaussian representations. Quantitative metrics (PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS) are reported below each crop.

Fig. 4: Quantitative performance (PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS) of AGSR compared with native 3DGS and bicubic baselines across varying training degradation factors (tf ). As the training factor increases, the quality of the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates substantially. AGSR becomes increasingly advantageous as the underlying representation degrades, with the strongest gains observed under moderate and severe degradation, outperforming the baselines across most settings and metrics.

TABLE I: Complexity analysis of the progressive aperture fusion network. We report the parameter count, computational complexity (GMACs), and full-pipeline inference speed (FPS) in both FP32 and FP16 precisions. Parameter counts and GMACs correspond to the cumulative deployed inference model required to produce each stage’s output. FPS is evaluated targeting Full HD (1920×1080) and includes both 3DGS rasterization and network inference overhead.
TABLE II: Quantitative comparison across multiple training degradation factors (tf ). Best performance highlighted in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes AGSR, a plug-in framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses multi-aperture rendering and uncertainty-guided feature aggregation to improve super-resolution and structural fidelity.
papers.title: AGSR: Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution for Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: AGSR improves 3D Gaussian Splatting super-resolution at inference time by fusing renderings with contracted Gaussian covariances and geometric uncertainty cues.

papers.abstract: Flat color-block drafts specify layout and regional color while leaving interior detail unspecified, yet pretrained flow-based generators can preserve their flat appearance even under photorealistic prompts. We trace this behavior to a cross-scale mechanism linking fine pixel variation to regional means in variational autoencoder (VAE) latent space. Flattening photo regions systematically shifts their latent means, with offsets concentrated along a shared channel direction within each backbone. Controlled field exchanges in FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image establish the effect of this displacement on texture generation: adding the photo-derived regional mean field to a flat latent restores texture, whereas adding its complementary field alone largely preserves flatness. A second-order encoding expansion explains how encoder curvature can convert zero-mean perturbations into mean shifts. An analytically solvable conditional Gaussian flow shows how regional noise averaging enables near-unit endpoint sensitivity at high signal-to-noise ratios. This mechanism motivates training-free rendering through pixel dither before encoding, mean-field scaling, and early boundary holding. Paired low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with draft conditioning improves content recovery and produces photo-like regional means under the standard velocity objective. Explicit regional mean guidance remains effective after adaptation, continuously controlling texture and improving color fidelity. These findings connect encoding shifts to persistent generation behavior and support interventions evaluated for texture, spatial fidelity, and semantic recovery.
authors: Zihan Gu, Jiangcan Jia, Hua Zhang, Lulu Zhao
bullets: Flattening image regions changes their latent means along backbone-specific channel directions, linking fine detail to regional statistics.
Controlled latent-field swaps in FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image show that restoring photo-derived regional means restores texture, while complementary fields mostly preserve flatness.
A second-order encoder analysis and a conditional Gaussian-flow model explain how zero-mean detail and regional averaging can produce persistent mean shifts and high endpoint sensitivity.
Training-free interventions—pixel dithering, mean-field scaling, and early boundary holding—enable texture control without retraining.
Draft-conditioned LoRA improves content recovery and photo-like regional means; explicit regional mean guidance remains effective and improves texture and color fidelity.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the mechanism of texture generation in flow-based models, revealing how regional mean latents govern spatial fidelity, which is relevant to geometry-aware generation.
papers.title: Why Flat Drafts Stay Flat: Region-Mean Latents Govern Texture in Flow-Based Image Generation
papers.tldr: Regional mean shifts in VAE latents largely determine whether flat drafts remain textureless or recover photorealistic detail in flow-based image generators.

papers.abstract: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sofilyzia/Fast-JEPA.
authors: Yao Zhang, Bin Yu, Shijie Lian, Haishan Liu, Changti Wu, Yu Wu, Kai Chen
bullets: Targets the high test-time cost of comparing plans through recursive state prediction.
Builds a goal-directed plan and directly predicts complete candidate outcomes for efficient search refinement.
Achieves 96.50% average success with 2.41× faster planning than INTACT across four tasks.
Maintains competitive success and low latency across different search budgets, candidate counts, and refinement depths.
Introduces DynaGoal to test planning under distribution shifts, deadlines, and response delays; Fast-JEPA reaches 73.83% on Shift and 87.67% on Deadline.

papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in qualitative spatial reasoning, but remain limited in quantitative spatial reasoning. Current work leverages the VLM agent to invoke external vision tools to perform computation. However, these methods usually bind each functional requirement to a single predefined vision specialist, implicitly resulting in fixed and rigid tool pipelines. In practice, addressing diverse spatial scenarios and tasks demands a broader diversity in pipeline orchestration and vision specialist selection to achieve robust spatial reasoning. However, such diversity leads to a combinatorial execution space, making it challenging for the agent to orchestrate the optimal pipelines and specialists for different scenarios. In this work, we propose SpatialMem, a memory framework that enables a VLM agent to accumulate tool-use experience and leverage that memory to orchestrate vision specialists to solve the spatial reasoning problem. SpatialMem builds a two-level memory structure, with task memory capturing tool orchestration and scene memory capturing tool selection. It further introduces a dual-state trajectory optimization process to preserve successful tool experiences and refine suboptimal ones. Moreover, existing spatial reasoning benchmarks suffer from quality issues and limited coverage of scene types and tasks. To address these gap, we propose MetricBench, a benchmark covering both indoor and outdoor scenes and three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on MetricBench, Q-Spatial, and SpatilRGPT-Bench, outperforming best VLM baselines by 32% on MetricBench. Additionally, the memory design yields a 9.1% absolute gain over a memory-free agent on MetricBench.
authors: Zinan Zheng, Nuo Chen, Jia Li
bullets: Targets VLMs’ limitations in quantitative, rather than qualitative, spatial reasoning.
Uses task memory for tool orchestration and scene memory for selecting vision specialists.
Applies dual-state trajectory optimization to retain successful tool-use experiences and refine weaker ones.
Introduces MetricBench, covering indoor and outdoor scenes across three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks.
Reports state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks, with a 32% improvement over the best VLM baseline on MetricBench and a 9.1-point gain over a memory-free agent.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes SpatialMem, a hierarchical memory framework for VLMs to perform quantitative spatial reasoning by accumulating tool-use experience and orchestrating vision specialists.
papers.title: SpatialMem: Building Quantitative Spatial Reasoning Agents with Hierarchical Memory
papers.tldr: SpatialMem equips VLM agents with hierarchical memory to learn tool orchestration and selection for more robust quantitative spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: When a constraint puzzle has several correct answers, language models tend to give the same one.We study four open-weight models from three families on symbolic puzzles and multi-solution ZebraLogic variants with exactly known solution sets.Repeated samples concentrate on one default solution far beyond uniform sampling, and different models often share it.Yet models usually produce even rarely sampled solutions when added clues uniquely identify them.On held-out symbolic puzzles, we compare visiting entities in name order with visiting those with the fewest initial candidates first. Both searches try values in the stated order. Where their pre-specified predictions differ, the latter matches a larger share of responses in all four models, by 26 to 40 percentage points.Reversing the stated value order or specifying a search order shifts responses towards the solution that the new order favours, on both testbeds. Randomising the presentation or supplying a random search order raises breadth (the effective share of solutions in use) by 26 to 42 percentage points on the symbolic task and 11 to 26 on ZebraLogic. The largest observed validity losses are 3 and 4 percentage points, respectively. Randomised presentation broadens answers more than a random-choice instruction in each of the three main models.
authors: Qinhan Hou, Jing Tang
bullets: Across four open-weight models, repeated samples overproduce one solution rather than sampling uniformly, often the same solution across models.
Models can usually produce rare solutions when additional clues make them uniquely identifiable.
Searches that select entities with the fewest candidates better predict model responses than name-order searches, by 26–40 percentage points where predictions differ.
Reversing value order or specifying random presentation/search orders shifts responses and broadens solution coverage, with limited validity losses of up to 3–4 percentage points.
Randomized presentation broadens answers more than a random-choice instruction in the three main models tested.

(B) Shared defaults across model pairs (filled) and the uniform-choice level (open). (C) Free frequency (solid) and cued success (dashed) by rank: name order at B = 6 (Symbolic), free frequency at B = 4 (ZebraLogic, original runs).

Figure 2: Testing the ordered-search explanation. (A) Example: excluded cells grey; columns: remaining candidates and each procedure’s visit order; markers: first solutions, outlined if different. (B) Same requests: share matching the MRV-like minus the name-order prediction; open: gpt-oss-120b. (C, D) Change in a predicted solution’s share when the prompt reverses (C) or specifies (D) an order. Percentage points; 95% intervals.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of how search order shapes LLM default solutions on constraint puzzles; relevant to LLM reasoning behavior.
papers.title: Many Solutions, One Answer: Search Order Shapes the Default Solutions of Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models’ default answers to multi-solution puzzles are strongly shaped by the order in which search options are presented or explored.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised foundation models are often said to need fewer labels than supervised training. We test this on a forestry task: classifying 20 tree species classes in 0.2 m aerial images from the TreeSatAI dataset. We compare a frozen DINOv3 model pretrained on 493 million satellite images, with only a linear classifier trained on top, against an ImageNet ResNet-50 that is fine-tuned end to end. On the official split, fine-tuning wins clearly (macro F1 0.764 vs. 0.685). However, 28.8% of the official test patches overlap a training or validation patch, and copying the label of the nearest such patch is correct for 83.6% of them. We therefore build a spatial split that holds out whole 2 km squares with a 200 m buffer. On this split the comparison becomes inconclusive (0.648 vs. 0.640, paired 95% CI of the difference [-0.054, 0.016]), and the learning curves of the two models overlap at every label budget from 343 to 33,126 training patches. On the five rarest classes, the frozen model achieves a higher mean F1 (0.566 vs. 0.445), although the confidence interval for this difference includes zero ([-0.05, 0.23]). Diagnostics show that the frozen features mainly miss differences between closely related species, such as the two native oaks. Choosing the input size and layer on validation data (224 px, block 16) raises the frozen model to 0.662 on the spatial split. A comparison that looks decisive on the official split is thus inconclusive under geographically separated evaluation. We release the spatial split and our code.
authors: Dharani Deivasihamani, Nandakishore Puttashamachar
bullets: Studies 20-class tree-species mapping in 0.2 m aerial imagery from TreeSatAI.
Compares a frozen DINOv3 encoder with a linear classifier against end-to-end fine-tuned ImageNet ResNet-50s.
On the official split, fine-tuning scores higher, but substantial patch overlap may inflate performance.
On a spatial split with held-out 2 km squares and buffers, performance is statistically inconclusive and learning curves overlap across label budgets.
Frozen features perform better on the rarest classes but mainly confuse closely related species; validation-based input/layer selection improves them.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Official vs. spatial evaluation on TreeSatAI. (a) In the official split, test patches lie between training patches, and many overlap one (filled squares). The same 2.4 km window is shown in both maps; each square is one 60.8 m patch. (b) Our split assigns whole 2 km squares to training, validation or test, and drops patches within 200 m of a square with another role. (c) Over all 20 classes, the clear lead of the fine-tuned ResNet-50 on the official split becomes inconclusive on the spatial split. (d) On the five rarest classes, the fine-tuned model loses much more than the frozen DINOv3 model; the remaining difference on the spatial split has a confidence interval that includes zero. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals from resampling whole 2 km squares.

Figure 4. Spatial test macro F1 against the number of training patches (mean ± s.d. over 3 random class-stratified subsets; one run at 100%). Grey markers: DINOv3 trained on 50 patches per class, drawn at random or spread as far apart as possible.

papers.selection_reason: Empirically compares frozen foundation model features against fine-tuned CNNs for tree species mapping, highlighting the efficiency and data leakage issues in current evaluation splits.
papers.title: Does It Depend on the Split? Frozen Satellite Features vs. Fine-Tuned CNNs for Tree Species Mapping
papers.tldr: Fine-tuned CNNs outperform frozen satellite features on the official split, but geographically separated evaluation makes the difference inconclusive and favors frozen features for rare species.

papers.abstract: Although memory-augmented architectures have expanded the ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to process long videos, existing retrieval processes still largely rely on global semantic matching and lack state-driven temporal control, often returning fragmented or redundant evidence and failing to maintain a coherent evidence chain. To address this challenge, we propose EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent guided by self-evolving retrieval skills. EvoMem constructs a hierarchical time-indexed memory, where different types of evidence are aligned onto a unified video timeline; during retrieval, temporal cues from acquired evidence are further converted into explicit signals that constrain subsequent memory access. To address recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering, such as unclear retrieval targets, improper memory access paths, or premature stopping, EvoMem introduces retrieval skills to provide process-level guidance, enabling the agent to dynamically adjust retrieval content, memory operations, and target temporal ranges according to the current evidence state, while deciding when to stop. Furthermore, inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate skill evolution as a reward-guided policy improvement process. Each candidate skill is treated as an external policy patch, and rewards are assigned according to answer-correctness state transitions on the validation set. In this way, effective skills are accepted and low-quality skills are rejected without updating model parameters. Experiments on four long-video question answering benchmarks show that EvoMem significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 60.1% and an average improvement of 8.6 percentage points over the previous best methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-video reasoning.
authors: Yutong Guan, Meixing Shi, Haoran Sun, Bing Sun, Yuxiang Cai, Yankai Jiang
bullets: Builds a hierarchical, time-indexed memory that aligns diverse evidence along a unified video timeline.
Uses temporal cues from retrieved evidence to constrain and guide subsequent memory access.
Introduces retrieval skills that adapt search targets, memory operations, temporal ranges, and stopping decisions based on the current evidence state.
Evolves skills through reward-guided policy improvement, accepting useful policy patches without updating model parameters.
Across four benchmarks, achieves 60.1% average accuracy and an 8.6-point average gain over prior best methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall pipeline of EvoMem: hierarchical time-indexed memory construction, skill-guided retrieval over textual, interval, and visual evidence, and reward-guided active skill bank updates without modifying model parameters.

Figure 1: Motivating example of EvoMem. (a) Base VLMs suffer from redundant frames and limited context. (b) HippoMM’s textcentric semantic memory may miss fine-grained visual evidence. (c) WorldMM lacks explicit temporal control for maintaining evidence chains. (d) Skill-free retrieval lacks guidance on what to seek, where to search, and when to stop. (e) EvoMem uses self-evolving skills for time-aware memory retrieval and coherent long-video reasoning.

Table 2: Ablation of EvoMem components.
Table 3: Generalization of retrieval skill guidance under different retrieval-model configurations on Ego-R1 Bench.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces EvoMem, a memory agent for long-video reasoning that uses self-evolving retrieval skills guided by RL, addressing procedural errors in long-context video understanding.
papers.title: EvoMem: Self-Evolving Skills for Time-Aware Long Video Memory Agents
papers.tldr: EvoMem improves long-video question answering by using time-aware memory retrieval and self-evolving skills to maintain coherent evidence chains.

papers.abstract: Micro-Doppler radar enables contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but deployment robustness remains underexplored. We compared full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using subject-disjoint in-distribution cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer. Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failures. We paired DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA), to our knowledge the first application of a self-supervised image foundation backbone to radar micro-Doppler HAR. DINOv3-PiSSA ranked first among PEFT methods in every evaluated setting. Under our protocol, its Small variant matched the in-distribution accuracy of the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art using 4.5x fewer total parameters, with only 3% trainable. It surpassed a size-matched variant of that baseline in every evaluated setting, with transfer gains increasing with shift severity: 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations attributed improvements to both pretraining and adapter recipe, with the pretraining contributing most under compound shift. Code and protocol are available at https://github.com/KeryanChelouche/udoppler-ssl.
authors: Keryan Chelouche (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France, Fondation L\'eonie Chaptal, Sarcelles, France), Petr Dobias (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France), Nistor Grozavu (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France), Olivier Romain (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France)
bullets: The study evaluates full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and PEFT under in-distribution and few-shot distribution-shift settings.
Full fine-tuning fails under cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapt to cross-orientation shifts; PEFT avoids both issues.
DINOv3-PiSSA is presented as the first use of a self-supervised image foundation backbone for radar micro-Doppler HAR.
Its Small variant matches prior Base-size PEFT in-distribution accuracy with 4.5× fewer total parameters and only 3% trainable.
It ranks first among evaluated PEFT methods, with transfer gains of 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points as shift severity increases.

Transfer under the three shifts used ten labeled target examples per class, with subject-disjoint support and test sets. Full fine-tuning collapsed on cross-dataset, while frozen probing under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failure regimes.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that parameter-efficient fine-tuning of self-supervised vision backbones (DINOv3) effectively handles distribution shifts in radar micro-Doppler human activity recognition, contributing to test-time adaptation and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Self-supervised Vision Backbones Survives Distribution Shift in Radar Micro-Doppler HAR
papers.tldr: Parameter-efficient adaptation with DINOv3-PiSSA improves robustness of radar micro-Doppler HAR under age, orientation, and dataset shifts while using far fewer trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Accurately extracting and mapping road surface elements is crucial for applications such as high-definition maps, road asset management, and intelligent transportation systems. This study first provides a comprehensive review of the benchmark datasets for extracting and mapping road elements, encompassing overhead-to-perspective data, large-to-local scales, and coarse-to-fine details. Subsequently, we thoroughly review the relevant approaches for extracting road surface elements. However, we argue that existing datasets still require enhancements in semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity. To bridge these gaps, this paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset for fine-grained road surface mapping to address these shortcomings. WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of diverse Chinese highways and urban streets. It features a rich combination of MLS point clouds, associated panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, detailed vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations for road surface elements. The dataset carefully annotates 15 distinct categories of road elements, including common markings like road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, as well as 10 types of direction symbols. To our knowledge, WHU-Road3D stands as the first multimodal dataset for mapping such a comprehensive range of road surface elements, designed to facilitate cutting-edge research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction and mapping on road surfaces. Beyond these immediate applications, WHU-Road3D also provides a valuable source for hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation. The dataset, along with the code for our benchmark methods, will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}.
authors: Xiaoxin Mi, Zhen Cao, Chong Liu, Yuhao Li, Zhen Dong, Bisheng Yang, Yang Jia, Shengwu Xiong
bullets: Addresses gaps in existing datasets, including limited semantic richness, modality diversity, and scenario complexity.
Covers approximately 100 km of Chinese highways and urban streets.
Combines MLS point clouds, panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance labels.
Annotates 15 road-element categories, including boundaries, crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, and 10 direction-symbol types.
Supports research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction, road mapping, topology reasoning, map updating, and street-scene generation.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a large-scale multimodal dataset (point clouds + images) for fine-grained road surface mapping, which is a critical component for autonomous navigation and map building in embodied AI.
papers.title: WHU-Road3D: A dataset and benchmark towards fine-grained road surface mapping
papers.tldr: WHU-Road3D is a large-scale multimodal benchmark for fine-grained mapping and instance-level understanding of road surface elements.

papers.abstract: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.
authors: Linjia Kang, Binhan Jiang, Juan Yang, Zhiqin Song, Xiangsen Wu, Qionglin Ren, Jiang Liu, Zhongjiang He, Hao Sun
bullets: Addresses limited guidance for intermediate decisions and the cost of repeated planning in tool-augmented VLMs.
Uses policy learning and experience evolution, including RSPO for process-aware training and WDL for weakness-targeted demonstrations.
At inference, LAWR reuses suitable workflows for a fast path, while a ReAct-based path handles novel tasks.
Label-free feedback from execution, workflow adoption, and cost savings updates workflow memory.
Across three benchmarks, reports up to 8.0% relative improvement and up to 52.1% lower token consumption.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of StarTV-Agent. (A) ReAct-based Tool Orchestration: A shared VLM policy coordinates frozen traffic experts through task planning, tool selection, argument generation, and evidence verification. (B) Policy Learning: RSPO combines role-sensitive process and terminal advantages, while WDL provides targeted teacher demonstrations for weak tasks. (C) Inference with Experience Evolution: The agent follows a fast path by reusing suitable parameterized workflows or a slow ReAct-based path for adaptive reasoning. Label-free execution feedback guides workflow reuse and memory updates.

Figure 3 RL training diagnostics comparing StarTV-Agent (w/o WDL) with terminal-only RL. (a) Mean raw task reward during training. (b) PPO approximate KL divergence. (c–d) Validation performance on TUMTraf VideoQA and Traffic-VQA. papers.selection_reason: Tool-augmented VLM agent for traffic scenario understanding with spatial and temporal reasoning and workflow reuse, relevant to multimodal foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Generalist Meets Specialists: An Evolving Multimodal Agent with Persistent Tool Orchestration for Traffic Scenario Understanding
papers.tldr: StarTV-Agent improves traffic scenario understanding by combining adaptive tool-based reasoning with persistent workflow reuse, boosting performance while reducing token usage.

papers.abstract: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.
authors: Junyoung Hong, Minsu Kim, Jaehyun Kim, Jeonghwan Cho, Jiwoo Lee, Seon Joo Kim
bullets: Studies proactive spatial reasoning: answering whether and when a queried spatial condition becomes true as video unfolds.
Introduces ProSpace-Bench with nine object-, camera-, and scene-level reasoning tasks, plus ProSpace-Train for supervised learning.
Injects causal geometric encodings into intermediate VLM layers, uses the KV cache as spatial memory, and selects spatial tokens for efficient streaming.
Experiments show a substantial VLM–human gap, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines.
Analyzes how the model retains previously observed spatial information across viewpoint changes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Task overview of ProSpace-Bench. Bounding boxes mark target objects in object-level tasks. The blue needle in Ego Rotation indicates the camera’s viewing direction; the star in Origin Return and the cylinder in Visual Homing mark the starting position.

Figure 3. Architecture of ProSpace-VLM. A causal geometry encoder estimates 3D point maps and camera poses from incoming frames. The resulting geometric encodings are injected into visual tokens. The model reads the cache through causal attention to assess the current spatial state and decide when to respond.

Figure 4. Analysis of attention visualization. Rows below the observed frames show the decision token’s attention over cached visual tokens, placed at their 3D positions. Boxes mark each model’s response frame.

Figure 8. Analysis of object permanence. Top: target bearings decoded from decision-token states by a linear probe after the target leaves view. A and B denote different scenes. Bottom: bearing error vs. time out of view (median; shaded: 95% bootstrap confidence interval over streams).

Figure 6. Analysis of failure cases. On Object Re-finding, GPT4o [18] responds to a look-alike chair, citing its position relative to another identical coffee table. papers.selection_reason: Proposes ProSpace-VLM for proactive spatial reasoning in streaming video, combining VLMs with explicit geometric encodings for spatiotemporal understanding.
papers.title: Thinking in Streams: Proactive Spatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: ProSpace-VLM enables vision-language models to make timely spatial decisions in streaming video by maintaining geometric memory across changing viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Lifelong model editing requires continuously incorporating new facts into deployed large language models (LLMs) without expensive retraining or compromising existing capabilities. Memory-based editors offer an appealing solution by keeping the base parameters untouched, yet their practical use is hindered by linearly growing storage requirements and deteriorating retrieval performance as edits accumulate. To tackle these problems, we introduce BiSpace, a lifelong model editing framework that decouples memory retrieval from knowledge injection across two distinct representation spaces. BiSpace routes queries and identifies relevant edits in an external semantic space, while injecting the corresponding knowledge into the internal representation space of the LLM through sparse and storage-efficient updates. Extensive experiments show that BiSpace shrinks each entry's storage to only about 10.2% of the original and shows strong resilience to long edit sequences of up to 16K edits. On a more challenging benchmark, BiSpace further improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods. These results advance memory-based editing toward reliable long-term model maintenance at scale.
authors: Yue Che, Jingze Wang, Chen Guoyi, Yujie Wu, Xuming Ran, Mingkun Xu
bullets: Addresses growing storage costs and declining retrieval quality as lifelong edits accumulate.
Retrieves relevant edits in an external semantic space while injecting knowledge into the LLM’s internal representation space.
Uses sparse, storage-efficient updates while leaving base model parameters untouched.
Reduces per-entry storage to about 10.2% of the original and remains resilient through up to 16K edits.
Improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods on a challenging benchmark.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of BiSpace. Knowledge retrieval is decoupled from injection by constructing edit keys and queries in an external semantic space. Sparse codebook values reduce storage costs and are reconstructed on the fly for updates in the internal representation space.

Figure 3: Overall Performance over 10K sequential edits on ZsRE, WikiBigEdit, and CounterFact using LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. BiSpace maintains consistently higher performance as edits accumulate, with larger advantages on the more challenging WikiBigEdit and CounterFact benchmarks.

Figure 2: Layer-wise analysis of knowledge retrieval and injection in HoReN after 1,000 edits on CounterFact across two models. The primary performance bottleneck lies in memory routing rather than knowledge injection.

Figure 8: Seven representative cases for each model on WikiBigEdit. BiSpace produces the target output, while all four baselines generate incorrect or incomplete responses.
Figure 9: Seven representative cases for each model on CounterFact. BiSpace produces the target output, while all four baselines generate incorrect or incomplete responses.

Figure 6: Overall Performance on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 over up to 10K sequential edits across ZsRE, WikiBigEdit, and CounterFact. BiSpace consistently outperforms UltraEdit across different editing scales and shows a clear advantage over HoReN on the more challenging WikiBigEdit and CounterFact benchmarks.

Table 8: Unstructured knowledge editing performance after 1K sequential edits on the full UnKEBench across three backbone models. Values before/after ’/’ denote performance on exact edit prompts/paraphrases, respectively. FC. denotes Factual Correctness. papers.abstract: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.
authors: Yifan Lu, Gaoyang Guo, Wen Chen, Ziyun Zou, Jian Wu, Han Zhu, Imran Razzak
bullets: Addresses outdated or misapplied preferences caused by storing interaction content without tracking currentness or scope.
Models the user as a latent preference state updated and revealed by every interaction, including the current request.
Stores relevant beliefs with supporting evidence, scope, and status rather than raw history alone.
Uses a trained writer to produce belief records for a frozen agent.
Achieves the best results among evaluated memory systems across two agent families and two benchmarks; request conditioning improves answering, while auxiliary tasks improve tool use.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HabitusMem. It then projects only the beliefs that bear on the user query to the agent, which answers or acts on the user query. Here, the bland diet and the late-shift hospital address shape the dinner order, whereas the partner-specific vegetarian preference and the one-off oat-milk instruction are kept but not projected. A single writer learns these steps from four tasks: direct writing, state update, request projection, and action projection.

papers.abstract: Table question answering with large language models remains difficult to scale: tables range from compact to million-token sizes, while questions require precise grounding of columns, values, and computations. Existing methods often specialize in a fixed inference strategy, which is brittle across different table scales and model capabilities. Full-table reading is efficient for compact inputs but suffers from irrelevant context. Table reduction helps long inputs but depends on reliable evidence localization, while execution is required when tables exceed the model context window and remains sensitive to schema and value grounding errors. We propose TableRoute, a capability-aware routing framework with evidence-conditioned inference for scalable TableQA. TableRoute first generates validated question--table evidence and identifies the required operations, then routes each instance among these three strategies according to serialized table length and calibrated estimates of how reliably the base model handles these operations. The validated evidence supports the selected route by grounding columns, values, and conditions. Across WikiTQ, WTQ-L, BirdQA, and TableBench, TableRoute consistently improves accuracy through complementary routing and evidence conditioning across table scales, while reducing online token cost. Code will be made available upon publication.
authors: Yuxiang Wang, Junhao Gan, Jianzhong Qi

Generates validated question–table evidence and identifies required operations before inference.

papers.abstract: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.
authors: Zhengru Fang, Zehao Liu, Mingyu Tsoi, Yaoyu Zhu, Junlong Li, Fengmao Lv, Sijie Cheng, Yuanliang Sun, Fang Yang, Jun Zhang

papers.abstract: Flow matching enables high-quality image and video generation, but its iterative sampling process requires repeated evaluations of large neural networks. Existing few-step methods can distort the output and reduce its agreement with a many-step reference. We propose TrajCal, a training-free calibration framework for few-step sampling. Based on scatter search, a well-established metaheuristic for difficult optimization problems, TrajCal starts with diverse seed schedules, deforms and combines these candidates, and selects one fixed schedule by final output fidelity for reuse on new inputs. For both image and video generation, TrajCal achieves higher reference fidelity than all compared baselines at low evaluation budgets while maintaining competitive visual quality. The search is effective even with randomly generated seeds, while trajectory-based seeds further improve fidelity. For cross-style generalization, photography-calibrated schedules also improve fidelity on unseen image styles.
authors: Junchi Zhang, Zihan Gu, Jiangcan Jia, Lulu Zhao, Wenbo Su, Hua Zhang
bullets: Addresses quality degradation and reference mismatch caused by few-step flow sampling.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.
authors: Qiming Huang, Hanze Dong, Jipeng Zhang, Mike Zheng Shou, Xinxing Xu, Furu Wei
bullets: Introduces Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four medical image types with answer-relevant masks and multiple renderings.
Shows that different presentations of the same mask can substantially alter model behavior.
Finds that masks can reveal missed diagnostic evidence but also induce incorrect associations, even when the mask is correct.
Introduces TUNE, which manages evidence acquisition, presentation, and answer updates.
TUNE improves mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points for a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone across three public medical VQA benchmarks, and by 9.1 points over direct tool use across seven benchmarks.

papers.title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management
papers.tldr: Medical VLM agents need to manage how segmentation evidence is presented and whether it should change an answer—not merely acquire the right mask.

papers.abstract: Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page: https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/
authors: Runze Wang, Fei Zha, Bing He, Ke Xu, Zhongyuan Wu, Yuxuan Xie, Wenzheng Wu, Zhongyuan Liu, Youcheng Cai, Ligang Liu
bullets: Targets generative renderers that lose continuity and fail to follow evolving gameplay conditions.
Uses Dynamic-Context Learning for chunk-level interaction supervision and Recurrent History Compression to maintain continuity within a bounded token budget.
Introduces Cross-Representation Flow Alignment to support generalization across diverse scene proxies and target appearances.
Provides WorldPrism, a dataset of agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos with renderings and chunk-level annotations.
Improves reconstruction and visual quality on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench; qualitative results show sustained interactive rendering under changing prompts and references.

papers.abstract: Spurious correlations can give image predictors high in-distribution accuracy but poor generalization under distribution shift. We introduce $\textbf{Rank2Replace}$, which transfers knowledge of task-relevant evidence from pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) to small predictors through training-time augmentation for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. The VLM ranks object-centric slots by task relevance and guides rank-dependent replacement with same-rank slot embeddings from another image. This augmentation retains the original image's label, encouraging reliance on preserved task evidence as incidental cues change, and supports combination with existing OOD methods. Across four datasets and six splits under shared frozen slot embeddings, the default cross-entropy configuration reaches macro-averaged average-group and worst-group accuracies of $80.43\%$ and $65.28\%$ without environment labels or dataset-specific replacement tuning. Slot corruption improves both macro-averaged metrics for all fourteen OOD training methods. Combining it with slot ranking and IRM reaches $81.96\%$ and $72.68\%$. Controlled ablations support the ranking and replacement design, with gains across five ranking VLMs and six extractor--predictor combinations. Permutation-invariant predictors further improve both macro-averaged metrics over their unaugmented counterparts while using VLM guidance only during training for efficient inference.
authors: Bo-Han Feng, Keng-Te Liao, Shou-De Lin
bullets: A VLM ranks object-centric slots by task relevance, then replaces slots with same-rank slots from another image.
The method preserves the source label while changing incidental visual cues, encouraging predictors to use task-relevant evidence.
It works without environment labels or dataset-specific replacement tuning and can combine with existing OOD methods.
Across four datasets and six splits, the default setup achieves 80.43% macro average-group and 65.28% macro worst-group accuracy; combining ranking with IRM reaches 81.96% and 72.68%.
Benefits are observed across 14 OOD methods, five ranking VLMs, and six extractor–predictor combinations; VLM guidance is needed only during training.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a VLM-guided slot replacement method for out-of-distribution generalization, offering a novel technique for improving VLM robustness.
papers.title: Rank2Replace: VLM-Ranked Slot Replacement for Out-of-Distribution Generalization
papers.tldr: Rank2Replace uses VLM-ranked object slots to create label-preserving training augmentations that reduce reliance on spurious cues and improve OOD generalization.

papers.abstract: Industrial bin picking requires pose estimates that are accurate under clutter, partial occlusion, and the reflective, texture-less nature of manufactured parts. Most recent approaches to 6D pose estimation follow multi-stage pipelines. These achieve high accuracy, but incur memory and runtime footprints that do not cope with the operational constraints of many real-world industrial deployments. Holistic pipelines estimate poses in a single pass, with cost controlled through indiscriminate subsampling or lowered resolution. Continuing this line, we present SCCV-6D, a fully sparse multi-view RGB-D estimator. We reconstruct the 3D space at millimeter precision, prune background via a staged heatmap mechanism, and predict class, translation offset and rotation at highest resolution for an arbitrary number of objects simultaneously. Rotation is formulated as canonical coordinate voting. Points vote for their canonical object coordinates with an associated confidence, enabling closed-form pose recovery with a symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve. Along an in-cluster point recovery induced by offset votes, this removes time-consuming post-processing stages. We reuse the task-supervised attention priors from the heatmap formulation for a novel attention-gated distillation objective that reweights teacher-student feature alignment. On the IPD test split we report competitive 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene, significantly faster than the leading entries. On MV-YCB our approach reaches 96.1 ADD-S, and remains competitive even on the densely packed bins of ROBI.
authors: Nico Leuze, Samed Dogan, Maximilian Hoh, Henry Schaub, Alfred Sch\"ottl
bullets: Reconstructs millimeter-precision 3D space and uses staged heatmaps to remove background points.
Predicts object classes, translation offsets, and rotations at high resolution for multiple objects in one pass.
Uses canonical-coordinate voting with confidence-weighted, symmetry-aware Procrustes pose recovery, avoiding costly post-processing.
Introduces attention-gated knowledge distillation guided by task-supervised heatmap priors.
Reports 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene on IPD, 96.1 ADD-S on MV-YCB, and competitive performance on densely packed ROBI bins.

figures.caption: Figure 2. SCCV-6D. n RGB-D views are fused into a sparse TSDF, yielding P . Two sparse, voxel-based heatmap stages focus taskrelevant foreground regions I′, before recovering to point-level resolution Q. A shared PTv3 trunk feeds all three estimation heads. The translation votes uj naturally form clusters. Along class predictions, these gate a FiLM-conditioned canonical-coordinate head, and one single batched symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve returns 6D poses [(R̂k, t̂k)].

Runtimes of competing entries are self-reported on heterogeneous hardware and indicate a trend rather than a matched comparison.

papers.title: SCCV-6D: Sparse Canonical Coordinate Voting for Holistic Multi-View RGB-D 6D Pose Estimation in Robotic Bin Picking
papers.tldr: SCCV-6D is a fully sparse, holistic multi-view RGB-D system for fast 6D pose estimation in cluttered industrial bin picking.

papers.abstract: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which decisions they may act on unattended, and a record that explains each one. We study a small, fully specified reconciliation contract: commit the target model's greedy answer (the anchor), draw one or two greedy checks that reach the answer by a different route (an alternate prompt, or a model from another family), and let a pure function return one of five outcomes, of which only Agree is acted on. On 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, with every method given access to verbalized confidence as a tie-breaker, the main finding concerns where calls come from: pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, and a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. As complete pipelines, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples differ by less than one point, with intervals containing zero. As detectors of the anchor's errors, the contract is ahead of pooled entropy with 3 and 5 samples under both tie-breaker conventions; with 10 samples the point estimates differ by less than one point and the sign depends on the convention. Under the strict Agree gate it automates 70% of items and still acts on 16% of errors. What the contract adds is a fixed committed answer, an explicit outcome and a decision replayable from its record; generation itself was not reproducible on the hosted API.
authors: Sivakameswara Reddy Chejarla
bullets: Evaluates an anchor answer against one or two greedy checks from alternate prompts or model families using a pure five-outcome reconciliation function.
Pooling samples from another model family improves semantic-entropy error detection, while same-model temperature checks perform worst.
The three-call contract performs comparably to pooled semantic entropy as a complete pipeline and detects anchor errors better at 3–5 samples.
A strict Agree gate automates 70% of items but still acts on 16% of errors.
The hosted API did not make generation itself reproducible; only the reconciliation decision is replayable from its record.
