papers.selection_reason: Proposes auditable cross-prompt and cross-model reconciliation for LLM decisions, relevant to LLM reasoning and reliability.
papers.title: Anchor and Check: Deterministic Cross-Prompt, Cross-Model Reconciliation for Auditable LLM Decisions
papers.tldr: A deterministic reconciliation contract makes LLM decisions auditable by acting only when independently generated checks agree with a committed anchor, though it still acts on some errors.

papers.abstract: Temporal action localization (TAL) detectors must identify actions and estimate their temporal boundaries, but localization remains a major source of detection errors. While understanding what determines boundary placement requires faithful attribution of temporal evidence, existing attribution methods have not sufficiently addressed the temporal structure of TAL or the need to tailor attribution to boundary localization. We introduce a structure-aware attribution framework that averages contributions across random evidence-restoration orders following the Shapley-Shubik principle. We make it tractable by using the detector's receptive field to limit which time steps are ordered individually, and by approximating each order with a soft gradient path. For boundary predictions, we further introduce cell-structured restoration orders and boundary-anchored references that selectively remove adjacent evidence. We also adapt faithfulness evaluation to assess the joint effects of contiguous temporal evidence and the direction of boundary displacement. Experiments on THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer demonstrate improved attribution faithfulness over existing methods. Attribution analysis and controlled interventions further reveal that class-score changes do not reliably track boundary displacement, providing input-level evidence that classification relies on content less informative about boundary placement. Code and evaluation artifacts will be publicly released.
authors: Ruoshan Lan, Zongru Shao, Chieh Tsai, Mihai Surdeanu
bullets: Addresses the lack of faithful, boundary-specific explanations for temporal action localization errors.
Averages contributions over Shapley–Shubik-inspired evidence-restoration orders, restricted by the detector’s receptive field and approximated with soft gradient paths.
Uses cell-structured restoration orders and boundary-anchored references to model adjacent evidence and boundary displacement.
Introduces faithfulness evaluation for contiguous temporal evidence and directional boundary shifts.
Experiments on THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer show improved attribution faithfulness; analyses indicate class scores do not reliably reflect boundary placement.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Random-order path attribution, shared by all targets and used directly as the class map (Sec. 3.2). Its path attributions aπ are averaged over R random orders of the units into apath; the baseline is the dataset mean m. Two approximations reduce the cost: (b) only the steps in the receptive-field window Wq are ordered independently, and (c) each order is integrated along a soft path whose cost does not depend on the number of units N . (d) Each candidate uses the faster of exact forward differences and the soft path, which for the wide windows of coarse pyramid levels is the soft path.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses temporal action localization with a structure-aware attribution framework, contributing to the understanding of temporal dynamics in video.

papers.abstract: Preference training is the standard recipe for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models, and each new method reports a lower CHAIR score. We ask what that reduction consists of. Every trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes the part of the gain that comes from saying less; the remainder is compared with what a deliberately weak, frozen, eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images can reproduce. All criteria were specified in the analysis code and frozen before the outputs they judge existed. For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two thirds of what training removes beyond saying less for 7 of 8 methods on COCO, 8 of 8 on AMBER and 6 of 8 on Object HalBench, with RLAIF-V the consistent exception; a later public method released for both LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL (SENTINEL) meets the same bar on both. On our own DPO checkpoints the accounting holds on Qwen2.5-VL but fails on InternVL2.5 on COCO (2 of 4 training designs). At matched recall, the base model plus the probe beats truncation for 8 of 9 LLaVA-1.5 systems on COCO and 9 of 9 on AMBER, on the two newer backbones, and when realized as actual sentence deletion. The same measure prices training signals: DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or by an object-level CLIP score recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the beyond-brevity gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO on Qwen2.5-VL (the probe 0.73 on InternVL2.5), both beat length-matched random labels, and CLIP labels buy more than probe labels on COCO. Human judgements show that the sentences the probe deletes are wrong more often than those truncation would delete; a human check of the CHAIR evaluator's precision falls below our pre-set bar, which we report as a limitation.
authors: Lingkai Bu, Qian Gao
bullets: The study separates CHAIR improvements into reduced verbosity versus genuine hallucination reduction by matching object recall with truncated base-model captions.
A frozen, 11-feature probe trained on 500 annotated images reproduces at least two thirds of beyond-brevity gains for most evaluated methods, with RLAIF-V as the main exception.
At matched recall, the base model plus probe generally outperforms truncation across LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5, COCO, and AMBER evaluations.
Probe- or CLIP-based preference labels recover substantial portions of ground-truth-labelled DPO gains, while outperforming random labels; CLIP labels perform better on COCO.
Human checks support the probe’s deletions, but also identify insufficient precision in the CHAIR evaluator as a limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'cheap pruning' techniques in vision-language models (VLMs) to reduce object hallucinations, directly addressing efficiency (token pruning) and VLM robustness.
papers.title: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest
papers.tldr: Much of anti-hallucination training’s apparent benefit comes from shorter captions and can be replicated by a cheap post-hoc probe, though some methods and backbones retain gains beyond brevity.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
authors: Filippo Galgani, Ziwei Ji, Omri Homburger, Ganesh Jawahar, Michelle Ramanovich, Ivan Korotkov, Luciano Martins, Utku Evci, Edouard Yvinec, Pooja Consul, Vivek Kumar, Tal Schuster
bullets: Addresses the need for lightweight, accurate draft generation in speculative decoding.
Uses a shared drafting head with target activation injection, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention, and clustered vocabulary projection.
Evaluated with the Gemma 4 family, achieving reported speedups of up to 3.1× on server-side setups and 2.2× on a smartphone GPU.
Introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes that require up to 1.83× fewer target-model forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
Scope: results are reported for Gemma 4 models and the specified hardware environments.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Architecture of the optimized Multi-Token Prediction (G-MTP) module. The input to the drafter is constructed by concatenating the token embedding (𝑒(𝑥)) with the backbone hidden state (ℎ(𝐿)), both of dimension 𝑑target, and reducing to the drafter dimension 𝑑draft. The draft tokens are then propagated through the MTP layers, utilizing cross-attention against the backbone’s frozen KV Cache to bypass prefill computations before recursively triggering the next forward step. For subsequent drafting steps, the drafter’s output state is up-projected (𝑊up), concatenated with the embedding of the sampled draft token, and down-projected (𝑊down) to form the next input (Equation 3).

Across successive drafting steps, the positional encoding (𝑝1) remains constant, as the drafter repeatedly queries a static, pre-computed KV snapshot.

papers.selection_reason: Optimized multi-token prediction drafting accelerates LLM inference and reduces KV-cache memory overhead.
papers.title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
papers.tldr: G-MTP is an optimized multi-token drafter that accelerates speculative LLM decoding across server and mobile hardware while remaining efficient and adaptable under domain shift.

papers.abstract: We present FAB (Fast and Accurate Body estimation), a human body estimator that jointly improves inference efficiency and body-recovery fidelity. Rather than predicting only parametric mesh-model parameters, FAB directly predicts human skeleton joints and dense surface points. In images, it predicts dense 2D and 3D body points alongside a parametric Momentum Human Rig (MHR) head, then fits SMPL in one learned pass followed by two Gauss-Newton steps. Its ViT-L student, FAB-L, distilled from a fine-tuned SAM 3D Body, runs in real time for one person on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, from detection to a fitted body, at 4.6x the speed of SAM 3D Body's eager-PyTorch body-only path, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks. The same network predicts heel, toe, hand, and knee contacts, which connect the body to the scene. FAB also estimates world-space motion, fuses static-scene depth around the visible person, and aligns body and scene using predicted contacts. For human-to-humanoid real-to-sim transfer, an in-model G1 head and FAB-Retarget, a motion-level retargeter that reads dense points or the fitted mesh, map motion to a Unitree G1. FAB-Retarget produces references that follow the person more closely than specialized retargeters including SOMA, GMR, UMR, and OmniRetarget, and substantially more closely than Fast SAM 3D Body retargeted with our sequence IK. Project page: https://www.jinkuncao.com/FAB.
authors: Jinkun Cao
bullets: Predicts dense 2D/3D body points and an MHR representation, then fits SMPL with one learned pass and two Gauss–Newton steps.
FAB-L runs from detection to fitted body 4.6× faster than SAM 3D Body’s eager-PyTorch body-only path on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks.
Estimates foot, hand, and knee contacts to align the body with static scene geometry and support world-space motion recovery.
FAB-Retarget transfers motion to a Unitree G1 using dense points or fitted meshes, producing closer-following references than several specialized retargeters and an IK-based SAM 3D Body pipeline.

papers.abstract: Organizations monitor their workers' activity for insider threats, in which workers misuse their legitimate access, by copying confidential files before leaving. Detectors score how unusual each day of activity is, flagging the most unusual for an analyst to review. Prominent current approaches use opaque neural networks, so explanations of a flag point to internal features: patterns of neuron activity most active on days of misuse. We audit such explanations for language-model detectors trained on CERT's simulated workplace logs. To test an explanation, we see what happens to the detector's score when we remove its features inside the model. We compare this to a control: a change that is as similar as possible to the removal, but without actually removing the features. Because defining "similar" requires choosing a metric, our central contribution is the tipping radius: a first-order prediction of how far that metric must move before the difference between removal and control disappears, a measure of how fragile the result is to that choice. In 33 of 34 runs of seven language models, the tipping radius is at most 18% of the distance between two standard choices of metric. Moving that far removes at least 58% of the difference or reverses it, while random moves of the same size leave it largely intact. The result replicates in thirteen of fourteen pre-declared primary runs on openly released models, though on our trained detectors the difference is often too small to measure. We also find that a flag's score partly reflects who the worker is, not what they did, and that the features named depend on whom they are compared against. Audits should therefore fix the control's metric in advance, report its tipping radius, and disclose that comparison.
authors: Suramya R. Angdembay
bullets: The study audits explanations that identify internal neuron features behind anomalous workplace-activity flags.
It introduces the tipping radius, estimating how much a control metric must change before the explanation’s apparent effect disappears.
Across 33 of 34 runs involving seven language models, small metric changes—at most 18% of the distance between two standard metrics—removed or reversed much of the explanation effect.
The findings replicated in 13 of 14 pre-declared runs on open models, while effects were often too small to measure in the authors’ trained detectors.
Flag scores partly reflect worker identity, and identified features vary with the comparison group; audits should predefine and disclose the control metric and tipping radius.

papers.tldr: Explanations from language-model insider-threat detectors are often fragile because their apparent importance depends strongly on the chosen comparison metric and reference worker.

papers.abstract: Multimodal safety guards increasingly generate rationales alongside safety predictions, yet whether these rationales are reliable remains largely unexplored. We systematically study *rationale hallucination* from two perspectives: visual rationale hallucination, where rationales contain unsupported visual facts, and safety attribution hallucination, where grounded content is assigned an incorrect safety interpretation. Across rationale-generation methods, multiple vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, we find that rationale hallucination is widespread and does not consistently diminish with higher classification accuracy or increased model scale. Further analysis of the Think-with-Image paradigm shows that hallucination is concentrated in fine-grained attributes and relations, while visual tools are often invoked infrequently or without sufficient spatial focus. Based on these findings, we propose *Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning* (TCG-RL), which rewards tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference. TCG-RL substantially reduces rationale hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance. By revealing the gap between prediction correctness and rationale reliability, our study motivates a shift in multimodal safety guarding from outcome-only evaluation toward safety decisions that are both accurate and verifiably grounded.
authors: Yingshuo Wang, Weixiang Zhao, Guancheng Li, Jiahe Guo, Yu Zhang, Yanyan Zhao
bullets: Rationale hallucination includes unsupported visual facts and incorrect safety interpretations of grounded content.
Hallucination remains common across generation methods, vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, even with higher classification accuracy or model scale.
Fine-grained attributes and relations are especially problematic; visual tools are often underused or lack sufficient spatial focus.
Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning (TCG-RL) rewards tool use only when it improves grounding over a tool-free reference.
The findings support evaluating safety guards for both prediction accuracy and verifiable rationale grounding.

papers.title: When Safety Rationales Hallucinate: Diagnosing and Grounding Multimodal Safety Guards
papers.tldr: Multimodal safety guards can produce accurate predictions with hallucinated rationales, but contrastive reinforcement learning that rewards useful tool grounding substantially improves rationale reliability without sacrificing safety performance.

papers.abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10{\deg} off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.
authors: Wai Ka Sun, Waiyiu Pong, Bowen Wang
bullets: A collision-free route can still fail when the robot approaches a stair or ledge with the wrong position or heading.
A 27-minute teaching session records one successful crossing for each terrain transition as reusable route events.
Before each transition, an entry gate triggers turning or backing up when the robot is more than 10 cm or 10° from the taught approach.
Under localization noise, compliant crossings increased from 24.1% to 88.6%; simulation and real-robot tests also showed improved recovery and reliable completion.
The method was demonstrated over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain, with six autonomous successful runs in competition.

papers.abstract: Routing states in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps. If changing routing also changes a model's step-level verification judgment, it is tempting to conclude that the judgment follows what routing encodes. We test this inference with RouteVerify, a controlled intervention study that replaces selected internal activations from one solution trace with activations from another, while keeping the evaluated input unchanged. Across nine MoE checkpoints, we compare three intervention interfaces: router logits, MoE outputs, and post-MoE residual states. We vary the layers and token positions at which activations are replaced. We measure changes in a verification margin that quantifies the model's preference for INCORRECT over CORRECT. We also evaluate the same input with activations from correct versus erroneous steps to test whether the resulting judgment depends on the source step's correctness. We report four linked results. First, probes on router logits separate correct from erroneous steps in eight checkpoints (AUROC 0.80-0.88). Second, replacing router logits across all routed layers changes the judgment in all nine checkpoints, and by more than a norm-matched random replacement. Third, this change rarely depends on whether the source step is correct. At one layer, routing from erroneous steps and from correct steps produces indistinguishable margins in all nine checkpoints. Under all-layer routing, their difference is resolved and positive in only one. Fourth, the same difference is positive for local residual replacements in eight of nine checkpoints, so the measure does detect such dependence where it exists. Correctness is therefore readable from routing, and routing replacements move the judgment, but the movement rarely follows correctness.

Replacing router logits changes verification margins in all nine checkpoints, more than norm-matched random replacements.
The judgment change usually does not depend on whether replacement activations came from correct or erroneous steps.
Local residual interventions reveal correctness dependence in eight of nine checkpoints, showing the measure can detect it when present.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates routing mechanisms in mixture-of-experts models using controlled interventions to understand step-level verification, contributing to the understanding of LLM architectures and interpretability.
papers.title: RouteVerify: Routing Interventions for Step-Level Verification in Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.tldr: RouteVerify shows that although MoE routing encodes step correctness and affects verification judgments, routing interventions rarely transfer correctness-dependent judgments.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.
authors: Youngwoo Shin, Jongsuk Kim, Junmo Kim
bullets: SFT can make VideoLLMs rely on textual regularities instead of video evidence, even when in-distribution accuracy improves.
VETO intervenes in the fine-tuning update rather than defining or filtering shortcut-related data.
It identifies the subspace occupied by text-only inputs and projects updates onto its orthogonal complement.
Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves in-distribution SFT gains and improves performance on six shifted-distribution benchmarks.
The method is designed to ground answers in the full video-text input, though its scope is evaluated on the reported models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.
authors: Hao Wu, Sipeng Chen, Jingwen Fu, Yuwang Wang
bullets: Diffusion language models can decode multiple tokens in parallel, but quality often drops when denoising steps are reduced.
CaRR is a training-free framework for improving outputs from a fixed editable checkpoint within the existing edit schedule.
Token Commitment Remasking refills selected replacements using updated context, while Submission Commitment Recovery rescues supported candidates that fail output requirements.
Experiments in code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent accuracy gains across four inference budgets, especially under tight budgets.
At one-eighth of the full budget, CaRR raises six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 percentage points, including 11.37 on MBPP and 10.05 on MBPP+.

papers.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.
authors: Yajie Qi, Wei Wei, Lin Li, Lijun Zhang, Jianye Hao
bullets: Addresses sparse rewards, long horizons, and inconsistent goals from prompt-only language-model guidance.
Introduces CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset built from Craftax-Classic interaction trajectories.
Uses offline KLTDPO fine-tuning to align the VLM with goal preferences, followed by online goal-guided RL.
The method collects diamonds earlier and achieves the highest score and reward in experiments.
It attains the highest success rates on most achievements; results are scoped to Craftax-Classic.

papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA
authors: Jiaming Liu, Linghe Kong, Guixu Zhang, Huaxi Huang
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and poor failure recovery in pipeline-style 3D visual grounding agents.
Uses a semantic anchor for optical-flow tracking and VLM-based local verification.
Uses a geometric anchor for voxelization and multi-keypoint projection to reason over 3D space.
The two anchors exchange information in a closed-loop tool-calling process to select subsequent perception-action steps.
Achieves 73.6% Acc@0.25 on ScanRefer and 70.4% overall accuracy on Nr3D in zero-shot evaluation.

papers.abstract: Revising every answer from a long-term memory can consume substantial inference budget and damage facts that were already correct. We introduce MemMend, a modular selective revision framework that routes potentially incomplete answers to an editor, represents corrections as bounded exact-text replacements, and accepts only edits with resolvable source coordinates and valid edit operations. The editor preserves the current answer when no legal repair is proposed; accepted edits require no additional semantic-verification call. On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, MemMend achieves 67.17 conversation-macro F1 and 88.35 mean Judge score, improving over a verified revision chain by 0.82 and 1.24 points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls. Routing uses 54.15% fewer revision calls than ungated local review, with similar F1 but a 0.67-point lower Judge score. Applied directly to native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, the editing interface raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points. It outperforms same-gate rewriting and saves 49.85-83.72% of editing calls relative to ungated editing, which retains higher F1 in this adaptation. A source-by-editing factorial supports local editing for F1 but leaves an independent quality benefit from source obligations unresolved. Transfer to 451 LongMemEval-V2 Small questions also favors revision efficiency, while an external PerLTQA dialogue subset reveals a completeness gap. These results support selective editing as a reusable quality-cost operating point.
authors: Sheng Shi, Geng Li
bullets: Targets the cost and risk of revising every answer, which can damage already-correct facts.
Routes uncertain answers to an editor that performs bounded exact-text replacements with valid source coordinates and legal edit operations.
On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, it improves over a verified revision chain by 0.82 F1 and 1.24 Judge points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls.
Direct editing improves native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, with gains of 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 F1 points, respectively.
Results support selective editing as an efficient quality–cost tradeoff, but show a completeness gap on an external PerLTQA subset and unresolved source-obligation effects.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.
authors: Yukun Dai, Tianshi Wang, Fengling Li, Jingjing Li, Xin Li, Lei Zhu
bullets: Targets world action models with one shared ℓ∞-bounded (4/255) perturbation across frames, tasks, and camera views.
Across eight models on LIBERO and RoboTwin, the attack drives task success near zero and shifts actions toward the chosen target; control attacks cause little target-direction shift.
Restoring future tokens removes 61–94% of the targeted effect in five models, while constrained attacks can make current-frame tokens more important.
Restoring only 0.36% of FFN neurons in layers 10–29 removes 72–96% of the effect in six models.
Low-energy residual directions can still be critical: removing directions 2–16 cancels most of the targeted effect despite containing only 11–18% of shift energy.

Bottom: three analyses intervene at the sites b–d and measure the remaining targeted effect T ′. (b) For one token group, we restore clean K/V in the attacked run or inject attacked K/V into the clean run. (c) For the top-k FFN neurons ranked by SteerTrace, we restore clean activations in the attacked run or inject attacked activations into the clean run. papers.selection_reason: Targeted attack and internal tracing for world action models; directly relevant to world-model safety and VLA action prediction.
papers.title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
papers.tldr: SteerTrace shows that tiny universal perturbations can reliably steer world action models toward attacker-chosen actions and identifies the internal tokens, neurons, and residual directions responsible.

papers.abstract: In recent years, GPUs have incorporated increasingly specialized support for low-precision computation, from Hopper's FP8 to Blackwell's FP4 Tensor Cores. Precision formats have evolved alongside this hardware, from MXFP4 and NVFP4 on Blackwell to E2M1 FP4 with direct UE5M3 block scaling on Vera Rubin, which we term as $\boldsymbol{VRFP4}$. These advances help serve larger language models at lower cost, but four-bit activation quantization can substantially degrade model quality. We introduce VR-SparseQuant, which uses Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 sparsity to recover accuracy while retaining native FP4 execution. By allowing two sparse streams to overlap, we use the same FP4 value budget as dense quantization to refine activations with larger errors. Offline scale-ratio calibration avoids runtime search, while a shared-weight GEMM accumulates both streams efficiently. On Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, VR-SparseQuant reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from $\boldsymbol{6.85}$ to $\boldsymbol{5.57}$ versus dense RTN W4A4. Including activation preparation, our native Rubin kernels for VRFP4 achieve up to $\boldsymbol{3.1\times}$ GEMM and $\boldsymbol{2.7\times}$ MoE speedup over BF16. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of adaptive activation quantization using Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 structured sparse FP4 instructions.
authors: Samir Khaki, Wei-Chen Wang, Song Han, Ryan Hanrui Wang
bullets: Addresses quality degradation from four-bit activation quantization for large-language-model inference.
Uses overlapping sparse streams to refine high-error activations without increasing the FP4 value budget.
Applies offline scale-ratio calibration and shared-weight GEMM accumulation to avoid runtime search and improve efficiency.
On Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, lowers WikiText-2 perplexity from 6.85 to 5.57 versus dense RTN W4A4.
Native VRFP4 kernels achieve up to 3.1× GEMM and 2.7× MoE speedups over BF16, including activation preparation.

papers.abstract: DeepStack-style vision-language models feed visual tokens to the language model at its input, and again at deeper layers. We call these the main entry and the later entries. What do the later entries add when the model already has the image? We give the entries versions that differ in one object's color and see which one the answer follows. On photographs, the original DeepStack follows the later entries, while Qwen3-VL-8B/32B follow the main entry. Does weakening the main entry give the later features more influence? On synthetic images, we keep this conflict and reduce color saturation at the main entry only. The unchanged later features gain a stronger effect on the relative scores of the two colors, in all four models, including Granite Vision. This holds even under mild desaturation, when accuracy without the conflict stays at 100%. To test whether later features can also correct errors, we degrade both entries and restore only the later ones. The same blur costs both Qwen models 50 percentage points of accuracy on stripe orientation. The 32B model recovers 48 points and the 8B model only 8. Accuracy with one clean entry predicted which entry each model can lose, and five of six tested predictions held on new GQA attribute questions. With the other entry zeroed, Qwen3-VL-8B loses only 0.3 points on its main entry alone, and DeepStack at most 3.45 points on either entry alone. In split inference on these questions, DeepStack can then send only its main-entry features at higher precision. This takes 49% fewer bytes than all entries at a shared precision, at similar accuracy.
authors: Yucheng Du, Yi Nian, Ruixue Lian, Yue Zhao, Xiyang Hu
bullets: The study compares conflicting object-color information placed in the main input entry versus later-layer entries.
On photographs, DeepStack follows later entries, whereas Qwen3-VL-8B/32B follows the main entry.
Reducing saturation only at the main entry increases the influence of unchanged later features across four models, even when normal accuracy remains 100%.
When both entries are blurred and only later features are restored, Qwen3-VL-32B recovers 48 of 50 accuracy points, while the 8B model recovers 8.
Entry-specific influence predictions generalize to most tested GQA attribute questions, enabling DeepStack split inference with 49% fewer bytes at similar accuracy.

papers.abstract: Human proficiency estimation is challenging because skill is a high-level and often subjective property that is not captured by action identity alone. Existing approaches leverage multimodal observations such as ego-exo video, gaze, pose, and inertial signals, but the gap between sensor-level evidence and abstract proficiency labels remains difficult to bridge. We present SkillLens, a proficiency estimation framework that uses atomic action descriptions as temporal guidance, rather than direct semantic supervision, to localize proficiency-relevant windows for dense visual-dynamics extraction. Each window is summarized into an action-dynamics feature and scored by a high-low prototype margin against higher- and lower-proficiency executions from the same activity-action category. Fusing these ego/exo PDM cues with a global ego-exo-gaze baseline through CORAL ordinal calibration, our method achieves 0.542 accuracy on Ego-Exo4D. Our project page is available at https://skill-lens.net/
authors: Deokhyun Ahn, Hyukjin Kim, Jae-Ho Han, Bumsub Ham, Heeseung Choi, Ig-Jae Kim, Haksub Kim
bullets: Targets the gap between multimodal sensor observations and abstract proficiency labels.
Uses temporal action guidance to localize proficiency-relevant windows for dense visual-dynamics extraction.
Scores window features via margins between higher- and lower-proficiency executions within the same activity-action category.
Fuses ego/exo visual-dynamics cues with global ego-exo-gaze features using CORAL ordinal calibration.
Reports 0.542 accuracy on Ego-Exo4D; the abstract does not specify limitations beyond the task’s inherent subjectivity.

papers.abstract: We enable accurate low-bit recovery from small synthetic pools by improving both image synthesis and student preparation. A grid with lower local response error can incur greater error in the student's block context. Functional Grid Calibration (FGC) selects activation scales and integer offsets against full-precision responses constructed from the student's current block input. With weights fixed during calibration, FGC evaluates candidates only at their consuming operators, bringing block context to calibration at nearly local-scoring cost. For DeiT and ViT, progressive inversion updates the same images through increasingly deep teacher prefixes. With 1,000 images, the complete pipeline exceeds MimiQ's reported accuracy in all 18 W4A4/W5A5 settings across nine backbones. With 256 images, DeiT-S and ViT-S reach 68.20% and 66.90% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at W4A4 in 26-27 minutes on one RTX 5090. The pipeline outperforms strengthened 1K-image MimiQ by 13.03 and 24.36 percentage points at lower preparation cost and the same recovery-update count. The same low-budget checkpoints retain their advantage on ImageNetV2.
authors: Haowen Hua, Sen Lin, Yaokun Huang, Zeyi Shao, Hao Zhang, Wei Sui, John See, Zeyd Boukhers, Cong Yang
bullets: Targets accurate W4A4/W5A5 recovery when only synthetic calibration data is available.
Functional Grid Calibration selects activation scales and integer offsets using full-precision responses from the student’s current block input.
Progressive inversion refines the same synthetic images through increasingly deep DeiT/ViT teacher prefixes.
With 1,000 images, the pipeline surpasses reported MimiQ accuracy across all 18 settings and nine backbones.
With 256 images, it achieves 68.20% top-1 on DeiT-S and 66.90% on ViT-S at W4A4; gains also persist on ImageNetV2.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.
authors: Aryan Jain, Abhishek Jha, Anish Nediyanchath, Promod Yenigalla
bullets: Addresses the limitation of memories that record what happened but not how experiences shape user behavior.

Projects event-as-edge knowledge into relational embeddings to transfer insights across users and infer missing knowledge for cold-start users.
Reports gains on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, and LongLaMP, including cross-user improvements at 5% graph sparsity.

papers.abstract: Multimodal image fusion traditionally generates a single fused image from paired observations at a specific viewpoint, limiting comprehensive scene perception and adaptability to diverse perceptual objectives. To overcome these limitations, we present LIFT, a novel framework for our proposed language-controlled 3D image fusion (L3D-IF) paradigm that extends multimodal image fusion from 2D images to free-viewpoint 3D scenes, enabling language-guided fusion tailored to diverse perceptual objectives. First, LIFT formulates Semantic Modality Binding (SMB), which interprets language instructions to identify semantic targets and their associated modality preferences and grounds these targets in corresponding regions of a shared Gaussian scene, establishing persistent semantic-to-spatial correspondences for consistent fusion control across viewpoints. Second, Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance (LCGA) is developed to achieve scene-wide multimodal appearance modeling by combining adaptive multimodal blending with language- and viewpoint-conditioned appearance refinement, enabling spatially adaptive realization of diverse fusion appearances while preserving source fidelity at pure-modality endpoints. Finally, we construct a Multi-View Language-Supervision (MVLS) dataset that associates language instructions and calibrated viewpoints with modulated fused images, providing effective supervision for learning instruction-dependent fusion from finite multi-view observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIFT achieves coherent multimodal fusion across continuous viewpoints, accurate semantic target localization, and consistent regional fusion control under diverse language instructions.
authors: Jingning Tian, Hao Zhang, Yumin Huang, Zizhuo Li, Xingyu Jiang, Erdun Zhao, Jiayi Ma
bullets: Addresses the limitations of single-view fusion by supporting coherent fusion across continuously varying viewpoints.
Uses Semantic Modality Binding to map language-described targets to spatial regions and preferred modalities in a shared Gaussian scene.
Uses Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance for adaptive, viewpoint- and language-dependent fusion while preserving pure-modality source fidelity.
Introduces the Multi-View Language-Supervision dataset with language instructions, calibrated viewpoints, and corresponding fused images.
Experiments show accurate target localization and consistent regional fusion control under diverse instructions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on visual feedback throughout manipulation, making them vulnerable to persistent texture attacks. However, optimized patterns can stand out from their surroundings, making an attack easier to notice and its carrier more likely to be inspected or removed. To address this limitation, our key insight is to search the structured image distribution of a diffusion model for natural-looking textures while using closed-loop feedback to identify task-disruptive candidates. Based on this idea, we propose DMT-Attack, a gradient-free gray-box attack that generates textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths. A frozen text-conditioned diffusion model defines the search space, and an eight-expert latent proposal network is initialized from evaluated teacher latents and refined using rollout feedback. We evaluate DMT-Attack against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. DMT-Attack achieves a macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (cASR) of 57.9%, compared with 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures. It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45% versus 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior.
authors: Jun Xia, Shangwen Wang, Jun Ma, Ruichao Ren, Zhouyang Jia, Xin Zhao, Huijun Liu, Jie Yu
bullets: Targets the vulnerability of VLA policies that continuously depend on visual feedback during manipulation.

Evaluated on pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites, achieving 57.9% cASR versus 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures.
Produces higher scene similarity and a lower detector flag rate than optimized patch baselines, motivating defenses that assess appearance and task behavior jointly.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images and videos, but every sampling step requires a full network evaluation. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing or forecasting network outputs across steps, but common approaches use per-model calibrated skip criteria or maintain per-layer prediction histories. We present D3-Cache, which applies Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to Diffusion sampling: it fits DMD to a short history of exact velocities and forecasts only the velocity that the scheduler consumes. A horizon-aware gate decides when to skip: whenever the network is evaluated, its output is compared with the forecast for that step, and the larger the error, the sooner the network is evaluated again, up to a cap on consecutive skipped steps. D3-Cache requires no training or per-model offline calibration curve and adds negligible memory. It shares one history length and risk tolerance across the four evaluated models. On four state-of-the-art image and video models, D3-Cache achieves speedups of 2.6-3.8x with high fidelity to the base model output.
authors: Yanbo Li, An Xiang, Xiaoxin Hu, Feng Wang, Cheng-zhong Xu, Kejiang Ye, Xitong Gao
bullets: Targets the cost of full network evaluation at every diffusion sampling step.
Fits Dynamic Mode Decomposition to a short history of exact velocities and forecasts the next scheduler-consumed velocity.
Uses a horizon-aware error gate to determine when to reevaluate the network, with a cap on consecutive skips.
Requires no training or per-model offline calibration and adds negligible memory.
Across four image and video models, reports 2.6–3.8× speedups with high fidelity to base outputs.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of D3-Cache. (a) After warmup, each sampling step either runs a full evaluation or reuses a DMD forecast of the velocity. The estimated risk grows with the horizon since the last full evaluation; exceeding τ or reaching the skip cap S triggers a refresh. papers.abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.
authors: Xudi Ge, Yepeng Liu, Haifeng Liu, Enze Shi, Liangqi Zhang, Yongchao Xu
bullets: Addresses action drift caused by illumination changes despite unchanged physical states.
VASE estimates visual action reliability from a frozen policy’s sensitivity to illumination perturbations.
TACE compares predicted and measured touch during execution to detect discrepancies.
Combines visual reliability and tactile discrepancies to gate bounded corrections for unexecuted actions.
Trained only in normal lighting, it achieves 87.5% success under normal and 73.8% under challenging unseen lighting across four real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/VC-VQA.
authors: Jiatong Ma, Yuchen Liu, Longteng Guo, Yichen Yuan, Yuze Wu, Dongze Hao, Ru Zhen, Yanhao Zhang, Haonan Lu, Jing Liu
bullets: Models must use visual evidence both before and after knowledge retrieval, including identifying clues, retrieving images, and localizing or verifying matched knowledge.
The benchmark distinguishes internal versus external images and provides traceable textual and visual evidence in a controlled multimodal knowledge base.
Twenty-one MLLMs are evaluated across no-knowledge, provided-evidence, knowledge-base retrieval, and open-web search settings.
Results show that vision-centric reasoning remains difficult, with fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition as the main bottleneck.
Agentic retrieval suggests benefits from multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context-goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.
authors: Kai Shi, Shiqi Zhao, Zimo Li, Hairong Qu, Hongyu Ma, Yongsong Yang, Jiahao Ai, Ziran Yin, Peng Yin
bullets: Addresses the gap between local latent reachability and persistent, task-level execution.
Uses a frozen LeWorldModel with a proposer for intermediate targets and CompassFlow to search trajectory-prior actions under limited evaluation budgets.
Adds patch-token spatial feedback and observation-based memory for phase transitions and bounded recovery.
State-indexed targets enable cross-episode context-goal composition.
Achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach on 1,000 TEST Cube trials; predictive ranking improves matched PushT success from 4.7% to 44.9% and TwoRoom from 33.8% to 77.7%.

papers.abstract: Given past images and known actions, visual continuation generates future frames from one evolving scene state. Keeping this state revisable matters when an object reappears or a later view changes an earlier interpretation. Once past images cannot be replayed, a summary sufficient for current rendering can lose candidates needed after correction. We establish matching sparse and dense bounds on the bits needed for later correction under stable observations and bounded disagreement. For static streams at the stated smoothness and margin scales, correction incurs at least logarithmic overhead in one dimension and polynomial overhead in higher dimensions. Coherent Archive Memory (CAM) stores geometric summaries with exact updates under clipped expansion and coordinate assignments, then uses historical existence constraints to select one state for all requested frames. Exhaustive photographic tests show strict worst-truth image-risk gains from joint witnesses, while controlled neural continuations recover positions hidden in the current view.
authors: Xiyang Zhang, Yuanhe Tian, Hongzhi Wang, Yan Song
bullets: Correction requires extra memory because render-sufficient summaries may discard plausible past explanations.
Theoretical bounds show logarithmic correction overhead in 1D and polynomial overhead in higher dimensions under stated assumptions.
Coherent Archive Memory stores geometric summaries and updates them exactly using clipped expansion and coordinate assignments.
Historical existence constraints select a single state consistently across requested frames.
Photographic and neural continuation tests show improved worst-case image risk and recovery of currently hidden positions.

papers.abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.
authors: Jiayi Chen, Lizhe Chen, Yujia Chen, Shihan Dou, Ming Zhang, Chendi Ge, Shiguang Ni, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang, Maxm Pan
bullets: Measures compaction by inserting compression points into successful agent trajectories and evaluating continued task completion.
Uses controlled retention ratios with an iterative adjustment procedure for fair comparison across compactors.
Covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks.
Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, but aggressive compaction still causes substantial accuracy degradation.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction in long-horizon agent tasks, a form of memory management at inference time.
papers.title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
papers.tldr: CompAct-Bench evaluates how well LLM agents compress working context without harming completion of long-horizon tasks, finding that compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models.

papers.abstract: Early interactions can reveal physical properties that later observations no longer show. These properties can still gov- ern the effects of future actions. Inspired by the distinction between retention and selective readout in working mem- ory and cognitive science, we introduce LATER, an action- conditioned world model built on CF-JEPA. LATER stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories that remain fixed during candidate rollouts. A response bridge queries these memories using the current state and candidate action, while multi-cut auxiliary supervision trains the memory writ- ers. On distracted Two-Stage PushT, LATER raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA. In a separate comparison across six models and two scratch- training seeds, LATER achieves the lowest mean physical readout error in both clean and distracted views, reducing along-push mean absolute error (MAE) under distractors by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA. Controlled history interventions show that later predictions depend on earlier physical evi- dence even when query observations and actions are fixed, with larger effects during pushing than waiting.
authors: Zihan Zhou, Wenxi Xu, Qilin Wang, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses the problem of physical properties becoming unobservable in later frames while still affecting future actions.
Stores completed transitions in fixed, partitioned memories and uses a response bridge to retrieve evidence based on the current state and candidate action.
Trains memory writers with multi-cut auxiliary supervision within a CF-JEPA-based world model.
On distracted Two-Stage PushT, improves terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA.
Achieves the lowest mean physical readout error across six models and two seeds, reducing distractor-induced along-push MAE by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA.

papers.tldr: LATER improves predictive world models by retrieving early physical evidence conditioned on future actions, helping preserve properties hidden by later observations.

papers.abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.
authors: Yanjing Li, Sheng Xu, Baochang Zhang, Xianbin Cao, Yawei Li
bullets: Targets the storage and computation costs of full-precision latent reasoning in VLMs.
Dynamics-Guided Quantization preserves rotary-key structure to reduce distortions in vision-language information retrieval.
Dynamics-Preserving Distillation aligns latent thoughts, readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher.
On ScienceQA-IMG using Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM reaches 90.43% accuracy.
Reports 16.64× fewer bit-operations and 6.40× lower measured latency than explicit chain-of-thought.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware quantization and distillation framework for efficient chain-of-thought reasoning in Vision-Language Models.
papers.title: Efficient Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language Model via Dynamics-Aware Quantization and Distillation
papers.tldr: QL-VLM makes latent chain-of-thought reasoning in vision-language models more efficient by combining dynamics-aware 4-bit quantization with distillation to preserve reasoning quality.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.
authors: Zhihao Liu, Zixiong Guo, Shuo Shao, Yu He, Wenli Wang, Meihui Chen, Di Wang, Yuke Hu
bullets: Addresses privacy risks in remote LLM inference, where sensitive user queries are exposed to the service provider.
Hides the real query among dummy queries and randomly shuffles the set before server-side inference.
Uses shared-prefix transformer KV-cache reuse to reduce the efficiency cost of processing augmented queries.
Evaluated on classification, generation, and QIA, EIA, and GPT-based privacy attacks.
Reports strong inference-time privacy, near-plaintext utility, and improved inference efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference method that reuses shared-prefix KV caches to improve efficiency while maintaining privacy.
papers.title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
papers.tldr: DP-SPD protects LLM queries by mixing them with client-generated dummy queries, shuffling them, and reusing shared-prefix KV caches to preserve utility and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies must react while visual inference is still running. Overlapping computation and execution reduces waiting, yet leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected. We present CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller that aligns perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction with actual robot execution. Rather than forecasting pixels or physical states, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history, supervised through action-sensitive distillation to retain the frozen expert's control response. Conditioned on this updated memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training. On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA reaches 93.8% success at 5.04$\times$ inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness.
authors: Xu Pan, Chubin Zhang, Xingrui Yu, Runmin Lan, Zihao Wang, Wenkai Guo, Bofang Jia, Bo An, Ziwei Wang
bullets: Addresses stale visual memory and disconnected action chunks caused by overlapping perception and execution.
Uses a Causal Latent World Model to predict current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history.
Applies action-sensitive distillation to preserve the frozen expert’s control behavior.
Uses Predictive Flow Warm-Starting for single-step correction of the remaining action horizon without additional training.
On LIBERO-10, achieves 93.8% success with 5.04× inference throughput, alongside improved robustness and motion smoothness.

papers.abstract: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Chenyuan Zhou, Chaoyi Huang, Zibo Wang, Zhiyuan Li, Yong-Lu Li
bullets: Addresses cross-tool manipulation by identifying geometric features shared across tools with similar functions.
Uses an embodied agent to reconstruct demonstrations in simulation, form and test affordance hypotheses, and refine extraction skills.
Encodes discovered functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone for training and inference.
Builds a reusable affordance-extraction skill library for unseen tools.
Achieves 86.1% simulated cross-tool trajectory-retargeting success and improves real-robot task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$ across three tasks.

papers.abstract: Machine translation with large language models requires both high translation quality and low generation latency. Accelerating translation while preserving quality is therefore essential for practical deployment. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate tokens at arbitrary target positions through iterative denoising, offering a new paradigm for parallel translation beyond sequential autoregressive decoding. However, existing methods still incur redundant computation: fixed target generation lengths waste computation on unused positions, while confidence-only commitment delays medium-confidence tokens whose predictions have largely stabilized. To address these issues, we propose TRAC, a training-free adaptive decoding method for diffusion machine translation. TRAC adapts the target generation length using source length and translation direction, with a conservative fallback to the maximum length for empty or unusually short outputs. It preserves high-confidence commitment while identifying temporally stable medium-confidence tokens for early commitment using cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-$K$ distributions. On bidirectional Chinese-English translation across FLORES-200, WMT23, and NTREX-128, TRAC reduces model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and achieves sentence-level generation speedups of 1.91 to 2.19 times over Fast-dLLM, with only a 0.02-point decrease in macro-average COMET. These results demonstrate that adaptive generation lengths and stability-aware token commitment improve the efficiency of diffusion machine translation.
authors: Tianyuan Li, Xihan Yang, Chenglong Wang, Yuzhang Wu, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Targets redundant computation from fixed output lengths and delayed commitment of medium-confidence tokens.
Uses source-length- and direction-aware target length estimation with a fallback for empty or unusually short outputs.
Commits tokens based on high confidence plus temporal stability measured by cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen–Shannon divergence over Top-K distributions.
Training-free evaluation on bidirectional Chinese–English translation reports 24.9%–36.8% fewer forward calls and 1.91×–2.19× sentence-level speedups over Fast-dLLM.
Macro-average COMET decreases by only 0.02 points; scope is limited to the reported translation directions and benchmarks.
