papers.tldr: TRAC accelerates diffusion-based machine translation by adapting output length and committing stable token predictions earlier, substantially reducing decoding cost with minimal quality loss.

papers.abstract: Federated reinforcement learning enables a fleet of robots to jointly learn a shared navigation policy without exchanging raw experience. In practice, however, the robots rarely operate in the same conditions: an open aisle is far easier to navigate than a cluttered room, and takes less learning to master. Standard federated aggregation rules ignore this. Uniform averaging weights every client equally, whether or not it is still learning, and weighting by episode return is worse, since easy environments permit high returns by construction. Both failures stem from what we call the \emph{plateau problem}: once a client masters its environment, its updates carry little new information even though its reported return remains high. We propose \emph{FedDIA}, which scores each client by how much its local training improves the global model it received, amplified by the difficulty of its environment. Difficulty is inferred from the model's own performance, without requiring any description of the environment. Both signals are measured against the global model, so they are comparable across clients. On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA reaches a mean success rate of $75.5\%$ across training and held-out environments, against $68.7\%$ for the strongest federated baseline. Its advantage holds when the models are transferred to hand-authored warehouse and living-space layouts, or when one of the clients is defective.
authors: Ye Lin Tun, Chu Myaet Thwal, Eui-Nam Huh, Choong Seon Hong
bullets: Standard uniform or return-based aggregation suffers from the “plateau problem”: mastered, easy environments can receive undue influence despite providing little new information.
FedDIA estimates environment difficulty from the model’s own performance, requiring no environment descriptions.
It scores client updates by improvement over the received global model and amplifies contributions from more difficult environments.
On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA achieved a 75.5% mean success rate versus 68.7% for the strongest federated baseline.
The advantage persisted on hand-authored warehouse and living-space layouts and with a defective client.

figures.caption: Figure 3: One communication round of FedDIA. The server broadcasts the global model 𝜃𝑘. Each client evaluates it before local training and its updated model after, obtaining returns 𝑟pre𝑖 and 𝑟post𝑖 . Both are sent to the server with updated parameters 𝜃𝑘𝑖 . From these, the server derives an improvement signal 𝑐𝐼𝑖 and a difficulty signal 𝑐𝐷𝑖 , combines them into a per-client score, and computes aggregation weights by softmax. Across the two example clients, a plateaued easy client receives low weight, while a still-improving hard client receives high weight.

Figure 1: Federated reinforcement learning across heterogeneous environments. In each communication round 𝑘, the server broadcasts the global model 𝜃𝑘 to all 𝑁 clients. Each client trains the policy 𝜋𝜃𝑘 in its own environment 𝑖, and returns the updated parameters 𝜃𝑘𝑖 . The server combines these into the next global model 𝜃𝑘+1 using aggregation weights {𝑤𝑖}.
Figure 5: Success rate (%) of the global model over communication rounds, averaged across the five environments (1000 episodes each). Shaded regions show one standard deviation over three seeds.

Figure 4: Top-down view of the five obstacle modes. Empty, random and grid are used for training, while mixed and multi-gate are held out for evaluation. Random obstacles are shown in blue and grid obstacles in red. The goal is the green marker.

Figure 6: Aggregation weight received by a client in each environment group (averaged within the group) for one representative seed. The lines show a five-round moving average. The dashed line at 1∕8 = 0.125 is the uniform weighting of FedAvg.

Figure 2: Training curves for one easy client (no obstacles) and one hard client (dense obstacles) under FedAvg [12] over three seeds. Shaded regions show standard deviation. The easy client’s success rate saturates near round 30, while the hard client continues to improve throughout training, illustrating the plateau problem: uniform averaging weights both clients equally, even though only one is still contributing new information.
Figure 8: Success rate (%) with 40 clients, 8 sampled per round, at round 60. Mean ± standard deviation over three seeds.

papers.title: Beyond Easy Clients: Difficulty- and Improvement-Aware Aggregation for Federated Reinforcement Learning in Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: FedDIA improves federated reinforcement learning for heterogeneous robot-navigation environments by weighting clients according to environment difficulty and how much their updates improve the global model.

papers.abstract: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.
authors: Yutao Li, Chen Wang
bullets: Single-reference squared-error evaluation may favor blurred or prematurely stopped videos that reduce prediction variance.
The authors formally decompose this bias and show that Physics-IQ can improve as generated futures collapse, even when their distribution worsens.
Kernel Physics-IQ removes the incentive in expectation using two independent samples per condition.
Across five image-to-video models, two-step sampling lowered Kernel Physics-IQ; for CogVideoX, the official score rose by 0.055 while the proposed score fell by 0.131.
Controlled physical-system tests show the new metric prefers the true outcome distribution over collapsed predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Tied official scores hide different futures. (a) Predictors in a pendulum world that swings left or right with equal probability: each card shows what the predictor draws (line weight: probability; dashed: never drawn), and the pixel mean blends both swings into one video (diamond: mean position). (b) Exact scores, averaged with a ball dropped onto a peg: the raw official composite ties the first four, whereas Kernel Physics-IQ ranks the true distribution first, as it does among all 34 predictors. (c) Mask distance: staying still wins below the thresholds of Prop. 2.

Figure 3. What one sample cannot see. A sample is scored by its distance to the recording (blue), which on average is the kernel score plus half the self-dispersion (green). Two-step samples disperse less: the dispersion premium they collect (dashed) outweighs their kernel loss, so single-sample scoring prefers them. A second sample measures the self-dispersion, which Kernel Physics-IQ subtracts. Frames: paper-smoke 2 s after the switch frame (Wan2.2, two seeds). Brackets (root-mean-square) and bars: Wan2.2 ST IoU distances on whole clips, mean over 66 scenes.

Figure 4. Fewer steps align seeds far more than they match truth. (a) Recording (x̄) vs. seed overlap (ȳ) with Eq. (6) contours and the 0.695 no-overlap line. (b) Dispersion-premium and kernelpart bars behind net diamonds for the official split. (c) Spatial masks behind x and y: Wan2.2 seeds 43 and 44 on rolling-reflection (Fig. 2b) against take 1 (teal). papers.selection_reason: Analyzes evaluation of video generators as world models and denoising-step effects; relevant to world models and video diffusion.

papers.tldr: Physics-IQ can reward video world models for producing less varied, less realistic futures; Kernel Physics-IQ corrects this using two independent samples per condition.

papers.abstract: Do video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss, or merely imitate motion? Overall motion and appearance scores cannot settle it. We investigate this through nonlinear forced response: an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. We introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapt six image-to-video backbones to predict this motion using only the flow-matching loss. Wan predicts motion accurately and generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes. Counterfactual tests suggest capabilities beyond replaying training videos. But what laws have they learned? We design three tiers of tests using Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry. All six reproduce the linear response, including resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics, including nonlinear softening. Remarkably, softening is barely present in training: only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts. Yet learned dynamics may fail to appear when state estimation or propagation goes wrong. We turn these tests and findings into strategies to improve video training and generation.
authors: Yutao Li, Chen Wang, Wangmeng Zuo, Hui Li
bullets: Tests nonlinear forced responses by shaking the support of suspended objects.
Uses dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapts six image-to-video backbones without a physics loss.
All six models reproduce linear response and resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics such as nonlinear softening.
Wan generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes, with counterfactual tests indicating more than training-video replay.
Performance is limited when state estimation or temporal propagation fails; sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts.

papers.abstract: Current multi-shot video generators render only limited durations per pass, requiring long movies to be stitched from local segments across which narrative progression and visual identity drift. To synthesize long-horizon movies with Coherence across Time, we present CaT-Movie, a multi-shot generation system consisting of a global story planner and a local window renderer. The planner expands user requests via a large language model to preserve, infer, and complete story details, while deterministic code maintains the resulting storyboard across shots to compile self-contained shot prompts and index reference frames from generated history. To execute this guidance, the renderer applies reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention to route identities from the indexed frames while isolating per-shot textual conditions. Given the scarcity of high-quality open-source multi-shot data, we construct a dataset of over 350K film shots annotated with semantic state transitions, entity grounding, and multi-granularity requests. We further build CaT-MBench, a benchmark on held-out films with the same annotations. It gives every baseline its native format and counts cross-shot consistency only when a cut opens a new camera setup, preventing repeated framing from passing as consistency. On CaT-MBench, CaT-Movie attains the highest average score and the most consistent characters among all methods. The project page is available at https://jinplu.github.io/CaT-Movie/.
authors: Jinpeng Lu, Haoyuan Shi, Yuanshen Guan, Jiyuan Xia, Bin Wu, Yinda Chen, Zhiwei Xiong
bullets: Addresses narrative progression and visual-identity drift when stitching short video segments into long movies.
Uses an LLM-based planner and deterministic storyboard tracking to create self-contained shot prompts and retrieve relevant prior frames.
Applies reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention to preserve identities while isolating shot-specific conditions.
Introduces a dataset of over 350K annotated film shots and the CaT-MBench held-out-film benchmark.
Achieves the highest average score and most consistent characters among evaluated methods on CaT-MBench.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the dataset and benchmark. One film pool and one schema feed the training data, (a) curation and annotation and (b) entity grounding, and CaT-MBench, (c) stories and questions and (d) cut-gated judging. The center chart gives the composition of both.

Figure 2. Overview of CaT-Movie. A planner writes one storyboard, from which a prompt compiler maintains cross-shot state and derives per-shot text ck, the frames each shot recalls, and an identity line cref for each recalled frame. The renderer denoises each window jointly with reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention, placing recalled frames before the reading shot’s first latent frame.

Figure 1. Cross-window drift, copied framing, and cut-gated evaluation. Each film strip is one generation pass. Joint generation switches camera setup at the cut from shot 3 to 4 but changes the man in the next pass, from shot 4 to shot 6, whereas memoryaugmented generation keeps the man yet repeats the framing of shot 3 across planned cuts. Scores average character and scene consistency over all 11 shots, and the cut gate of CaT-MBench fails consistency checks across planned cuts that keep the camera setup.

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison on a test story of 11 shots and 28.4 s, which HoloCine generates in three windows. Each of four shots is shown at its middle frame. Icons mark characters that CaT-MBench judges inconsistent, enlarged at the bottom right of the shot, and crossed scissors mark planned cuts where the video keeps the camera setup.

Figure 6. (Left) Character checks passed by time from first appearance to return, pooled over the test stories, with 95% intervals. (Right) Consistency by window distance on development stories, where Recent is recent-shots recall and W/o refs trains without references.

papers.abstract: Learned models for radio access networks (RANs) are often developed using simulation, yet their predictions can shift when exposed to physical propagation conditions, protocol behavior, and equipment implementations. This paper presents a cyber-physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework for AI-RAN that connects a task-oriented student model, an experiment-planning coach agent, a calibratable virtual environment, and a physical host agent. Physical measurements are organized as evidence for both model adaptation and subsequent experiment planning. We examine an implementation of the physical-feedback pathway using ping-pong handover as a case study. The system completes 12 physical executions organized into six baseline--candidate pairs, updates the student from measured outcomes, and evaluates the revised model on reserved physical configurations. In the observed short-window tests, increasing the time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280\,ms changes the ping-pong count from three to zero. The updated student achieves a grouped-validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.673 round trips/min, while a common three-configuration physical evaluation yields MAEs of 1.240 and 1.601 round trips/min for the pre-feedback and post-feedback models, respectively. These results characterize both the operational feedback loop and the parameter-dependent generalization behavior revealed by new physical experiments.

In 12 physical executions, increasing time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280 ms reduced ping-pong events from three to zero.
The case study highlights parameter-dependent generalization and the operational behavior of the physical-feedback loop.

papers.abstract: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary (tub) hybrid general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that minimizes low-order accumulation latency, while retaining value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. Post-place-and-route INT4 yields 14%/9% smaller area for Splice-BP/Splice-LUT, compared to the systolic array.
authors: Prabhu Vellaisamy, Hsien-Fu Hung, Andrew Kim, Shawn Blanton, John Paul Shen
bullets: Introduces two PE variants: Splice-BP, based on bit planes, and Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in one cycle.
Across 26 INT4 CNN and LLM workloads, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.4%/76.4% versus a binary systolic array.
Splice-LUT improves geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces energy-delay product by 6.13× across the evaluated configurations.
For W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, both variants reduce tile energy by 77.3–88.1%.
Post-place-and-route INT4 implementations reduce area by 14% (Splice-BP) and 9% (Splice-LUT).

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.
authors: Yichen Guo, Yanlong Chen, Xinyue Zhang, Mohan Liu, Song Zhang, Yawei Li
bullets: Targets W4A4KV4 deployment of world action models on onboard robot computers.
Uses a reader metric to measure future errors by their impact on actions, and read counts to allocate activation/cache precision across denoising steps.
Adds gaze-guided refinement, giving action-relevant tokens a second 4-bit quantization pass in the denoising loop and cache.
On LIBERO-Plus, achieves 76.4% and 83.3% success—within 1.2 points of 16-bit models—while compressing 3.8×, reducing peak memory 2.3×, and running 1.66× faster.
On a real AgileX PiPER arm, reaches 47.0% success versus 52.0% for 16-bit and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.

At every control step, gaze-guided refinement (d) gives the tokens selected under the current gaze a second 4-bit code in the linear layers and in the cache, and the attention of the action tokens gives the gaze for the next step.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon world modeling in partially observable environments requires compact memories that preserve spatial structure despite accumulated localization drift. Inspired by hippocampal episodic and spatial memory and the multi-periodic coding of entorhinal grid cells, we propose HiSTFormer, a hierarchical spatiotemporal world model, which adopts a layer-wise organization of local temporal RoPE and multi-periodic spatial RoPE, together with content-conditioned address offsets, to capture recent temporal context and long-range spatial structure. A fixed-capacity memory keeps KV storage and per-step attention cost bounded as the sequence grows. On MemoryMaze and HM3D, HiSTFormer outperforms strong world-model baselines within the training sequence length and generalizes substantially better to prediction horizons far beyond those seen during training, while using a compact model. The hierarchical spatiotemporal design remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, with consistent gains as depth increases. These results show that hierarchical spatiotemporal organization and content-adaptive spatial addressing provide effective inductive biases for efficient long-horizon world modeling.
authors: Tiantian Li, Junfeng Lu, Yifei Wang, Zhaoyang Zhang, Lei Wang, Tianyi Qian
bullets: Targets spatial-structure loss caused by localization drift in partially observable, long-horizon environments.
Combines layer-wise local temporal RoPE, multi-periodic spatial RoPE, and content-conditioned address offsets.
Maintains fixed-capacity KV memory, keeping storage and per-step attention cost bounded as sequences grow.
Outperforms strong baselines on MemoryMaze and HM3D, with stronger generalization to horizons beyond training.
The approach remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains. However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another. Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD)}, a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy. PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy. A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by $3.5$ points on NavTest and $5.0$ points on NavHard. Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions. These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.
authors: Chengkai Xu, Yicheng Guo, Jiaqi Liu, Yiming Cui, Shiyu Fang, Peng Hang, Hao Zhang, Jian Sun
bullets: Addresses the problem that more demonstrations may be redundant or harmful, and that data value differs across planners.

Controlled group-removal experiments support the directional fidelity of PAD’s valuations.

Policy-specific curation improves EPDMS and consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across multiple planner types while reducing scene-level regressions.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.
authors: Haotian Zhai, Leqi Liu
bullets: Prediction accuracy may not reflect the cost of decisions made from LLM outputs.
DFRL uses negative downstream decision regret as the reinforcement-learning reward and does not require convex or differentiable optimization problems.
Heuristic warm-starting and reward correction reduce the need for expensive exact reward evaluations.

Experiments on synthetic problems, knapsack, and H&M inventory planning show improvements over prediction-loss baselines; the best inventory configuration reduces regret by 31.4% versus SFT and 12.4% versus the strongest conventional forecasting baseline.
The method is evaluated within the reported synthetic, knapsack, and inventory-planning settings; broader generalization is not established by the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1 DFRL pipeline with RLOO as an example. (1) Context. The input x provides task-relevant information, including text and structured data. (2) Predict parameters. The LLM independently samples K parameter predictions ĉ1, . . . , ĉK ∼ πθ(· | x). (3) Solve downstream optimization problems. Each prediction ĉk is passed to the optimizer, which returns a decision w⋆(ĉk) that is optimal under the predicted parameters. (4) Evaluate regret. Each decision is evaluated under the observed parameters c and compared with the optimal decision under c, yielding reward rk = −ℓ(ĉk, c). (5) Update the LLM policy. RLOO subtracts the average reward of the other K − 1 predictions from rk to obtain advantage Ak. These advantages weight the policy gradients used to update θ, without differentiating through the downstream optimizer. The hindsight cost F (w⋆(c), c) is shared across predictions and cancels from the advantages, so solving under c is unnecessary for the RLOO update.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.
authors: Anh Dao, Xinxin Liu, Hang Yu, Jeffrey A Chan Santiago, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: WAMs are costly because they combine video generation with action prediction using large transformers.
A shared six-block core is recurrently applied to execute 30 layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert; video and action experts use different depths.
Elastic self-distillation trains one checkpoint to support varied action-depth and sampling-step budgets.
The 0.58B-parameter model reports 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, with 7.4× lower peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched measurements.
On real hardware, it achieved 71.3% success over 80 trials; performance degrades when action depth is aggressively reduced without budget-aware training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. (a) Each expert stores a prelude, a shared core, and a coda, and loops the core Kv times in the video expert and Ka times in the action expert (shown for Kv=4, Ka=2). The video expert encodes the current frame once per query and caches its keys and values. At every sampling step, the action expert reads them in a joint attention; late alignment lets action loop r attend to video loop σ(r), so even a single action loop sees the deepest visual features. Both experts also cross-attend to frozen text embeddings of the instruction, and future frames are predicted only during training. (b) One student learns every setting (Ka, N) in S. The target of each macro step is the frozen teacher’s fine Euler map started from the student’s own state (Llocal), and the final chunk is matched to the teacher’s chunk from the same noise (Lend).

Figure 1. LoopedWAM is small, fast, and elastic. (a) Each expert stores 12 blocks and loops its shared 6-block core K times. One checkpoint thus reaches the 30-layer depth of its dense donor with 2.4× fewer parameters, and the depth is chosen at test time. (b) RoboTwin 2.0 success against parameters, as reported by each paper. At 0.58B, LoopedWAM (91.9%) is the best model below 2B and on par with the ∼6B Fast-WAM (91.8%). (c) LIBERO success against latency on one H100 for each setting of action loops Ka and sampling steps N of LoopedWAM-E. One checkpoint spans 24.7–86.2 ms at 95.2–96.2% success, and at (2, 2) it is 3.9× faster than Fast-WAM.

papers.abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.
authors: Xinze Shi, Litian Zhang, Zhenjie Su, Zelong Yu, Yuting Zhang, Qihua Feng, Zifeng Kang, Chaozhuo Li, Zhengxuan Hu
bullets: The issue arises from the Bradley-Terry objective itself, not from faulty comparisons; its pre-training optimum predicts the eventual distortion.
In a simulated robot-push task, an initially accurate model shifted 33–43 percentage points of probability to outcomes absent from the enumerated branches.
The effect persisted on unseen conditions, across five candidate laws, and with denser outcome enumeration; about 29 percentage points remained after excluding impossible events.
Distortion inflated hazard probabilities and reduced threshold-based utility by about 3 percentage points on trained and 1–2 points on unseen conditions when impossible events were included.
A likelihood that models the judge’s rule avoided the probability shift, while audits traced the Bradley-Terry effect from probabilities to actions.

papers.abstract: An age prompt can change how a vision-language model (VLM) rates the emotion evoked by an image. Does the change predict how people of different ages rate that same image? We evaluate 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images using young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts and estimate image-specific age differences from ratings by 822 participants. Without an age cue, models closely track average human valence (median Pearson $r=0.891$). Under an older-adult prompt, 16 of 17 models assign lower valence on average than under a young-adult prompt. Yet after adjusting for image pleasantness, correlations between model and human age effects range from $-0.030$ to $0.093$, against an estimated ceiling of $0.595$. The discrepancy is clearest on 54 sensitive images rated as pleasant. Across models, the older prompt reduces valence by $0.845$ points on average, while older participants rate these images $0.443$ points higher than younger participants. Providing human ratings from other images improves agreement on the direction of age differences, although image-specific fidelity remains modest on 600 held-out images ($r_{\mathrm{part}}=0.105$). These results show why evaluations of demographic personalization in foundation models need human comparisons at the level of individual stimuli. Project page available at https://shahriyar-zaman.github.io/age-conditioned-emotion-reasoning/
authors: Shahriyar Zaman Ridoy, Azmine Toushik Wasi, Lin Gu, Ruogu Fang
bullets: Evaluates 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images with young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts, comparing them with ratings from 822 participants.
Without age cues, models closely match average human valence, but age-conditioned effects show near-zero agreement with human age effects.
Older-adult prompts lower model valence for 16 of 17 models, whereas older participants often rate sensitive pleasant images more positively than younger participants.
Human ratings from other images improve prediction of the direction of age differences, though image-specific agreement remains modest.
Findings emphasize evaluating demographic personalization against human judgments for individual stimuli, not only aggregate behavior.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Baseline valence, age contrasts, and agreement with human ratings. (a) Without an age cue, 17-model mean valence tracks pooled OASIS valence (median per-model r = 0.89; fitted slope 1.22; calibration slopes 1.04–1.39); sensitive-flagged images highlighted. (b) Older-minus-young valence shift with 95% intervals (also used in panels c and e): 16 of 17 models are negative, 13 after Benjamini–Hochberg correction (hollow: q ≥ .05). (c) rpart with image-bootstrap intervals: point estimates lie within [−0.03, 0.09], far below the ceiling of 0.595 (dashed); the best model reaches 15.6% of it. (d) Pairwise correlations of model valence age effects: models agree with one another (mean r = 0.43 over 136 pairs) but weakly with human age effects (mean rpart = 0.03, bottom row). (e) On flagged pleasant images (n = 54), models lower valence by 0.85 on average, while older human raters score them 0.44 higher (participant bootstrap [0.10, 0.86]; 25 raters aged 60+).

Figure 2. Stimulus-matched evaluation of age-conditioned affect. OASIS ratings (a) yield per-image human means H̄i, age effects ∆Hi, and uncertainty τi (b). 17 VLMs rate the same images under four age conditions (c), returning valence, arousal, an emotion label, and a description (d). We measure competence, responsiveness, and fidelity (rpart between ∆Mi and ∆Hi) (e), run diagnostics (f), test reasoning-only and human-grounded mitigations on 300 images (g), and validate S4 on 600 held-out images (h).

Figure 4. Examples of age-conditioned descriptions and ratings. Three OASIS images (none sensitive-flagged), each with two models from different developers. Beside each image: pooled human valence and arousal (V, A; 1–7), the direction of the image-specific age effect among OASIS raters aged 60+, and the 17-VLM mean older-minus-young valence shift (O−Y). For each model: valence and label under the young (Y) and older (O) personas with their verbatim descriptions (shortened with an ellipsis). Older ratings are green when they move in the direction of OASIS older raters and red when opposite; vulnerability, memory and excitement words are coloured. In all three cases, leisure and nature scenes turn risky, frail or threatening under the older persona, although older raters rate them slightly more pleasant.

Figure 5. Grounding improves alignment but remains below the human ceiling. All results use the same 300 images. Groups follow §3.4: 17 VLMs is the direct prompt (S0) on every model, reasoning agents are S1–S2, human-grounded agents are S3–S5 and VERA-Cal, and S4 panel is the grounded contrastive panel alone; human ref. is the attainable ceiling rmax from §3.3. (a) Mean image-level fidelity, rpart, for each group, with the ceiling marked. (b) Direction agreement with human age effects. (c) Fidelity as a percentage of the ceiling with joint image bootstrap comparisons.

Aversive net: net images gaining an aversive label under the older persona. ↑ higher is better; →1 closer to 1 is better. papers.abstract: Robotic planning from visual observations and signal temporal logic (STL) requires grounding task requirements in scene evidence while adapting plans to execution feedback. We present GraF-VTA, a graph-based framework that extends Vision-TL-Action with structured task representations, causal observation history, and closed-loop trajectory generation. Bidirectional cross-attention fuses STL syntax tokens with visual features, while an optional frozen automaton embedding supplies complementary untimed task structure. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations and compresses older frames to provide recent execution context. Conditioned on these features and robot state, a flow-matching model generates plans whose action prefixes are executed before replanning from refreshed observations. Across five simulation environments, the single-graph configuration achieves higher open-loop Success@$K$ than TeLoGraF and Vision-TL-Action on four environments at the reported budgets $K\geq16$. On Panda, matched-update ablations increase Success@256 from 53.91\% without observation history to 62.50\% with pyramid memory. In closed-loop Dubins evaluation, it reaches 64.06\% Success@1024, compared with 12.50\% for adapted S-MSP and 27.34\% for adapted Logic-VLA. These results support combining structured visual conditioning with observation history and replanning to improve coverage of STL-satisfying trajectories.
authors: Zezhi Liu, Zhiwei Zheng, Hanqian Luo, Deyun Qin, Shizhen Wu, Yongchun Fang
bullets: Represents task requirements with STL syntax, optional automaton embeddings, and graph-based visual–logical fusion.
Uses bidirectional cross-attention, temporal-pyramid memory, and robot state to condition a flow-matching trajectory generator.
Executes action prefixes, refreshes observations, and replans to adapt trajectories during execution.
Across five simulated environments, the single-graph model outperforms TeLoGraF and Vision-TL-Action on four environments at reported budgets of K≥16.
Observation history improves Panda Success@256 from 53.91% to 62.50%; closed-loop Dubins Success@1024 reaches 64.06%.

The fused features, DFA embedding, and current state condition a Temporal U-Net to generate the planned trajectory via an ODE solver.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models are advancing embodied navigation, but frequent inference incurs substantial computational cost. We present Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy. Retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback determine the cognitive horizon, or how many cached waypoints the robot executes before refreshing its prediction. At the policy's stop request, local visitation history guides a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls. CHAC reduces vision-language model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points, respectively. Success rate and success weighted by path length improve per model call on both benchmarks. Across four physical navigation tasks with 40 runs per method, CHAC achieves 18 successes versus 14 for native execution, reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.
authors: Weile Gong, Zijian Lu, Jiahao Zheng, Bo Xu, Yiping Zuo, Jiajia Guo, Xin He, Weijun Wang, Weibei Fan
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of frequent inference in multimodal embodied navigation.
Uses a frozen navigation policy and retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback to set an adaptive cognitive horizon.
At stop requests, local visitation history enables a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls.
Cuts model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with corresponding success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points.
In physical tasks, achieves 18 versus 14 successes, while reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on persistent memory to plan tool calls and complete multi-step tasks, which exposes them to memory drift: an adversarial or misleading memory alters the execution path and final outcome. In this work, we investigate online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. We identify two fundamental challenges. (1) Content-level features are insufficient for causal memory-drift attribution, as perplexity or retrieval relevance alone cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized; (2) Counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, as it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory, exceeding real-time serving budgets. To address these challenges, we propose DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. Specifically, DriftGuard first constructs causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score (MDS) that captures action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. Guided by this supervision, DriftGuard then learns an online risk model that estimates MDS from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories via its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DriftGuard-7F0B.
authors: Licheng Pan, Yuzhou Chen, Zhixuan Chu, Yichen Sun, Han Zheng, Zhiyu Wang, Hao Wang, Yan Wang, Bingyu Zhu, Haiwen Hong, Longtao Huang, Kui Ren
bullets: Persistent agent memory can drift and redirect tool use or task outcomes when memories are misleading or adversarial.
Content signals such as perplexity and retrieval relevance do not reliably identify causally influential memories.
Offline, paired counterfactual replays compare original and single-memory-neutralized trajectories to build component-wise memory drift scores.
An online risk model estimates these scores from pre-action information and flags memories using their maximum component risk.
Experiments show accurate identification of drift-inducing memories and efficient online defense, without serving-time counterfactual rollouts.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.
authors: Hang Zhang, Yuzhi Pan, Ziyao Zhong, Chaokun Wang, Shuo Cao, Zeyu Huang, Yue Xue, Fang Niu, Bofan Xie, Guanchen Ge, Zecheng Li, Leqi Zheng, Ziyang Liu, Wei Wang, Miao Gu

GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest reported average score of 56.1, compared with 44.4 for the composite Human-SOTA baseline.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems. We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This delivers 1.29--3.95$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 1.12--2.34$\times$ energy efficiency improvement over SSD-based retrieval.
authors: Yuseon Choi, Sanghyeon Park, Eunjong Lee, Hanseo Lee, Sangjin Kim
bullets: Retrieving successful experiences to warm-start DiT denoising helps embodied agents adapt to OOD environments while reducing inference cost.
FlashX combines high-bandwidth parallel pSLC key search, interleaved Compute-in-Flash engines, and dense TLC latent storage.
Proprioception-aware clustering reduces search overhead and supports incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering.
Across VLA and WAM workloads, FlashX improves task success by up to 12.24 percentage points and search throughput by 2.57× over prior NAND search.
Compared with SSD-based retrieval, it provides 1.29–3.95× end-to-end speedup and 1.12–2.34× energy-efficiency improvement.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models are increasingly adapted into task specialists to expand their embodied capabilities. Yet these capabilities remain fragmented across separate policies, and existing model-merging methods do not reliably preserve them during closed-loop execution: parameter-space alignment provides only an indirect proxy for behavior, while regression may fail to preserve behavior at states not covered by its calibration inputs. We present Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR), an execution-aware, gradient-free framework that consolidates robot specialists into a single policy. Across two complementary timescales, TCR collects calibration inputs from expert rollouts spanning different stages of task execution and from intermediate states within iterative action generation. To account for representation shifts introduced by merging, TCR recomputes each block's input through the already merged blocks. It then uses each expert's computation within the block to form module inputs and fits merged weights to match the experts' linear outputs. A two-pass calibration procedure further refines the merged policy using separate rollout caches while retaining the frozen specialists as teachers. The resulting model preserves the original inference graph and requires neither expert routing nor additional gradient training. On LIBERO, TCR merges four $\pi_{0.5}$ specialists and achieves 77.83% success across 1,200 evaluation episodes, outperforming FeatCal, RegMean, and direct weight averaging by 9.50, 24.17, and 33.00 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Wenshuo Chen, Honglei Jin, Le Yang, Jianfei Song, Shaofeng Liang, Lei Wang, Junze Zhu, Kailong Wang, Zhengxi Jin, Haozhe Jia, Honglin Chu, Songning Lai, Xiucheng Wang, Yutao Yue

papers.abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.
authors: Zihan Xiao (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Boshen Xu (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Pei Fu (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jianzhong Ju (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Zhenbo Luo (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jian Luan (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Qin Jin (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China)
bullets: Video MLLMs face major memory and latency costs from large numbers of visual tokens.
Existing compression methods are difficult to compare fairly because evaluations use different setups, tasks, and models.
VidToC provides a controlled framework spanning representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time-encoding strategies.
Experiments across three video-understanding tasks show that compression behavior depends on the task, compression placement, time encoding, and backbone.
The study offers empirical guidance for selecting compression strategies, including across hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures.

papers.abstract: Global medium-range weather forecasting must not only generate ensembles efficiently to characterize uncertainty in future states, but also serve downstream applications such as extreme-event warnings and cross-sphere coupled simulations. We introduce WeatherCraft, a framework that unifies probabilistic generation and reinforcement learning alignment through discrete weather tokens, bringing the GPT-style pretraining--post-training paradigm to global medium-range weather forecasting. A multiscale tokenizer represents atmospheric states as a coarse-to-fine token hierarchy, while a Transformer models causal dependencies across time and scale and predicts tokens within each scale in parallel. Direct sampling generates diverse ensembles, and exact token log-probabilities enable Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to maximize downstream task rewards without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models. On the ERA5 benchmark, WeatherCraft's eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% relative to the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and, with KV caching, achieves an approximately $18\times$ inference speedup over GenCast. Direct fair-CRPS adaptation improves ensemble probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves forecasts of persistent land temperature extremes and coupled ocean heat extremes. This work establishes discrete autoregressive modeling as a general foundation for scalable, task-alignable Earth system foundation models.
authors: Jinhan Li, Zhisheng Chen, Yuxuan Li, Yuan Gao, Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Jinlong Du, Kun Wang
bullets: Targets scalable global medium-range ensemble forecasting while supporting warnings and coupled Earth-system simulations.
Uses a multiscale coarse-to-fine tokenizer and a Transformer with parallel prediction within each scale.
Generates diverse ensembles by sampling and applies GRPO using exact token log-probabilities, without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models.
On ERA5, its eight-member ensemble mean lowers day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% versus the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and is approximately 18× faster than GenCast with KV caching.
Fair-CRPS adaptation improves probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves persistent land-temperature and coupled ocean-heat extreme forecasts.

papers.abstract: Aerial sensing must combine uncertain overhead context with current observations while budgeting prediction, movement and image processing. AeroBelief uses the next executable action as the unit of verification against reference scores. It groups candidate views by first action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, and selectively queries a structured world model (WM). Calibrated group bounds support strict commitment; a six-query controller connects selective prediction with belief updates, acceptance checks and scheduled sensing. Across four layout families, 40 worlds and 960 closed-loop executions, the AeroBelief controller completes 75.42% of tasks, compared with 73.33% for exhaustive WM scoring and 65.83% for line-of-sight geometry, using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations than exhaustive scoring. In fixed-reference replay with a six-query cap, proposer-scaled anchored bounds raised first-action certificate availability from 36.25% to 54.69% and reduced mean queries per state by 13.54% relative to unit-scale anchored bounds. A complete ground-hosted pipeline processes 2,685 self-collected 20-megapixel unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images from seven DJI Mavic 3M routes. Context-guided admission and feedback retain all eight independently supported target confirmations with 76.05% fewer processed images and 70.02% less accumulated active processing service than uncapped all-frame processing; feedback saves another 5.17% of images relative to static context. The studies connect budgeted action selection with evidence-driven processing of recorded flight imagery.
authors: Tianren Li, Dongbo Li, Hongkai Chen, Jie Liu, Guoliang Xing
bullets: Groups candidate views by their next executable action and uses an inexpensive proposer before selectively querying a structured world model.
Uses calibrated group bounds, belief updates, acceptance checks, and scheduled sensing under a six-query controller.
Completes 75.42% of tasks while using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations than exhaustive scoring.
In replay, increases first-action certificate availability from 36.25% to 54.69% and reduces mean queries per state by 13.54%.
On 2,685 UAV images, retains all eight supported target confirmations while processing 76.05% fewer images than uncapped processing; scope includes four layout families, 40 worlds, and seven routes.

papers.title: AeroBelief: Budgeted First-Action Verification for Evidence-Guided Aerial Sensing
papers.tldr: AeroBelief improves budgeted aerial sensing by verifying candidate first actions selectively, achieving similar or better task completion with far fewer world-model evaluations and processed images.

papers.abstract: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.
authors: Amit Feldman, Ilan Shimshoni, Rotem Dror
bullets: Addresses the need to identify and assess procedural mistakes before recovery is no longer possible.
Uses observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions to recognize completed steps, localize them temporally, and classify execution errors.
Compares separate modular components with a joint model that predicts step identity, timing, and correctness together.
The joint model improves binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 from 80.7% to 84.1%, with the largest gain for slips.
The dataset split is revised to include erroneous videos across all splits; omitted steps are identified only after the video ends.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the two approaches. At each call, the system receives the current window V [τ, t] (sampled at 1 fps), the task description d, the instruction list I , and its prediction history. (a) The modular approach chains a Step Identifier, which selects an instruction s ∈ I or EXTRA; a Temporal Localizer, which predicts the attempt’s boundaries [a, b]; and an Execution Verifier, which classifies the cropped attempt V [τ+a, τ+b] as CORRECT, MODIFICATION, SLIP, or CORRECTION, using its previous execution labels as context. Extra actions are labeled ADDITION without verification. (b) The joint approach predicts all fields in a single structured response, conditioned on up to 12 previous predictions. In both, a NOT COMPLETED output (dashed) keeps the window start τ and extends the window by ∆ = 5 s; an accepted record updates the history and starts the next window at the predicted end.

papers.abstract: A prompt for in-context learning (ICL) can describe a task in addition to, or instead of, demonstrating it through examples. Yet how task descriptions work remains poorly understood theoretically. Through the Bayesian view of ICL, we model descriptions as informative priors characterized by their specificity and reliability. We adapt the effective sample size (ESS) from Bayesian statistics, quantifying a description's predictive value as an equivalent number of demonstrations. For in-context linear regression, we show that a reliable description's ESS grows with its specificity and with the task's dimension. A description that may be irrelevant, however, gains little from its specificity unless demonstrations are given. In practice, do in-context learners use descriptions as a Bayes-optimal predictor would? Our experiments show that meta-trained Transformers come close to the Bayes-optimal ESS when tested on their training distribution. Pretrained language models, however, make too little use of highly specific descriptions when answering without reasoning; most of them closely match the Bayes-optimal predictor only when reasoning is enabled. These results extend the Bayesian analysis of ICL from demonstrations to descriptions.
authors: Bruce Nguyen, Bei Jiang, Linglong Kong
bullets: Models descriptions as informative Bayesian priors and measure their predictive value using effective sample size (ESS), interpreted as an equivalent number of demonstrations.
For in-context linear regression, reliable descriptions become more valuable with greater specificity and higher task dimension.
Potentially irrelevant descriptions benefit little from added specificity unless demonstrations provide supporting context.
Meta-trained Transformers nearly achieve Bayes-optimal ESS on their training distribution, while pretrained language models often underuse highly specific descriptions without reasoning.
The analysis extends Bayesian theory of in-context learning from example demonstrations to task descriptions.

(a) Descriptions generated and stated with standard deviation 30, so c = 4. (b) With standard deviation 10, so c = 36. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes in-context learning and task descriptions in LLMs through a Bayesian effective sample size framework.
papers.title: Is a Description Worth a Thousand Demonstrations? Specificity and Reliability of Task Descriptions in In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: Task descriptions can substitute for demonstrations in in-context learning, but their value depends on specificity, reliability, and whether the model reasons over them.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video prediction lets robots anticipate the visual consequences of their actions for planning and policy evaluation. Existing predictors denoise each future from noise without using their own estimate of it, which limits the quality of the predicted future, in particular of the manipulated objects, and requires many network calls. We present TwoPass, a self-conditioned training-and-inference framework that keeps the standard flow-matching objective. Self-Generated Draft Training supplies a detached clean-video estimate from the shared network as conditioning at the same noisy state. A Refinement-Only Late Adapter applies a dedicated residual transformation when a draft is present. At inference, Draft-Reuse Iterative Refinement obtains both a solver update and the next draft from each velocity prediction, requiring as few as 4 function evaluations (NFE) per video chunk. Training samples discrete solver-query noise levels and updates the pretrained backbone. Extensive experiments on Bridge and Language Table show that TwoPass achieves state-of-the-art results with 4 NFE, far fewer than the 50-59 calls of existing predictors. Code: https://github.com/PlantPotatoOnMoon/TwoPass.
authors: Yijun Liu, Shijia Ge, Tongtong Feng, Xin Wang, Yuan Meng, Yuwei Liu, Zhi Wang, Wenwu Zhu
bullets: Targets low-quality predictions of manipulated objects and the high inference cost of existing video predictors.
Uses self-generated draft training to condition predictions on a detached clean-video estimate at the same noisy state.
Adds a refinement-only late adapter that applies a residual transformation when a draft is available.
Reuses each velocity prediction to produce both a solver update and the next draft during inference.
Evaluated on Bridge and Language Table, with 4 NFE versus 50–59 calls for existing predictors.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of TWOPASS. (1) Self-Generated Draft Training: on feedback-enabled updates (probability 0.5), two passes share weights and the noisy state. The first runs without gradients and produces a detached draft d = sg(xσ − σṽ) for the supervised second pass. (2) Refinement-Only Late Adapter: a bottleneck with a zero-initialized up-projection sits before the shared prediction head; the role flag r disables it when no draft is available (draft call) and enables it for draft-conditioned (refine) calls. (3) Draft-Reuse Iterative Refinement: inference starts without a draft, then reuses each clean estimate while the solver advances the noisy state, so each solver step costs one network call. Draft training and draft reuse are stages of the same self-conditioning mechanism.

Figure 4. Additional predictions on Bridge. Rows show GT, IRASim, ORV and TwoPass (NFE = 4), at frames 6–15 in the top and bottom examples and at frames 8, 12, 16, 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 29 and 31 in the middle example. Top: moving a blue cloth; TwoPass places the cloth closest to the ground truth, and both baselines place it with an offset. Middle: closing the flap of a box; in the last three frames TwoPass follows the closing flap, and the flap of both baselines remains partly open. Bottom: moving a metal pot and setting it upright; TwoPass stays close to the ground-truth position and size of the pot, IRASim’s pot lags behind, and ORV’s pot shrinks in the middle frames. Red boxes use coordinates derived from GT and shared across methods. Methods share the initial observation and actions.

Figure 1. Motivation and concept of TWOPASS. (a) Planning and policy evaluation repeatedly predict the outcomes of candidate actions, so prediction must be accurate and fast. (b) Prediction must capture changing regions and frame-to-frame visual changes; orange contours show simplified outer boundaries of the main regions that change between frames. (c) Self-Generated Draft Training teaches the model to use its own imperfect predictions; a Refinement-Only Late Adapter gives draft-conditioned correction its own pathway; and DraftReuse Iterative Refinement recycles clean estimates without extra network calls. The draft and supervised training passes share a noisy state, whereas inference advances the solver state between calls.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents can now build interactive 3D worlds and games, yet these worlds, like those built by people, often contain glitches such as floating objects, walls that can be walked through, or objects that change when no one is looking. An automatic auditor could check such worlds at scale and provide rewards for agents that build them, but only if it is both accurate and cheap. Auditing requires three abilities, namely navigating to the objects that may contain a glitch, triggering glitches that appear only after a specific behavior, and recognizing what is wrong. Current auditors are either accurate but slow and expensive or cheap but unreliable. We study how much of the audit small models can take on. A 4B vision language model fine-tuned end to end on verified trajectories of a frontier teacher guided by Bayesian search learns to navigate and trigger, and six such explorers together match a frontier model on both, but recognition stays far behind. We therefore build an auditor in which a swarm of small explorers navigates and triggers, and a frontier model reviews what they record and report. On WorldAuditBench, our auditor succeeds on 55.9% of 213 tasks in Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js worlds, 13.6 points above the strongest auditor reported, at less than a quarter of its cost. It matches the frontier reviewer exploring on its own at 4.6 times lower cost and about half the latency. Without further training, it also answers embodied questions about real-world scans, matching the frontier reviewer exploring on its own and surpassing four other frontier models by 6.4 to 16.6 points.
authors: Jingbo Yang, Ziyan Jiang, Li An, Jiabao Ji, Yujian Liu, Tommi Jaakkola, Yang Zhang, Shiyu Chang
bullets: Targets three auditing challenges: navigating to suspicious objects, triggering behavior-dependent glitches, and recognizing faults.
A fine-tuned 4B vision-language model learns navigation and glitch triggering from teacher-guided verified trajectories; six explorers match a frontier model on these abilities.
Recognition remains weaker in small models, so a frontier model reviews explorers’ recordings and reports.
On 213 WorldAuditBench tasks, the system succeeds on 55.9%, improving 13.6 points over the strongest reported auditor at under one-quarter the cost.
It also answers embodied questions about real-world scans without further training, matching the frontier reviewer and outperforming four other frontier models.

papers.tldr: A swarm of small vision-language explorers plus a frontier reviewer enables accurate, lower-cost auditing of interactive 3D worlds.

papers.abstract: States with identical protected observations can admit different future interventions. Each transition specifies its successor, response increment, required initial reserve and net consumption. Composing these records in execution order distinguishes protocols with equal net consumption and different initial reserve requirements. At a fixed state, a weighted Gram operator determines the linear response ellipsoid and a quotient identifies directions attainable only through cooperation between blocks. Nonlinear systems with identical complete affine data can have incomparable finite-budget response sets. In regular charts, the first correction to quadratic minimum cost is a covariant cubic form involving the third derivative of cost and the Hessians of protection and response. At singular gates, sequential feasibility depends on the peak reserve along the path. A history-weighted operator detects responses outside the old channel's range closure. Controlled congruence characterizes exact reductions of deterministic labelled dynamics, and a two-cut value identity separates the effect of paid verification from that of subsequent action selection. On Qwen2.5-7B Base, two projected policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens under a per-position KL ceiling of $2\times10^{-5}$. Over 200 arrivals they recovered 391 of 396 initial rejections. Each yielded over 1,200 times the held-out cross-entropy reduction of historical-channel-only AdamW. Under an expanded 2,560-position contract, fixed continuation and neutral renewal began on the same protected logit fiber in distinct structural strata. Both admitted all 200 subsequent writes. Fixed continuation yielded 1.74 times the held-out loss reduction per unit squared write cost. Renewal had a smaller KL excess on the first candidate tested at every arrival and used fewer full verification scans.
authors: Qinyou Wang
bullets: Equal protected observations may conceal different intervention futures, initial reserve requirements, and sequential feasibility constraints.
Weighted Gram and history-weighted operators characterize attainable response directions, including cooperative and previously inaccessible channels.
The theory covers nonlinear cubic cost corrections, singular-gate reserve peaks, deterministic reductions, and a two-cut decomposition of verification and action-selection value.
On Qwen2.5-7B Base, two projected policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens and recovered 391 of 396 initial rejections over 200 arrivals.

Under the expanded contract, both policies admitted all 200 writes; fixed continuation achieved 1.74× greater loss reduction per squared write cost, while renewal had lower first-candidate KL excess and fewer full scans.

papers.tldr: The paper develops a framework for distinguishing protected-state dynamics by execution history, response geometry, nonlinear cost, and verification structure, with supporting experiments on projected language-model policies.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models process large numbers of visual tokens, making token pruning important for efficient inference. Training-free pruning methods differ in whether and how they use the user query, and the value of query conditioning remains unclear. We present a controlled study of training-free, pre-LLM video token selection. Using a shared Qwen-3-VL backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings, we compare 21 pruning principles spanning query-agnostic, shallow query-conditioned, structured query-conditioned, and holistic strategies. To instantiate the last two categories, we introduce Structured Query Pruning, which decomposes the question into semantic anchors, and a Pareto variant, which combines anchor relevance with query-agnostic visual diversity. Across Video-MME, MVBench, and LongVideoBench, relevance computed from the raw question embedding is unreliable (8--16 points below the best methods), whereas anchors derived from query decomposition avoid this failure. However, query access is not inherently advantageous: strong query-agnostic coverage methods remain competitive or superior in the full-field comparison. Relative to a redundancy-only baseline, structured selection helps most on evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; on broad tasks, the holistic selector improves over either relevance or redundancy alone. Further, pruning reduces cost and memory. These results support a practical design rule: preserve visual coverage by default, and add structured relevance when the task and token budget demand selective evidence retrieval.
authors: Divya Kothandaraman, Timo Kumkel, Jaclyn Pytlarz
bullets: Compares 21 training-free video token pruning strategies under shared backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings.
Raw question-embedding relevance is unreliable, performing 8–16 points below the best methods across evaluated benchmarks.
Structured query decomposition avoids this failure by selecting tokens linked to semantic anchors.
Query access is not always beneficial: strong coverage-based, query-agnostic methods can match or outperform query-conditioned approaches.
Structured selection helps evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; holistic selection helps broad tasks, while pruning reduces cost and memory.

Tokens are ranked and the top-k are retained for LLM generation. The hybrid Pareto strategy jointly optimizes semantic relevance and visual diversity.

papers.abstract: In multimodal multi-turn dialogue, dialogue history plays a dual role: reliable responses provide useful context for subsequent turns, whereas hallucinated responses can propagate errors across turns. Existing training-free methods globally adjust the effect of dialogue history on generation, making it difficult to suppress misleading information without weakening useful context. To address this trade-off, we introduce Support-Guided Triadic Decoding (SGTD), a training-free framework that selectively controls the influence of unreliable history and fuses complementary predictions during decoding. Specifically, Historical Answer Support Estimation measures the visual support of historical responses against type-matched alternatives and identifies low-support content that may mislead later generation. Support-Targeted Attention Intervention then weakens the influence of this content while preserving the surrounding dialogue, producing a support-refined prediction. Triadic Decoding combines this prediction with the full-history prediction and answer-free visual evidence, while the Support-Adaptive Plausibility Constraint filters implausible tokens using visual agreement and historical support. Experiments on MMHalSnowball and VisDiaHalBench across representative LVLMs show that SGTD consistently achieves the highest accuracy under hallucinated histories while preserving the benefits of factual context.
authors: Yiheng Li, Wenhao Wang, Xingyi Li, Zhilin Tang, Zichang Tan, Zhen Lei, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets error propagation from hallucinated responses in multi-turn multimodal dialogue.
Uses historical answer support estimation to identify responses with weak visual grounding.
Applies targeted attention intervention to suppress misleading history while retaining useful context.
Fuses full-history, support-refined, and answer-free visual predictions with plausibility filtering.
Evaluated across representative LVLMs on MMHalSnowball and VisDiaHalBench, achieving the highest reported accuracy under hallucinated histories while preserving factual-context benefits.
