papers.title: Support-Guided Triadic Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Dialogue with LVLMs

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.
authors: Jiachen Tao, Gengyu Zhang, Haoxuan Wang, Bing Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses the failure of robot policies to compose reliable atomic skills over long-horizon tasks.
A VLM observes camera images and provides the next step in the policy’s instruction format; successful rollouts are relabeled and used for fine-tuning.
On stalled states, next-step coaching increases subgoal completion by 4.6× over the original task instruction.
Unassisted success on unseen long-horizon scenes improves from 47.4% to 59.3%, outperforming human-demonstration and self-collected-success fine-tuning at equal data budgets.
The action backbone remains frozen; the approach is scoped to leveraging existing skills through language guidance.

papers.tldr: CoachSI uses a frozen vision-language model to tell a robot policy the next atomic step, improving long-horizon task success without generating actions.

papers.abstract: Despite strong multimodal capabilities, large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate when linguistic priors outweigh visual evidence or when predictions are grounded in irrelevant or misleading image regions. Training-free contrastive decoding mitigates hallucinations by contrasting the original prediction with an auxiliary one that exposes linguistic priors. Yet existing methods focus on altering the auxiliary input or computation and do not ensure that either branch uses query-relevant visual evidence during decoding. We propose Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding (VEGD), a training-free framework that identifies query-relevant visual evidence and guides its use throughout contrastive decoding. VEGD locates this evidence by aggregating localization heads with strong visual responses and coherent spatial structure, then selectively weakens it in the auxiliary image. During generation, VEGD directs visual-carrier heads in both branches toward the same evidence location, strengthening access to intact evidence in the main branch while anchoring the auxiliary branch to its weakened counterpart. An adaptive distribution fusion strategy then combines or contrasts their predictions according to distribution divergence. Experiments across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that VEGD consistently reduces hallucinations.
authors: Yiheng Li, Wenhao Wang, Xingyi Li, Mingda Jia, Zichang Tan, Yinhang Tang, Zhen Lei, Yang Yang
bullets: Addresses hallucinations caused by linguistic priors and irrelevant or misleading image regions.
Uses localization heads to identify query-relevant evidence with strong visual responses and coherent spatial structure.
Selectively weakens the identified evidence in the auxiliary image and guides visual-carrier heads in both decoding branches to the same location.
Adaptively fuses or contrasts branch predictions based on their distribution divergence.
Experiments across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks show consistent hallucination reduction.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding. papers.abstract: We propose MergeableRF, a method for radiance field relighting through model parameter merging. Given multi-view images of a scene under known basis lights, our goal is to relight the scene by directly combining the parameters of radiance fields trained under these lights. This is motivated by the linearity of light transport: the image under a mixture of lights is the same weighted combination of the images under each light. However, combining the parameters of independently trained radiance fields does not produce the corresponding combination of images. To address this, we represent a scene with shared geometry and a separate appearance network for each basis light. We start these networks from the same initialization and introduce merge-aware training, which teaches their parameter combinations to reproduce the corresponding combinations of images. Given a target HDR environment map, we compute its basis-light coefficients and use them to merge the appearance networks into a single relit model. Our method supports both Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), without material estimation, additional relighting networks, or target-specific optimization. Unlike image-space blending, it requires only one rendering pass per viewpoint. Experiments on synthetic Neural Gaffer objects and real OLATverse captures demonstrate relighting quality competitive with methods trained on the same multi-light observations.
authors: Yinan Wang, Rohan Kadkol, Hyunjin Yoo, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Lalonde, James J. Clark
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between combining independently trained radiance-field parameters and combining their rendered images.
Uses shared scene geometry and separate, identically initialized appearance networks with merge-aware training.
Relights a target HDR environment by computing basis-light coefficients and merging the corresponding appearance networks.
Supports both NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, requiring one rendering pass per viewpoint.
Demonstrates competitive relighting quality on synthetic and real multi-light captures.

papers.abstract: We present DRVEXO-4B-Unified, a modular multimodal assistant built around a 4B language backbone. A self-contained checkpoint combines text, image, and speech inputs with reference-conditioned speech output and structured interaction. A temporal residual connector adapts acoustic sequences to the language interface; explicit text boundaries support incremental speech synthesis; and three task-conditioned scoring heads rank supplied action candidates alongside generative tool calls. These interfaces connect conversation to application-defined choices while leaving action authorization to the application. The system obtains 74.22% on all 900 MMMU validation questions, exceeding the published validation scores of Gemma 3 4B IT and InternVL3.5-4B without test-time scaling. Strict prompt-level IFEval accuracy is 82.26% and MATH-500 accuracy is 89.40%, above the original Qwen3-4B non-thinking report's 81.2% and 84.8%, respectively. On NVIDIA GB10, the model achieves a speech-synthesis first-chunk latency of 390 ms. For concurrent text generation, a growth-aware admission policy completes a 128-answer batch at 594.41 output tokens/s, including filling and draining, without preemptions. We plan to release the model weights and accompanying code under Apache License 2.0, retaining applicable third-party terms.

Achieves 390 ms speech first-chunk latency and 594.41 output tokens/s for a concurrent 128-answer batch on NVIDIA GB10.

papers.abstract: Smoothed online learning has recently been studied as a way to bypass hardness results for the fully adversarial setting, which can be overly pessimistic. In this framework, the adversary is constrained to generate contexts from distributions having a bounded density with respect to some fixed base measure $\mu$. Prior work makes the strong assumption that $\mu$ is known to the learner, with notable exceptions including Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). In this paper, we study sequential probability assignment (a.k.a., online learning with log loss) with smooth, well-specified data in the more general setting where $\mu$ is \emph{unknown}, without the Lipschitz condition imposed in the work of Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). We prove regret upper bounds against both adaptive and oblivious smoothed adversaries: the adaptive bound is controlled by empirical $\ell_\infty$ Hellinger entropy, while the oblivious bound improves this dependence to empirical $\ell_2$ Hellinger entropy, the notion that has been shown to characterize the complexity of learning with i.i.d. data (Bilodeau et al., 2023). Both bounds are obtained through algorithms based on truncated empirical Hellinger covers. We complement these results with a general lower bound, showing that our upper bounds are essentially tight for some natural classes, which implies a separation in the difficulty of smoothed online learning between regimes where $\mu$ is known and where it is unknown.
authors: Ziyi Liu, Daniel M. Roy
bullets: Studies smooth, well-specified online learning with log loss without assuming the learner knows the base measure or that model classes are Lipschitz.
Provides regret bounds for both adaptive and oblivious smoothed adversaries.
The adaptive bound depends on empirical ℓ∞ Hellinger entropy, while the oblivious bound uses the less stringent empirical ℓ2 Hellinger entropy.
Both algorithms are based on truncated empirical Hellinger covers.
A general lower bound shows the guarantees are essentially tight for some classes and reveals a difficulty gap between unknown- and known-measure settings.
papers.selection_reason: Sequential probability assignment with regret bounds is a direct instance of online learning.
papers.title: Sequential Probability Assignment against Smoothed Adversaries with Unknown Base Measure
papers.tldr: This paper develops near-tight regret guarantees for sequential probability assignment against smoothed adversaries when the underlying base measure is unknown.

papers.abstract: Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSEPose, which derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations. We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those inside a tolerancedilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is consistent across camera frames and metric scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across benchmarks.
authors: Junghoon Seo, Hakjin Lee, Jaehoon Sim
bullets: Addresses mesh-dependent reconstruction targets for unseen object instances from partial RGB-D observations.
Maps observed 3D points into normalized object coordinates and selects support within a tolerance-dilated pose-and-size envelope.
Combines the envelope target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context.
On REAL275 and HouseCat6D, closely matches surface-based supervision and remains stable across boundary perturbations and viewpoints.
Supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across both benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression often treats salience or similarity as a proxy for transcription importance. Complete document OCR breaks this assumption: small symbols and repeated entries can be indispensable to the transcript despite being visually inconspicuous. We present Select and Compensate, a two-stage framework built on a simple idea: choosing where to retain a token need not determine all the evidence it carries. Selection combines adaptive encoding resolution with global importance and local contrast to choose which tokens to retain as anchors. Compensation enriches these anchors with nearby discarded content and its relative position, without adding tokens. The OCR backbone remains frozen, and native coordinates and structural tokens are preserved. We evaluate complete page transcription across five backbones on OmniDocBench and document reconstruction on MPDocBench. With half the original visual tokens, our input-adapted configuration reaches 95.42 OmniDocBench Overall on Ovis versus 96.09 for the uncompressed model, and paired evaluations show gains over simply reducing the input resolution on both benchmarks. With the original input grid, our method stays within 0.17 points of the uncompressed model at 75% retention and exceeds a learned global selector by 4.70 points at 25%. On a fixed 200-page Ovis workload at the same 50% visual-token budget, only 3 of its outputs hit the length limit, versus 30-34 for the evaluated RTPrune, DivPrune, and HiPrune adaptations, and it finishes the batch 35-40% sooner. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Yixuan Huang, ShengFan Zhang, Jiawei Chen
bullets: Targets a key OCR limitation: visually subtle symbols and repeated entries may be essential despite low salience.
Selects anchor tokens using adaptive resolution, global importance, and local contrast.
Compensates retained anchors with nearby discarded content and relative positions without adding tokens; the OCR backbone remains frozen.
At 50% of the original tokens, Ovis reaches 95.42 OmniDocBench Overall versus 96.09 uncompressed, and paired evaluations outperform simple input-resolution reduction.
At 25% retention, it exceeds a learned global selector by 4.70 points; at a 50% budget, it also reduces length-limit hits and finishes a fixed workload 35–40% sooner.

papers.abstract: 3D worlds can now be captured, reconstructed, and generated at scale, yet the objects in them stay still: a pressed pillow does not compress, and a pulled door does not swing. Bringing these objects into interactive 4D world models requires a representation of how they can move, deform, and respond physically to user actions in real time. We present PRIO, a pre-trained representation for interactive objects. Given static geometry, PRIO predicts an object-specific configuration space in a single forward pass. This space provides generalized coordinates for Lagrangian mechanics, allowing physical laws and user actions to govern motion. Configurations are linear in these coordinates, allowing the quantities needed by the dynamics to be precomputed. Dynamics then run at interactive rates without further network inference. Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories, PRIO learns priors over object configurations that generalize to unseen shapes. It supports meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians, bringing objects in reconstructed and generated scenes into interaction. We demonstrate its use in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation. In addition, compared with existing 4D generation methods, PRIO generates dynamics faster and follows user actions more faithfully.
authors: Shixun Huang, Lifu Wei, Yue Chang, Chen Geng, Heng Zhang, Jinhyung Ahn, Caoliwen Wang, Siyuan Chen, Donglai Xiang, Jiajun Wu, Peter Yichen Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making reconstructed or generated 3D-world objects physically interactive.
Predicts an object-specific configuration space in one forward pass from static geometry.
Uses linear generalized coordinates with Lagrangian mechanics, so dynamics quantities can be precomputed and simulated without further network inference.
Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories to generalize configuration priors to unseen shapes and support meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians.
Demonstrated in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation; reported faster dynamics and more faithful response to user actions than existing 4D generation methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PRIO. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a pre-trained representation for interactive objects in 4D worlds, enabling real-time physical interaction and dynamics simulation for robot manipulation.
papers.title: PRIO: Pre-trained Representation for Interactive Objects in 4D Worlds
papers.tldr: PRIO predicts a compact, physics-compatible representation of how objects move and deform, enabling fast interactive 4D simulation from static geometry.

papers.abstract: Deficits in reactive balance can increase fall risk among older adults and individuals with neuromuscular impairments, motivating the need for interventions that improve balance recovery. Wearable robotic exoskeletons offer a promising approach to addressing this need by augmenting balance control. However, developing controllers that deliver appropriately timed and scaled assistance remains challenging, as evaluating each candidate strategy requires repeated exposure to destabilizing perturbations. We propose a simulation-to-real framework that combines motion imitation and reinforcement learning to develop balance-assistive ankle exoskeleton control. A muscle-driven neuromusculoskeletal model was trained using a small set of motion-capture data from a single subject to reproduce kinematic and kinetic responses to backward-translation perturbations. This model served as a virtual human for training a reinforcement-learning exoskeleton controller. The resulting controller generated bilateral ankle assistance using only inertial sensor measurements, without explicit perturbation detection. We implemented the controller on-board a bilateral ankle exoskeleton and evaluated it in five healthy subjects whose data were not used for training. Assistance increased the perturbation magnitude that subjects could withstand without stepping by 11.8% and reduced peak center-of-mass displacement and velocity by 13.5% and 28.2%, respectively. Individual benefits varied with baseline recovery strategy and body mass. These results indicate that a single virtual human can yield transferable balance assistance, and that more diverse virtual humans could further improve its effectiveness.

bullets: Targets fall risk caused by impaired reactive balance and the challenge of tuning assistance without repeated physical perturbations.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained models provide transferable representations for class-incremental learning (CIL). However, sequentially adapting these representations introduces optimization costs and may disrupt old-class feature structure. This motivates us to explore whether the discriminative potential of these representations can be further exploited by continually accumulating class information while keeping the encoders frozen. To this end, we propose TAP, a new and novel framework for tapping the discriminative potential of frozen representations in class-incremental learning. It accumulates visual and semantic class information in the frozen CLIP embedding space with only lightweight optimization. TAP comprises three modules: class-conditional visual distribution modeling, class-adaptive semantic calibration, and visual-semantic posterior fusion. The first module retains class means and within-class scatters, combining class-specific and shared covariances to stabilize distribution estimation. The second module learns class-specific weights over text templates from current-task images, adapting text representations to downstream classes. The third module combines the visual and semantic posteriors through a weighted product of experts for prediction over all seen classes without retaining images from previous tasks. Across nine datasets under two incremental protocols, TAP achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining the highest average incremental and final-stage accuracies among the compared methods. The code is provided as an ancillary file.
authors: Zihao Wang (Shandong University), Yu-Wei Zhan (Zhejiang University of Technology), Xiao-Qian Liu (Shandong University), Zhen-Duo Chen (Shandong University), Weitong Liu (Shandong University), Xin Luo (Shandong University), Xin-Shun Xu (Shandong University)
bullets: Addresses the optimization cost and feature disruption caused by continually adapting encoders in class-incremental learning.

Fuses visual and semantic posteriors with a weighted product-of-experts for prediction across all seen classes.
Achieves the highest average incremental and final-stage accuracies among compared methods across nine datasets and two protocols.

papers.abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.
authors: Bo Li, Taoyong Cui, Bob Zhang, Mengran Li, Chengyang Zhang, Yang Zhang, Pheng Ann Heng, Wanli Ouyang, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
bullets: A frozen language model writes programs that directly read, construct, or modify network weights using task knowledge and existing weights.
Programs enable unseen command compositions and a new pickup action, with reported gains up to 99.8% exact match and 98.4% success while preserving prior capabilities.
On ImageNet, four programs improve robustness by 8.84–17.62 points without reducing clean accuracy, outperforming matched fine-tuning baselines.
Causal analysis in Vision Transformers links gains to selectively activated noise-correction gates that preserve clean performance.
Programs transfer across independently trained networks and can be composed with prior edits, supporting reusable and accumulating capability installation.

papers.abstract: Deploying fruit instance segmentation in real agricultural settings requires generalizing across unseen species, orchards, and imaging conditions under strict onboard compute and annotation budgets. We introduce SegAnyFruit (SAF), a data construction and progressive training framework that distills foundation-model priors into lightweight, prompt-free segmenters. SAF combines generic mask pre-training, broad mid-training on automatically annotated web imagery from our curated WebFruits dataset, and human-verified agricultural refinement post-training on PaperFruits, together spanning 733K images and 9.66M whole-fruit masks across 165 fruit types. Across seven benchmarks, zero-shot SAF-RF-DETR-XL reaches 69.06 average mask AP50:95 (+4.76 over SAM 3) while remaining deployable on edge devices. SAF initialization also boosts few-shot to full-shot adaptation across five agricultural domains while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Finally, we systematically analyze training stages, data scale, model capacity, and generative augmentation, and validate our pipeline's transferability to underwater, cell, and human segmentation. We will release our datasets, code, and SAF models.

papers.abstract: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.

papers.abstract: Analyses of error feedback bound the memory buffer through a compressor contraction constant -- $r/p$ for the best rank-$r$ approximation of a $p$-dimensional spectrum -- which survives into the rate. We show it need not appear at all. When the compressed momentum is re-injected into the pre-compression accumulator, the previous compressed momentum $\beta_1 M_{t-1}$ is an admissible competitor in the projection, and the buffer obeys $\|E_t\|_F \le (1-\beta_1)\|G_t\|_F + \gamma\|E_{t-1}\|_F$, free of the dimensions $m,n$ and of the rank $r$. The argument uses only that the compressor is a metric projection onto a closed cone, so it covers top-$k$ selection as well as truncated SVD, holds for every selection from the projection set with no condition on singular-value crossings, and in its trajectory-tracking form assumes nothing about the gradients. In the two-stage template of the standard analyses it replaces a Stage-2 constant of order $p^2/r^2$ by one of order $1$, against $\Theta(p/r)$ for the sharpest contraction-based bounds. Transferring the full rate costs a leakage term, which we bound by the step-weighted gradient mass $\sum_{u\le t}\eta_u\|G_u\|_F$ and show tight up to a factor $\sqrt{2}$; the price is an additive $O(\log^2 T)$ floor, not a slower rate. On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$ the feedback decay costs under $0.008$ validation $F_1$.
authors: Alireza Moayedikia
bullets: The buffer bound depends on gradient norms and decay, not matrix dimensions or approximation rank.
The proof applies to metric projections onto closed cones, covering top-$k$ selection and truncated SVD without singular-value separation assumptions.
In standard two-stage analyses, a dimension-dependent factor of order $p^2/r^2$ improves to order $1$.
Rate transfer incurs a leakage term controlled by the step-weighted gradient mass, producing an additive $O(log^2 T)$ floor rather than a slower rate.
On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$, feedback decay reduces validation $F_1$ by under $0.008.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning enables sequential tasks to be represented as compositions of separately trained skills. This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, comparing their training requirements and task performance with flat reinforcement learning baselines. The evaluation concerns complete pipelines with task-specific observation, reward and control structures. In navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manually specified high-level plans. In manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment and lifting are trained separately, with downstream skills initialised from states collected during predecessor rollouts. Across unseen navigation layouts, the hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms the evaluated flat DQN baselines while requiring fewer training interactions. In manipulation, the hierarchical chain requires fewer training steps than flat SAC and exhibits lower observed variation across seeds. The frozen Pick and Lift skills are further reused for stacking by training an additional Place skill.
authors: Madeleine Nouri, Gelareh Mohammadi, Francisco Cruz
bullets: Evaluates complete hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation.

Uses fewer training interactions or steps than evaluated flat DQN and SAC baselines, with lower observed seed variation in manipulation.
Reuses frozen Pick and Lift skills for stacking by adding a Place skill.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role. However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.
authors: Linfeng Dong, Jianwei Niu, Jiuyi Zhao, Ruibing Feng, Xinghao Wu, Wu Yang, Shuai Tao, Wulong Liu, Mu Li

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ActMem. (a) A pretrained vision-language backbone (Qwen3-VL) encodes the instruction, the timestamped historical frames, and the current perception, and performs latent memory reasoning inside the backbone to produce the subtask together with its Latent Memory CoT states Ct, which condition a flow-matching action expert; Perception Attention additionally routes the current visual features to the action expert. (b) Inside the backbone, the subtask tokens that form Memory CoT follow the history and the current view in the sequence, so under the causal mask they read both, and their hidden states become Ct; the action expert receives only Ct, not the history tokens. (c) Efficient Memory CoT Inference. Consecutive decisions usually share the same subtask, so the previous subtask is reused as a draft and verified against the updated context in a single parallel pass. If it is accepted, its hidden states are recomputed to give the new Ct, with no token-by-token decoding.

papers.abstract: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.
authors: LoongForge Team
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and fragmented, model-specific training stacks of embodied models.
Uses a common abstraction layer to share infrastructure without restricting model architectures or execution requirements.
Combines reusable and hardware-aware optimizations spanning computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8 communication for DDP/FSDP.
Also provides unified data infrastructure, egocentric-to-robot data synthesis, and concurrent simulator evaluation.
Reports 1.47×–4.38× higher training throughput and 4.1×–23.2× faster evaluation than corresponding open-source baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LoongForge-Embodied system architecture. The framework unifies heterogeneous VLA and WAM models under a single native-PyTorch training stack, combining an integrated data pipeline (Ego2Robot, unified data loaders, and composable transforms), an acceleration toolkit of shared optimizations with model-specific execution paths, distributed training with FP8 communication, and an integrated evaluation orchestrator. The right-hand panels preview representative results on training speedup, trainingloss consistency, and benchmark success rates (Section 8).

Figure 3: Training-aligned evaluation architecture. A unified entry point launches a benchmark client process and a model inference server process, which exchange only model inputs and predicted actions over WebSocket RPC. Numbered markers denote the four pipeline stages: observation adaptation (1), payload construction (2), and action decoding (4) run in the client, whereas action prediction through the shared training-side predict_action interface (3) runs in the server, which also hosts the model registry/factory and the action-chunk cache. The client loop returns from each environment step to observation adaptation until the episode terminates.

Figure 2: Unified data architecture of LoongForge-Embodied. Heterogeneous embodied datasets are integrated through a format abstraction layer that exposes a common sample contract. Model-specific data processing is supported through extensible registries for transformations, preprocessing, collation, and sampling, enabling diverse VLA and WAM models to share the same data infrastructure.

Figure 5: Training-loss alignment between the original reference implementations and LoongForgeEmbodied across eight embodied models. The solid blue and dashed orange curves denote the reference and LoongForge-Embodied, respectively. papers.abstract: We study how to obtain a task-specific Vision-Language Model (VLM) for language-guided path generation between start and end points on remote sensing images. We explore this question from three aspects. First, we implement three widely used architectural approaches and compare their performance. Second, we design a scalable method for constructing pre-training data and build an effective pre-training dataset with a degree of diversity. Methods trained on this dataset achieve promising zero-shot performance. Third, we construct three benchmarks that support stratified evaluation and design three metrics for path generation. We investigate this problem through extensive experiments. The results show that the zero-shot performance of methods trained on the constructed pre-training dataset can exceed that of some advanced commercial VLMs. Code and Dataset can be available at https://github.com/jzdang/RemoteVLPG
authors: Junzhe Dang, Mengmeng Zhang, Yuxiang Zhang, Wei Li
bullets: Compares three widely used VLM architectural approaches for the task.
Introduces a scalable method for constructing diverse pre-training data.

Reports that trained methods can outperform some advanced commercial VLMs in zero-shot evaluation.

papers.abstract: We present a stereo visual odometry (SVO) framework that integrates geometric feed-forward models (GFMs) for dense depth prediction with factor-graph-based visual odometry to achieve accurate localisation and dense metric mapping. Our key idea is to exploit sparse but reliable metric geometry estimated from stereo and temporal multi-view observations to calibrate dense GFM predictions, while retaining the robustness and efficiency of model-based SVO. Rather than directly conditioning the GFM on potentially noisy stereo depth, optimised 3D landmarks are used to jointly estimate a scale-shift transformation over all keyframes within each local submap, yielding metrically consistent dense depth predictions. To balance accuracy and computational efficiency, we introduce a hierarchical factor-graph architecture. At the local level, sliding-window optimisation estimates high-frequency camera poses and multi-view-refined 3D landmarks. Dense predictions are generated only for selected keyframes and registered within each submap using SE(3) Generalised ICP. Consecutive submaps are further aligned in Sim(3) using their shared geometry, allowing residual scale inconsistencies to be corrected. These intra- and inter-submap constraints are incorporated into a global factor graph to produce a consistent trajectory and dense metric reconstruction. Extensive experiments on public and in-house datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive odometry accuracy against geometric and learning-based baselines while providing accurate dense metric reconstruction and improved robustness to failures in learned depth prediction.
authors: Fahira Afzal Maken, Sagun Man Singh Shrestha, Edward Vanderfeen, Lucas Carvalho de Lima, Rongxin Li, Changming Sun, Milad Ramezani

Aligns dense keyframes with SE(3) Generalised ICP and consecutive submaps with Sim(3) geometry alignment.
Experiments report competitive odometry, accurate dense metric reconstruction, and improved robustness to learned-depth failures.

papers.abstract: Advances in video generation and avatar synthesis enable new ways to answer user questions through visual explanations. This task requires a system to formulate a correct answer, translate relevant information into visual material, and deliver the explanation through an avatar's speech and actions. Existing benchmarks rarely assess whether avatars point to the visual content being discussed. We introduce VisualTalk-Bench for question-driven avatar-led video explanations in finance and Chinese and English education. It includes 800 curated reference videos and 100 independent evaluation requests, assessing Content Factuality, Speech-Visual Consistency, Visual Quality, Motion Smoothness, and Avatar-Content Pointing. Yet end-to-end video generators often struggle to align gestures with specific visual targets. To explore this challenge, we develop Avatar-O Agent, a modular reference implementation with explicit interaction planning. Experiments across six agents show that factual precision and visual quality do not guarantee accurate pointing. A 26-participant study comparing four agents finds that Avatar-O Agent receives the highest average ratings for visual guidance, perceived pointing accuracy, and explanation effectiveness. We will release the data and code.

papers.abstract: Tree-structured speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models (VLMs) by verifying multiple candidate continuations in parallel. However, long visual contexts increase the cost of speculative computation, making candidate coverage and redundant expansion important considerations beyond tree topology adaptation. We propose Raptor, a training-free framework that uses rejection feedback to jointly regulate candidate coverage and drafting effort. Our key insight is that acceptance length alone cannot distinguish insufficient candidate coverage from excessive deep expansion, and these conditions require different allocation decisions. Raptor therefore extracts complementary rejection-aware signals to characterize speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion. These signals jointly guide bounded, momentum-smoothed updates of tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget, together with execution control that limits unnecessary drafting and progressively restores expansion when appropriate. Extensive experiments with two VLMs across seven multimodal benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Raptor, achieving up to 2.39x average speedup over autoregressive decoding.
authors: Qishu Hu, Haozhao Wang, Zicong Hong, Yufeng Zhan, Yuanqing Xia
bullets: Addresses the high speculative-computation cost of long visual contexts, including insufficient candidate coverage and redundant expansion.
Uses rejection-aware signals for speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion rather than relying only on acceptance length.
Adaptively updates tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget with bounded, momentum-smoothed control.
Experiments across two VLMs and seven multimodal benchmarks report up to 2.39× average speedup over autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.
authors: Payman Behnam, Elaheh Sobhani, Saad Amin, Yahya Hassan, Daniyal Khan, Biswadeep Chakraborty, Tanish Patwa, Souvik Kundu, Alexey Tumanov
bullets: Targets redundant, low-utility tokens in long reasoning traces, which can nevertheless receive high attention scores.
Uses uncertainty-guided pruning: retains more cache during uncertain phases and prunes more aggressively when confidence is high.
Uses redundancy-aware selection to favor informative and diverse tokens over content similar to recent reasoning.
Co-designs the method with vLLM through fused CUDA decode kernels while preserving paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture.
Across three benchmarks and two reasoning models, improves accuracy under constrained cache budgets; for one 8B model, reports up to 1.43× speedup and 45% higher throughput versus Full-KV.

papers.abstract: Combining fine-tuned models by composing their parameter updates has become a standard alternative to multi-task training. We formalize composability as a property of a collection of task vectors and prove that the excess loss of the merged model is controlled by an interference functional of the cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of the updates. In the quadratic regime this functional equals the excess loss, giving a criterion that is necessary as well as sufficient and that measures the angle between task vectors in the curvature metric rather than the Euclidean one. Fine-tuning under a curvature-guided regularizer -- constructed from curvature statistics of the kind memory-efficient optimizers maintain -- keeps displacement in the base curvature metric below a ceiling set by the penalty coefficient at every iterate, at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ non-convex rate. Under a single Loewner comparison between the base statistic and the task curvatures, this control converts into a ceiling on the interference functional, inversely proportional to the penalty coefficient, so that the curvature term of the bound is controlled during training. A first-order term, present because regularized solutions are not stationary for the task loss, is not reduced in the same way. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the budget and the ceiling, show the first-order term dominating for strong penalties, and find the curvature-guided penalty slightly better than an isotropic one. In a three-seed transformer study the functional is rank-correlated with merging degradation, but no more strongly than the Euclidean displacement norm.
authors: Alireza Moayedikia

The regularizer does not similarly reduce the first-order term caused by solutions being nonstationary for the task loss.
Experiments confirm the predicted budget and ceiling; the functional tracks merging degradation, but is no more rank-correlated than Euclidean displacement in a transformer study.

papers.abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.
authors: Boyin Tan, Jiadong Zhang, Xiaosong Ma, Chun Jason Xue, Xiaowei Huang, Youcheng Sun
bullets: Addresses a limitation of outcome-level self-evolution, which cannot distinguish incorrect instructions from instructions the agent failed to follow.
Uses coverage labels—follow, not-follow, or not covered—to guide targeted skill revision.
A persistent root-cause analysis agent validates revisions on subsequent runs, while a maintainer builds a shared strategy library across tasks.
Across three benchmarks and executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7%–70.5% of tasks, outperforming initial skills and the strongest baseline.
Removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

papers.abstract: We study the problem of computational efficiency for linear bandits in high-dimensional settings with a finite arm set. In linear bandits, the increase in the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors leads to growing computational costs of $O(d^2)$ at each round of update. Traditional low-rank approximation methods such as SOFUL reduce computation via fixed-size matrix sketching, yet run the risk of incurring vacuous linear regret when the spectral tail of the data is heavy and the approximation rank is inadequately selected. To guarantee regret convergence and effectively reduce computational costs, we introduce a clustering mechanism and propose the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm. Our method preserves the full covariance information in each cluster by maintaining an exact orthonormal basis of the cluster's column space together with a low-dimensional coordinate representation, which guarantees robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities. It performs cluster switching by assigning a sentinel for each cluster, and reduces per-round update computation to $O(\bar r^2)$ in the cluster's effective dimension $\bar r=\min(r,l)$, where $r$ is the intrinsic rank of the data and $l<d$ is a tunable rank bound.
authors: Hantao Yang, Hong Xie, Defu Lian
bullets: Targets the $O(d^2)$ per-round update cost of high-dimensional linear bandits.
Avoids the vacuous linear regret risk of fixed-rank sketching under heavy spectral tails.
Maintains an exact orthonormal basis and low-dimensional coordinates for each cluster.
Uses cluster sentinels for switching and reduces updates to $O(\bar r^2)$, where $\bar r=\min(r,l)$.
The abstract states sublinear regret and computational savings, but gives no numerical experimental results.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a clustering mechanism (Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit) to reduce computational costs in high-dimensional linear bandits, improving efficiency.
papers.title: Coordinate Basis Linear Bandits with Sublinear Regret over Low-Rank Clusters
papers.tldr: CBL accelerates finite-arm linear bandits by clustering arms and preserving exact low-dimensional covariance structure, achieving robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail failures.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in universal multimodal embedding models. However, this understanding does not ensure that their embeddings preserve the evidence needed to distinguish relevant items from confusable alternatives. To preserve essential discriminative evidence in embeddings, this paper proposes DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework that combines task guidance with on-policy retrieval feedback. Specifically, a few learnable queries are used to encode task-relevant information in a compact latent space. Reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision shape these representations to support both task understanding and retrieval discrimination. To address task-specific discriminative needs, we design shared-private expert adaptation that integrates cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning. Building on this, the on-policy hard-negative distillation is introduced: the student retrieves confusable candidates, and a reverse KL divergence objective aligns its embedding-based similarity distribution with the teacher's fine-grained relevance distribution over these candidates. Candidates are periodically refreshed using updated student snapshots, tying teacher supervision to the student's evolving retrieval behavior and confusions. Across four model configurations that span two backbone generations, DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB, and MRMR, demonstrating its effectiveness across modalities and tasks.
authors: Ben Kang, Junda Wang, Yuxuan Yuan, Hang Li, Yuhan Liu, Xin Chen, Wanting Geng, Tong Lin, Pei Fu, Dong Wang, Jian Luan, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Addresses the gap between multimodal understanding and embeddings that can distinguish relevant items from confusable alternatives.
Uses learnable queries, reasoning instructions, and auxiliary answer-generation supervision to encode task-relevant information compactly.
Applies shared-private expert adaptation to balance cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning.
Distills teacher relevance distributions over hard negatives retrieved by the student, with candidates refreshed as the student evolves.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across MMEB-v2, UVRB, and MRMR for four configurations spanning two backbone generations.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.
authors: Zhengbo Zhou, Dooman Arefan, Shandong Wu
bullets: Addresses the risk that visual-token compression removes contextual information needed to interpret subtle mammographic lesions.
Uses a bilateral-guided token selector to prioritize lesions and their local and contralateral-breast context within a shared token budget.
Applies a bilateral reward to encourage diagnostic reasoning that benefits from preserved cross-image evidence.
Experiments on datasets built from CBIS-DDSM and VinDr-Mammo report better evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained token budgets.
Inference benchmarking shows reduced prefill latency.

papers.abstract: Recovering accurate visible-surface depth from a single RGB-D image and an object mask is essential for robotic grasping and manipulation of transparent objects. Specular reflections cause missing depth, while refraction corrupts nonzero returns with background depth, making raw measurements unreliable as surface anchors. Under a fixed sampling budget, refining an initial single-view prediction within a single search interval either misses large refraction offsets or sacrifices fine local resolution. To resolve this single-view trade-off, MIR-Depth constructs Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses: a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth. Selective Recurrent Refinement then introduces out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update inverse depth from these volumes using a multi-scale ConvGRU. Finally, Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel spatial gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial geometry without imposing raw sensor readings as hard constraints. Experiments on TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D show that MIR-Depth achieves lower error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD. Real-robot evaluations confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction. Code and pretrained models will be publicly available.
authors: Xinzhe Fu, Qi Shao, Yuanfei Xie, Taoyu Wu, Zhihao Cao, Long Hu, Hong Liang, Xianzhi Li, Anh Nguyen, Baoru Huang, Rongsheng Li
bullets: Addresses missing and corrupted depth caused by specular reflection and refraction in transparent-object RGB-D images.
Builds coordinate-aware global and local multi-range inverse-depth hypotheses around a prior-guided prediction.
Uses recurrent refinement with out-of-bounds masking and validity-aware fusion, followed by spatially gated residual correction.
Reportedly achieves lower error than several prior methods across five datasets.
Real-robot evaluations show improved surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of MIR-Depth. A frozen Depth Anything V2 model provides the relative-depth prior. Transformer and CNN encoders extract RGB-mask, relative-depth, and raw-depth features, which are summed at each scale. The summed features provide multi-scale context, while a decoder and depth head predict initial depth D0. Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses construct one shared global inverse-depth volume aggregated by a 3D hourglass alongside medium and fine pixel-wise local volumes filtered by depth-axis convolutions. Selective Recurrent Refinement queries these volumes, encodes lookup features together with per-offset validity indicators, and fuses active ranges to update inverse depth through a multi-scale ConvGRU. Spatially Gated Correction weights the full-resolution residual relative to D0 to produce completed depth for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models plan from pixels with model predictive control, yet often fail on tasks their model should handle. Test-time adaptation attributes such failures to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode, without checking this attribution against the planning loop itself. We follow the executed planning loop on pushing tasks. In most settings, with and without distribution shift, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, where the object stays in place while the model predicts progress. The warm-started gradient-descent (GD) planner then returns nearly the same plan, a fixed point where the agent mostly idles. We propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning before deployment with a fixed-weight loop breaker: a residual memory of the episode's prediction errors or random re-initialization at every replan. With GD, Unstick recovers most of the adaptation gain on pushing tasks with the memory, and with re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts. A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, present with and without distribution shift, which a planner with fixed weights can break. Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/unstick.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Dongheon Lee, Kyu Sung Choi
bullets: At least 96% of observed failures are stalls: the object remains stationary while the model predicts progress.
Stalls arise both with and without distribution shift, challenging the attribution of failures solely to model error.
Unstick combines on-policy fine-tuning with a fixed-weight loop breaker: prediction-error memory or random re-initialization at each replan.
Residual memory recovers most adaptation gains on pushing tasks; re-initialization works well for shape shifts but less for visual shifts.
The findings identify planning-loop fixed points as a major limitation of warm-started gradient-descent planners.

papers.title: Stuck in Place: Stall Diagnosis and Remedies for JEPA Planners

papers.abstract: When reconstructing high-quality 3D assets from images, existing approaches often excel at one objective while compromising another, and frequently overlook the intrinsic quality of the reconstructed surfaces. We present MODL, a framework that jointly optimizes geometry and view-dependent appearance directly on a watertight triangle mesh. Our approach combines Laplacian-preconditioned optimization for smooth vertex updates with curvature-adaptive remeshing to preserve fine details and well-shaped triangles. The triangle mesh is optimized subject to multi-view normalized cross-correlation constraints, but without segmentation, geometric supervision or alpha-blending. Evaluations on object reconstruction datasets demonstrate that MODL achieves competitive novel-view synthesis while producing geometrically accurate models with superior intrinsic mesh quality. Our results highlight the potential of direct mesh optimization to unify photorealistic rendering, geometric reconstruction, and practical 3D asset creation.
authors: Nathaniel Burgdorfer, Philippos Mordohai
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between novel-view appearance and intrinsic mesh quality in image-based 3D reconstruction.
Optimizes a watertight triangle mesh using Laplacian-preconditioned vertex updates and curvature-adaptive remeshing.
Uses multi-view normalized cross-correlation constraints without segmentation, geometric supervision, or alpha-blending.
Evaluations show competitive novel-view synthesis alongside geometrically accurate models and superior mesh quality.
Scope: focused on reconstructing textured objects from images.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of the output mesh geometry and appearance between several GS methods and MODL.
Figure 5. Output 3D assets for MODL on the Aria DTC [9] dataset.

Figure 2. Radar chart of the metrics assessing 3D asset quality. BER, SIR, and AR focus on mesh quality, CD measure geometric accuracy, and PSNR portrays image synthesis capability (see Section 5.3). Methods using TSDF Fusion for post-processing provide competitive geometric accuracy and intrinsic mesh quality, but are lacking in well-formed triangles and rendering capabilities. Triangle Splatting [20] without TSDF Fusion is the antithesis, providing the best rendering capabilities and well-formed triangle shapes, but lacks in mesh quality (since the output is a triangle soup) and geometric accuracy. MeshSplatting [19] provides a nice balance between rendering and geometric quality, but the meshes are nonmanifold and have poor connectivity overall. MODL yields the most balanced 3D assets in terms of the combined mesh, geometric, and photometric quality.

Figure 3. The remeshing operations of Botsch and Kobbelt [2]. To maintain a desired target triangle edge length, edges are: (a) split if the actual edge length exceeds the target length; (b) collapsed if the current edge length is smaller than the target length. In practice, we use a buffer size around the target edge length such that triangle edges that are close to this length are not split or collapsed. Following the Botsch and Kobbelt [2] algorithm: (c) edges are flipped when doing so improves the vertex valence distribution of the mesh; and (d) vertices are moved towards their one-ring neighborhood centroid in a local tangent plane and are then projected back onto the surface.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86$\times$--4.28$\times$ end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Overdue-Lin/WAMotor
authors: Zexun Lin, Yuan Feng, Xike Xie
bullets: WAMs incur high latency from multi-step denoising during robotic control.
The method addresses dual nonuniformity: velocity residuals vary sharply across denoising stages, and integration step sizes unevenly amplify state errors.
It derives a trajectory error tolerance bound linking velocity residuals and integration steps to final action-distribution error.
WAMotor selects reliable anchor velocities, delays speculation when needed, and uses integration-step-aware verification thresholds.
Evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show 2.86×–4.28× speedups with maintained success rates.

papers.title: WAMotor: Accelerating World Action Models via Speculative Inference under Dual Nonuniform Denoising Dynamics

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in parameterized layout generation via tool-augmented code synthesis. However, LLMs lack spatial awareness, making one-shot generation unreliable. While layout quality can be evaluated with established techniques, a critical gap remains: geometric-domain evaluation outcomes cannot be directly translated into actionable code-level fixes, trapping iterative refinement in blind refactoring. We propose SGLayout, a self-refining framework that closes this gap via a schema-guided mechanism. Upon code execution, a structured schema captures the correspondence between each code-level instance and its geometric attributes, establishing a bidirectional link between code space and geometry space. Emulating engineer review practices, SGLayout evaluates layouts along two complementary dimensions: intent compliance through quantitative structural checking and qualitative vision-language assessment, and rule compliance through DRC. All identified violations are then back-projected through the schema onto precise code targets, enabling surgical repair. This closed-loop process iterates until layout convergence. On a curated benchmark of 112 parameterized layout generation tasks using GDSFactory, SGLayout achieves a 76.79% pass rate, compared with 50.89% for the strongest baseline.
authors: Siyang Chen, Yuan Pu, Yuhan Qin, Zhaotan Lin, Siyuan Liang, Zhuolun He, Lining Zhang, Bei Yu
bullets: Addresses unreliable one-shot layout generation caused by LLMs’ limited spatial awareness.
Uses a schema to bidirectionally map code instances to geometric attributes.
Combines structural and vision-language checks for intent compliance with design-rule checking for rule compliance.
Back-projects violations to code targets and iteratively repairs layouts in a closed loop.
Passes 76.79% of 112 GDSFactory benchmark tasks, versus 50.89% for the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to recognize small visual entities and understand their relationships. Scene graphs offer a natural way to represent this information, organizing visual entities as nodes and their relationships as edges. However, we identify two challenges: existing scene graph benchmarks provide insufficient coverage of fine-grained entities and the relationships among them, and existing methods for fine-grained visual understanding have yet to effectively leverage such graph-structured information in MLLMs. To address these challenges, we introduce Fine-Grained Multimodal Scene Graph Benchmark (FG-GraphBench) and FiGRA. FG-GraphBench is a benchmark comprising three complementary tasks: fine-grained visual question answering (FG-QA), image captioning (FG-Caption), and image description generation (FG-Description). We develop a two-stage construction pipeline that discovers and grounds fine-grained entities and establishes their relations to construct the fine-grained multimodal scene graphs (MSGs) in FG-GraphBench. Building on these MSGs, we propose FiGRA, a Fine-grained Graph Representation Augmentation method for MLLMs. FiGRA adopts a two-stage training strategy. It encodes multimodal entity and relation features as continuous graph tokens, and integrates them into the MLLM. Experiments show that FiGRA significantly outperforms strong baselines across three tasks of FG-GraphBench. Further analyses confirm the effectiveness of FG-GraphBench and highlight the importance of preserving fine-grained entity and relation information for visual understanding.
authors: Sicheng Liu, Xunkai Li, Ziyu Han, Xingnan Zhang, Ru Zhang, Rong-Hua Li
bullets: Targets limited coverage of fine-grained entities and relationships in existing scene-graph benchmarks and methods.
Introduces three tasks: fine-grained visual question answering, captioning, and description generation.
Builds fine-grained multimodal scene graphs using a two-stage entity discovery, grounding, and relation-construction pipeline.
FiGRA encodes multimodal entities and relations as continuous graph tokens and integrates them into MLLMs through two-stage training.
Experiments report significant improvements over strong baselines across all three benchmark tasks; analyses emphasize preserving fine-grained information.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents rely on stored records to recover a person's state as facts change. Reliable answers depend on how facts are recorded, retrieved, and presented to the reader. We treat a long-form persona dossier as a memory representation of a known latent state, an invariant identity plus a timeline of facts, routines, and decision rules tied to life phases. We present ChronoDossier, a benchmark of 311 synthetic dossiers of 1k-10k words written by seven generators from dated timelines. Intrinsic metrics evaluate the records against their intended states; extrinsic metrics test recovery by five readers on a seeded 32-persona GPT-5.1 panel balanced across lengths (520 rated turns per condition). The linked states, records, evidence packets, and answers support tests of construction and evidence delivery. In a contextual-stress control, tag-scoped writer inputs remove detected out-of-scope anchor copying. Frozen questions authored on staged dossiers transfer less reliably to one-pass dossiers of the same states. In matched evidence controls, whole sections repair 29 of 32 GPT-5.1 and 25 of 30 Sonnet 4.6 failures labeled as packaging, compared with 2 of 8 and 1 of 8 answer-formation failures. Attribution uses separate key-based and key-free support measures, with model disagreements retained. Length remains confounded with persona and question composition; the observed between-bucket widening depends on excerpt construction. The benchmark supports offline evaluation against known facts. Memory acquisition from interaction and validation against real users remain outside its scope.
authors: Noah Sturgill, Jinho D. Choi
bullets: Models personas as an invariant identity plus time-linked facts, routines, and decision rules across life phases.
Introduces 311 synthetic, 1k–10k-word dossiers from dated timelines, evaluated with intrinsic state-matching and extrinsic reader-recovery metrics.
Matched evidence experiments found whole-section packaging repaired many packaging failures, but rarely corrected answer-formation failures.
Frozen questions transferred less reliably from staged dossiers to one-pass dossiers representing the same states.
Length effects are confounded by persona, question composition, and excerpt construction; interaction-based memory acquisition and real-user validation are out of scope.

papers.abstract: Despite learning transferable features, fake image detectors may struggle on unseen domains due to mismatched decision boundaries. Our analysis shows that features extracted by the frozen forensic encoder remain discriminative, but the source-trained decision boundary does not fully exploit this information. However, correcting this boundary without source data or target labels remains challenging, as unreliable source predictions may lead to incorrect adaptation. To address this issue, we propose Graph-Regularized Residual Adaptation (GraRA), which refines the source decision boundary using only unlabeled target data. To determine which classifier directions to update, GraRA constructs a compact residual subspace from uncertainty-weighted target features and keeps it orthogonal to the source classification direction. To guide these updates, it uses source-score anchors to generate soft labels through target-graph diffusion, while neighborhood consistency regularizes residual learning within the constrained subspace. The learned correction is merged into the source classifier, requiring only 32 optimized coefficients and no additional inference branches. On diverse unseen OpenMMSec domains, GraRA achieves 84.36\% accuracy and 91.34\% AUC, improving over the source detector by 4.33 and 3.50 percentage points, respectively. Further analysis shows that reliable source predictions and locally consistent neighborhoods help guide residual learning, allowing GraRA to correct ranking errors that a simple threshold shift cannot address. \textcolor{cvprblue}{Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Shichuang Xie, Qishuai Ding, Tong Qiao, Liquan Shen, Guorui Feng
bullets: Frozen forensic features remain discriminative across domains, but the source-trained decision boundary can misclassify target images.
GraRA learns a compact residual correction in an uncertainty-weighted target-feature subspace orthogonal to the source classification direction.
Source-score anchors, target-graph diffusion, and neighborhood consistency provide soft supervision without source data or target labels.
Using only 32 optimized coefficients and no extra inference branch, GraRA reaches 84.36% accuracy and 91.34% AUC on diverse unseen OpenMMSec domains.
It improves over the source detector by 4.33 and 3.50 percentage points, correcting ranking errors beyond what threshold shifting can fix.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of GraRA. Given unlabeled target images, a frozen source detector extracts target features and source logits. GraRA then adapts the source classifier in three stages. (a) An Uncertainty-Aware Residual Subspace is constructed from uncertainty-weighted target features and kept orthogonal to the source classification direction to constrain classifier updates. (b) Source-Guided Target Graph Diffusion uses real and fake anchors to guide semantic diffusion on a target k-NN graph, generating graph-refined soft targets. (c) GraphConsistent Residual Optimization combines semantic consistency and graph smoothness losses to optimize residual coefficients within the constrained subspace. The learned residual is merged into the source head for target inference.

Figure 5. Understanding boundary adaptation in GraRA. (a, b) Decision boundaries of the source classifier, shifted source classifier, and GraRA on two representative targets. (c) Relationship between 5-NN label purity and final AUC gain on unseen target domains.

Figure 1. Motivation for GraRA. (a) The source classifier separates real and fake samples in the source domain. (b) Domain shifts can cause decision boundary mismatch even when frozen features remain discriminative. (c) Unconstrained adaptation may amplify errors from unreliable source predictions. (d) GraRA combines graph-refined supervision with constrained residual learning to correct the source decision boundary.
