papers.abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.
authors: Chengyang Dong, Ze Chen, Kai Ye, Chutian Wang, Heng Xu, Wei Mo, Maomao Li, Jiayan Xu, Jiayuan Wu, Yihao Xiao, Linhua Ye, Zhonghua Peng, Ruize Han, Jialong Sun

Theory links estimation variance to convergence limits in high-dimensional, small-population settings.

papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies from demonstrations typically samples trajectory segments uniformly or relies on static offline data curation before training. However, we find that demonstration data vary sharply in supervision value across temporal windows, and that each window's value to the policy evolves substantially during training rather than being fixed or captured by raw loss alone. Motivated by this finding, we propose RefreshGrad, an online adaptive data-sampling framework that periodically scores temporal windows from the evolving policy using five policy-native signals and dynamically adjusts their sampling weights during training. RefreshGrad focuses optimization on informative, learnable windows without altering the policy architecture, training objective, or inference cost. Across ten LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks, RefreshGrad boosts average success from 60.7% (Uniform) and 68.2% (FAKTUAL) to 76.1% under visual perturbations, and from 57.4% and 73.3% to 81.3% in clean scenes.

papers.abstract: Continual SAR interpretation requires multimodal large language models to learn incoming sources while retaining earlier task abilities. This is difficult when acquisition and geographic shifts alter visual evidence, regionally concentrated categories bias answers, and historical images are scarce. We address this problem with Historical On-Policy Distillation (HOPD), which reuses source-acquisition LoRA states as persistent teachers for one evolving student. Archiving each state before consolidation preserves a stable source reference. The teachers supervise student-generated prefixes, transferring historical behavior to the student's changing generation contexts. To enrich sparse replay, original-view teachers guide augmented historical student views while preserving spatial coordinates. This knowledge is consolidated into a single deployed adapter that requires no source identity. On SARVQA-CL, our source-incremental evaluation protocol, HOPD achieves the highest final mean score of 54.51 among the compared methods, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.96 points. It also improves the final source-macro score in every evaluated task over shared-memory Replay-SFT, with gains across source orders. These results support source-acquisition history as supervision for retaining earlier task performance during continual SAR adaptation. Code and data: https://github.com/zcablii/HOPD.

papers.abstract: Panoramas can serve as shared scene backgrounds for multi-shot video generation, but most existing panorama generators take text alone or a single input image. We present a single model that generates a full equirectangular panorama from a text caption and K in {0,...,4} perspective conditioning views taken by a four-camera rig at one viewpoint. We fine-tune a pretrained text-to-image rectified-flow transformer in two stages. In the first stage, each conditioning view is appended to the token sequence together with the ID of its camera slot, and the number of views varies during training, so one set of weights serves every input setting. In the second stage, we improve the region not covered by any conditioning view. Supervised training computes its loss on noisy latents of the ground truth and never scores a panorama the model has generated and decoded, so we propose Uncovered-Region GRPO (UR-GRPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that rewards the candidates a vision-language model prefers in pairwise comparisons on crops around this region. Because the slot ID alone does not tell the model which way the rig points, we also offer an optional variant that writes each view's camera direction into its position encoding, which lets the user decide where each view appears in the output. With one conditioning view, our model outperforms the previous state of the art, 360Anything, trained on the same data and evaluated with the same code, on Laval Indoor and gives mixed results on an indoor subset of SUN360; the second stage improves the results for every number of conditioning views.
authors: Rui Hong, Xugang Ye, Jana Ko\v{s}eck\'a, Kai Fan
bullets: Addresses panorama generation for multi-shot video by combining captions with up to four views from a four-camera rig.
Fine-tunes a pretrained text-to-image rectified-flow transformer with camera-slot-aware view tokens and variable numbers of inputs.
Introduces Uncovered-Region GRPO, using vision-language-model preferences on crops of regions not covered by conditioning views.
An optional direction-aware positional encoding lets users control where each view appears in the panorama.
With one view, it outperforms 360Anything on Laval Indoor, shows mixed results on SUN360, and the second stage improves results for all view counts.

papers.abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.
authors: Xuwei Ding, Skylar Zhai, Linxin Song, Jiarui Feng, Dongqi Fu, Huajun Xi, Junnan Li, Jingcheng Liang, Jieyu Zhao, Yinglong Xia, Hong Li, Jian Kang

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a lightweight policy model to mitigate the difficulty of handling higher-dimensional action spaces in reinforcement learning (RL), alongside an algorithm to effectively train it. To address this, we focus on drifting models, which can implicitly represent complex distributions and infer actions in a single forward pass. However, while drifting models can be straightforwardly trained via backpropagation of the Q-gradient, this alone cannot be expected to appropriately capture the desired action coordination. Therefore, this paper constructs a three-step learning algorithm to encourage the action coordination. First, the source distribution of the drifting model is co-optimized as a diagonal policy model. This conditions the drifting model to attach the coordination, which cannot be expressed by a diagonal distribution, as residuals. Second, a discriminator model before and after drifting is introduced with adversarial training for a regularization term. This actively promotes the extraction of the coordination that fundamentally separates the two distributions. Third, best-of-N sampling is applied for action selection during rollouts in order to give directionality toward/beyond the regions where the coordination is insufficiently extracted/sufficiently discovered. The proposed method consistently improves the sample efficiency and the final control performance over the conventional diagonal distribution modeling across three locomotion tasks with high-dimensional action spaces. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that this improvement is achieved by reducing variance in certain action dimensions, effectively coupling them with other actions as action coordination.
authors: Taisuke Kobayashi
bullets: High-dimensional actions are difficult to coordinate when modeled with conventional diagonal distributions.
The method uses a drifting model that represents complex action distributions and generates actions in one forward pass.
Training combines co-optimization of a diagonal source policy, adversarial discrimination before and after drifting, and best-of-N rollout sampling.
Across three high-dimensional locomotion tasks, it consistently improves sample efficiency and final control performance over diagonal modeling.
Analysis attributes the gains to reduced variance in some action dimensions and stronger coupling among actions.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) now render long, legible text in images, and feature caching is a standard way to accelerate them. Caches are judged by image-level metrics, which do not check whether the rendered text is still correct. We find that caching silently rewrites this text. On Z-Image, TaylorSeer at 2.9x fewer FLOPs lowers word accuracy from 62% to 46%, while ImageReward and CLIP Score barely change. Sampling with fewer steps at the same compute keeps almost all of this text, so the loss comes from how the cache predicts the skipped steps. Decomposing the cache error along classifier-free guidance (CFG), we trace this loss mainly to the guidance term, the difference between the conditional and unconditional predictions, which caches extrapolate worst on text. Correcting the guidance inside the text alone recovers most of the lost text. We therefore propose GuideCache, which recomputes both CFG branches only on the tokens with the largest predicted guidance error, using the guidance terms that the cache already stores. At 2.4x fewer FLOPs, GuideCache restores full-compute prompt fidelity on Z-Image and Qwen-Image, and on Z-Image it renders text as well as or better than ToCa, TeaCache, and FasterCache while staying much closer to the full model's output. GuideCache works with caches of any order, and on top of fewer sampling steps it keeps more text than step reduction at a higher speedup. These results suggest that acceleration methods for text-rendering models should be evaluated on the text they render.
authors: Kun Zhou, Wenmian Yang, Zhensheng Wang, Weijia Jia
bullets: Feature caching can silently rewrite image text even when image-level metrics such as CLIP Score and ImageReward barely change.
The text loss primarily comes from caching errors in classifier-free guidance, especially the difference between conditional and unconditional predictions.
GuideCache recomputes both guidance branches only for tokens with the largest predicted guidance errors, using cached guidance information.
At 2.4× fewer FLOPs, it restores full-compute prompt fidelity on Z-Image and Qwen-Image and outperforms or matches prior caches on Z-Image text rendering.
The work argues that acceleration methods for text-rendering models should be evaluated directly on rendered-text accuracy.

papers.abstract: Underwater vehicle-manipulator systems distribute actuation across thrusters and joint motors. Whole-body model predictive control (MPC), rather than separate vehicle and arm controllers, can coordinate both to extend the workspace and exploit the system's full kinematic capability. Doing so, however, requires a hydrodynamic model and derivatives throughout the prediction horizon. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) captures geometry-dependent forces and moments for such a model, but is too expensive to evaluate online. We present a differentiable analytical hydrodynamic model combining smooth spherical-harmonic force and moment fields with a coupled added-inertia matrix identified from CFD. It compactly represents velocity and acceleration-dependent loads and provides their derivatives in closed form. These derivatives are propagated through free-floating vehicle--manipulator dynamics for whole-body trajectory optimization and receding-horizon control, jointly optimizing thruster forces and joint torques for reaching and continuous tracking. Held-out CFD tests validate the principal translational-force and rotational-moment fields and the added-inertia response. The analytical Jacobians evaluate faster and avoid the step-size sensitivity of central finite differences. Closed-loop Stonefish experiments demonstrate whole-body MPC in an independent marine simulator. By making geometry-dependent hydrodynamics directly available to gradient-based control, the model incorporates water forces and their sensitivities into motion allocation between the vehicle and arm, rather than treating them only as disturbances.
authors: Hefan Wang, Yvan Petillot, Carlos Mastalli
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of using CFD hydrodynamics online for underwater vehicle–manipulator control.
Combines smooth spherical-harmonic force and moment fields with a CFD-identified coupled added-inertia matrix.
Provides closed-form hydrodynamic derivatives propagated through free-floating vehicle–manipulator dynamics.
Held-out CFD tests validate key force, moment, and added-inertia responses; analytical Jacobians are faster and avoid finite-difference step-size sensitivity.
Closed-loop Stonefish experiments demonstrate coordinated whole-body MPC for reaching and continuous tracking.

papers.abstract: Existing weakly supervised image manipulation localization (IML) methods typically rely on annotation-specific training strategies, hindering the joint use of diverse annotations within a single model. This limits the scale of usable training data and constrains further progress. We propose UniIML, a teacher-student framework that maps diverse weak annotations into a unified representation to guide the Segment Anything Model (SAM) in generating multiple candidate masks. However, SAM is designed for general-purpose segmentation and has limited sensitivity to manipulation traces; its predicted quality scores alone may therefore fail to reliably identify the candidate that best delineates the manipulated region. We introduce Ordinal Safe Consensus (OSC), which first filters candidates using trusted weak-annotation constraints encoded in the unified representation. It then ranks the remaining candidates separately by consistency with weak annotations, SAM-predicted quality scores, and cross-view stability, aggregating these rankings for an initial selection. To assess how changes in the evaluation criteria affect candidate selection, OSC repeats ranking and selection while omitting one criterion at a time. The most frequently selected candidate is adopted as the final mask, and its relative selection frequency quantifies selection stability. We construct soft pseudo-labels from the selected candidate's predicted probabilities and estimate pixel-level supervision weights based on selection stability, pixel-level agreement among candidates, and predictive certainty. The student receives direct supervision in regions defined by weak annotations and learns from soft pseudo-labels elsewhere through reliability-weighted distillation, enabling unified training across weak annotation types. Experiments show that UniIML achieves superior average performance compared with state-of-the-art IML methods.
authors: Songlin Li, Hui Ma, Zhiqing Guo, Dan Ma, Gaobo Yang, Xin Liao
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing weakly supervised IML methods use annotation-specific training strategies.
Uses a teacher–student framework to convert diverse weak annotations into a shared representation that guides SAM to generate candidate masks.
Introduces Ordinal Safe Consensus (OSC), which filters and ranks candidates using annotation consistency, SAM quality, and cross-view stability.
Builds soft pseudo-labels and pixel-level supervision weights from selection stability, candidate agreement, and predictive certainty.
Experiments report superior average performance over state-of-the-art IML methods, without specifying numerical results in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen visual reasoning by repeatedly applying weight-tied modules. However, their decoding memory grows with recurrent depth and limits the image size and batch size that fit in a fixed memory budget. Each recurrent step produces its own key-value (KV) states, so the cache holds several copies of the same image. We find that, after an exact prefill, earlier steps still need access to visual information but can reuse the final visual KV within the same module. We propose FoldCache, which compresses visual KV along the recurrent axis while preserving the full prefill computation. FoldCache partitions recurrent steps within each module into groups and retains the final visual KV of each group for its members to share during decoding. Sharing stays within module boundaries, while question and answer KV remain separate for each step. The grouping granularity controls the degree of compression, and folding can be combined with token eviction and quantization to further reduce memory use. On LoopVL, FoldCache approximately halves prefix KV memory while matching full-cache accuracy on five open-ended benchmarks. These memory savings support batch sizes up to 1.7 times those of a full cache under the same GPU memory budget, and up to 2.6 times with the more aggressive FoldCache-Lite.
authors: Kun Zhou, Wenmian Yang, Zhensheng Wang, Yanzeng Li, Weijia Jia
bullets: Looped VLMs store separate visual KV states for each recurrent step, limiting image and batch sizes under fixed memory.
FoldCache preserves exact prefill computation, then groups recurrent steps within each module to share the final visual KV during decoding.
Question and answer KV states remain separate, and grouping granularity controls the memory–compression trade-off.
On LoopVL, it approximately halves prefix KV memory while matching full-cache accuracy across five open-ended benchmarks.
The method enables up to 1.7× larger batches, or up to 2.6× with the more aggressive FoldCache-Lite; it can also combine with token eviction and quantization.

(c) At decoding, each invocation of a sample attends to its group’s visual segment, stored once per group and sample, and to its own question and answer KV, and the two results are merged by log-sum-exp.

papers.abstract: The success of manipulation policies is closely tied to the spatial relationship between the robot and the target object, as well as the task being performed, making the ability to adjust the robot's pose critical for successful execution. When the robot starts away from the task, such adjustments require coordinating navigation with local manipulation. Jointly training these capabilities incurs substantial computational and data costs, while navigating toward a predefined goal pose limits the flexibility needed to adapt to task-specific manipulation requirements. To address these challenges, we propose Learning to Move from and for Manipulation Policies (M4M), a framework that learns manipulation-aware mobility directly from pretrained manipulation policies. By leveraging the hidden representations of the policy's action-generating network as dense supervision, together with a limited number of manipulation execution outcomes, we learn a spatially conditioned embedding that captures task-dependent manipulation success across candidate robot poses. From the robot's current stereo observations, this representation estimates manipulation success at unvisited poses without rolling out the manipulation policy at each location. It is further integrated into navigation policy training, while a learned handoff policy decides when to transition from navigation to manipulation, enabling the robot to move and manipulate in a unified, task-aware manner. Across eight articulated-object tasks in unseen RoboCasa kitchens, M4M achieves 47.0% mean task success, compared with 26.5% for the strongest baseline and 19.2% for direct manipulation execution, and refrigerator-closing experiments show consistent improvements across four frozen manipulation policies.
authors: Siyuan Zheng, Zhong Cao, Henry X. Liu
bullets: Addresses the need to coordinate navigation and manipulation when the robot starts away from the task, while reducing the cost of jointly training both capabilities.
Uses hidden action-policy representations and limited manipulation outcomes to learn a spatially conditioned embedding of manipulation success across robot poses.
Predicts success at unvisited poses from stereo observations without executing the manipulation policy at every location.
Integrates the learned representation into navigation and uses a handoff policy to decide when to switch to manipulation.

Achieves 47.0% mean success across eight unseen RoboCasa kitchen tasks, versus 26.5% for the strongest baseline and 19.2% for direct manipulation; refrigerator-closing tests improve across four frozen policies.

papers.title: Learning to Move from and for Manipulation Policies: Spatializing Latent Action Representations for Goal-Pose-Free Mobile Manipulation

papers.abstract: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination should therefore preserve Jev's fast local action selection while introducing LLM reasoning when execution stalls. We observe that recurring state-action pairs can signal stalled execution. We therefore propose LoopRoute, a simple but effective action router that uses this signal to allocate control within an agent. The decision model acts by default. When a loop is detected, the LLM provides brief, feedback-driven assistance and then returns control to the decision model. Later loops can request further assistance. The rule requires neither additional training nor model-specific confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves task success over standalone Jev with only limited use of the LLM policy. The mean gains are 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on ALFWorld, MapReader, and TextWorld cooking, respectively. Compared with full LLM control, LoopRoute also substantially reduces the mean cumulative API time and API-call cost per task. The same rule also improves the success rates of six frozen decision models.
authors: Zeming Yu, Huamin Ma, Yingyu Chen, Yuan Sun, Peng Hu, Yang Qin
bullets: Addresses stalled execution in decision agents that repeatedly select actions without progressing.
Routes control to the decision model by default and requests brief, feedback-driven LLM assistance upon loop detection.
Requires no additional training or model-specific confidence calibration.
Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, improves success over standalone Jev by 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1%, while reducing API time and cost versus full LLM control.
Also improves success rates for six frozen decision models.

papers.selection_reason: Loop-triggered routing reduces LLM invocation cost and improves task success in agent benchmarks.
papers.title: Stop Going in Circles:Loop-Triggered Routing for System 1 Decision Agents
papers.tldr: LoopRoute keeps fast System 1 action selection by invoking an LLM only when repeated state-action loops indicate the agent is stuck.

papers.abstract: Argumentation frameworks (AFs) provide explicit, formal mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts and thus have been incorporated into large language model (LLM) decision-making. The benefits vary and depend on how arguments and their relations are constructed, evaluated, and incorporated into the decision process. {We abstract a workflow consisting of four stages based on existing argumentation-augmented methods} and investigate their design choices over tasks of debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification. Our evaluation with recent LLMs shows that existing methods do not consistently improve performance across the considered tasks. Motivated by this observation, we develop two task-specific methods. The first is called Qnt-Arg, which organizes arguments around the original speakers in debate materials and aggregates model-estimated argument strengths and candidate-answer priors under gradual semantics. The second is Qlt-Arg that uses credibility estimates to establish preferences between conflicting evidence items and applies grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for subsequent LLM inference. We examine the roles of generative and decision models within the two methods. In the debate setting, Qnt-Arg consistently outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods across matched configurations; Qlt-Arg improves retrieval-based fact-verification performance compared with the baselines. These findings demonstrate the value of combining formal argumentation and LLM while highlighting the importance of aligning with tasks in argumentation construction, model selection, and the role of formal semantic reasoning.
authors: Bochen Han, Anshu Xiong, Mingyang Ma
bullets: The study analyzes a four-stage workflow for incorporating argumentation frameworks into LLM decision-making.
It evaluates design choices for debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification.
Qnt-Arg groups debate arguments by original speakers and combines estimated argument strengths with answer priors using gradual semantics.
Qlt-Arg ranks conflicting evidence by credibility and uses grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for LLM inference.

papers.abstract: Visual world models such as DINO-WM and JEPA-WM plan with an optimizer that searches for actions whose predicted outcome has the lowest cost, its distance to a goal image. A plan can thus fail in two ways: the optimizer never tries a good action that the cost would prefer (a search failure), or the cost, computed on predictions, ranks a bad action first (a scoring failure). The two need different remedies, more search or a better model, but a planner does not record which one occurred. We tell them apart by executing the optimizer's candidates, scoring a known solution with the planner's own cost, and comparing costs on predicted and real outcomes. An error model explains when each arises and so how to use retrieved demonstration windows (DemoProp): start the search from them (a warm start) when prediction errors are small, and average them without the model when large errors make the optimizer pick overrated actions. Across four simulated environments and three world models, on short tasks whose goals the planner can represent, PushT and Wall fail mostly by search, while Metaworld and RoboCasa fail by scoring because the cost, sound on real outcomes (AUROC 0.94 on Metaworld), is at chance on predictions (0.54). The diagnosis tells which remedy pays off: a four times larger search lowers the real-outcome cost only where failures come from search (clearly for DINO-WM), and where they come from scoring, averaging the windows without the model solves 127 of 168 new Metaworld tasks, against at most 87 when the model chooses among them. Within PushT, degrading only the model flips which use is better, and our rule, frozen in advance, follows the flip and solves 678 of 960 new episodes, against 530 for the best fixed use.
authors: Haoxuan Jia, Yang Liu, Shang Luo, Chenhao Wu, Zixiang Ni, Yingguang Yang, Feng Zhang, Chongyang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Kefu Xu, Congjing Ran, Jifeng Zhu, Bin Chong
bullets: Planner failures are separated into search failures—good actions are not tried—and scoring failures—predictions rank bad actions as best.
The diagnosis executes candidate actions, evaluates a known solution, and compares costs on predicted versus real outcomes.
DemoProp warm-starts optimization when prediction errors are small, but averages retrieved demonstrations without the model when errors are large.
Across four environments and three world models, PushT and Wall mainly exhibit search failures, while Metaworld and RoboCasa mainly exhibit scoring failures.
Adaptive remedy selection outperforms fixed demonstration use in the reported PushT evaluation, solving 678 of 960 episodes versus 530 for the best fixed strategy.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.
authors: Bowen Xue, Saeed Hadadan, Fabrice Rousselle, Zahra Montazeri, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Milos Hasan
bullets: Targets reconstruction errors in scene layout, scale, lighting, and unseen-surface completion.
Uses shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates to coordinate scene planning and component construction.
Agents generate parameterized Blender programs, with visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail selection.
Adds inferred unseen regions, fitted lighting, motion support, programmatic checks, and visual comparison-based revision.
Evaluated on 100 scenes, showing better original-view fidelity than direct-agent reconstruction and stronger novel-view content similarity than compared video-to-3D methods.

papers.abstract: Generating realistic 3D assets remains constrained by classical representations: surface meshes and compact physically based materials struggle to express objects whose appearance arises from fine geometry or complex light transport, while existing Gaussian-splatting generators typically bake fixed illumination into appearance. We introduce VideoRNG, a two-stage method that generates complete, relightable 3D assets from a text prompt or a single image without prescribing a mesh or analytic material model. A video generator fine-tuned from a pretrained video diffusion backbone first produces a structured RGBA turntable sequence under a known pose, camera, and illumination. A feed-forward large reconstruction model initialized from a pretrained video diffusion backbone then maps the video-VAE latent frames of selected turntable frames directly to millions of anisotropic Gaussians with learned neural appearance features. A shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer turn this representation, which we call ray-traced Relightable Neural Gaussians (rtRNG), into radiance under novel viewpoints and illumination. To preserve high-frequency appearance while learning geometry, we introduce depth-anchored appearance training, and we make million-Gaussian reconstruction practical through foreground token selection and cost-aware distributed sampling. VideoRNG generates complex assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs that can be interactively rendered, relit, and integrated into scenes.
authors: Bowen Xue, Saeed Hadadan, Fabrice Rousselle, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Zahra Montazeri, Milo\v{s} Ha\v{s}an
bullets: Addresses the limitations of meshes, analytic materials, and illumination-baked Gaussian representations for complex appearance and light transport.
Uses a fine-tuned video diffusion model to generate structured RGBA turntable sequences with known pose, camera, and lighting.
Reconstructs selected video-VAE latent frames as millions of anisotropic Gaussians with learned neural appearance features.
A shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer support novel-view rendering and relighting.
Demonstrates interactive scene integration for assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs.

The MLP labeled “4L × 64” is the per-asset decoder distilled from the nine-layer, width-512 shared decoder described in Section 3.4 for final rendering. (d) The resulting asset supports novel views and lights through stochastic Gaussian ray tracing.

papers.abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world models have shown strong predictive capabilities, they still struggle with the heterogeneous dynamics arising from diverse object interactions. To address this in a unified framework, we decompose robotic interactions into distinct physical regimes and assign each to a specialized motion expert. We introduce MoRE, a 3D world model with a mixture of motion experts organized around rigid, deformable, and prehensile dynamics. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific priors. Trained on mixed simulation and real-world data, MoRE integrates with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to support diverse manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MoRE improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance. Code, data, and project website are available at https://alwaysleepy.github.io/MoRE-WM-site/.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Shaowei Liu, Albert J. Zhai, Henry Che, Wei-Chiu Ma, Shenlong Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling heterogeneous physical interactions in robotics.
Assigns distinct motion experts to rigid, deformable, and prehensile physical regimes.
Trains on mixed simulation and real-world data and integrates with Model Predictive Control.
Improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes and strengthens real-world MPC performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MoRE. Given the current and historical object states and actions, represented as point clouds, we first encode the scene and actor inputs into point tokens using two encoders. An explicit gating network then selects among specialized motion experts, each tailored to a distinct physical regime, to predict the next object state in 3D. P = prehensile, NP = non-prehensile.

Figure 4: Model Predictive Control (MPC) performance. (a) Box pushing and (b) toy manipulation results. Each section details the prediction error across planning steps (left) and success rate vs. error threshold (right). MoRE achieves lower error and higher success than the baselines.

Figure 3: Qualitative results on DROID evaluation. We compare model predictions with ground truth on challenging DROID scenes with clutter, diverse objects, and partial observations. Even for small, low-resolution manipulated objects, our model produces accurate dynamics, demonstrating robustness to occlusion and noise.

Figure 5: Real world dynamics predictions. We visualize predictions of point motion on real world data. The red points are the end-effector (action) points. The Vanilla model struggles to treat the box as rigid and the toy sloth as soft. In contrast, our model correctly handles the different cases.

Figure 6: Benchmark tasks visualization: Simulation and real-world benchmarks covering rigid and soft objects under non-prehensile and prehensile interactions, designed to evaluate generalization across diverse physical regimes.

Table 2: Dynamic model comparison across interaction types and physics. We report geometric accuracy (MSE, CD) and material structural metrics (rigidity or Laplacian). Privileged experts (gray) are domain-specific and assume known interaction types at test time, while our Mixture-of-Experts model handles diverse interactions in a unified framework with consistently strong performance.
Table 4: Comparison with Point-World on the DROID dataset. Our method performs better across all three cases, showing strong generalization to real-world object dynamics.

Table 5: Gating Network Accuracy. Expert selection accuracy (%) evaluated over 50 random interactions per task category. The gating network maintains consistently high accuracy across diverse regimes, indicating reliable expert routing for different physical dynamics.

Table 3: Ablation of MoRE under different interaction types and physical regimes. We evaluate the impact of expert specialization, routing strategy, and self-rollout training using geometric and structural metrics. Performance degrades when removing expert specialization, explicit routing, or self-rollout training, highlighting the importance of each component for robust dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: Sign language translation and recognition have been shown to benefit from various pretraining approaches. We propose a novel two-stage pretraining approach for the motion encoder, which first learns to reconstruct masked motion, followed by joint masked prediction of pseudo-gloss units and motion. Pseudo-glosses serve as an intermediate structured representation of natural language text and are obtained from the captions by a large language model. We curate a corpus of about 1,100 hours of American Sign Language from five public datasets, estimate 2D pose for all clips and define an evaluation protocol. We then reproduce state-of-the-art translation methods and evaluate them using the same train and test splits. We propose a translation model built on our pretraining strategy, and this model outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods Uni-Sign and SHuBERT, as well as the YouTube-ASL baseline, on the How2Sign, ASL STEM Wiki and OpenASL datasets. Furthermore, the gain from the joint pretraining using motion and pseudo-gloss grows as translation data shrinks. A classifier built on the same encoder also achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ASL Citizen isolated sign recognition and outperforms our reproduction of Uni-Sign on WLASL2000.
authors: Rui Hong, Jana Ko\v{s}eck\'a
bullets: Uses a two-stage motion-encoder pretraining strategy: masked-motion reconstruction, then joint masked prediction of motion and LLM-derived pseudo-gloss units.
Curates approximately 1,100 hours of ASL video from five public datasets, estimates 2D poses, and defines a common evaluation protocol.
The resulting translation model outperforms prior methods and the YouTube-ASL baseline on How2Sign, ASL STEM Wiki, and OpenASL.
Joint motion–pseudo-gloss pretraining is especially beneficial when less translation data is available.
The shared encoder achieves state-of-the-art isolated-sign recognition on ASL Citizen and surpasses a Uni-Sign reproduction on WLASL2000.

papers.abstract: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy's action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.
authors: Clinton Enwerem, Saleh Kemal, John S. Baras, Calin Belta
bullets: Residual reinforcement learning adapts an imitation policy under a limited environment-interaction budget.
The method separates a phase’s failure frequency from its impact on full-task completion by estimating completion gain from paired episodes.
Positive gain estimates select which action components to correct and how to distribute training episodes across phases.
In docking and bimanual assembly simulations, gain-based allocation targeted phases that were not always the most failure-prone and improved completion.
A release-phase residual policy improved held-out completion from release-start states by 16.9% in one assembly configuration.

papers.abstract: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.
authors: Sergey Musienko
bullets: Uses a frozen encoder with a control ladder: factory decoder, Bayesian head, affine map, and full fine-tuning only as an escape hatch.
A conjugate Normal-Inverse-Wishart Bayesian head updates from labelled trials without gradient optimization.
Clean-referenced gating reduced adaptation entry from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the factory decoder retained for about 87% of clean cells.
Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matched or exceeded frozen-trunk accuracy across five encoder architectures at roughly 23× lower fit time than full fine-tuning.
Natural-drift checks showed no reliable head accuracy gain, emphasizing cost efficiency and clean-data safety; adaptation severity varied across datasets.

papers.abstract: A Bayesian learner may retain an issued action while updating its posterior, trading predictive loss against adjustment charges. We assume population curvature, boundary control, an order-$1/n$ lower bound on expected posterior uncertainty about the optimal action, and an observable unbiased gradient witness whose squared norms are uniformly integrable. Sample losses may be unbounded or nonconvex. Cumulative expected excess measures the loss increase relative to current predictive Bayes actions. For bounded nonnegative nondecreasing charges $c$ with $c(0)=0$ and nondecreasing profiles $G: \mathbb{N} \to [1,\infty)$ with $G(J)=o(J)$, we characterize joint attainability of cumulative expected excess $O(G(J))$ at horizons $T=2^J$ and finite expected lifetime charge. Here $J$ indexes logarithmic time. The criterion is finiteness of a prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, equivalently its decreasing-weight dual. Adaptive timing and private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region. For each feasible pair, a horizon-independent deterministic checkpoint policy attains the profile with lifetime-cost moments of every positive order. For excess $O((\log T)^r)$, $0<r<1$, every policy needs $\Omega((\log T)^{2-r})$ revisions in expectation, and a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound for every feasible charge. We verify the assumptions for logistic decision models with nondegenerate covariates, finite second moments and a locally positive smooth prior density, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors.
authors: Viet Bac Nguyen
bullets: Studies retaining actions while updating beliefs, balancing predictive loss against costs for changing actions.
Provides an attainability criterion based on prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, with an equivalent decreasing-weight dual.
Shows adaptive timing and private randomization do not expand the attainable region.
For excess O((log T)^r), 0<r<1, proves every policy requires Ω((log T)^(2−r)) expected revisions, while a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound.
Verifies the framework for logistic decision models, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors, under stated regularity assumptions.

figures.caption: Table 1: Feasibility for logarithmic charges cα. Equality is infeasible at every strict threshold.

papers.selection_reason: The theoretical framework for a Bayesian learner updating posterior beliefs and deciding when to change actions under adjustment costs is relevant to test-time adaptation and deployment-time learning.
papers.title: Prescribed Bayesian Efficiency under Lifetime Adjustment Costs
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes when a Bayesian learner can jointly achieve low cumulative predictive excess and finite lifetime adjustment costs, and gives matching revision-rate bounds.

papers.abstract: A unified 3D medical foundation model promises reusable, frozen features that serve a wide variety of tasks such as segmentation, classification and registration on MRI, CT and PET as well as specialist models do. Generalist models still need separate backbones for localized and global tasks, specialist models are confined to a single modality, with the concern that spanning modalities under-emphasizes fine anatomy, and both typically rely on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive. We present VoxForge, a single encoder that integrates recent advances in 3D architecture, self-distillation and cross-modal curricula to learn transferable features from permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes. We evaluate it strictly frozen, the test a reusable foundation model must pass, against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models on segmentation, classification and registration across MRI and CT, and on PET, which it never sees. VoxForge has the best or tied-best average rank in every task group, serves localized and global tasks across modalities at the level of state-of-the-art specialists, and is extremely label-efficient, matching top-performing models on TotalSegmentator CT with a tenth of the labels.
authors: Rushil Anirudh, Jayaraman J. Thiagarajan
bullets: Addresses the need for one reusable model across localized and global tasks and multiple imaging modalities.
Combines 3D architectural advances, self-distillation, and cross-modal curricula, trained on permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes.
Evaluated strictly frozen across segmentation, classification, and registration on MRI and CT, with zero-shot evaluation on PET.
Achieves the best or tied-best average rank in every task group and performs at specialist-model levels across modalities.
Shows strong label efficiency, matching top-performing TotalSegmentator CT models with one-tenth of the labels.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding maps a screenshot and a natural language instruction to the coordinates of the intended interface element. Existing approaches improve grounding through visual scaling, instruction scaling, and sampling scaling, yet it remains unclear which grounding bottlenecks these strategies address and where their gains saturate. To address this gap, we introduce ScaleDiag, a controlled diagnostic framework that isolates the effects of visual input, instruction information, and prediction sampling on GUI grounding by independently varying target scale and surrounding context, target-specific information and auxiliary descriptions, and candidate coverage and selection, respectively. We evaluate ScaleDiag across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models and find that each scaling strategy operates within a much narrower regime than commonly assumed. (1) Visual scaling is governed by target occupancy rather than a fixed crop ratio, with full-screen errors typically rescued once the target occupies only 0.32% of the cropped view, while further zooming eventually becomes harmful. (2) Instruction scaling is driven by information that identifies the target rather than description richness itself, as even ground-truth-derived attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful, while appearance and spatial descriptions account for over 90% of the achievable gain. (3) Repeated sampling exposes a different limitation, as correct coordinates are frequently generated but remain difficult to select, leaving 5.1--11.0 points of oracle headroom while geometric consensus provides almost no improvement. Together, these results show that test-time scaling is constrained by distinct operating regimes rather than benefiting monotonically from more visual focus, richer instructions, or additional samples. Our code is available at https://github.com/YenanLiu/ScaleDiag.
authors: Chen Liu, Zhen Fang, Xin Yu, Dadong Wang, Ling Chen
bullets: Visual scaling depends on target occupancy, not a fixed crop ratio; zooming too far can hurt.
Instruction scaling benefits mainly from appearance and spatial cues, while added attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful.
Repeated sampling often generates correct coordinates but fails to select them, leaving 5.1–11.0 points of oracle headroom.
Geometric consensus provides almost no improvement, indicating that sampling and selection have distinct bottlenecks.
Findings are based on five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our controlled diagnostic framework for GUI grounding. (a) Controlled visual interventions vary the visual evidence while keeping the instruction fixed. We construct target-centered, aspect-ratio-preserving crops at different area ratios, and separately add resized distractor screenshots while preserving the target screenshot at its native resolution. (b) Controlled instruction interventions keep the screenshot and target fixed while modifying the instruction. Rule-based attribute injection appends ground-truth-derived position, color, size, or shape cues, whereas an LLM generates natural descriptions from appearance, spatial, functional, and goal-oriented views. (c) Repeated sampling keeps both the screenshot and instruction fixed and generates multiple coordinate predictions, allowing us to compare greedy decoding, coordinate-medoid consensus, and oracle candidate coverage. Together, these interventions isolate the effects of visual evidence, instruction information, and candidate selection.

Fig. 5. Instruction utility depends on target-identifying information. (a) Effects of appending annotation-derived coarse attributes, including position, color, size, shape, and their combination. Bars show the mean accuracy change relative to the original instruction over models and four benchmarks, while points show the corresponding per-model averages. (b) Grounding accuracy along an information ladder, from a generic instruction without target identity, through truncated and original instructions, to coarse and fine location clarifications. Qwen3.5 models are emphasized with darker curves. (c) Grounding accuracy under the original instruction and selected GPT-5.2-generated single-view and multi-view descriptions. Each bar is averaged over seven models and five benchmarks, and the dashed line marks the original-instruction baseline.

Fig. 4. Difficulty-gated visual scaling under target-centered cropping. OCC denotes the ratio of the target bounding-box area to the visible image area. (a) Grounding accuracy across retained crop areas, grouped by native OCC measured on the full screenshot. Each point reports the accuracy of one native-OCC group at a given crop scale. (b) Within-item accuracy gain over the full-frame input as a function of post-crop OCC. Each crop prediction is compared with the full-frame prediction for the same item, and the resulting changes are averaged within OCC bins. Rescue OCC is the post-crop target occupancy at the least aggressive crop that converts a full-frame miss into a hit. The shaded region shows its interquartile range across rescued items, while the dashed line marks its median. Both panels pool approximately 34.9k model–benchmark–item instances.

Fig. 6. Repeated sampling improves candidate coverage but leaves a selection gap. Sampling uses K = 8 predictions at T = 0.7, while Greedy uses one prediction at T = 0. (a) Grounding accuracy under Greedy, coordinate-medoid selection, and Oracle@8, averaged over five benchmarks with 500 items each. Medoid selects the coordinate with the smallest total distance to the other samples, whereas Oracle@8 counts an item as correct if any sample hits the target. (b) Distribution of the number of correct samples m, pooled over four models and five benchmarks (N = 10,000), with items categorized as all wrong (m = 0), partially correct (0 < m < 8), or all correct (m = 8). (c) Recoverable items as a function of m. Bars show the proportion of items missed by Greedy but covered by Oracle@8; curves show the normalized GRPO opportunity score, reward-variance factor, and Greedy hit rate.

Fig. 3. Effects of target-centered cropping on GUI grounding performance. (a) Grounding accuracy across crop area ratios for each model and benchmark. (b) Accuracy gain of the best crop over the full screenshot.

Fig. 1. GUI grounding failures can arise from insufficient target visibility, missing target-identifying information, or unreliable candidate selection. These bottlenecks require different interventions, including visual scaling, instruction refinement, and verifier-guided sampling.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images, but iterative sampling remains computationally expensive. Feature caching reduces the number of full network evaluations, yet its approximation error can become more severe under short sampling schedules, where fewer full-compute steps and a coarser sampling grid can make history-based extrapolation less reliable. In this paper, we propose CalibCache, a lightweight offline calibration method that corrects systematic discrepancies between cached and full-compute feature dynamics. Specifically, CalibCache calibrates feature acceleration, defined as the second-order finite difference across sampling steps. Using only a single pair of full-compute and naive-cache trajectories at each setting, CalibCache fits scalar acceleration maps offline by centered least squares. These maps are then applied during sampling without additional full-network evaluations or online optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image on DrawBench and DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, CalibCache consistently improves fidelity or generation quality over TaylorSeer under 20-step sampling at cache intervals $N=3,4,5$. At $N=5$, it reduces FLUX.1-dev LPIPS from $0.563$ to $0.429$ while achieving a $2.86\times$ denoising speedup over full-compute sampling, and lowers DiT-XL/2 FID from $16.39$ to $10.37$ relative to TaylorSeer.
authors: Mingyu Liang, Dingkun Xu, Jingwei Xu
bullets: Targets growing cache approximation errors caused by few sampling steps and coarse sampling grids.
Calibrates feature acceleration—the second-order finite difference across sampling steps—using one full-compute/naive-cache trajectory pair per setting.
Fits scalar acceleration maps offline with centered least squares and applies them during sampling without online optimization.
Improves fidelity or generation quality over TaylorSeer across FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, and DiT-XL/2 at 20 steps and cache intervals of 3–5.
At cache interval 5, reports FLUX.1-dev LPIPS of 0.429 with a 2.86× denoising speedup, and DiT-XL/2 FID of 10.37 versus TaylorSeer’s 16.39.

papers.abstract: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.
authors: Hector G. Rodriguez, Marcus Rohrbach
bullets: Pointwise rewards that map correct answers to confidence 1 and incorrect answers to 0 lose useful distinctions between answer confidences.
CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation) rewards confidence rankings across question sets using thresholds induced at different risk tolerances.
This enables models to abstain or defer on lower-confidence questions while maximizing coverage under a target error rate.
On math benchmarks, CARE raises 5% risk coverage from 0.8% to 42.4%; on out-of-distribution QA, it raises coverage from 12.3% to 23.6%.
The approach is evaluated for selective prediction and confidence estimation, with reported gains across several in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: The paper proposes a reward estimation method for training LLMs to produce reliable confidence scores and abstain, directly relevant to language foundation model training and reasoning reliability.
papers.title: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: CARE trains LLM confidence scores relative to other questions, substantially improving reliable selective answering at low risk.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as text classifiers, but their labels are only useful when we know to what extent we can trust them. We compare black-box methods (verbalised confidence and sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (P(True), and multiple logit-scoring methods using constrained generation). We evaluate eleven open-weight LLMs (1B-32B parameters) on five classification datasets with 3 to 151 labels, measuring classification performance (accuracy, F1-macro), discrimination (AUROC), and calibration (ECE and Brier score). The choice of confidence method rarely impacts accuracy significantly, but logit-based scoring methods lead to much better discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) than black-box methods (AUROC 0.57-0.66). Replacing labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but costs 3-6 accuracy points on average. We also introduce decision-only scoring, which only scores positions where labels diverge in the prefix tree (trie). It reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets and performs comparably to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method configurations (Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B) are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.
authors: Owen Cook, Xingyi Song
bullets: Evaluates black-box confidence methods against token-probability and constrained-generation scoring across 11 open-weight LLMs and five classification datasets.
Confidence method choice has little effect on accuracy, but logit-based methods achieve much stronger discrimination (AUROC 0.74–0.77 vs. 0.57–0.66).
Replacing natural labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but lowers accuracy by 3–6 points on average.
Decision-only scoring reduces decoding steps by 88–96% for the largest label sets while performing comparably to full-label scoring.
Top open-weight configurations are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.

papers.title: LLMs Are Already Confidence-Aware Zero-Shot Classifiers

papers.abstract: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.
authors: Anish Khazane, Alex Saad-Falcon, Guanchu Wu, Marcio Porto, Jasper Shan, Fei Yu, Eugene Shulga, Intaik Park, Yongzhe Zhang, Xiaoyu Deng, Sheng Luo, Xiaoya Wang
bullets: Targets memory pressure from large sparse embedding tables in recommendation systems.
Assigns higher pruning rates to embedding tables associated with less important features, replacing size-based heuristics.
Validated across three large-scale models and reproduced on DLRM with the Criteo 1TB dataset.
Enables training with fewer GPU trainers, higher per-GPU throughput, and over 1,000 fewer GPU-hours per model launch.
Evaluates the end-to-end tradeoff, including the cost of computing feature importance.

papers.abstract: Point-image alignment learns useful object representations, but different local feature patterns can produce the same pooled descriptor and receive the same alignment signal. We introduce MS-Point, a cross-modal pretraining framework that directly supervises intermediate point features and their neighborhood responses. At selected encoder stages, we compute neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling and align their branch descriptors with image features. Branch-level objectives align each representation with its visual target, while cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion coordinate information across branches. A common interface of intermediate features and spatial neighborhoods supports both graph encoders and point Transformers. Evaluations across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning demonstrate the transfer value of this design. Same-backbone comparisons and capacity-matched and computation-matched controls connect these improvements to the structure of supervision. Together, our findings support directly supervising intermediate features and neighborhood variation to learn transferable, geometry-aware representations across modalities.
authors: Hai-tao Yu, Jun Xia
bullets: Addresses ambiguous supervision from aligning only pooled point-cloud descriptors.
Computes neighborhood averages and residuals at multiple encoder stages before pooling.
Uses branch-level cross-modal alignment, cross-level consistency, and adaptive fusion.
Supports both graph encoders and point Transformers through a shared intermediate-feature interface.
Evaluations show transfer value across classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning.

papers.abstract: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem. What is essential is the multi-view agreement (Accord), which is considered in SLAM as a source of geometric self-consistency. Accord anchors each keyframe window to metric 3D points triangulated from the filter poses, then exploits bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to estimate and correct per-image scale errors while preserving the metric scale established by the anchors. Context keyframes further improve depth prediction, and the resulting submaps are fused in a factor graph. We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset. With nothing tuned per dataset/setup and every map aligned only by Accord's own trajectory, Accord achieves consistently best/second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform. Accord is open-source along with the phone-rig dataset for the benefit of the research community
authors: Jaafar Mahmoud, Arthur Movsesyan, Cuong Huynh, Mikhail Iumanov, Sergey Zagoruyko, Sergey Kolyubin
bullets: Addresses the gap between metric-but-sparse VIO geometry and dense-but-scale-ambiguous monocular depth.
Anchors short keyframe-window submaps to metric 3D points triangulated from VIO poses.
Uses bidirectional dense depth agreement across co-visible images to correct per-image scale errors while preserving metric scale.
Adds context keyframes and fuses submaps in a factor graph for online dense mapping.
A single untuned configuration performs consistently among the best across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset; code and data are released.

papers.abstract: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.
authors: Marco Roschkowski, Hannes Gernandt
bullets: Addresses slow training in continuous-time state-space models caused by repeated neural-network evaluations during numerical integration.
Uses compact nonlinear dynamical components arranged in parallel and series.
Implements custom Triton GPU kernels to reduce launch and memory overhead during sequential evaluation.
Also introduces a port-Hamiltonian variant and evaluates accuracy and training time through benchmark comparisons.

papers.abstract: We propose the radiometric camera, a model that lifts any central geometric camera model to a radiometric one. The lifted model keeps the projection of the geometric model and adds a finite aperture, a free-form focus surface and a generic vignetting function. We calibrate it by inverse rendering directly on the relative irradiance of the sensor, from the same images of standard calibration targets used in geometric calibration. Geometric calibration absorbs the bias of its feature detections. The proposed radiometric calibration uses no features, and our radiometric cameras have lower reprojection errors on held-out test sets. The focus surface extends defocus modeling from the thin lens to any central camera, and we use it in a first multi-view radiometric reconstruction, which recovers the in-focus reflectance of a texture from defocused images. The vignetting is estimated jointly and accurately reproduces a flat field measured through a diffuser. Because every standard camera model lifts to a radiometric one, the radiometric camera naturally and directly extends generative scene models beyond multi-view geometry to multi-view radiometric ones, where phenomena such as lighting and attenuation can be accurately estimated.
authors: Ties Harder, Felix Seegr\"aber, David Nakath, Hendrik Sauer, Kevin K\"oser, James Pritts
bullets: Models finite aperture, free-form focus surfaces, and generic vignetting while preserving the original camera projection.
Calibrates directly from sensor irradiance using standard calibration-target images, without feature detections.
Achieves lower reprojection errors on held-out tests than geometric calibration, according to the abstract.
Supports multi-view reconstruction of in-focus texture reflectance from defocused images and jointly estimates vignetting.
Provides a foundation for extending multi-view geometry to radiometric scene models involving lighting and attenuation.

papers.abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Bangji Yang, Qinglong Zheng, Ziwen Wang, Chaoran Cheng, Changyi Yang, Hanqi Mao, Ge Liu
bullets: Targets repetitive thinking loops in small vision-language models that waste the token budget and lose answers.

Independent editors locate the issue in middle-layer attention outputs, where the smaller VLM stops consulting the image during loops.
Across six image benchmarks on Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B, Keel removes most loops, shortens answers, and improves average accuracy; it also combines well with budget forcing.

papers.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
papers.tldr: Keel uses a frontier multimodal model to diagnose and edit a VLM’s weights, removing image-reasoning loops without retraining or increasing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. papers.abstract: Agentic cyber-physical systems rely on perception and state estimation to support autonomous decisions. Degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations can therefore propagate through an autonomous pipeline and create security-relevant failures. This work presents a synthetic Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) testbed developed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for repeatable stress testing of perception and tracking algorithms supporting agentic decision-making. A simplified quadrotor follows scripted trajectories while co-located virtual sensors generate synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative IR-like observations. The testbed varies target range, motion, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability, with future stress cases including sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and false observations. As an initial exemplar, a nonlinear coordinated-turn Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. Position error and uncertainty are compared as LiDAR observations degrade and are lost. The framework provides a reproducible environment for studying how sensing degradation affects downstream autonomous estimation and resilience in agentic C-UAS systems.
authors: Ivan A. Fernandez, Jingdao Chen
bullets: Addresses security-relevant failures caused by degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations in autonomous C-UAS pipelines.

Varies target range, motion, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability; planned cases include dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and false observations.
Demonstrates a nonlinear coordinated-turn EKF evaluated with LiDAR target-centroid measurements as observations degrade or disappear.
Assesses position error and uncertainty over a 20-second maneuvering trajectory.
