papers.abstract: Can a distilled image generator save time by reusing features between its few remaining denoising steps? We study a fixed branch cache that replaces selected attention and MLP evaluations while preserving the student's noise schedule. One full trajectory and one raw-cache trajectory from the same initial noise supply a scalar correction for each branch type and reuse position. At $1024^2$, one internal reuse reduces four-step Qwen-Image-Lightning denoising time from 1.279 to 0.977 seconds. Three reuses yield $1.51\times$ speedup on eight-step Lightning and $1.53\times$ on eight-step Hyper-FLUX. We evaluate image quality on all 200 DrawBench prompts. With the reuse positions held fixed, correction improves mean same-seed image fidelity over raw reuse by 0.66 and 0.87 dB on the two Lightning students. On Hyper-FLUX the PSNR difference is 0.01 dB, while LPIPS improves from 0.1625 to 0.1546. These results measure the effect of branch caching and correction while retaining each student's original sampling grid.
authors: Mingyu Liang, Dingkun Xu
bullets: Reuses selected attention and MLP features across denoising steps without changing the student’s noise schedule.
A scalar correction is computed per branch type and reuse position from full and raw-cache trajectories with the same initial noise.

Across 200 DrawBench prompts, correction improves Lightning same-seed fidelity by 0.66 and 0.87 dB over raw reuse; Hyper-FLUX shows similar PSNR and better LPIPS.
Results are scoped to fixed reuse positions and preserve each model’s original sampling grid.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3\% task success, compared with 61.7\% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3\% for the VLM alone, and 46.7\% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30$\times$ fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.
authors: Chrisantus Eze, Christopher Crick
bullets: Addresses the lack of grounded scene-change reasoning in VLM-generated multi-step manipulation plans and the inefficiency and drift of pixel-level world models.
Imagines candidate plans in DINOv2 feature space using a flow-matching world model with action cross-attention and causal temporal history.
A dual-head critic evaluates imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before robot execution.
On six language-conditioned tasks, it achieved 83.3% success, outperforming the reported latent-world-model, VLM-only, and pixel-diffusion baselines.

All executed plans were verified successfully; remaining failures came from low-level grasp or placement slips, while simulation results showed strong CALVIN and cluttered nut-assembly performance with 30× fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification.

Stage 3: a goal head scores the terminal latent state against the goal, and a temporal consistency head checks consecutive imagined states; the best verified plan is executed.

papers.abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.
authors: Sanidhya Vijayvargiya, Rahul Lokesh
bullets: Addresses the limitation of continual-learning-style memory systems that retain information indefinitely.

papers.abstract: Ferrofluids are liquids containing magnetic nanoparticles, enabling shape control through external magnetic fields. This deformability supports their use as soft robotic bodies that can navigate confined spaces and manipulate objects. Their nonlinear continuum dynamics, however, make reliable control challenging. Existing work shows how spatial magnetic fields from electromagnet arrays can establish and maintain desired ferrofluid configurations. A complementary objective is to exploit the fluid's dynamics under limited actuation to reach prescribed shapes that may not be sustainable at equilibrium. Here, we use deep model-based reinforcement learning to control these transient shapes. Learning directly through physical interaction, our policies select current commands for a single fixed electromagnet based on visual observations, guiding the moving ferrofluid toward prescribed geometries. The learned policies repeatedly attain a variety of shapes spanning polygons, asterisks and pentominoes. These results demonstrate that learning directly from physical interaction enables reliable fluid shaping, opening new possibilities for controlling ferrofluid-based soft robots.
authors: Anthony Czubarow, Antonio Terpin, Raffaello D'Andrea
bullets: Ferrofluids are promising soft-robot bodies but are difficult to control because of nonlinear continuum dynamics.

The work demonstrates reliable fluid shaping under limited actuation for potential soft-robot applications.

papers.abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP.pdf and GDP.xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.
authors: Anima Singh, Suhas Yogin, Weicheng Kuo, Ivor Rendulic, Ivan Jurin, Antoine Yang, Oran Kelly, Rohan Doshi, Hammad Ayyubi, Ioana Bica, Sergi Caelles, Matthew Conniff, Dan Graur, Anastasija Ili\'c, Ahmet Iscen, Chao Jia, Tomasz K\k{e}pa, Chunyuan Li, Noah \'O Donnaile, Filip Pavetic, Goran Petrovic, Khalid Salama, Zhicheng Wang, Polina Zablotskaia, Yiqian Zhang, Ming Zhao, Benjamin Caine, Mario Lu\v{c}i\'c, Melvin Johnson, Radu Soricut, Jean-Baptiste Alayrac

Uses expert-weighted rubrics and a sandboxed agentic autorater, which matched human expert judgments on 96.2% of criteria (κ = 0.91).
Claude Fable 5.2 achieved the highest Climb-WSR (56.6%) and overall WSR (73.3%), followed by Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% and 71.9%); Carbon used 5.7× fewer tokens.
Even the strongest evaluated models scored below 57% on frontier criteria, indicating substantial room for improvement.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.
authors: Takahiro Miki, Robin Schmid, Manthan Patel, Turcan Tuna, Julia Richter, Julian Nubert, Joonho Lee, Matthias M\"uller, Marco Hutter
bullets: Targets robust autonomous navigation in diverse, unstructured real-world terrain.
Uses a VLM to interpret scenes, assess risks, understand signs, and assign navigation costs.
Converts semantic outputs into a real-time dense risk map through open-vocabulary segmentation.
Conditions pre-trained RL policies for agile locomotion and local navigation.
Real-world trials achieved kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, while exposing limits in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the ROAM pipeline. The proposed system bridges high-level reasoning from vision-language models (VLMs) with low-level actuator commands for autonomous robot control. It processes RGB images and robot descriptions through a VLM to generate object labels enriched with risk, preferred area, and steppable values. These labels are converted into semantic images using open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, which operates at a higher frequency than the VLM analysis. The semantic images are then fused with elevation maps to create an environmental representation that reinforcement learning (RL) policies utilize for fast and robust robot control.

papers.abstract: Tracking a hidden object through a video is effortless for humans, yet it remains a bottleneck for vision language models (VLMs). In the shell game, where a ball is hidden under one of several identical cups that are then swapped, VLMs that answer directly stay near chance, thinking models fail on long games, and fine-tuning learns only the lengths it has seen. We argue that the limit is serial computation: each swap must be composed with the last result, and a VLM of fixed depth has only a fixed number of state transitions for it. To address this, we propose RecurrentVLM, which makes every attention layer of a pretrained VLM recur over time by computing the keys and values of finished frame groups from the layer's own output. With a single answer token, RecurrentVLM reaches 100% on VET-Bench and 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps. We also observe several interesting phenomena: length generalization emerges suddenly at an aha moment; without recurrence, each swap costs an attention layer; the ball's state forms in the first four attention layers; and recurrence keeps the latest state at the cost of details of earlier moments. These results suggest that recurrent VLMs are a potential solution for tracking the states of unobserved objects in video. Code will be released.
authors: Dingqiang Ye, Jiacong Xu, Wen Zhang, Yiqun Mei, Vishal M. Patel
bullets: VLMs struggle with shell-game tracking because each swap requires composing a new state with the previous one.
RecurrentVLM applies every attention layer recurrently, recomputing keys and values from completed frame groups while using a single answer token.
It achieves 100% on VET-Bench, 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps.
Length generalization appears abruptly, while recurrence preserves the latest state but loses details from earlier moments.
The findings suggest recurrence can support tracking unobserved object states in video.

papers.abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/
authors: Arthur Bucker, Pramod Anantharam, Jonathan Francis, Jean Oh
bullets: Addresses OOD failures caused by scarce, multimodal robotics data and policy overfitting to small distribution shifts.
Combines LVM/VLM semantic reasoning with object-relational distance pairs along meaningful geometric axes to form task-specific guidance.
Transfers motion patterns from successful in-distribution rollouts without retraining the policy.
Works in simulation for pose and task-goal shifts and on a real robot for cable placement and unseen-object steering.
In reported experiments, it more than doubled success one grid step outside training positions and nearly eliminated object confusion when steering toward unseen objects.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our visual-geometric policy steering framework. Offline analysis (at task initialization, once per episode): (1) we retrieve the most relevant successful in-distribution rollout τ∗ by weighted image (DINOv2) and text (CLIP) similarity; (2) a VLM selects the task-relevant object-relational distance pairs per motion phase (e.g., gripper–cube distance d1, cube–table distance d2, gripper orientation θ), evaluated per timestep into the reference trends Φ; (3) a VLM with SAM2 matches the demonstration objects to the live OOD scene (e.g., the cylinder takes the cube’s role), re-targeting each pair. Online steering (every action chunk): (4) perception projects the live scene into the same distance space and aligns each pair to Φ within a window, giving the reference d∗. At every denoising step, a differentiable dynamics model F forecasts the features d(A) of a candidate chunk A, and a line-searched gradient step on the trajectory loss corrects the frozen policy’s velocity field, yielding the steered chunk A′.

Fig. 5. Positional generalization. Every rollout is plotted at the Mahalanobis distance of its measured cable position (dots near 100 are successes, near 0 failures), with per-zone success rates and 95% Wilson intervals (squares) and a per-method logistic fit, crossing 50% at 2.8σ (base) and 3.4σ (VG-Steer).

Fig. 9. Visual-geometric guidance via VLM-selected distance pairs. Offline (a–c): the demonstration is segmented (Gemini 3 Flash + SAM2) and split into sub-trajectory phases (STRAP); the VLM selects each phase’s entity pairs, projections, and sub-goal constraints. Online (d–e): the live scene is matched to the demonstration, and the guidance steers the frozen policy so the selected projected distances track the reference.

Fig. 4. Positional sweep on cable bagging, in the camera view. (a) Training distribution of the 110 cable grasps in the demonstrations. (b) The single reference rollout, with its end-effector path split into sub-trajectories. (c, d) Per-cell outcomes: dots mark the measured cable position of every trial, filled green for success, red rings for failure.

Fig. 2. Differentiable guidance injection. At each denoising step, the candidate chunk is rolled out by forward kinematics, and the guidance loss (position, orientation, gripper) is differentiated; a golden-section line search sets the step size, and the correction is applied to the policy’s velocity field, steering the trajectory without modifying weights.
Fig. 8. Real-world outcome breakdown (share of rollouts, counts on bars). Residual failures concentrate in grasp and transport, which the guidance does not address.

Fig. 7. Task variation on cable bagging. Left: the single reference rollout above the new setting in which cable, banana and spoon share the workspace. Center, right: confusion matrices (instructed object in rows, reached object in columns) for the base and the guided policy.
Fig. 6. Disambiguating the target object in a cluttered scene. In red and blue, the distance pairs used per sub-trajectory (ST0 approach, ST1 transport).

Fig. 3. Per-action-chunk inference overhead on π0.5 (mean over the four suites, CUDA-synchronized). With VG-Steer a chunk takes ∼73 ms in total (1.2× the base’s ∼61 ms), comparable to gradient-only VLS (∼70 ms total); full VLS costs ∼20× more, scaling with its particle count (20 here).

papers.abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.
authors: Luca M. Hartmann, Parinaz Naghizadeh
bullets: Targets the verification and interpretability limits of self-play RL driving policies.
Replaces a trained PPO teacher’s action head with DiffMPC enforcing road-boundary and agent-ellipse constraints.
Uses DAgger in the teacher’s self-play simulator to train the constrained student.
Across 9 seeds, students match or outperform teachers on nuPlan, CARLA, and out-of-distribution Waymo scenes.
Distillation requires no more than 30% of the teacher’s training time.

papers.abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g.~MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.
authors: Ioana-Sabina Stoian, Florinel-Alin Croitoru, Vlad Hondru, Andreea Iuliana Ionescu, Andrei Paun, Radu Tudor Ionescu
bullets: Addresses unsupervised medical anomaly detection when labeled abnormal data are unavailable.
Combines image-based JEPA representation learning, target-encoder distillation, and pseudo-anomaly classification.
Evaluated across six datasets spanning MRI, OCT, X-ray, and histopathology.
Achieves competitive performance and ranks first on three datasets; ablations support the value of all three stages.
Code is publicly released; the approach is scoped to learning normality from healthy-patient images.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of MADJEPA. Our pipeline is divided into three training stages: 1⃝ self-supervised training via I-JEPA; 2⃝ target encoder distillation to a randomly-initialized student; 3⃝ A: prompt-based pseudo-anomaly generation, and B: normal vs. pseudo-anomaly classification. Together, these training stages build a strong and calibrated representation of normal data. Best viewed in color.

papers.abstract: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.
authors: Zirui Song, Jiadong Zhang, Zheng Lu, Xiaosong Ma, Xiaojun Chang, Xiuying Chen
bullets: The pipeline compares task instructions with checker code to predict possible disagreements.
It recreates suspected cases in simulation and uses multi-view renderings for visual verification.
Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 test cases matched the predicted checker verdict.
Auditing identified 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks: 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures.
The study recommends testing both incomplete executions and valid task completions that differ from expert demonstrations.

papers.abstract: JEPA-based video encoders learn strong representations for video and image understanding through prediction in latent space. However, their standard pretraining predicts features within individual images or video clips, without explicitly exploiting paired camera views of the same object or moment. Consequently, the learned representations may not reliably support matching across different camera viewpoints. To solve this problem, we introduce multi-view predictive post-training to strengthen cross-view instance and temporal correspondence while retaining independent single-view inference. A shared encoder processes masked context views independently, and a training-time predictor jointly predicts latent tokens for masked context regions and a fully held-out view. We alternate cross-view prediction with single-view masked prediction on general image and video data to help retain the encoder's pretrained capabilities. After only 9,000 post-training updates on a single GPU, MV-JEPA improves cross-view instance retrieval and coarse cross-camera moment retrieval on various datasets, with further gains in zero-shot action-phase retrieval and frozen-feature classification on AE2. Frozen-probe evaluations further indicate that post-training largely preserves motion recognition, image recognition, and dense semantic segmentation performance on the evaluated benchmarks. Together, these results demonstrate that multi-view predictive post-training can strengthen instance and coarse temporal correspondence in JEPA video encoders without modifying the encoder architecture or single-view inference interface.
authors: Yangchen Zhao, Ali Payani, Caiwen Ding
bullets: Addresses weak cross-view instance and temporal correspondence in standard JEPA pretraining.
Uses a shared encoder with a joint predictor for masked context views and a fully held-out view.
Alternates multi-view and single-view masked prediction to retain pretrained image and video abilities.
With 9,000 post-training updates on one GPU, improves cross-view instance retrieval, coarse cross-camera moment retrieval, and some zero-shot and frozen-feature tasks.
Evaluations suggest motion recognition, image recognition, and dense segmentation are largely preserved; scope is limited to evaluated benchmarks and coarse temporal matching.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.
authors: Arjun Choudhry, Aditya Narayanan, Raghav Mallampalli, Po-han Li, Sai Shankar Narasimhan, Raimi Shah, B. Aditya Prakash, Shubhankar Agarwal
bullets: Time-series forecasters cannot use future information to verify candidate forecasts, unlike language models.
BGAA uses rolling-origin backtests on the series history to evaluate structured context transformations.
It discards views that underperform the original context and averages the survivors’ predictive distributions.
Across tested benchmarks, BGAA reduces MASE by 0.5–5.9%; a 313M model with TTC outperforms larger models in its family.
The remaining gap to oracle view selection highlights window-level view selection as a key challenge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: BGAA system overview. (1) The observed context is the only input available at test time. (2) A fixed pool of transformed views is generated, and (3) each is forecast with the same frozen TSFM. (4) Forecasts are mapped back to the original observation space. (5) A leak-free rolling-origin backtest scores the views against the base and admits the best candidates. (6) The admitted forecasts are aggregated with the base forecast to produce (7) the final predictive fan.

Figure 2: Test-time compute improves MASE under estimated inference-FLOPs scaling. On GIFT-Eval (97 configurations), lines connect four test-time compute budgets for each frozen model; stars denote published models at 1× compute. Each rung uses the model’s measured benchmark PFLOPs scaled by its measured forward-pass ratio (base + gate + apply)/base. The CRPS ladders also improve over their corresponding bases.

Figure 3: Pareto curves for accuracy vs computational cost. (fev-bench, 100 tasks). Lines are our test-time compute ladders over a frozen model, cheapest rung first; stars are published models on fev-bench. A rung sits at its model’s measured 1× benchmark PFLOPs times the measured forward-pass ratio (base+gate+apply)/base. As in Section C.1, charging each extra pass at the base-pass cost is a conservative accounting convention for models with variable-length computation, since some views shorten the context.

Figure 9: Views move the same contexts toward different regions of each model’s rollout distribution. We use ancestral rollouts from each model’s quantile head as a proxy for its learned forecasting behavior and visualize the resulting 20-dimensional shape-feature space with joint t-SNE. Colored points are rollout samples, grouped by kmeans mode; black points are real GIFT-Eval contexts; arrows show the mean displacement induced by each view. We use the same contexts and views for both models, but diff moves toward different rollout modes: for CHRONOS-2, a low-iqr over std, high-step max mode with mass 0.07; for TIREX-2, a high-kurtosis, high-skew mode with mass 0.02. This provides the geometric counterpart to the fingerprint result. t-SNE preserves local neighborhoods, but distances should not be interpreted metrically.

(c) These displacements can align with different modes of each model’s rollout distribution. The top-1 hit rate is therefore about 15× chance. Ranked per window, the top-1 hit rate falls to about 11%. (b) Share of the hindsight MASE gain recovered by the top-k: the per-config top-1 recovers 32–33%, while the per-window top-1 recovers about 27%. The first “realized” column uses all 97 configs; the others use the 53 configs that can be cross-fit. The labelranked gate keeps the deployed policy fixed but ranks views with held-out labels. The reported realized/label-ranked ratio is the realized improvement divided by the label-ranked improvement. The best-view gain (x-fit) selects one view per config on one half of its windows and evaluates it on the other. The per-window hindsight selection selects the best view per window using its realized labels. These label-based quantities are diagnostics, not deployable verifier targets.

papers.abstract: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. Players choose positions to maximize their expected shares of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses. We utilize the game's kernel-general theoretical criterion for when co-located positions become locally unstable to separation. We evaluate InflEns on a corpus assembled from seven safety-related benchmarks, which demonstrates that the highest-share expert has the lowest held-out response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on approximately 90% of prompts across four kernels under a sharpened simplex representation, compared with approximately 15% after permuting allocations across prompts. We demonstrate that the method performs comparably to published learned gates without having to train an explicit gate on the experts. Because the router is fixed, we can trace harmful behavior to a single expert and retrain only that expert, which lowers HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following. The game also gives us several controls over how the experts specialize, including the kernel choice and its parameters, the trait-space geometry, and the number of experts. Importantly, InflEns is a general framework that can be extended to any encoder and data distribution.
authors: Mark Lovett, Denis Lim, Soroush Vosoughi
bullets: Experts choose positions in a fixed prompt-trait space to maximize their expected share of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses.
A kernel-based stability criterion guides when co-located experts separate and specialize.
On seven safety-related benchmarks, the highest-share expert had the lowest held-out NLL for about 90% of prompts, versus about 15% with permuted allocations.
The fixed router performs comparably to published learned gates and enables tracing harmful behavior to one expert for targeted retraining.
Specialization can be controlled through the kernel, trait-space geometry, and number of experts; the framework is intended to generalize across encoders and data distributions.

papers.title: Game-Theoretic Data Allocation for Expert Specialization and Routing
papers.tldr: InflEns uses one game-theoretic data-allocation process to both specialize LoRA experts and route prompts to the expert expected to perform best.

papers.abstract: Human-object motion synthesis requires coordinated human participation as objects move toward specified goals. However, reaching object targets does not ensure that contact is established and maintained, while adjustments that improve contact may interfere with task completion. We introduce CoRelate, a diffusion framework that coordinates full-body human-object motion through explicit interaction relations and task feedback for rigid and articulated objects. We represent intended participation through hand-part relations that specify the participating hand, its part-relative reference position, and participation interval. These relations serve both as generation conditions and as references for measuring interaction realization. At each denoising step, a temporal refiner trained jointly with the generator combines relation deviations, task residuals, and motion features from the current prediction to jointly update human and object motion across the sequence. After generation, temporal motion correction addresses remaining contact failures by optimizing local motion segments while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion. Experiments demonstrate improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success over the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies support the benefits of relation conditioning and the complementary roles of task and relation feedback.
authors: Zhiwen Qiu, Daisy Lin, Diyu Zhou, Jialin Wu, Rosita Ji, Saleh Kalantari
bullets: Targets the challenge of achieving both object-goal completion and sustained human–object contact.
Conditions generation on participating hand, part-relative reference position, and interaction interval.
Uses a temporal refiner to jointly update human and object motion from relation deviations, task residuals, and current motion features.
Applies local temporal correction after generation to fix contact failures while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion.
Experiments report improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success; ablations support relation conditioning and combined feedback.

(B) R conditions the generator Dθ and is the reference for relation feedback z (blue paths). At each denoising step, Fψ combines z, task residuals etask, and features f to update human and object motion, with R and goals g fixed. (C) Temporal correction then edits local hand motion with the object trajectory fixed followed by finger refinement.
Figure 4. Qualitative ablation visualization. We progressively add task and relation feedback to the no-feedback baseline and highlight incorrect interactions.

Table 3. Ablation study. Each design choice contributes and task and relation feedback show complementary gains when combined.

papers.title: CoRelate: Coordinated Human-Object Motion Synthesis through Interaction Relations

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models learn to plan from data, and hand-written planners are widely treated as a thing of the past. We test whether this is justified: we implement sixteen textbook planners, each combining a path source (reference line, A*, hybrid A*, RRT*) with a trajectory method (Frenet lattice, nonlinear optimization, $s$--$t$ search, dynamic window), and evaluate them on three benchmarks: open loop on nuScenes, closed loop on nuPlan with ground-truth perception, and photorealistic closed loop on HUGSIM. On HUGSIM, they replace only the planner of the end-to-end model UniAD and read its frozen perception, without an HD map or other privileged information. On nuScenes and nuPlan, the best textbook planners are competitive (L2 error of 0.735\,m against 0.947\,m for UniAD's planner; a nuPlan score of 79.3 against 76.1 for the rule-based PDM-Closed on Test14-hard with reactive agents). On HUGSIM, nine of the sixteen score above UniAD's learned planner on the same perception,. The best, a hybrid A* path followed by nonlinear trajectory optimization, raises HUGSIM's driving score (HD-Score) from 32.0 to 41.8. The gain is largest with standing and oncoming cars; against cars that steer at the ego, there is none. In 31 of the 182 runs in which UniAD's planner hits a car, the best textbook planner completes the route on the same perception: these crashes are due to the planner, not the perception.
authors: Andreas Look
bullets: The study evaluates 16 planners combining four path sources with four trajectory-generation methods across nuScenes, nuPlan, and HUGSIM.
On nuScenes and nuPlan, the strongest textbook planners are competitive with learned or rule-based baselines.
Replacing UniAD’s planner with a hybrid A* plus nonlinear optimization planner improves HUGSIM HD-Score from 32.0 to 41.8.
Nine of 16 textbook planners outperform UniAD’s planner on HUGSIM under identical perception.
Planner failures explain some UniAD crashes: the best textbook planner completes 31 routes that UniAD fails, though it provides no gain against cars steering directly toward the ego vehicle.

papers.title: Old-School Planners Drive (Sometimes) Better Than Learned Ones
papers.tldr: Classical hand-written planners can outperform learned planners in end-to-end driving, especially against standing and oncoming vehicles, even when using the learned model’s frozen perception.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.
authors: Yangchen Zhao, Ali Payani, Caiwen Ding
bullets: Long-horizon planning suffers from compounding prediction errors and weak guidance from distant goal similarity.
GEMS generates structured intermediate subgoals and selects relevant states from Latent Experience Memory (LEM).
A distance gate chooses whether to evaluate predicted outcomes against the generated subgoal or a retrieved memory state.
Across manipulation, navigation, and reaching tasks, GEMS achieves success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World.
The method outperforms evaluated world-model planning baselines, while relying on a frozen world model.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.
authors: Ziyan Yang, Taiwei Shi, Jieyu Zhao
bullets: Addresses context-window limits and the information loss caused by summarization, masking, and structured memory.
Uses only an append-only text log plus on-demand grep-style regex search—no embeddings, indexes, memory extraction, or extra models.
Trains Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning across five context-management strategies and evaluates multiple long-context memory tasks.
Achieves 95–97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and beats SUPO summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi.
Remains effective as input streams grow and stays on the accuracy–token-cost Pareto frontier across the evaluated tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: GREPMEM Overview. (a) The basic agent loop generates responses and tool calls from its active context, while GREPMEM additionally appends these interactions and tool results to a persistent history log. (b) Context compaction generates a summary when the working context reaches the compaction limit, allowing the agent to resume execution with a compacted context. GREPMEM builds on SUPO’s summarization loop. Extending this framework, GREPMEM enables (c) on-demand retrieval through grep_history and (d) a lossless, append-only full history log containing user messages, tool calls, tool results, summaries, and agent responses. By combining context summarization with a log preserving every message and tool output verbatim, GREPMEM enables grep_history to retrieve matching log lines after the first compaction without embeddings, a retrieval index, or an additional model.

Figure 1: Mean Accuracy vs. Token Cost After RL. We compare four context management strategies by their mean accuracy and token usage across five evaluation tasks. SUPO compresses context through summarization, while Masking discards older tool outputs to free context space. MemGPT maintains editable working memory, archival memory, and searchable message history. Our method, GREPMEM, combines summarization with a lossless, searchable history log, enabling on-demand retrieval through grep without a retrieval index. Token usage includes prompt and generated tokens across all model calls. Figure 5 reports per-task results.

Figure 3: Evaluation Performance of Five Context Management Strategies During RL Training. Scores are averaged over the evaluation samples available at each checkpoint. Evaluation details are provided in Appendix E.

Figure 4: ContextBench Performance Across Stream Lengths. We evaluate how stream length affects ContextBench performance before (dashed) and after RL (solid) training.

Figure 6: Per-Task Accuracy vs. Runtime After RL. We compare the accuracy and wall-clock runtime of RL-trained strategies on each evaluation task. Runtime is measured in minutes per episode, or per stream for ContextBench, and is shown on a logarithmic scale. Dashed lines indicate the Pareto frontier. Runtime measurements are approximate because episodes ran concurrently on shared inference and retrieval servers.

Table 3: Accuracy Before and After RL Training. We compare the accuracy (%) of five context management strategies using Qwen3.5-9B before and after training with the same RL recipe (§4). Within each block, bold marks the best value in each column, and underlining marks the second best. Table 2: Evaluation Task Sizes. Questions are totals per evaluation run. Timing indicates whether questions are revealed before or after the relevant input.

Length groups are defined by whether trajectories fit within the 32K-token context window, with trajectory counts shown in parentheses. Question types cover recall, causal inference, state updating, and state abstraction. Bold text marks the best value in each row.

papers.abstract: Localizing object boundaries is important for embodied visual systems, since small boundary errors can change the inferred geometry of physical surfaces. We study whether deep stereo models produce boundaries consistent with simple shape priors when local image and disparity cues are weak. We create a synthetic stereo dataset consisting of objects drawn from a highly constrained family of shapes, with randomized depth, slant, color and texture. Despite the simplicity of this shape space, we find that several state-of-the-art stereo models retain systematic boundary errors, even when finetuned or trained from scratch on the dataset. We then introduce a simple generative stereo model that jointly predicts disparity and a distance field representing object boundaries. The model improves boundary localization and produces contours that adhere more closely to the underlying shape space. These results expose limitations in the boundary predictions of current stereo architectures when local evidence is weak, and motivate further study of whether generative models can better combine regional grouping evidence with global geometric structure.
authors: Linbo Tang, Aneel Damaraju, Todd Zickler
bullets: The study tests whether stereo models learn simple global shape priors for boundary localization.
A synthetic dataset varies depth, slant, color, and texture across objects from a constrained shape family.
Several state-of-the-art models retain boundary errors even after training or fine-tuning on this dataset.
A generative stereo model jointly predicts disparity and an object-boundary distance field.
The findings highlight limitations of current architectures and motivate combining regional evidence with global geometry.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of HDiT-Stereo. Per-view image features and correspondence features from a trainable photometric encoder and a frozen DINOv2 semantic encoder condition an HDiT denoiser. From noise the model jointly generates disparity and an unsigned boundary distance field through iterative denoising. Flame and snowflake symbols indicate trainable and frozen components.

Figure 4: Recovered foreground shapes. For each scene, the upper row shows disparity maps with ground truth on the left; the lower row shows recovered foreground shapes overlaid on ground truth. Dark regions indicate agreement, orange regions indicate disagreement, and solid black lines mark ground-truth contours. Our model achieves the highest shape IoU.

Figure 1: Boundary errors when texture and disparity cues are weak. Left panel: input stereo images and true disparity. Right panel: locations where each model’s predicted disparity error is greater than two pixels, along with overall Bad 2.0 percentage. Despite being finetuned or trained from scratch on our heavily constrained shape distribution, several deep stereo models retain substantial errors near object boundaries. Our diffusion-based HDiT-Stereo reduces errors near boundaries, particularly where local evidence is weak.

Figure 2: Dataset examples. Shapes are slanted planar regular polygons up to degree eight with randomized appearance. Difficulty is controlled by similarity in object appearance, object slant, and object depth. The extreme case (bottom right) provides no local evidence for much of the objects’ boundaries, requiring nonlocal shape information for successful grouping.

Figure 7: Disparity predictions and boundary errors. For each scene, rows show disparity maps, cyan-box enlargements, Bad-2 error maps, and their enlargements; stereo inputs appear at left. Black pixels indicate disparity errors exceeding 2 px. HDiT-Stereo better preserves polygonal contours and achieves the lowest Bad-2 rate in both examples.

Figure 6: Our sampled posterior can be bimodal for ambiguous figure-ground scenes. Left: Four sampled disparity and boundary predictions. Disparity remains consistent while the boundary predictions capture both valid figure-ground interpretations. Right: t-SNE embedding of 100 boundary samples, forming two clusters near the two valid contour maps (orange and green stars). Grey bands indicate the predicted zero-level boundary contours.

Figure 5: Sample variation identifies unreliable predictions. Left: Mean disparity error versus sample standard deviation, binned separately for boundary and interior pixels across all test scenes. Higher uncertainty indicates larger errors. Right: Mean error among pixels retained by predicted uncertainty (orange) or ground-truth error (gray). Removing uncertain pixels substantially reduces error without requiring ground truth for selection. Computed on a 100-scene test subset, and the dashed line is RAFT-Stereo on the same subset.

Table 1: Contour fidelity and global accuracy. Boundary-localization metrics (left columns) are this paper’s focus; global metrics (right columns) are reported for completeness. Results use 1000 test scenes and variability is reported as ± IQR/2 across scenes. Beneath each method are its total and trainable parameters in millions. Our model is sampled 10 times per scene, and we report the average metric across the samples (Mean) and the oracle Best-1-of-10, which for each metric is the best value among the 10 samples, selected using ground truth. In every column, bold marks the best value and underline the second best, excluding Best-1-of-10. Our model leads the boundary and global Bad-X columns and is mid-field for global EPE.

Table 3: Inference cost for one 128× 128 stereo pair on a single A100-40GB in fp32. HDiT-Stereo uses 50-step DPM++(2M) SDE sampling, while the baselines use a single forward pass. Best in bold, second best underlined among Mean rows. Best-1-of-10 uses an oracle and is excluded from ranking.

papers.abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.
authors: Xianzhe Fan, Chi-Pin Huang, Fu-En Yang, Jing Wang, Yecheng Wu, Yu-Cheng Chou, Johan Bjorck, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Jan Kautz, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Zhiding Yu, Hengshuang Zhao, Zhiqi Li
bullets: Targets coordinated manipulation, where each robot’s move affects teammates’ future actions.
Jointly generates future views and executable action chunks for all robots in one sample.
Uses cross-agent attention to denoise shared action and future-view tokens while retaining separate control interfaces.
Achieves 67.8% mean success across three real-robot tasks and 90.3% across eight simulated tasks with up to four arms.
Ablations show cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision are important for coordination.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance, and uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals. We propose VisAlloc, a dual-level framework combining sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting. A fixed paired-teacher filter retains samples answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced negative crop. At the token level, both EMA teachers score the same student-generated response, and their absolute log-probability differences measure view sensitivity. Additional supervision targets tokens admitted by sensitivity or teacher-distribution disagreement, with shared frozen-prior, template-bigram, and student--teacher divergence gates. Inverse-frequency redistribution preserves the total additional weight within each micro-batch, while the positive teacher remains the sole distillation target. Inference requires only the full-image student. Across eight benchmarks, our 4B and 9B models achieve macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, outperforming Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points, respectively. Code on GitHub: https://github.com/Kaelyn01/VisAlloc
authors: Haoran Xu, Tian Chen, Yuhe Wu, Yanbo Zhao, Junchi Liao, Hongyu Wang, Jiaze Li, Wentao Wang, Yanfeng Li, Rui Qian
bullets: Filters training samples using positive evidence-centered crops versus spatially displaced negative crops.
Reweights tokens based on view sensitivity and disagreement between positive and negative visual teachers.
Uses multiple gates and inverse-frequency redistribution while keeping the positive teacher as the only distillation target.
Inference requires only the full-image student, avoiding teacher or crop-based overhead.
Across eight benchmarks, the 4B and 9B models reach macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, respectively, exceeding Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of VisAlloc. (A) Paired-view construction produces an evidence-centered positive crop and a spatially displaced negative crop. A fixed paired-teacher filter then retains samples that the positive teacher answers correctly and the negative teacher answers incorrectly, after annotation-quality checks. Each retained sample keeps its full image and paired teacher views. (B) Both teachers score the same student-generated response under aligned prefixes. (C) Realized-token sensitivity supplies the continuous base; sensitivity or teacher-distribution disagreement admits a bonus under shared context gates, and inverse-frequency redistribution preserves its total before mean normalization. (D) Only the positive teacher supplies the weighted JSD target, and EMA updates once after the actor update. The displayed redistribution is for E > 0, and zero-budget batches retain zero bonus. The views and bonuses are schematic (λ = 4, 4B).

Figure 4: Training dynamics of five 4B settings on a shared 0–65 step axis: (a) response length for five runs, (b) bonus admission for three, and (c) logged low-frequency bonus share for two. Orange: VisAlloc (spatial-only); gray/blue/green/purple: Vision-OPD, contrastive base, targeted extrapolation (p90), and routed spatial/mask. The first three runs extend to step 65; orange/purple end at step 60. (a) Mean response length decreases from ≈80–95 to 66–77 tokens; no collapse is observed over the recorded steps. (b) Final 10-step mean bonus admission is 8.2% for VisAlloc, ≈2.3× p90 extrapolation (3.6%) and slightly above routed spatial/mask (7.8%). (c) Trailing 5-step means of the logged low-frequency share stay within 77–90% (ending at 82.4/82.9; raw single-step values span 64–92%). Thin traces show raw logs and thick traces show trailing 5-step means; the recorded budget ratio is 1.000.

Figure 1: Conceptual comparison of OPD, Vision-OPD, and VisAlloc. OPD provides uniform text-only teacher feedback. Vision-OPD adds a privileged evidence crop but retains uniform token weights. VisAlloc contrasts positive and negative teacher views to allocate a conserved token-weight budget. Fixed paired-teacher selection precedes allocation, and both teacher views are geometry-matched crops.

All methods are evaluated using the same protocol, following Vision-OPD. ‡ Our reproductions of Vision-OPD and OPD-V. Among open-source models (single forward pass), the best results are highlighted in bold, and the second-best are underlined. VisAlloc-9B achieves the highest six-benchmark average in this group. Baseline results are from Yuan et al. (2026).
Table 3: Implementation settings for the reported 4B and 9B experiments. Backbone-dependent frozen artifacts are constructed separately for each model size.

Table 4: Sequential component and negative-view ablations. Upper-block rows cumulatively add the named component or change the admission quantile. Filtering is followed by frequency redistribution and then the teacher–teacher JSD OR branch. p90/p80 denote realized-token sensitivity admission. ∆ is the precedingrow macro-average change (lower block: relative to the spatial-only row). papers.abstract: Gas Source Localization (GSL) with mobile robots is challenging because wind and gas measurements are spatially sparse, noisy, and potentially affected by robot motion. Indoor airflow can vary substantially across space, while detailed environmental layouts, boundary conditions, or precomputed airflow fields are often unavailable. Moreover, hazardous sources must be localized as quickly as possible, making exhaustive exploration impractical. This paper presents a lightweight physics-informed probabilistic framework for efficient GSL under spatially varying indoor airflow. As the robot navigates, it continuously collects wind and gas measurements and reconstructs the spatially varying airflow field online. The estimated wind field drives a forward dispersion model that predicts the gas pattern for each candidate source location. These predictions are compared with the measured gas pattern to update a probabilistic belief over the source location. As the wind field is reconstructed incrementally, the framework also accounts for the spatially non-uniform reliability of wind field estimation and its influence on the source estimation. The resulting belief map is then used for informative path planning to guide the robot toward informative regions. High-fidelity simulations provide a comprehensive evaluation of the individual components and their integrations within the complete system, while physical indoor experiments assess the system performance under realistic sensing, motion, and airflow conditions. The results demonstrate that incorporating lightweight physical knowledge significantly improves localization robustness under spatially complex airflow and enables more efficient exploration.
authors: Wanting Jin, Thomas Wiedemann, Han Fan, Achim Lilienthal, Alcherio Martinoli
bullets: Addresses sparse, noisy gas and wind measurements in spatially varying indoor airflow without requiring precomputed airflow maps.
Online reconstruction of the airflow field supports forward gas-dispersion predictions for candidate source locations.
A probabilistic belief over source locations accounts for the spatially varying reliability of wind-field estimates.
Informative path planning guides the robot toward regions expected to improve localization.
High-fidelity simulations and physical indoor experiments show improved robustness and more efficient exploration under complex airflow.

papers.abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/
authors: Amani Kiruga, Mark Hamilton, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, William T. Freeman, Vincent Sitzmann, Yilun Du, Ayush Tewari
bullets: Targets the poor out-of-distribution generalization of fast, feedforward 3D reconstruction networks.
Uses inverse generative modeling to recover latent variables that best explain a monocular image.
Combines a generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network to avoid degenerate flat reconstructions.
Reports stronger OOD reconstruction accuracy than feedforward networks across controlled synthetic and real-world tasks.
Introduces adaptive test-time inference that allocates more computation to ambiguous inputs.

papers.abstract: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.
authors: Yao Zhang, Zhuchenyang Liu, Yu Xiao
bullets: Targets multi-step household interactions involving movable objects, such as picking up and throwing a toy into a basket.
Specifies motions with positions, paths, and poses, then measures execution errors and revises the control plan.
Introduces Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks across 31 apartment furniture layouts, with one to three chained goals per task.
Achieves task completion rates of 98.7%, 93.3%, and 82.7% with three evaluated language models.
Ablations show spatial control is essential for task completion, while quantitative feedback improves motion precision.

papers.abstract: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model. At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps. Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.
authors: Ido Nitzan Hidekel, Dan Raviv
bullets: Model-merging interference can be estimated before fully evaluating candidate merges, reducing expensive coefficient search.

Full multi-task merges require two evaluations along the merge path rather than one.
LR-Merge freezes receiver-local responses to form an affine surrogate and optimizes coefficients via convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes.
The method improves tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified mergers; its surrogate supports new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.

papers.abstract: Understanding how stable psychometric traits and time-varying states jointly inform behavior is an important problem in computational behavioral science. Existing personalized agents commonly condition actions directly on a static profile, leaving realized state transitions unused as an explicit source of supervision. We introduce a profile-conditioned state world model that uses observed environment--behavior state transitions to learn transition-informed representations for behavioral prediction. During training, a posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions, while a prior predicts the resulting codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context. The prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator-grounded execution. Thus, the world model provides structured transition supervision instead of treating personality as a direct action descriptor. We evaluate the framework in VEET, a controlled behavioral simulator with human trajectories, and in AgentSociety as a structurally different synthetic environment. A participant-disjoint split of 240 training, 25 validation, and 48 test participants evaluates generalization to unseen people. On VEET, the model reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95\% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL. Ablations associate continuous next-state modeling with most of the Top-1 gain, while discrete codes and prior alignment mainly improve Top-3 and distributional alignment. These results establish transition-informed world-model supervision as useful for subject-generalized behavior prediction, without implying causal psychological mechanisms or calibrated long-horizon state dynamics.
authors: Ziyuan Qin, Yang Qiao, Summer B. Frandsen, Michael T. Treadway, Liang Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of conditioning behavior directly on static personality profiles while ignoring realized state transitions.

Evaluated in VEET and AgentSociety with participant-disjoint splits; VEET achieved 0.904 Top-1 accuracy and 0.0033 Macro KL.
Ablations link continuous next-state modeling to Top-1 gains, while discrete codes and prior alignment improve Top-3 and distributional alignment.

papers.abstract: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.

papers.abstract: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.

papers.abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.
authors: Seojin Kim, Noseong Park
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks in long-context LLM inference.
Propagates token importance across attention-induced transition graphs beyond recency or immediate attention.
Evaluated on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning across multiple LLM families.
Maintains competitive task performance under moderate to aggressive compression, including up to 90%, with low end-to-end overhead.
Scope: performance is demonstrated across the reported tasks and model families, with a favorable accuracy–memory trade-off rather than universal superiority.
